The Tiger I, officially known as the Panzerkampfwagen VI Tiger Ausf. E, stands as one of the most iconic and formidable tanks of World War II. Developed by Nazi Germany, this heavy tank earned a fearsome reputation on the battlefield. My fascination with the Tiger I stems from its engineering brilliance, historical significance, and the enduring legacy it has left in both military history and popular culture.

One of the most compelling reasons to admire the Tiger I is its advanced engineering. Introduced in 1942, the Tiger I was a marvel of military technology. Its 88 mm KwK 36 gun was one of the most powerful tank guns of its time, capable of destroying enemy tanks at long ranges. This firepower, combined with its thick armor, made the Tiger I a formidable opponent. The frontal armor was up to 100 mm thick, and its side armor was 80 mm, providing substantial protection against most Allied anti-tank weapons.

The tank's suspension system was another notable feature. The overlapping road wheels, while complex and prone to maintenance challenges, provided excellent weight distribution and stability, crucial for the tank's performance on various terrains. Additionally, the Maybach HL230 P45 engine, despite its initial reliability issues, delivered the necessary power to propel the 57-ton behemoth.

The historical significance of the Tiger I is another aspect that captivates me. It was a game-changer in armored warfare, altering the strategies of both the Axis and Allied forces. The mere presence of Tiger tanks on the battlefield could influence the tactics of opposing forces, often leading to significant changes in Allied strategies to counter this formidable adversary. Its debut at the Battle of Leningrad and subsequent engagements on the Eastern and Western Fronts showcased its capabilities and the psychological impact it had on enemy troops.

Moreover, the Tiger I symbolizes the peak of German tank engineering during World War II. Despite being introduced later in the war and produced in relatively limited numbers, its impact was disproportionate. Stories of lone Tiger tanks holding off entire columns of Allied armor have become legendary, contributing to the mythos surrounding this vehicle. This reputation for invincibility, whether entirely accurate or not, speaks to the Tiger I's formidable design and the respect it commanded.

The Tiger I's legacy extends beyond its wartime service. It has become a cultural icon, frequently depicted in films, documentaries, and video games. This ongoing presence in popular media keeps the memory of the Tiger I alive and continues to inspire interest and admiration. For military enthusiasts and historians alike, the Tiger I represents a pinnacle of tank design, symbolizing both the technological advancements and the strategic challenges of its era.

In summary, my admiration for the Tiger I is rooted in its remarkable engineering, significant impact on World War II, and enduring legacy. Its combination of powerful weaponry, robust armor, and advanced design makes it a standout in the history of armored warfare. The Tiger I's ability to capture the imagination and respect of people long after its operational days is a testament to its enduring allure and significance.

The sound design is equally impressive, with realistic weapon sounds, explosions, and atmospheric effects that bring the battlefield to life. The game’s music and voice acting add to the immersion, providing a fitting soundtrack to the high-stakes action.

Final Verdict:
Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a triumph in the RTS genre, offering a deeply immersive and realistic depiction of WWII’s Eastern Front. Call to Arms: Gates of Hell Ostfront is what many of us see as the spiritual successor to Men of War: Assault Squad 2, and it definitely brings a lot to the table. This game offers a brutal and immersive World War II strategy experience that fans of the genre will appreciate.

[b]Gameplay and Mechanics[/b]

Gates of Hell Ostfront keeps the core elements of the Men of War series but adds some awesome new features. The direct control option is still there, letting you take over individual units, which is always a blast. The new units, improved physics, and realistic ballistics make the game feel more authentic. The addition of stealth and unit changes is a nice touch and adds some cool new tactics to play around with.

[b]Realism and Strategy[/b]

This game nails realism. From the accurate vehicle models to the destructible environments, everything is designed to pull you into the WWII setting. The strategic depth is intense—you’ve got to think about terrain, unit placement, and supplies. Every decision counts, and that makes for a truly engaging experience.

[b]Graphics and Sound Design[/b]

The graphics have gotten a major upgrade. The environments are detailed, and the units look fantastic. The sound design is also top-notch, with authentic effects that really bring the battlefield to life. It's one of those games where you can get lost in the atmosphere.

[b]Optimization and Performance[/b]

The game is pretty well-optimized, running smoothly on high-end systems. But watch out for high unit count battles—my FPS dropped to around 15 at times, even with an RTX 3090 and an i9 10th gen processor. It’s a bit frustrating, but it doesn’t happen all the time.

[b]Community and Mod Support[/b]

One of the best things about Gates of Hell Ostfront is the community and the mods. The active player base keeps pumping out new content and improvements, which keeps the game fresh. There are plenty of mods to customize your experience, adding even more replay value.

[b]Challenges and Learning Curve[/b]

The learning curve is pretty steep. The mechanics are detailed, and there’s a lot of micromanagement, which can be overwhelming at first. But if you’re willing to put in the time, it’s incredibly rewarding. The AI can be a bit inconsistent, which can be annoying, but it’s not a deal-breaker.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Call to Arms: Gates of Hell Ostfront is a fantastic spiritual successor to Men of War: Assault Squad 2. It’s got deep, rewarding gameplay, enhanced realism, and significant improvements in graphics and sound. While the learning curve and occasional AI issues can be a pain, the game’s strengths far outweigh these minor problems. If you love real-time strategy games, this one’s a must-play.

[b]Pros:[/b]

- Enhanced realism and strategic depth
- Detailed gameplay mechanics and direct control feature
- Significant graphical and sound design improvements
- Active community and extensive mod support
- Better optimization for smoother gameplay

[b]Cons:[/b]

- Steep learning curve for newcomers
- Occasional AI inconsistencies
- Performance dips in high unit count battles

[b]Rating: 9/10[/b]

A great spiritual successor to Men of War: Assault Squad 2, Gates of Hell covers the same realistic WW2 combat without loosing the great core gameplay. 
Unfortunately this game is more of a sidegrade than a all-around improvement. The reworked conquest system allows for much longer conquest games and much more dynamic gameplay. Graphics and sound design have also improved appreciably from Men of War: AS2, as well as welcome improvements to multiplayer and co-op. 

However, the old style Men of War conquest mode where new units are added as the match goes on has been dumped. The unit call-in system where units can be earned as you make progress has been removed as well. Now you must pick your units in deployment stages before battle and anticipate what you will face rather than simply spawn what you want. The battle AI is also much worse than Men of War; medics will not automatically heal your units requiring you to babysit infantry, and the horrible pathing will result in vehicles running over your own units or getting stuck. 
Lastly, for the price in comparison to Men of War: AS2 the content is lacking. Gates of Hell includes only Germany and the USSR in the base package, and the bare minimum of units. In comparison Men of War: AS2 included almost all the major axis and allied armies and units in the base game, as well as 5 or 6 times as many maps. 

Overall, while this game has many problems, some of which can be fixed via mods on the workshop, I would still recommend Gates of Hell. It offers a completely unique WW2 experience which is much more focused and refined than Men of War. If you are looking for a well made WW2 rts campaign and multiplayer, this is it. That being said, Men of War: Assault Squad 2 still is the king for single map conquest.

This is by far my favorite WW2 strategy game. It has very detailed units and deep tactical combat. This game gives you the opportunity to constantly make interesting tactical choices like "do I take the high ground with better visibility, or do I dig in on the objective," or "do I call in an extra infantry squad to reinforce my weakening flank, or do I save up points for an armored unit later, " or "do I hide this rifleman behind this bush where he is harder to spot, or do I hide him behind hard cover where he is harder to kill?"  And every decision you make has an impact on the outcome of the battle. 

While some gamers might feel that this level of detail involves too much micro management, I have had a lot of fun when resources are running low and I plan a raid on an enemy position to capture a mortar so that I can finally deal with a pesky MG nest on the other side of the map.

Infantry are very soft and die quickly when caught in the open, but when used correctly, are the dominant units in the game. The moments when you get an MG set up just in time to shred an enemy squad, or when your sole surviving rifleman buys you extra time by knocking the tracks off a heavy tank feel incredibly rewarding. I have frequently cheered out loud in joy when my plans come together.

Knowing the difference in capability between a Panzer IV F and a Panzer IV J can make a difference in a battle. While this might be more than most gamers care to know, I like learning about tanks and tank development and being rewarded for my interest feels great. 

On top of all of that, I think the maps a beautiful, tank shells screaming past sound amazing, you can take direct control of each unit when you want to be the hero, and watching French farm houses get ripped to splinters never gets old. 

If you are interested in the WW2 strategy genera but this game doesn't seem right for you, here are a few other options. (I own and play all of them.)

Company of Heroes is a great series that is closer to the arcade side of the spectrum. You wont have to worry about controlling each individual man in your squad or how many bandages they have left. But Gates of Hell has so much more depth that Company of Heroes feels flat to me now.

Men of War 2 is new and is still being improved, but it seems to split the difference on the arcade-vs-realism spectrum between Company of Heroes and Gates of Hell. It has more abstractions and less micro. There is a ton of content and I think it has a bright future, but right now Gates of Hell is more polished. 

If you are looking for a larger scale battle, try Steel Division. You wont have to worry about which bush to hid behind or what window to peak out of. But I feel like I lose some of the excitement when I zoom out to that level. Gates of Hell makes you feel much closer to the foxhole. 

I hope you get to play all four of these games!

Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a game that offers a detailed and historically accurate portrayal of the Eastern Front, providing a truely challenging and rewarding experience for strategy enthusiasts and history buffs alike.

Gameplay:
The gameplay in "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is deeply engaging, emphasizing tactical depth and strategic planning. Players command a variety of units, each with unique capabilities and vulnerabilities, requiring thoughtful deployment and maneuvering. The game offers both single-player campaigns and multiplayer modes, allowing for a range of experiences from solitary strategic contemplation to competitive engagements with other players.

One of the standout features is the realistic combat mechanics. The attention to detail in unit behavior, ballistics, and damage modeling creates a highly immersive experience. The ability to control individual soldiers and vehicles adds a layer of micromanagement that can be both rewarding and demanding. This complexity, while sometimes overwhelming, ultimately enhances the authenticity and depth of the gameplay.
The AI is on par with any other Men of War games and has to be microed a lot. If you persevere, you will get the hang of it and learn to master the specificity of controlling the AI.

Graphics and Sound:
Visually, Gates of Hell: Ostfront impresses with its detailed environments, outstanding looking graphics and meticulously modeled units. The battlefields are richly textured, reflecting the grim and gritty nature of the Eastern Front. The game makes me want and allows me to take really nice looking screenshots during ANY play session, It looks that good.

The sound design is equally remarkable. The roar of tank engines, the crackle of gunfire, and the distant booms of artillery create a palpable sense of battlefield chaos. The musical score, while somewhat understated, effectively complements the tense and dramatic atmosphere of the game. I found however that the OST annoyed me after hearing it for a while. That is easily fixed by any music mod on the workshop.

One of the most exciting aspects of "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is its vibrant and active modding community. The game supports a wide array of mods, extending its longevity and replayability significantly. These mods range from small tweaks and additional units to comprehensive overhauls that can transform the game entirely. Players can find modifications that cover various historical periods, including conflicts and scenarios beyond World War II.

Notably, some mods push the timeline well into the modern era, introducing contemporary military equipment, modern combat scenarios, and advanced technology. These mods provide a fascinating contrast to the base game’s World War II focus, offering fresh and varied experiences that can cater to different interests and playstyles.

The community-driven content ensures that "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" remains a dynamic and evolving platform. The availability of such a diverse range of mods keeps the game engaging long after players have exhausted the original content. For those who enjoy customization and exploring new possibilities within a familiar framework, the modding scene is a treasure trove of creativity and innovation.

Historical Accuracy:
A notable strength of "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is its commitment to historical accuracy. The game features meticulously researched units, weapons, and scenarios, providing an educational glimpse into the strategies and technologies of World War II. For history enthusiasts, the level of detail in the historical references and the authenticity of the unit designs is particularly satisfying.

Challenges and Learning Curve:
While the game’s depth and realism are commendable, they also contribute to a steep learning curve. New players may find the complexity daunting, with a need to grasp intricate mechanics and strategic nuances. However, for those willing to invest the time, the rewards are substantial, offering a profoundly immersive and strategically rich experience. What it is not however, is a balanced competitive multiplayer. It does not bode well to a ranked system and uses an old lobby system instead of matchmaking. Not that big of an issue to me as I play single-player or Coop most of the time.

"Gates of Hell: Ostfront" stands out as a meticulously crafted RTS game that delivers both strategic depth and historical authenticity. Its demanding gameplay, realistic combat mechanics, and detailed presentation make it a must-play for dedicated strategy fans and World War II enthusiasts. While its complexity may pose a challenge for newcomers, the game’s rich and rewarding experience makes it well worth the effort.

The extensive modding community further elevates the game, providing an endless stream of new content and extending the gameplay into different eras, including the modern age. For those seeking an RTS that combines tactical sophistication with a faithful representation of history, along with the flexibility to explore a wide range of scenarios through mods, "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is an exceptional choice.

Fog of war will bring the negative aspect of your units out, where they have goofy movement and your artillery is more dependent on you micromanaging as a result. The enemy Ai often favors extremely heavy artillery in their army compositions.

Gates of Hell: Ostfront stands tall as the new champion in the realm of World War II RTS games, dethroning even the stalwart Company of Heroes franchise. For players like me, disheartened by recent entries in the once-beloved series, Ostfront is a revelation. Its fusion of classic RTS mechanics with unprecedented 1st and 3rd person unit control elevates every encounter to an unparalleled level of strategic depth and personal engagement. Whether it's maneuvering a tank through dense foliage for the perfect ambush or directing a machine gunner to hold a crucial chokepoint, Ostfront puts you in the boots of every soldier, making every moment truly your own.

Immersion isn't just a buzzword in Ostfront; it's a defining feature. The painstaking attention to detail in modeling and representation sets a new standard for WW2 RTS games. From the meticulously crafted environments to the lifelike character models and authentic sound design, every aspect of Ostfront breathes life into the conflict, transporting players to the front lines of history. The result is an experience that is not only gripping and immersive but also undeniably grounded and realistic, capturing the essence of WW2 like never before.

In addition to its stellar base game experience, Gates of Hell: Ostfront boasts a thriving modding community that adds a whole new dimension to the gameplay. This vibrant community is home to incredibly talented individuals who craft a diverse array of modifications, total conversions, levels, and even entire new campaigns. What's truly remarkable is that many of these community-created mods are on par, and in some cases, even surpass the quality of content produced by the development team themselves. This ensures a constant stream of exciting and fresh new content, keeping the game experience dynamic and ever-evolving.

Moreover, Barbed Wire Studios, the developers behind Ostfront, have demonstrated an unwavering commitment to supporting their game through high-quality DLCs. Each new addition to the game not only expands the content but also pushes the quality bar even higher. These DLCs are not mere cash grabs but thoughtful expansions that enrich the gameplay experience, introducing new features, units, and scenarios that keep players engaged and coming back for more. With a combination of community-driven creativity and developer-driven excellence, Gates of Hell: Ostfront stands as a testament to the enduring power of passionate game development and community engagement.

As a dedicated player of single-player skirmishes and campaigns, I've already invested over 200 hours into Gates of Hell: Ostfront, and the journey is far from over. The sheer breadth of content and the endless possibilities for emergent gameplay ensure that each session is as fresh and exhilarating as the last. With Ostfront, I've found not just a game but a lasting passion, and I eagerly anticipate the countless hours of enjoyment still to come.

I have played this game on my brother's account for over 40 hours and have been playing almost all MOW games so I think I can confidently provide some insights.

Should you get the game?
Short answer:
If you are a strategy fan in general, interested in a more smaller scale battles, with some RPG elements, then YES, absolutely. You WILL miss out if you are hesitated. And I have not even mentioned the mods.

Long answer:
GAMEPLAY: 10/10
Generally, you will control a battalion size army to achieve various objects, whether its to eliminate all enemies on the map, or control a small area, or a specific object in campaign missions. The thing is: you can control in groups, advance to the enemy's position like in Company of Heroes, OR, you can control a single soldier to stealthily plant a bomb behind the enemy's tank, or take a MG-42 and go ham on the incoming enemy squads (very satisfying sounds btw), OR, you can control a King Tiger and shoot through (almost) anything in front of you, which is NEVER a boring thing to do. So there is a range of tactics and play style for you general to choose from. And that, to me, is very niche gameplay style that can't be replicated by many RTS games out there (oh yes, in case you didn't know already, this is an RTS game). And I don't think you will get bored with the game after even 100 hours (like me). 

SOUNDS: 8/10
The sound effects have come a long way. It is not that the sound were bad at all in the past, but it has been improved A LOT since the developer employed one of the game's mod creators out there, HangEmHighs, to work for them (which is AWESOME to hear), especially the recent updates of the cannon sounds. You can hear the brutally shreds of MG-42, the awe of the Russian artillery, or the screams of agony when the soldiers fall down. A very immersive experience.

GRAPHIC: 7/10
Gritty, brutal, realistic and you can get a very "dang" feeling when you hit the right spot on a tank and it blows off. If you are playing with friends, it will be so fun to admire the scenery of carnage together. Never a boring moment. But I want to remind you that you will need a somewhat decent setup to run this. I have a RTX 3060 12GB, an i5-12400F, 32 GB of RAM. And the game runs fine. Oh and put in on SSD too, since if you plan to fiddle with mods, the game can load quite slow. But hey, there are mods to improve the graphics, so don't worry.

MODS: 10/10
Yes, a lot. And I mean A LOT. Whether you want to turn this into a modern day setting with Abrams fighting Russian T90s, or Warhammer 40k, or Star Wars, or zombies... anything you think of, you will probably find a mod for it on the workshop. And the modding is not too hard either. Even with my limited knowledge of coding, I once managed to play around and put 2 30mm cannons on my King Tiger, a REMOTELY controlled 12.7mm heavy mg on top. So, yeah, go for it, and try anything you want.

MULTIPLAYER: 
I am not exactly into PvP that much. So I haven't played that much with others. But I do find it very enjoyable to play it with my friends sometimes. Sorry I cannot bring that much information in this area.

Final thought/score: 8.75/10
The game is not perfect. The loading can be quite long sometimes, the graphics is not exactly the best, optimization can use some work, the engine is not that great. But at the end of the day, it is a VERY solid game. And you will have a lot of fun time with it yourself I hope, whether you are a RTS fan, a WW2 fan, or a casual player that wants to change stuff up a bit.

When it comes to an authentic and realistic World War II RTS, "Call to Arms: Gates of Hell" is definitely at the forefront. The sound is well implemented, and although the graphics seem a bit outdated, they are still appealing.

Unfortunately, the AI of both the units and the enemy is inadequate, as if it hasn't evolved in the last 15 years. This flawed AI takes away a lot of the fun. A major issue is pathfinding. The AI has severe difficulties crossing rivers, often stopping before them and requiring direct control by the player, even though this would be feasible in the water. Additionally, the AI fails to recognize that a bridge is only a few meters away and does not use it.

The AI also does not check for obstacles. The vehicle AI does not avoid trees but instead takes the most direct route, carrying along any objects in its path. It would be significantly faster if it simply moved a meter to the side. Precise command is necessary to prevent the AI from making mistakes. Sending a tank quickly to another point while managing other units is almost impossible.

Target prioritization is another shortcoming. When I order a tank to attack an enemy tank, it only does so as long as there is no closer threat. If our tank is attacked by infantry, which poses no real threat, it switches targets and tries to combat the infantry, often resulting in a side hit to the turret. It would be better if it focused on the enemy tank, especially if there are enough anti-infantry units nearby.

Another problem occurs when sending infantry to a position: sometimes only one soldier moves, while the rest stay at the original location. This often leads to confusion about where one's troop has gone.

The AI requires intense "babysitting" to perform the actions desired, often preventing focus on more critical aspects of the game.

The enemy AI shows its strengths primarily in well-scripted campaign levels. However, outside of these scenarios, particularly in Conquest mode, its weaknesses become evident. It dispatches isolated troops and does not seem aimed at coordinating joint attacks. When the AI attacks, it feels like shooting clay pigeons, as one simply takes out the incoming units. In your own attacks, the main task is clearing flag points, encountering occasionally newly spawned enemy units. The AI does not attack in a coordinated manner nor does it attempt to cleverly combine units.

Ostfront is a functional RTS that suffers from anemic holdovers from previous games. On the surface, being able to control each and every unit as an option sounds like a fun mechanic and it is. However it goes past the point of being an option and instead becomes a mandatory part to functional normally. As many other reviewers have pointed out the AI in this game is questionable at best. Highly dubious pathfinding, the fact soldiers can't run while shooting, tanks can't drive over rocks and priority targets being completely asinine just to name a few. All of these issues stacked up with each other make it so that direct control of units is paramount to success.

Some RTS's like to proclaim "Clicks don't mean success!" but here they most certainly do. That being said, a few of the minor complaints like 3rd person camera angles being awkward, medics not being able to do their job automatically and tank targeting fixes are all mods you can download freely on the workshop. However some of these do come with their own "balance" suggestions, so be careful about which ones you install.

If you ignore the AI issues (Which will prove to be impossible) and other faults, you'll run headlong into Ostfront's biggest flaw. In that it does not convey enough information to the player. You'll consistently find that a tank or squad of yours has been wiped out for some time and you'll have had no feedback about it. No crew shouts, no commander announcement and depending on the damage it might not even disappear from your unit roster, let alone if you have multiple of that unit.

But truthfully, the biggest pain in the neck is the unclear vision system in the game. The view cone around a squad or a tank is just a flat out lie. All it tells you is the area in which it *could* spot something. It does not account for items like smoke, hills, walls or camouflage. So lets say a tank of yours pops smoke but other units in your roster are still spotting targets past its smoke screen. The game does not tell you who is doing this. The tank itself still says it can see past it, when it clearly cannot. So having to [b]manually[/b] pan the camera and check to see if a tank or a squad can see over a hill or around some smoke is a painstaking task, especially considering how important vision is to any RTS.

Yes, I am aware that Ostfront has two checks to make when making sure it can spot an enemy. But if this system comes at the cost of relaying information to the player, you should probably re-evaluate priorities.

For instance when you give a group of infantry an order to move to a building or trench for cover, without fail half will pause part way to reload(this I'll never understand), look around, point their rifles off into the distance, sometimes shoot at enemies or static weapons and draw their fire to the whole squad that is running in the open etc. This usually results in getting them shelled or mowed down by a machine gun. 

Defenders of the game will say that "you have to micro manage the units to get them to do what you want them to do." This would be fine but I expect that once I give the order to run to a trench for instance I shouldn't have to give order to the same unit 6, 7, even 8 times to get it to finish the order. I have literally had to give a unit the same order over and over and over again because it kept stopping in and open area to turn around and look at enemies behind him.

Another AI problem that is constantly mentioned, tanks will target single infantry all the way across the map with their turrets while ignoring enemy tanks in front of them. The argument I hear to counter this is lock the ammo selection to AT rounds but this only prevents them from shooting at the infantry with their main gun and not rotating their turrets to target with the MG. This is just bad threat assessment. 

I have heard it said that these AI shortcomings are due the limitations of the game engine. I'm sorry I don't buy this and it sounds like a cop out. It may be difficult to fix but I don't believe that game engine is preventing this. The proof of this is that the enemy AI controlled by the same game engine performs much better when comes to these issues. 

The tanks, artillery, mortars are lethal and very good at target selection. The enemy infantry while tend to rush in like zombies can also be very good at finding cover and targeting infantry especially in CQB where they use grenades and even melee with surprising effectiveness, Meanwhile the player AI stand around and look at their feet while they are getting assaulted.

I can't count how many times I have rage quit this game and it has always been because my AI have done something so completely frustrating after I had been so careful to prepare them for action. If they could fix these AI problems (the last update was supposed to improve the move orders but frankly it hasn't), this game would be so much fun. 

I think the devs for the most part are pretty responsive and want to produce a quality product. I just think they prioritize things like unit design and models which are very good in this game over the mechanics which need some help. If they can fix this problem I would gladly change to a thumbs up and write a review stating why.

I'm really glad I decided to check this out on a whim when it was on sale early this year. I had briefly remembered looking at the original Call to Arms years ago and being intrigued yet underwhelmed. But this version, now fully standalone from the original, is so much more high quality than the base game.  

This game reminds me a lot of World in Conflict, and I love it for that.  It plays similar in a number of ways, from a very quick time to kill on a lot of units, the types of battle strategies that it encourages, and the points system it uses to call in reinforcements instead of using base building and resource gathering.

The detail in the units, maps, and sound design (especially after recent patches) are unlike anything I've ever seen or heard in an RTS. The sound alone is better than most FPS games.  Mortar, artillery, and tank barrages are terrifying. The maps are large and littered with tons of details, destructible objects and buildings, building and bunker interiors, trenches, and detailed foliage.

Every troop has a kit, a random name (ex.Lt. John Smith), limited ammo, and limited resources that must be managed with supply trucks. Vehicles have ammo and fuel too, as well as full crews that can enter and exit any vehicle. Vehicles have individual parts that can be damaged and repaired as well. Despite all that, it's simple enough to manage it all and doesn't feel overwhelming.

The game also includes the ability to directly control units. Controlling foot troops is clunky and not that great, so I never use it, but controlling tanks and AT guns works incredibly well and its super immersive. It feels a bit like Warthunder, or like you're playing a scene from the movie Fury.

There's also ample modding support and the use of the Steam Workshop. Shoutout to the mod Valor for providing a number of high quality factions like Italy, Japan, France, and the UK in a way that makes them feel like official content.

This is easily one of the most capable entries in a long list of games using the GEM engine. First used back in 2004 in "Heroes: Soldiers of WW2" it has since been used in all of the many Men of War games as well as their re-releases. 

Now technically speaking, all of these games play pretty much the same way. So what makes this entry more special?

The touted conquest campaign, third person tank controls, improved graphics, the somewhat larger scale of battle perhaps? To me it's the attention to detail, as well as historical authenticity. 

There was never any reason to texture the hole for the Tiger I hand-crank starter. It's never used in-game and not many people will look that closely at the model. But they did it anyways. 

There was never any need to make a robust spatial sound design system using high quality audio. It's a strategy game, not Skyrim. But they did it anyway, and in post-launch updates no less!

And it's great to see and explore the early World War 2 equipment and battles which often get overlooked in favour of the late war (which, don't worry, is here too). 

So while the game itself is reiterative and the engine is aging and clunky, there is a clear passion by the developers to make a product they can be proud of. 

If you have any interest in World War 2 and real-time strategy games I would strongly recommend this game.

In an age where most (If not nearly all) Men of War spinoffs and alterations turn out to be either cashgrabs or shoddily made, Gates of Hell is the only one that actually wants to be good. Amazing graphics combined with a fantastic vibe and blissful audio results in one of the best products in the RTS genre out there today, but it still has some issues.

Campaign:
A series of individual missions that sometimes (not often) tie themselves into an overarching chapter. There are quite a few missions, and they all tend to be somewhat long. Some missions will test you more than others, but the main problem with the game itself (as opposed to engine issues) pop up here. A trap that many Men of War games end up in, is that they present a mission as a puzzle to be completed in a somewhat specific manner, reducing replayability as a result. Instead of getting a straightforward but open ended mission, like (Hold this point for 40 minutes) or just (Take control over this objective), there are often a series of minor objectives to be completed first, and side objectives are often rather mandatory affairs for a smoother experience. The missions that shine are those that allow you to pick your force composition, give you a list of objectives, and just sends you off to deal with them. Any 'cinematic' cutscene moment often ends up being more annoying than anything else, since oftentimes they show up when you are in the middle of combat. 

Conquest mode: 
The thing I've been playing the most is the conquest mode, wherein you duke it out with the ai over one or several points on a map, as part of a wider 'map'. At first it seems a bit basic, but you recruit your own dudes, manage your own research, and attempt to outcompete the AI before it grows too strong and too powerful for you, which to me is really fun. Playing as the Germans and trying to take over a factory with pioneers, only to see the soviets rush you with a few kv's, will always be a terrifying ordeal. In contrast to Call to Arms, the conquest maps in Gates of Hell are often quite large, way more detailed, and not annoying to play repeatedly. There are quite a few maps, the AI is competent enough to give you a run for your money, and both the AI and the game will punish you often.

Multiplayer: 
Your usual Men of War experience, very solid, not much to say. You get a map, get to select your doctrine (units available to you), and there you go. 

Engine:
The game looks stunning, but the engine shows its age. This is not a bad thing really, but for those used to playing the other Men of War games the mechanics are not only familiar to you, but also terrifying to dabble in. Due to the amount of micro you have to manage to do x or y (despite this game trying its best to make it more of a fluid experience), expect to click fast and click often. Resupplying your men is an easy affair, but switching weapons and adjusting inventory stuff requires some experience to do in a fast manner. 

Currently this is the best and ultimate Men of War style ww2 game, and with the plethora of mods it also becomes the best and ultimate Men of War style cold war game too. If you can stand a somewhat click-intensive interface and the fact that you oftentimes have to micromanage your soldiers and vehicles, this is the best ww2 fast paced rts of a modern nature out right now today. Coh 3 is dead in the water, coh2 wont get more support, Men of War as a frachise is held together by prayer alone, and steel division 2 is run by devs who are incapable of adding more maps or anything of any substance to their game.

Bought this on a whim because it looked like a modern Blitzkrieg and I was not disappointed at all. It's one of ~5 games (campaign wise) that I've completed in the last 10 years and I've been unable to put it down since I bought it. From the smaller scaled missions to full scale battles it's been a blast. It's given me some extremely tense and rewarding moments that few games have been able to do - planning a manoeuvre and seeing it come to fruition, successfully defending against the onslaught of the Soviets by placing 500 mines in the fields of Kursk, or shelling the living hell out of entrenched positions are dopamine hits that never got old. 

There can be a lot of micromanagement involved in your army, which not everyone will enjoy (but I did - being able to scavenge the battlefield for enemy armour and weapons and using it against them is very satisfying, especially in the Talvisota campaign when you're at a disadvantage). You have to resupply troops with ammo if they run out, vehicles with fuel, everyone with bandages, and revive fallen soldiers with your medics (keep them alive at all costs) but all of this really helps immerse you into the setting. The ability to control a single soldier/tank/artillery piece in third person is also great, just make sure your other troops are set up well because you can't manage them when you're in direct control. 

There are drawbacks but I believe some of them have been present in the game engine forever, such as path finding. The AI can be perplexing at times (if you snipe someone from far enough away and they're right next to other enemies, the living don't run and hide but just stand there). The tutorial leaves some things out (but they're reworking them as per the last community update). Your medics don't auto revive people which can be frustrating, but you can queue revives with shift + right click. 

You will get annoyed when an enemy mortar shell lands perfectly and wipes an entire squad, but then you can send back 50KG of high explosive and return the favour. If you want a less arcadey version of Company of Heroes with great graphics, a wide range of missions and weapons to play with, engaging and demanding gameplay, then get this game. It can be unforgiving at times, but when it goes well it is the best feeling.

The first truly functioning game on this engine.  It's got a good campaign with great scripting, it's got AI that actually utilizes terrain and spreads out during Conquest mode, and the UI/UX are flavorful and nowhere near as barebones as past titles.

It still has plenty of problems--Conquest AI are still mostly mindless lemmings charging in near-endless waves at the objectives, but unlike all other games on this engine, they will behave *somewhat* realistically.  Still, the difficulty is artificial--the AI don't get smart, they simply have 2x-3x your funding so they can call in tanks until you're firing your last AT shot and running out of ammo/medical supplies. It feels dramatic, but it's only because the AI overwhelms you, not because they play smart. 

This game gets a "Yes" from me because it's the first game that ACTUALLY takes a step forward for this engine. This engine, minus the atrocious AI, has more potential than any other RTS I'm aware of right now. The unit-level tactics are absolutely fantastic, and the immersion factor is remarkable.  Commanding a platoon to company-sized element, managing their individual inventories, executing one alphas with handpicked troops that follow you through the game, and taking individual control of any unit on the battlefield to play as a Shooter is really unique and incredible. 

Cheers to the team that actually made something worth playing from this engine.  Keep going!! You're sitting on an absolute gold mine here, and you have accomplished something all other devs using this engine have failed to--a *worthwhile* singleplayer experience in one of these games.

Short and sweet: One of the best real-time strategy games with a WWII scenario on the market.

The units are detailed, vehicles can be manned and have different hit zones that can also be repaired specifically. The entire environment is destructible (you can torch entire villages and forests with a flamethrower) and even explosion craters can be used as cover. You can build simple fortifications and positions on the battlefield. Units move realistically and infantry consume stamina when sprinting.

There is also the option to control units directly. Either from the normal game view with the swiveling camera or in the first person perspective. But be careful, when you're in the first person perspective, you don't really see what else is happening on the battlefield.

Each unit has an inventory. So you can loot dead people or vehicles and quickly get better weapons, grenades or ammunition if supply vehicles are too far away.

The game contains various single player campaigns, single player skirmish, single player dynamic campaign, multiplayer coop and multiplayer PvP on a wide variety of maps and number of players.

If you're interested in non-hectic, well-presented and comprehensive WW2 real-time strategy, you can't ignore Gates of Hell. In which game can you hit a suspected enemy tank behind a house, depending on the ammunition type, if you manually fire your tank's big cannon through the house walls?

"Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront," developed by Barbed Wire Studios and released in 2021, is a captivating strategy military game that delves into the Eastern Front of World War II. The game stands out in the strategy genre, offering a detailed and immersive experience for players keen on historically accurate warfare simulations. With its focus on realism, dynamic battles, and strategic depth, "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" provides an engaging and challenging platform for fans of military strategy.

One of the most striking aspects of the game is its commitment to historical accuracy. The meticulously researched units, weaponry, and maps recreate the Eastern Front with remarkable detail. From the iconic tanks and infantry units to the realistic terrain and weather conditions, every element contributes to an authentic portrayal of the brutal conflicts that unfolded on the Eastern Front during World War II. This commitment to historical accuracy enhances the overall immersion, making players feel like they are commanding real armies in a critical chapter of history.

"Gates of Hell: Ostfront" boasts a robust and dynamic battlefield experience. The game allows players to control a wide array of units, including infantry, tanks, artillery, and aircraft. The ability to switch between unit types seamlessly adds a layer of flexibility to strategic planning, enabling players to adapt to changing circumstances during the heat of battle. The realistic physics engine further enhances the combat experience, with accurate ballistics and destructible environments adding depth to the tactical decisions players must make.

The game's single-player campaign offers a series of challenging missions that span the Eastern Front, providing historical context and narrative depth. The campaign is well-crafted, immersing players in the evolving storyline as they progress through various scenarios. Each mission presents unique challenges, requiring players to employ diverse strategies and tactics to succeed. The inclusion of historically inspired missions adds an educational element to the gameplay, allowing players to experience key moments from the Eastern Front in a dynamic and interactive way.

The multiplayer component of "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is a standout feature, offering intense and strategic battles against human opponents. The variety of multiplayer modes, including cooperative missions and large-scale battles, caters to different playstyles and preferences. The game's active online community contributes to its longevity, with an abundance of user-generated content, mods, and custom scenarios available for players to explore and enjoy. The competitive multiplayer scene adds a layer of unpredictability, as each match unfolds differently based on the strategies employed by both sides.

The game's attention to detail extends to its graphics and audio design. The visuals are impressive, with realistic character models, detailed landscapes, and visually stunning explosions. The attention to detail in the sound design, including authentic weapon sounds and battlefield ambiance, adds to the overall immersion, creating a sensory-rich experience that complements the strategic depth of the gameplay.

The inclusion of a comprehensive modding toolkit further extends the game's longevity and appeal. The modding community has embraced "Gates of Hell: Ostfront," creating a wealth of additional content, including new units, maps, and gameplay enhancements. The developers' support for modding showcases a commitment to player creativity and ensures that the game remains a dynamic and evolving experience long after its initial release.

Despite its many strengths, "Gates of Hell: Ostfront" may have a steep learning curve for newcomers to the strategy genre. The depth of its mechanics, the intricacies of unit management, and the strategic considerations required for success may be overwhelming for those unfamiliar with military strategy games. However, for players seeking a challenging and authentic experience in World War II military strategy, the learning curve becomes an integral part of the rewarding journey toward mastery.

In conclusion, "Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront" is a standout title in the military strategy genre, offering a compelling blend of historical accuracy, dynamic gameplay, and immersive visuals. This game is the best realistic tactical/strategic game. It is not like Company of Heroes, which is a pure rts game, where different units mostly have only differences in health/armor/attack/range/vision, etc. This game requires you to consider many scenarios in combat, such as micromanaging a grenadier to crawl forward to the side and rear of an enemy tank and throw a grenade. These detailed scenarios excellently restore the appearance of real war: when attacking, you need air strikes, artillery, and infantry coordination; when defending, you need to build fortifications on high ground, lay mines and anti-tank obstacles. At the same time, in many single-player missions, you are no longer required to just monotonously ‘eliminate the enemy’, many times you need to infiltrate behind enemy lines to obtain intelligence, provide cover for friendly convoy transfers, or even operate bombers to pinpoint and eliminate specific enemy targets… People say War Thunder restores history, but I think War Thunder compared to this game, can only be considered a driving simulator. Because real war is multi-branch coordination, happening in the air and on the ground at the same time. The mighty Tiger tank can indeed easily destroy the Soviet T34 series, but without engineers clearing mines, it can only step on mines and break down in front of the enemy line; without the cover of grenadiers, rushing into the enemy line can only become a target for anti-tank grenades and rocket launchers; without accompanying anti-aircraft fire, it will become a feast for the IL-2 attack aircraft… Just around one tank, there can be so many variables and choices, let alone the cooperation between different branches, terrain and tactics are completely diverse. Here, as a commander, you can command an armored column to push the enemy line; you can choose to concentrate artillery and air force to let the enemy experience the ‘Von Fritsch ammunition quantity’; you can also transform into a Brandenburg assault team, infiltrate behind the enemy, and attack from the enemy’s line depth in reverse. There is no simple armor-piercing confrontation in war, the most important thing is system operation. There is no such thing as a single superior weapon that can sweep the enemy in this world, only the cooperation between different branches can highlight the true appearance of war, and this is also the unique feature of this game.

Greatest all around "war game" I have ever played. The amount of depth and things to do is mind boggling. Learn the systems. Watch YouTube tutorial videos and learn this game. You will NOT regret it. Bravo to the developers.

I also like being able to salvage enemy units and either sell them for currency or use in my own battlegroup. Just minor things like that - short moments of frustration that don't really detract much from the immersive gameplay - highly recommend.

[h3] Summary and Rating [/h3]
[b]Preliminary note[/b]: 60 hours of playing time, standard campaign completed (easy), first Liberation DLC missions started

[b]Summary:[/b] Great realistic real-time strategy game with exciting and challenging missions, extensive optional micromanagement, base-building content, very wide variety in infantry, vehicles and air force and the ability to control each soldier/vehicle from a first-person perspective to get straight into the action.
[b]Buying recommendation:[/b] Yes (also at full price)
[b]Rating:[/b] 8/10 based on 
Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10 
Sound, music and voices: 7/10 
Campaign: 9/10 
Technology: 8/10 
Extras: 9/10 (Editor + Modding)

[h3]Negative[/h3]
- no HUD scaling for higher resolutions (very annoying, should be introduced urgently)
- Revise training camp and make it more beginner-friendly / better define instructions
- sometimes missing designations for infantry

[h3]Performance / Bugs[/h3]
The game runs very well for me (32GB RAM, RTX 3060, Ryzen 7 5800X) on WQHD with ultra settings, the frames are stable, no major stutters. The game is largely bug-free, even if engineers sometimes install themselves and then can't move anymore (don't build tank barriers directly behind sandbags!). 

[h3]Campaign[/h3]
I really liked the missions in the standard game, even if the difficulty seems quite random and doesn't increase with each mission. This also depends on the different scenarios and the corresponding necessary knowledge about the game. Let's see how it works out in the second run on normal. I really like the design and content of the stories and intro videos. I also found the first missions of the Liberation DLC exciting, but I can't say anything final about them yet. Unfortunately, the training camp is very buggy and the instructions are sometimes completely unclear. At some point I gave up and started playing the real game. This is something that should be urgently improved for beginners, otherwise they will be put off before they really start playing. General tip: If a mission seems too difficult, you're probably using the wrong approach. Fundamentally rethink your tactics. Overall, the missions feel very dynamic, sometimes the main direction of battle changes or there are counterattacks after conquering the front or flanking opponents. In addition, there are small, fun secondary tasks that make the missions seem coherent. The only thing that sometimes bothers you is that the opponents unexpectedly come from directions that were not foreseen and defensive positions that have been built for 30 minutes are completely useless. But that's more exciting than annoying and doesn't happen all the time. Plus, it's probably realistic.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The game is diverse and the mechanics seem well-rounded and realistic. 
I find it interesting that - like in other games - you can't always use the same tactics to win. It is absolutely necessary to play map-based and, for example, to use the landscape to your advantage. Heavy gun positions must be covered with smoke from the front in order to then flank them with infantry and tanks. Alternatively, you can take them out from a distance with your own heavy guns or let a hidden infantry unit flank you unnoticed in order to switch off the gun so that the tanks can advance can. The battlefield/road must be checked for mines or you risk losing entire groups of vehicles. If your own tank is disabled due to mistakes, you may have to take out enemy vehicles at close range with grenades, dynamite or explosives, which in turn often requires smokes or clever preemptive hiding of infantry units close to future front lines. Of course you can also use anti-tank infantry if available. In general, the variety of infantry units is very high and everything seems appropriate. Short-range assault troops can be equipped with SMGs, riflemen and flamethrowers to storm trenches. They receive cover fire from the riflemen/MGs from a greater distance. The lieutenant is used for reconnaissance with his binoculars, while snipers operate in the background. Medics then in the second infantry group, so that they don't die on the first attempt if there is a machine gun hidden somewhere by the fog - everything feels great dynamic, there are regular surprises that you have to be able to deal with. Basically, I often noticed that realistic tactics are effective in this game, which increases the immersion enormously: you can often act in a way that makes sense. There are epic wedge-shaped attacks on an area of ​​the front line, followed by flanking attacks and ambush attacks to take the entire front line. 

The switch between offensive and defensive also keeps longer battles exciting; in the latter, the base building elements in particular are a huge added value because you can determine your own tactical positions (hills, forests, intersections, roads), which are then filled with sandbags, trenches, holes, Barbed wire and anti-tank barriers can be secured. In addition to the previously distributed anti-tank mines and anti-personnel mines. You then have to reinforce these defensive positions with the right types of infantry / heavy weapons (mortars, anti-tank guns, artielly) / vehicles and thus have a lot of individual control over the battle and the map. Environmental features such as differences in altitude or poor visibility in forests are noticeably relevant. Micromanagement often becomes relevant later in the course of the battle: ammunition and supplies have to be replenished, this can be done at stationary points or in the vicinity of certain mobile vehicles. Here, too, you have great control over the structure of your front line, for example by moving or building ammunition depots of medical tents near a new front line. If you run out of ammunition, you can loot any enemy (weapons, ammunition, bandages, supplies, explosives) - so you can turn a simple rifleman into a machine gunman. After damage, every enemy vehicle can be looted and repaired so that you can then use it yourself. However, depending on the damage, this takes a very long time and is not possible if the vehicle has been completely destroyed. In this respect, you should use the opportunity to switch off special parts such as the tracks or the gun turret in order to render the vehicle unable to move or combat. Micromanagement is sometimes a bit awkward, but largely optional. This is rounded off by the innovative first-person option, which you can activate at any time for any soldier and get straight into the action. Simply take on the perspective of a soldier dynamically in the game: great! And in some situations, a life saver!

[h3]Dynamic campaign[/h3]

In addition to the campaign, there is also the dynamic campaign, which is preferred by many and offers the possibility of large and long turn-based battles.

[h3]Editor[/h3]

There is also an extensive editor with which you can create your own scenarios. Very extensive, for example it is possible to adjust individual life point values ​​per soldier. However, the editor is complex and I have only dealt with it superficially. Nevertheless, something like this is an absolute plus point for me in general because it means the game can be played endlessly and you don't necessarily have to buy DLCs. Always fair when developers make something like that possible. And for me a reason to buy DLCs at full price because I won't be forced to do it.

[h3]Modding[/h3]

There are mods, but I haven't tried them yet.

[h3]Music and voices[/h3]

Okay, not great, but suitable. The narrator in the intro videos does a very good job.

It's Janky, but there are good bits. 6/10. I'd love to leave a positive review however more would need to be done. I support the devs however as i think they are going to turn this game into something really special.

Pro's

- Sound is amazing, from gun shots, that whipping sound of bullets as they pass units, explosions, the unit speech, engine sounds and pretty much all sound design and recordings are epic levels of good. Probably one of the best I've heard. 

- The graphics are decent, the effects, the maps themselves, it's great when it's paired with the sound effects as it really does simulate a real battlefield. 

- The game play is decent, there is a lot of mechanics at play, that feel rewarding when you get it right, though still janky.

- The Dynamic campaign and local AI skirmishes are the best modes.


Con's

- There is a LOT of jank, from clipping geometry ( invisible walls around terrain ) the way models interact with hit boxes particularly with the environment, you will notice this as your shots will hit invisible obstacles often, very pronounced in prone position or when your tank is hull down.

- The AI is rudimentary, from not responding, not shooting, Ai just running towards you, AI abuse vision mechanics the way a human can't. AI also get unlimited ammo, unlimited resources. Lazy way of making the game challenging. The developers know this is a challenge to code, because then they would need to write code of sending ammo to replenish it's units, which would be a massive job to code, so instead of actually doing that, they just give the AI unlimited everything, while you need to micromanage sending ammo boxes and supply trucks out to your units. 

- The moving path system mostly works okay, but units will often get stuck on geometry and obstacles in the environment and then just stop leaving you confused as to why they didn't move to where you asked them to.

- Bugs, where captured tanks won't move, but will rotate on same spot, units not responding to commands randomly.

- Basic things with the UI are tedious, for example if you want a crew to leave a vehicle you command them to exit, but then need to re-select the units to ask them to move, making you click a lot, the micro management is tedious rather than rewarding.

- The vision system is good in concept and works well for PVP, but for PVE or playing solo against AI, the AI abuses the mechanics and rather moves its units into places where you don't have vision. Basically, the AI checks where the player has no vision, then moves there, if you chase them down, they simply do it again, moving units specifically to where you can't see. It happens on a micro and macro scale which makes the fighting seem robotic and unnatural. After a few hundred hours you learn how to combat this silly behaviour but it's simply programmed that way in order to provide some artificial challenge.  To make it worse, AI on the player side does not do this, they never use smoke and don't abuse vision mechanics.

- The single player campaign missions are horrid, there is no open way to do things, you're told what to do in every single mission rather than giving the player the options on how they want to proceed. 

- All the good features like laying mines, building defences, sandbags, such a great idea, but the micro management you need to do by clicking and giving commands for everything renders it all useless because it takes you away from fighting for too long.

In the end, I'd say its a good game, I will thumbs it down because there is a lot that should be improved by default. 

There should also be more options to set up your own battles with your own settings, the custom settings in skirmish are so bareboned. It must allow us to set the parameters for every part of the battle, from which units are allowed, how many capture points.

The game has promising updates incomming, I will consider changing my review to positive if i deem the new features, content or efforts worth a thumbs up, the devs do seem like good people.

So it might actually be worth supporting them to make this product better.

Absolutely Fantastic! Realistic tactics, especially when it comes to tanks. Nothing beats the Tiger II, except maybe a direct hit from a 1000lb bomb or a player stupid enough to allow a flamethrower to get behind it and light the engine on fire. Some of the mods available on the workshop are must haves, like having Medics actually do their job without having to be told. 

Soviet play relies  heavily on infantry early on, but the second you can get a pair of T35s you'll be in good shape. T35s are mobile gun batteries and can handle any early tank or light vehicle head on, but beware anything above a 37mm will damage this thing quick and a 105 will blow this thing to hell and gone. Always keep bombers on standby as they are really the only thing you have that can deal with the later stage German tanks without getting instantly clapped. Heavy and clever usage of flame weapons is key and artillery is never a bad choice.

Germany is pretty heavy with the tanks. StuG III's will get you by for quite some time and the Flamethrower infantry can kill ANYTHING if they get the engine compartment alight. The second you can grab a Tiger II or perhaps a pair....its full on easy mode. Surviving long enough to get Tigers is another story.

US has an uphill battle at every turn. Your tanks are simply outclassed by Germany at every stage, I honestly still cannot believe how many 90mm shells a StuG III can weather and still kill the US counterpart with relative ease. The US excels at slapping infantry with tons of lead and even in the later stages of a campaign a Stuart is an invaluable friend to have. US tanks pack more punch than a lot of the German counterparts in the same stages but US tanks are made of paper while German tanks are solid rocks with guns attached. Even the Pershing gets slapped down by a Tiger II almost instantly, its for this reason Artillery is the US' best friend. Cumbersome to use, and VERY slow getting into position without a tow vehicle, but dish out the hurt from relative safety and at long range, oh and I never mentioned that later stage US tanks are actually howitzers on treads and unlike German counterparts can actually tow their own ammo supply. After spending over 100 hours playing "Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront," I wanted to give it a well deserved thumbs up.

The learning curve may seem steep at first, especially for those who haven't played "Men of War" series games before or even good old "Soldiers: Heroes of World War II." While the controls could be more intuitive, once you get the hang of them, the hybrid RTS/Action gameplay becomes captivating.

One of the aspects I really enjoy is the is the atmosphere and visual fidelity. Both vehicles and soldiers are exquisitely detailed, while the damage models further enhance realism. Moreover, the intense battles require good planing and adaptability.

In terms of content, and as game name suggests, base content revolves around the WW2 Eastern Front. Since the game's launch, the developers have diligently worked on improvements for the base game but they also released new content in the form of paid DLCs (quick recap):
[list]
[*]Scorched Earth adds content related to the Eastern Front, featuring new units and missions.
[*]Talvisota brings Finland as a playable faction, introducing new vehicles, units, weapons, and missions.
[*]Liberation introduces the U.S. as a playable faction, adding Western Front content, including vehicles, units, weapons, and missions.
[/list]

As a conclusion, I really do recommend "Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront". On the other hand, if what you're seeking is a more casual experience similar to "Company of Heroes", then I'd suggest checking out "Men of War 2", releasing later this year.

On a last note and personal wish, I sincerely hope that the developers introduce the Pacific Theater featuring playable Japanese faction.

I think the most painful thing this game does (and why my hand hurts) is making you manage individual soldiers' or vehicles' inventories and ammo types in the most difficult way. This happens in lots of places: missions where you don't have resupply crates that do it for you when your units run out of ammo; or if you have to load ammo into a tank; or having to find a particular item in a field of dead soldiers (yes, you have to click through each body while holding the highlight bodies key); or if you want to look through vehicles that might have the supplies you need; or if a tank has to switch between firing at long and short range, or from hard targets to soft targets and its ammo type is suboptimal. Yeah, you do all that manually and it is not only painfully click-heavy, but also not a fun experience. 

The squad management is another bizarre design choice. I couldn't easily set up manual control groups, I had to select multiple units that will auto merge into a squad, but there are no hotkeys for these groups, just an emblem you can click to select them all. If I click an individual soldier, it will break them out of the squad and I have to reselect the rest to merge them as a squad again. Unless I completely botched it, it feels like in 2023 we're still reinventing the wheel of RTS controls and UI/UX. Given how finicky this all is, finding the soldier you need for a task in a big group is hilarious because everyone looks the same. The good version of this is if you have a group of soldiers with the items you need, their actions will be done automatically by the right person or object if you know what to click. The bad part is, sometimes doing things like mounting a machine gun is manual and you need to use the incredibly fiddly inventory system. To revive soldiers, you have to have a person with bandages selected somewhere in your units (not everyone has one), then manually click every soldier that goes down. Good luck finding the person with the medkits in their inventory across a mid size battlefield while managing the rest of your besieged units! Same goes for tank repair, there's about 5 clicks to repair a tank if you don't have the repair kit on your soldier so this gets old fast.

There are also no alerts when your men are being killed offscreen, so you just have to figure out how to keep track of it yourself. Again, this is a basic RTS feature strangely absent here. And as people have mentioned, missions don't end sometimes, or they do but if you click "continue" instead of "next", then you get left on the same map and have to manually quit and select the next mission yourself. I stopped playing after I spent about 45 minutes trying to figure out how to end the second Russian mission. Hilariously, there is a secret objective on that mission but it doesn't tell you what it is once you reveal it, the camera just zooms in on a part of the road with some crates, and when you fail, it zooms in on the road even further. After I had found the intel briefcase and picked it up, it never gave me further instruction. I have to presume it bugged and just didn't progress.

There is clearly a lot of love for the RTS in here, but I don't recommend this as it stands because it feels like they've gone with a lot of interesting features but not thought about user experience or playtested enough. I thought this might be more accessible than Men of War 2, which didn't give me a tutorial when I started. Though CTA does provide a tutorial, it still leaves the average person wondering how to enjoy most of what the designers envisioned.

What is this game?
Basically Men of War. If you don't know what that means: you spawn units (infantry, tanks, support equipment) and control them. No base building & resources gathering.

What does it add compared to Men of War?
- Newer graphics
- Third person mode & first person mode (some vehicles)

What's single player like?
Note: I only played single player a little as it quickly felt repetitive and not fun.
You have several campaigns and a 'conquest' mode. They all come down to the same gameplay.
You kill the helpless enemies using artillery, tanks and well placed mines while minimising losses.
The challenge is fighting off wave after wave or assaulting a superior foe with limited resources.

What's multiplayer like?
Starting off the lobby system is broken and you will struggle to host or connect with lobbies regardless of your isp, region or pc. Say 1 out of 3 matches end quickly because someone fails loading or lags unbearably. Once in a match you can spawn units based on timers (look up men of war). Infantry, armoured cars and support guns are unlocked first, later tanks and heavy artillery at the end. Often a match snowballs hard and you won't even get to unlock your late game units.

MP game modes:
- conquest (coop vs ai dynamic campaign)
- coop (coop vs ai missions)
- battle zones (classical victory points mode)
- domination

There is no attack/defence mode unlike men of war (one of the reasons you're better off buying that).

Battle zones is straight forward, rush to capture points and hold them until your team reaches the required points. Losing units reduces your victory points. If you reach 0, you lose (depending on a setting). If you fail to rush the capture points, you have to attack and capture more. Sometimes this mode snowballs heavily but often the matches are somewhat interesting as there are many (> 5 typically) capture zones spread around the map. This mode tends to end quickly if the team that lost early on doesn't make a big comeback mid game.

Domination is in my opinion the best mode. Each team has a HQ sector, lose it and you lose the match. New capture zones are spawned every now and then in a semi-predictable pattern. Capturing these zones gives you extra manpower & victory points. This tends to move the battle around the map to some degree, which is good. The placement of the sectors can be very one sided. If the first few sectors spawn in territory you already control, you get extra manpower & victory points basically for free. This causes snowballing.

Performance:
Straight up terrible. No point lying here. The game looks good compared to men of war but it requires 7-17GB of ram runtime. Whenever 1 person lags in a match, the entire game becomes a slide show. I'm not sure if the devs simply didn't optimise it or if the engine is crap but the result is clearly terrible. Also players frequently suffer from lag spikes of whole seconds despite their internet working fine. I believe that is an issue with the game itself. An issue I did not experience in Men of War.

The balance:
The balance between factions and doctrines has shifted drastically several times. I think that overall it's not bad. It's neither Wehraboo heaven nor Soviet propaganda movie. Sadly the game suffers heavily from pay to win DLCs. Most DLCs add a new faction & new doctrines to the old faction (alongside maps & missions). To get people to buy the DLC, the new faction & doctrines are intentionally made more powerful than the existing factions & doctrines. This is called powercreep. By the time the next DLC comes out, the devs will/have nerfed the previous DLC to be about balanced.

So what about the gameplay itself?
You can order your units to move, fire, attack, etc, let them fire at will or directly control them. The difference between these is sadly massive. The units AI retarded (more on that below). This means that direct control or constant ordering is the only viable way to play. You don't have the resources (unless you play custom/test mode) to trust the unit AI.

Infantry combat boils down to grenades + (s)MGs + snipers (+ support guns). Tank combat supposedly is deterministic and realistic, but ends up pretty random as hit chance is random. If you aim the right spots with the right gun, tank combat is 1 hit kill. Note you can only hit these weakspots (somewhat) reliably if you use direct control.

As you are constantly required to micro units, you tend to play with 2 dozen infantrymen 1-2 tanks and some support guns. This hurts the setting of ww2, the largest scale war ever...
Also the micro makes the game stressful instead relaxing. And so it fails to be a proper game, it's more of a chore.

What's so bad about the unit AI?
- Infantry will lie down and cower behind cover and not fire. You can workaround this by putting them in the open and ordering them to lie down. If you like using cover to gain tactical advantage, I sadly have to recommend Company of Heroes over this.
- Vehicle path finding is terrible. Vehicles prefer to drive over roads (makes sense) except the roads almost always go through the center of the map where the enemy can easily hit you. To work around this you have to double right click (be sure to check the path preview) or manually drive (let's you go faster also).
- Units love to pick their own targets, often preferring to kill a harmless infantrymen vs an enemy tank or support gun.
- Infantry turns to face the direction of combat. Makes sense, you may think. Except they never turn back to face the way you want them to face. This makes keeping vision on an area micro intensive as you have to tell every infantrymen personally to face a certain direction. He will look away the moment he senses combat somewhere.
- Vehicles love turning on the spot instead of driving in an arc. This makes them slow and exposes their weak spots.
- Infantry does not use grenades or AT rockets automatically most of the time. Very rarely they do. It's so rare, you can't rely on it.

Other issues:
- Infrequent crashes to desktop.
- Poor map design with a lot of tiny height differences that are hard to spot. You can find them if you go first person mode or tilt your camera to the ground.
- Units have dementia and forget where the enemy is despite aiming at it. This is not so much an issue with artillery duels but mostly with tank combat.
- There are bombing runs you can call in but they are laughably easy to dodge by just stepping aside or towing a gun and driving away. Only useful vs vehicles with broken tracks or the karl gerat.

Summary:
Buy Men of War (any version) if you like to micro. It's cheaper and you won't miss anything.
If you want better unit AI and cover to matter, buy Company of Heroes (+ mods).

I keep coming back to this ambitious game but I'm often left with frustration and at this point cannot recommend the game. The largest reasons are:

* The game feels very buggy. In my current 14 hours of playtime I've ultimately lost or had to restart missions multiple times due to game issues. The most recent case caused an AT-gun to flicker in and out of existence right next to my valuable tank. EDIT: This seems to simply be an issue with fog of war as it happens repeatedly. Camo is apparently so advanced that a 75mm howitzer is completely invisible to a tank directly beside it, even while firing.
* The mechanics in this game ultimately amount to chance based on the accuracy of the unit or the driver. A enemy light tank can stroll straight up to your medium tank and kill it without a scratch, should your medium tank miss its necessary first shot. This applies to basically all encounters and can lead to some hero moments but can also lead to frustration when the AI suicide charges you with a unit much less expensive than yours.
EDIT after more hours: Pretty sure the AI gets accuracy buffs to makeup for their lackluster AI, even on lower difficulties. Have fun watching your emplacements miss multiple shots on enemy tanks as they stroll up only go get perfectly killed in one shot.
* There seems to be shortcuts missing from the game that are otherwise common among RTS games. The most glaring is the inability to queue orders, meaning you cannot order a unit to "move here, then attack target unit" for example. Another that I couldn't understand was that to deselect a unit from a squad, you have to click the unit itself in the game world. You cannot click it's icon to deselect it, which is especially annoying for individual soldiers.
* There are very little resources both in-game and on the broader internet that explain units composition, let alone their intended usage or strengths. 

Ultimately it's a very cool game and might be some fun if you can catch it on sale, but I would hesitate to say it's currently worth its full price.
