The good:
- What this game gets right is beautiful graphics and a good selection of units.

The bad:
- First things first: this is an unfinished game. Missing audio for the campaign missions, tons of bugs, missing animations/textures, etc. This is not something the devs themselves  deny, but somehow the game is being sold as a "stable" i.v. v1 release. This is an alpha at best. Know what you're buying.
- Dynamic campaign is repetitive and boring, lacks creativity, and so do the mission campaigns. You're not gonna learn anything serious from playing the missions. Instead of teaching new players about the game mechanics and units in the game, the devs instead chose to design missions that are lame and lacking in quality and depth, and certainly lacking in "strategy".

The ugly:
- Because this is based on the MOWAS engine, the game lacks user friendliness and simple, common sense features that would make the experience less frustrating. How about adding notifications about the skirmish game progress if you're trailing behind, or winning? There are no simple mechanisms for selecting soldiers that look so tiny in big maps, or attack-move commands that you could use to multi-task while taking direct control of your tanks or guns. What often happens is then you having to directly control every single unit, which makes this not a strategy game. It's like the devs are confused over what exactly this game should be: call of duty (1st person shooter) ? Company of heroes (real-time tactics) ? Nah, it's neither IMO and if it is, then it sucks in both, but this is def not an RTS game.  
- Frustrating MP experience: massive lag, poor performance esp on 3 vs 3 maps, so many bugs, crashes, and timeouts. You typically have a 50% chance of finishing the game. Horrid software design and bad coding imply tons of memory leaks and frequent crashes for the user. And I'm not sure these ever get addressed. In fact, the devs are probably creating more bugs as they add more features instead of fixing the current code.
- By far the worst thing about this game is the AI. It's not just the AI you play against that sucks, but also the one you rely on when you're not directly controlling your troops. You can "hope" your tank is going to hit back at that AT gun sniping it from a distance, but ... that's not how AI works in this game. In fact, you cannot even prioritize your tanks or AT guns to attack enemy tanks. Instead of improving the AI, the devs instead chose to make advanced AI (esp hardcore) cheat and have access to massive resources, which it uses to flood you with troops and tanks that do nothing intelligent. It is as dumb as they come.
- Primitive and unphysical path finding, which could leave your tank or truck stuck on a stone or a piece of wood. Troops inside trenches exit the trench if you order them to move to another section of the trench. Absolutely frustrating how often you have to take direct control of each unit just to make sure it doesn't get stuck. Remarkable how the basics in this game were not properly designed, probably because they're based on the MOWAS engine, which is total junk.

The only major complaint I have is that the infantry move at will AI behaves significantly worse than in MoWAS 2. This is due to the walking fire mechanic, which appears to override the default behaviour, leading to both friendly and enemy infantry being extremely unreactive to enemy fire if moving. A simple modification to remove the walking fire tag from infantry weapons fixes this, and allows infantry disperse, go prone and return fire automatically if in move at will mode, as they did in MoWAS 2. 

Other than the bugged walking fire mechanic, which can be disabled relatively easily, GoH easily surpasses MoWAS2 in performance and mechanics at this point in time. The game has also been updated consistently since launch with new content, and the developers have been very attentive to complaints and suggestions from the community. 

Although GoH only has two factions currently, the amount of content in terms of units, vehicles and missions rivals vanilla MoWAS 2 in terms of quantity, and is significantly higher and more consistent in terms of quality. 

Also, GoH unlike the base CtA, appears to have very high adoption among the MoWAS 2 mod community, so expect big things there.

Built by a small indie game team, Gates of Hell is one of the best RTS games you can buy on the market. 

Distinct mechanics separate it from your typical game in this genre that are only seen in the Men of War series and faithfully restored in this one as well. 
Things you may overlook such as inventory for every unit on the battlefield that can be fully customized, and the ability to have full fledged control of every soldier under your command are not implemented in any other game as well as they are for this one.

Other examples include vehicles with fully modeled components, very much like what would be seen in a game like War Thunder, and the ability to repair and reuse damaged vehicles later, including enemy ones. This can be very unforgiving for new players, but with practice can be used to your own effect equally as well.

Although the developer team may be slow to update the game at times, this has been easy to forgive considering the steady progress they have had since release given the size of their studio. 

However, it must be noted that the multiplayer player-base is very niche, and it can often be difficult to find good multiplayer games without personally knowing a regular lobby creator.

All in all, I highly recommend Gates of Hell to anyone who is looking for a fresh new take in the RTS scene, and with more popularity, the Multiplayer issue will eventually fade away.

Developers stuck to the same old game with a few ribbons to make it look different. 

There in NO strategic value in this game. The micro-management is soooooooooo cumbersome that the game becomes tactical at best. 

The game rewards playing lone wolf hero with 1 tank in direct-control to save the day. You know, like in the Hollywood movies of the 1960s.  

Campaign: Meh. The developers deny you of units to make it "difficult". Boring, lots of grind. No models to enjoy there. 

German faction: It's trash. They have the worse everything. Conquest becomes a race for the Tiger and the King Tiger tanks. Everything else is useless and their stupid bullets will bounce at the Russian tanks. Which comes to infantry, why wasting points in getting better units? They don't make a difference. The cheap ones will do since they drop like flies. OK, I get it the Nazis are bad, they lost the war, blah blah blah... So then make a game with nations of your acceptable political spectrum with EQUAL features. Give the player the chance to use both factions. I am tired of playing Russia !!!

German artillery: Far inferior in range to the Russian. 

German rockets: Waaaaaaay inferior to the Russians. They won't come on wheels and they will destroy themselves and the friendlies around them. This is another cynical feature that will make you rage given your limited resources. 

Conquest: Playable only if activating Workshop mods made by the community. 

Airplane: It is a cynical feature that doesn't belong. I quit several games because of this. It is not fun to be struggling with resources and then the PC just throws a bombing raid. 

Starting point: This is a total mess. I assumed the developers had learnt from all these years... What a waste of time by gathering units around all over the place. It would be so simple to make an off map base that is clear where units pop and drive into the map (and disabling all fire in this area to avoid off map action). 

Units: They are all beautiful as always and is a pleasure to see the models in combat. But they are incompetent and Kamikaze. They will always choose the worse path throwing themselves at the opponent. Infantry will not know how to move in trenches, so they will walk out offering themselves to the enemy. So again, going micro moving soldier by soldier... 

Arty and cannons: The still come without transports. So lot's of time wasted towing them to trucks and moving them to the battle. By the way, it takes lots of time towing anything. Sometimes you have to try several times. 

Repairs, digging, sandbagging, healing: It is worse than ever. The wait is soooooo long that is better to skip it and make the best with the items around the map. There is no reward in repairing vehicles it takes forever.  Just leave it and call for a fresh one. The toolboxes are consumables. So not only it takes forever to repair anything, but also you have limited repair uses. The units are so stupid that they will waste a repair kit to fix a wheel when the cannon, or the engine is out (no priority system). 

Fog of war: Disable this stupid thing. It only works for you. The computer has full view of the map. 

Officers: The are just for show. They have binoculars, look cool (they look awesome in fact), but have no effect on the battlefield. Cannons will waste their time with infantry and ignore tanks. The game is lacking an arty detail system, so you could, for example, make your officer order mortars to focus on infantry and cannons on tanks. Officers could be great assets if given influence over units. 

Pace of the game: This thing is soooo slow that you will make lot's of hours playing this thing. Probably the developers get paid by the hour you play.

Veterancy: I see no value here. The infantry will get killed in no time, cannons and tanks don't get any smarter. 

Shooting range: Good concept, but wasted opportunity. It should be a true shooting range in which you could call and try every single unit available in the game to experiment with it and learn its mechanics. So bring your COD/BF tactical self and learn how to shoot, throw grenades, drive/shoot with a tank. You will play like agent Smith from the Matrix movie. You have to take control of all your stupid minions if you want them to be effective.  

Workshop: This is the real value of the game. Great community, incredible mods. They have outdone the developers. For this guys, I almost placed a YES in my review, because they really are the game. But unfortunately, the rating should be for the developers, not the Workshop community.

This feels like the early Beta rather than a full release. Endlessly buggy AI, missing names for objects (Especially any HEAT ammo in tanks), and a general lack of polish leads to a frustratingly annoying gameplay loop about AI failing to do its job.

It appears that the player's units AI is even worse than the enemy when playing single-player. These issues have been present since the first Men of War games and have only been made worse with this installement:

- Tanks will absolutely always focus on engaging infantry, always automatically switching to HE rounds and turning towards enemy soldiers. Do they do at least kill infantry? No. They will allow themselves to get swarmed as they turn their hulls and turrets to track a soldier 400m away. This gets extremely frustrating extremely fast, as you can lose a handful of your best tanks to moronic engagement hierarchies, with no fault of your own. Many good mechanics have been added to this game, but it DESPERATELY deserves a "Infantry VS Tanks" engagement mode, so you can set up your tanks in critical spots and have them focus exclusively on anti-tank warfare. 
I have found that opening any tank/AT weapon's inventory, and manually ripping HE rounds out of it, helps to smooth the super aggressive infantry engagement mode, but this leads to another problem:
- Tanks have a 80% chance of completely ignoring engaging enemy tanks. I simply cannot make it easier for my tanks to shoot them - They have clear line of sight, the enemy is facing sideways, my tank has APHE/HEAT loaded, aim is on minimum, yet they refuse to engage. 
I have to manually click on the enemy tank for mine to engage - their turret will turn.
Then I click again - They begin to track infantry
Then I click again - Their turret will turn towards the enemy tank
Then I click again - They will start glitching out tracking between the tank and infantry
Then I go into manual aim mode - it misses
And repeat, over and over many times, my tanks will sit brain-dead whilst enemies engage.

- Planes have been added to the game. Great! You have the ability to buy AA trucks and guns to take them down. Great! The AA doesn't engage the plane. Great. And if it does, the spread is ridiculous and distance to engage too small for a plane rapidly coming in and out of range for the AA to do anything to it. Great...
Many games, I have set up 5 AA trucks, with 1 or 2 static AA guns, anticipating the one enemy plane attack, only for units to fail to recognise the plane and not engage, or when they do, miss extensively. The plane itself can take a lot of damage before going down, and without all guns shooting at it, you are guaranteed to lose at least one or a whole group of your units to a plane attack.
Furthermore, if the AA trucks are not in range, they will try to be, leading to them rapidly moving into each other and promptly making for target practice for the plane.

- Mortars are still a buggy mess. They will not engage on their own, even if within their engagement distance, leading to manually having to select every single mortar, selecting attack on ground on a target, and then rolling the dice on whether the mortar feels like shooting or not. I just want to set them up to engage at the furthest distance, and anywhere in between, without having to babysit them. 
I recently ran a match where the enemy and myself were battling in very close-quarters, and I was reminded of my mortar purchases after they sprung to life from being idle up to now, by showering the engagement in mortar shells, killing mostly my own units. I just sighed and quit the match, I can't deal with it anymore.

I am constantly having to battle my units to make them do what I want. This is not fun or engaging, it is frustrating. I cannot stress hard enough how annoying this is to play with. The game has VERY good potential, and I love the dynamic campaign and the many quality-of-life changes, but it DESPERATELY needs some love into it's AI, especially engagement hierarchies. I feel like my units are blind 99% of the time, and don't have enough energy to do 200 CPM just to micro every single soldier, mortar, tank and AT to move where I want to, yet alone anything more complex.

Maybe multiplayer is better, but I can't be asked anymore.

Despite being a great game and deserving of being called Men of War Assault Squad 3, it's difficult to recommend the game in its current state.
On one hand, it improves greatly on the foundation of the previous games, including more fortifications, tanks, smoother unit animations, a dynamic campaign (akin to that in Call to Arms), and 5 missions for both USSR and Germany that play very differently. Audio is also a step up, with more realistic gun sounds and movement through different terrain.
On the other hand, the rampant bugs, lack of quality care, voice overs for missions being absent (currently being added through updates every few days), unit pathing that STILL is clunky and will run infantry through open ground despite being in a trench, the cover suggestions being inaccurate, lack of faction variety (only Germany and USSR) and the very high price tag for newcomers ($50 base value!), make it a difficult game/dlc for me to broadly recommend.
In conclusion, if you're a die hard MOWAS fan, and really want a modern take on the series, then Ostfront might be worth it. However, if you're new to RTS games or are looking for a strategy game with in depth unit controls/realistic armor/artillery, then Men of War Assault Squad 2 is simply a more polished product with far more content.
If you like numerical ratings, I'd place Ostfront as a 7/10, simply because I'm a big fan of MOWAS.

This game is Men of War: Assault Squad 2 mixed with some of the more classic MoW games on steroids, and finally something decent created from Call to Arms. If you enjoyed any of the previous titles or the setting you'll be sure to enjoy this game. It’s realistic, fun & immersive. The single player seems to be a great middle point and compromise of what was good with the original missions in the series and the removal of the slog of capture points with waves of AI you had in assault squad. You have limited resources for the missions but are tasked with specific objectives and scenarios. Definitely a benefit than the generic missions for MoW:AS2. Before I continue, I would like to disclose that I received this copy for free - I was part of the closed beta testing group. However I still would have bought this if I hadn’t. I’m still looking to be able to buy and give the DLC to a friend or two of mine, but that option is not possible yet.
This game sets itself out from the previous titles in the franchise(s) / series. 

	There are immersive and more believable voice lines and dialogue than previous titles. Although I do wish they were in their respective native languages rather than accented English. No more terrible lines like american infantry screaming “aim is in the reach zone”,“Hurrah.”,  “for uncle sam!” which are not only terrible translations that make no sense but also terrible voice acting. The dialogue/narration is better coming from the experience of the preceding games with narration such as a “Japanese” (some random English speaker, no accent)  narrator saying in a complete monotone “Shosha thank goodness you’ve arrived”. It’s a step up from the previous titles.

	The variety of weapons and vehicles is astounding in comparison to all previous titles. In terms of tracked vehicles for the Germans alone there are 48 in comparison to the measly 20 MoW:AS2 had. The amount of content far surpasses any of the other titles by more than a factor of two when comparing a faction's weapons, vehicles, equipment and units. This does have the downside - there are no one to one counters or equals to vehicles in multiplayer - each vehicle/weapon has its strengths and weaknesses just in real life which looking back on MoW:AS2 was probably a key point in its design. Don’t expect to be on equal ground vehicle class to vehicle class. This is usually balanced by command point (cost that this unit incurs limiting the amount of overall units you can command up to your limit) and the manpower points - the amount of points required to call in that unit.
	
Cons:
	Introductory loading movies/cutscenes cannot be skipped. This can be annoying, especially after playing the mission more than twice.

	Conquest is rather boring, it’s better than Call to Arms but it’s not great. Conquest maps are around 2x the size of CtA’s. This allows for extensive flanking and movement which is a big improvement to the meat grinder littered with choke points in call to arms’ conquest. I’ve experimented both on the easiest of difficulties and the hardest. It’s gotten better as development has progressed but playing defensive missions on hardcore (highest difficulty) you can essentially go afk and come back to find you’ve won and taken no losses. This has happened to me in a co-op conquest session. Right now the conquest mode isn’t challenging or interesting. To someone new it’s probably the opposite but to someone who’s put time into the series you won’t find it engaging.

	Networking and replication need to be improved, and I expect it will be. The advertised overhaul implicated that the waiting for server freeze - where the person with the worst computer would hold everyone else back hasn’t been fixed. The only benefit at the moment is the freezing seems significantly less frequent but still happens. Rubber-banding (snapping from one point to another) is very apparent and common when a unit is in a move order. This doesn’t happen constantly but is definitely common. It doesn’t happen enough to make the game even remotely unplayable, it’s just very noticeable. This overhaul was not what I expected and so far have been somewhat let-down by it, from a technical perspective these issues shouldn’t be happening - especially for an RTS where the majority of input is event based- they should be utilizing prediction here but so far it either seems they don’t or don’t do it correctly. The bizarre part of this is that this rubber-banding only seems to happen outside of direct control of the unit - which is the opposite of what should be happening. 

	The individual unit AI for vehicles is not great - this is also prevalent in call to arms and is arguably worse there. This isn’t a game breaking issue, but it can lead to some very frustrating and often unfair situations.The AI in terms of targeting, awareness and activity often either feels possessed or straight up braindead. Units can straight up ignore or improperly prioritize which units to engage resulting in instances of what should be a easy engagement turn into losing a vehicle. For instance a tank can continue to shell a damaged unit (effectively no threat) and ignore the immediate threat in-front of it. Another issue for tanks is they will turn their turrets to the wrong direction by themselves where there are no units leaving them unprepared to engage units in front of them. A similar issue is where vehicles will not engage units to the near right (almost in front of them viewpoint wise - range doesn’t matter) or left and have to be manually told to do so. On top of this there seems to be the lack of awareness for vehicles, sometimes they will not engage tanks or other units in front of them despite being able to. It makes vehicle management very micro intensive and can be straight up tedious with large amounts of vehicles.

	Overall somewhat of a rough start, largely to no-fault of BarbedWire Studios. It's good game, and I expect it to be a great game going forward. It’s one that I’d recommend to anyone to buy if they enjoy either the setting or the franchise(s)/series. So far it's the best title to date.I acknowledge the price is a bit steep for some and with the given issues I described it’s understandable for some to wait until those issues are fixed or the game goes on sale. I’d say and include more but there’s a character limit for reviews...

Frankly speaking - nah. Just nah, don't bother. Even if you don't own the preceding game, Assault Squad 2, you're better off just getting that instead of this.
Gates of Hell is basically a paid (and incredibly pricy) version of either Valour or RobZ mods. 

Here's what you're getting for £40:

• 2 nations only (Valour/Robz offer over 8)

• Greatly improved visuals. That I can give to it. The game looks gorgeous, especially in winter settings. MLRS's leave clouds of lingering smoke, tanks erupt into fireworks. Skyboxes are neat and the player has been given much more liberty with the camera angles. Terrain and elevations feel more pronounced and realistic. Vegetation has seen a major upgrade.

• New animations for infantry, which is quite a welcome addition to the series that's been using the same outdated animations for well over 15 years. The new ones are still rather rough and unpolished, though. For instance, soldiers have different idle animations where they sit or lie down, but upon a single order immediately snap back into combat stance with zero transition. 

• 10 campaign missions, some of which are stealth-oriented. Yeah. Stealth in an RTS that has  an incredibly rudimentary and mostly broken stealth system. Some other missions have you take on an entire fortified and alert village with a single squad of partisans. Amusingly dumbfounding for a game attesting to historical accuracy. What's worse, all these missions are accompanied by very crudely made cutscenes with some characters having voice acting and others not, units behaving erratically, and remaining enemy troops shooting back mid-cutscene. The writing is rather wonk too.

• The Fog of War is a debacle. Units may happen to be located at point-blank range from each other and still not see one another. The time it takes for a unit to spot an enemy is unrealistically slow. It takes no less than 2 seconds for a unit to stare into any given spot for the enemy to magically materialise.

• Inconsistent AI. Particularly blatant in stealth missions. Some enemy units are completely oblivious to gunfire going off near them and act completely braindead even when having a target in LoS, while others notice and start spraying at incomprehensible ranges. Furthermore, pathfinding is botched for vehicles. They get stuck on steep slopes and inside indestructible walls. Units in general can't do anything on their own without constant babysitting.

• Appalingly bad netcode. 100ms latency translates to a whole second of input lag in co-op/multiplayer. Even just a single person in the lobby with a subpar PC makes the game borderline unplayable for the entire server. Loading times in multiplayer can take up to 2 minutes. 

• "Realistic armoured vehicles" with a really dubious damage model. Huge shells ricocheting in cases where the target should've been torn apart is not exactly realistic. And then there are T-34-85s that can single-handedly destroy a panther at combat range in a 1-on-1 fight. 

• Air units physics and behaviour have barely, if at all, changed since 2006. They still fly at incredibly low altitudes, can do an almost perfect 360 turn on the spot, drop bombs by spawning them underneath and letting them slowly touch the ground with zero acceleration.

• Sounds effects have changed for the worse compared to Valour/Robz. Where the latter had raspy and vivid sounds, the former has watered-down, on-the-nose, dulled pops. Just juxtapose the thunderous, rattling clap of the Tiger's cannon in RobZ to that of GoH's generic "plop" sound. Most cannon sounds in GoH feel underpowered and weak. MG42 isn't itself.

Is it worth it? Absolutely not for the current price. And for a hefty discount? Perhaps, when and if big overhaul mods come out. Otherwise, just get an Assault Squad 2 and one of the realism conversion mods for it. They offer a much grittier and realistic experience than this at the moment. And more of it as well. And for free, base game excluded.

Below you will find my initial review of CTA Gates of Hell: Ostfront, in which I did not recommend the game. I found the game to have a very steep learning curve, and I found the tutorial to be pretty substandard. I stand by the criticisms I made then, as they were true at the time. In tact, i was so traumatised by my tutorial experience that I have refused to go back to it. It might well be fixed by now., or perhaps not. You can find the entirety of my negative review below this updated one.

So, now I've clocked up another twenty or so hours in the game and I have decided to reverse my original judgement. So, why did I go back and keep playing? Partly, because I really wanted to like the game. It was clear that the devs had put a lot of effort into it, and the attention to detail and period authenticity were all there. There were also some very positive and enjoyable elements of gameplay. The game got under my skin. I wanted to keep coming back, despite my initial misgivings. And after several more hours of learning through  trial and error gameplay, I began to thoroughly enjoy my experience.

GRAPHICS AND SOUND DESIGN
The graphics are excellent for a strategy game. One feature is the ability to go down to take direct control of individual vehicles, or even individual soldiers. The graphics here would stand up as good enough for a third person shooter of a few years' age. For a strategy title, that's pretty darn good. The sound design is also very well done. The troops under your command are convincingly voiced, crying out to their comrades in either Russian or German. The sound of gunfire is good, with tank main armament and artillery effects being truly excellent.

GAMEPLAY
This is not a base-builder RTS (thank goodness), but one that gives you limited resources to carry out a specific set of objectives in each mission you play. The missions are organised into either scripted five-mission Campaigns for each of the German and Russian armies, or into dynamic Conquest campaigns which you can set various parameters for. Multiplayer is available, although I have not dabbled in this. As I mentioned above (and speak of at length in my original review), the learning curve for newcomers to the franchise is very steep. The game is also quite difficult. If you make a mistake, expect to be punished for it. Also, since it's an RTS game, if you're micro-managing one part of the battlefield, your pixel troops could be being absolutely trounced by the enemy elsewhere. And there is a great deal of scope for a great deal of micro-management. Do you want to fine tune the position of every soldier in your squad? You can. Want to loot dead bodies for arms and ammunition? You can. Want to fire a Rigid Composite AP shell instead of an AP shell with HE filler? You can, subject to ammo availability. Just remember to keep an eye on those flanks.

AI
The AI for your own troops is very basic. You can pre-set how they will behave when they see enemy troops (Fire at Will/Return Fire?Hold Fire) and that's about it. They don't appear to have any sense of self preservation, so if they come under a mortar barrage, they will simply stay at their post until they're all dead., or until you order them to bug out. So if you're obsessing about the load-out of a medic attached to a squad on the other side of the battlefield at the time, well I hope those extra bandages were worth it. The enemy AI is little better. They will defend their posts to the last man, but without any imagination. If they see your troops, they will shoot at them, until you manage to kill them all. When the enemy AI attacks, they move forward relentlessly, shooting as they advance. But they don't seem to take much advantage of cover or covering fire, and use the same paths for each successive wave. Once you work out where they're coming from, you can set up a kill-zone in the open and cut down wave after wave. The scripted attacks the enemy make in the Campaign missions are better executed, however, but in Conquest, the enemy makes up for this with sheer force of numbers. It's an inelegant solution, but it keeps the game challenging in its own way.

CONCLUSION:
CTA Gates of Hell: Ostfront suffers from a steep learning curve, with numerous mechanics which can be overwhelming at first, and which are poorly explained in the tutorial. The opportunities - and occasional necessities - to micro-manage can be fun at times, but a bit tedious at others. But the general gameplay loop is enjoyable and well executed, in spite of mediocre AI. The game can be very challenging at times - even at lower difficulty levels - but this adds to the sense of achievement when you lead your pixeltruppen on to victory. Oh, but did I mention that the tutorial is not the best? Well, you can read all about that below. Just be careful not to be swept away in the tidal wave of negativity, as the game is really rather good, especially for anyone interested in tactical level engagements on the WW2 Eastern Front.

I'm a veteran of tactical games like Close Combat, Combat Mission, Graviteam Tactics - all supposedly notoriously obtuse games; but even with all their complexities, pretentiousness, and navel-gazing, it always served a purpose, and mastering the mechanics offered true rewards. In this game? You gotta remind your soldiers, individually sometimes, to put their helmets on and unsling their rifles - and if that sounds daft I'm not even scratching the surface of the redundant, tedious micromanagement this game demands (it literally makes you mount an MG34 on a tripod in the tutorial - like WTF else am I gonna put on it? Edit (2024):

After a series of mostly good (not all!) DLC's, numerous updates and a better attitude (mine!), I am now happy to revise my review to very favourable. It has become a good game. Some room for AI improvements still, but otherwise has overtaken MOWAS2 in terms play-ability.

Not nearly as realistic as advertised (there are blatant health bars that appear when units take damage when in the first paragraph on the store description it says there are none, soldiers can easily walk off a burst of SMG fire, often even MG fire, and the accuracy of all weapons is abysmal at best even with the adjusted range for MOW type games, the lethal radius of artillery and similar HE/Frag shells is similarly underwhelming and often a squad must be packed together to ensure they are all incapacitated from most artillery), but it is a decent successor to vanilla MOW:AS 2 in its current state in my opinion, which is why I'm giving the game a positive review.  Fortunately, a few mods to increase the realism (more damage) have already been made, and more are on the way I am sure. The infantry AI is quite poor as of this review and require a lot of tedious micromanaging and support especially on the offensive to be effective, otherwise the entrenched infantry will usually win.

A few other points from my experience with the gameplay of beta and release:

GoH: Ostfront is described on the store as attempting to be almost synchronous with the back-and-forth brutality of the Eastern Front ("The time has come to experience the hell that soldiers endured"), the occasional crying/screaming of dying soldiers and atmospheric music are the only things that really affirm this. There is no gore whatsoever aside from blood pooling and blood stains on the environment from impact wounds. One could argue there are limitations with animations of the dying or decals put onto bodies, but that is not the case based on a few overhaul mods for MOWAS:2, the WH40K mod coming to mind. From the description without having played the beta I would have expected some depiction of realistic violence, after all, high caliber weaponry can often destroy and distort the human form in ways almost unimaginable, and flames will universally char and blacken men into skeletal defaced husks often devoid of semblance of a uniform when given time.

Conquest mode is my favorite mode by far, although often I'll find myself direct controlling a tank or AFV for a large period of time and clearing a point of infantry without ever directly engaging with my own infantry even with armored support. Sometimes I will end up catching a molotov or AT rifle round to the tracks but more often than not I am successful at clearing out infantry and moving my own in to hold it.

There is a lot of variety and attention to detail in the models and equipment in the game. SS camouflage and Splittertarn smocks and zeltbahns are used by the Germans by select units like Snipers and Brandenburgers, as well as Amoeba pattern camo used by Soviet reconnaissance units. The older Stahlhelm-like SSH-36 and the Adrian helmet is even available for Soviet border troops and conscripts. The AVT, G41 (W), and MkB 42 (W) are also in the game, the last time I've seen these 3 rifles in the same game was when I was played Red Orchestra 2.

Overall it makes a good basis for a MOW:AS2 successor from my experience, although I'd prefer it went its own path and attempted to try its hardest to bring a vivid and accurate depiction of combat on the Eastern Front to Men of War terms.

Short version: Gates of Hell is an excellent entry in this long running series.  Easily the best looking (and sounding) of all and the first that really gives you the atmospheric sense of being there.  It also continues the amazing variety of ways to play that these games offer in big ways and small.

Note: my experience with this game is playing the conquest/dynamic campaign mode in single player and coop multiplayer mostly during the beta, but also since release.

For series veterans, I have been playing this series of games since SHOWW2.  I am also the programmer for the Dynamic Campaign Generator mod for most of the games in this series (not a Workshop mod - it's on moddb).  Despite the limitations they are currently working within, I think the conquest/dynamic campaign mode in this game is well done (the best since the feature appeared in the series).  Provided your expectations are in line with what a randomized campaign can be, this offers a truly endless singleplayer and coop multiplayer experience.

For newcomers, these games are very unique in the variety of ways they let you play.  They are extremely accessible with well known RTS gameplay, while at the same time they have a wealth of options for anyone who wants to dig deeper.  For instance, the direct control mechanic allows you to jump in as the driver of any tank or gun to find the prefect hull down position, or to play the gunner and use your knowledge of tank armor and ballistics to try to land the perfect shot.  Details like the ability to button up a tank allow you to make the classic trade-off between better spotting or keeping commanders safe from small arms fire.  Each of the vehicles and soldiers have inventories and you can scrounge for ammo or other necessities in desperate situations.  The maps  are destructible, so you can knock down part of a house with a tank and then use the remains as cover for your infantry.  And the list goes on and on...

In addition, these games have a the full-featured editor and support almost unlimited modding.  So, in addition to the team continuing to work hard on supporting the game, you will undoubtedly see a wide variety of interesting mods.

In conclusion, this game offers an experience that is almost as technically detailed as a game like War Thunder when it comes to tank warfare, but with all the things that games like that are missing such as infantry!  It offers a variety of ways to play as well as open ended modding.  It evokes the feel of classic tactical wargames like Close Combat or Squad Leader, while also providing a great visceral experience with top notch visuals and sound.

Six months ago, I was absolutely ecstatic for the release of this game. As a veteran MOWAS 2 player with over 1400 hours, I was excited for something new, the supposed "MOWAS 3". [i] Wow, unrivaled realism? Different ammunition types for tanks? This was going to be a standalone version of the RobZ mod! [/i] Unfortunately, this naviete was broken once I got my hands on the Open Beta. I first thought "This feels off, but I think that the devs will change things throughout the course of the Open Beta" Here we are, and nothing has changed. Not to mention that the devs decided to release this game in a bundle for $35,. IMHO, it's pretty scummy to charge nearly forty dollars for such a half-baked product. Oh, and more "paid expansions" are on the way? I feel as though this is DMS trying to find a way to milk more money from the MOWAS 2 fanbase. Remember when the GoH devs said that "there would not be any FPS direct control"? I sure do. And then the community complained, and the devs buckled. I've always been a strong believer that the new direct control that CtA brought was nothing more than a gimmick. I understand that you're able to toggle between different options, however, I believe that the Direct Control should've never been tampered with. Whatever happened to "no healthbars"? Call to Arms, for the failure of a game it is, had the option to toggle healthbars. You know what's the worst part? The Open Beta closes and the very next day they release. I'm not an expert, but that doesn't seem like a whole lot of time to make a myriad of bug fixes and tweaks, The game is incredibly unpolished. Text in loading screens isn't formatted correctly (runs off into the background), a quote from Zhukov was given to Eisenhower? How are these things missed?

Movement of units feels clunky, even worse than MOWAS 2. Often I will double click to have units sprint, and instead they will have a Sunday afternoon walk to the frontline. Units will not dive out of the way of an enemy grenade. MOWAS 2, with its punishing AI, did this better. Explosion effects are paltry, and the only real feedback you get is obnoxious screen-shake that you cannot disable in the options. The devs have said that this is for "immersion and disorienting the player". Obnoxious screenshake is used to compensate for terrible explosion effects because the devs couldn't be bothered. MOWAS 2, a game from 2014 had more weight and feel. Without screenshake, explosions are often just a puff of smoke and then nothing. 

Don't get me started on the combat. The TTK is that of vanilla MOWAS 2, and in game I feel as if I need to hose down a single soldier with a coaxial MG for an eternity before he falls. For a game that champions on itself on immersion and realism, it sure feels real arcady. The tank combat is horrendous. Light tanks will have slugging matches with each other, while a FlaK 36 will bounce a shell off the side of a BT-7 because the game said so. The infantry units feel all the same. Ammunition compatibility is a joke. A PPSH-41 that has been arbitrarily assigned "stick magazine" is magically not able to use drum magazines. Overall, the combat feels like a carbon copy of vanilla MOWAS 2. The bullets move at the same speed, and the AT guns feel like they have the muzzle velocity of a wet noodle. I'm not asking for Combat Mission: Shock Force here, but I would've thought that a game that was in development for like six years would outdo a free mod for MOWAS 2. 

The bugs and crashes are another beast entirely. When I was playing the Open Beta I thought, "hmm the bugs don't seem too bad" The full release looks like No Man's Sky on launch in comparison to the Beta. I'm unable to progress through the third mission of the German campaign because the scripting on it is faulty. Did those YouTubers with press copies actually play any else other than the Dynamic Campaign? The game holds your hand the entire way. On the second German campaign mission, the defenses ARE PRE-MADE. You literally don't have to do anything. I don't expect to grab a shovel and dig an anti-tank ditch myself, but PLEASE let me play the game, for goodness sake! Or, for the first Soviet mission, the game goes "put dummy guns here pretty please :))"

I'm not a big stickler for graphics, but the models for infantry are disappointing. Sure, they're better than MOWAS 2, but my dog could probably make better models than MOWAS 2. The (FREE) RobZ mod for MOWAS 2 had better graphic fidelity in terms of infantry models, vehicles, mounted weapons, etc.  Did I mention that the Blau Division volunteers have randomly generated German names and speak German? Instead of y'know, Spanish names and dialogue? Where's the immersion? Mine sure is broken. The devs promised an "immersive representation of the Ostfront" and yet, are so far away. So this game is centered completely around the Ostfront, huh? Where are the Romanians, Italians, Hungarians and Czech? Where are the nearly 300,000 Italians that fought and died on the Eastern Front? [i] Oh wait, maybe it'll be for a paid DLC! Oh joy! [/i]

I feel like this game needed another year of development. The final product feels rushed, and I'm sad to say that I don't enjoy playing the game. I know this entire review I've been really harsh. That's because I'm disappointed. I REALLY wanted this game to be good. However, as the days rolled closer towards release, I realized that this wouldn't be the case. Maybe in a year or two, this game will be better, but without realism mods for an already "realistic" game, I can't recommend. For those interested in this game and have never played a MOW game, go buy MOWAS 2 and download the RobZ realism mod. You'll get a much more realistic experience for cheaper. And for veterans of MOWAS 2, I feel you. I know your excitement. Save your money. 
I'm tired of YouTubers kissing this game's ass and hailing it as the greatest thing to grace RTS players since RobZ. It's blind endorsement for a product that hasn't even gotten major bugs and crashes figured out. 

I know I mentioned MOWAS 2 more than a cow goes moo, and that's for a reason. Why spend a steak dinner's worth of money for a reskin of something you already have? I mentioned the RobZ realism mod often because I believe that was the pinnacle of the MOWAS 2 experience. It brought life to a community that was aching for something new, something fresh. Theodore John Kaczynski (/kəˈzɪnski/ kə-ZIN-skee; born May 22, 1942), also known as the Unabomber (/ˈjuːnəbɒmər/), is an American domestic terrorist and former mathematics professor.[3][4] He was a mathematics prodigy, but abandoned his academic career in 1969 to pursue a primitive life.[5] Between 1978 and 1995, he killed three people and injured 23 others in a nationwide bombing campaign against people he believed to be advancing modern technology and the destruction of the environment. He issued a social critique opposing industrialization and advocating a nature-centered form of anarchism.[6] Kaczynski's critiques of civilization bear some similarities to anarcho-primitivism, but Kaczynski rejected and criticized anarcho-primitivist views.[7][8][9]

In 1971, Kaczynski moved to a remote cabin without electricity or running water near Lincoln, Montana, where he lived as a recluse while learning survival skills to become self-sufficient. He witnessed the destruction of the wilderness surrounding his cabin and concluded that living in nature was becoming impossible, resolving to fight industrialization and its destruction of nature. He used terrorism to fight this industrialization, beginning his bombing campaign in 1978. In 1995, he sent a letter to The New York Times and promised to "desist from terrorism" if the Times or The Washington Post published his essay Industrial Society and Its Future, in which he argued that his bombings were extreme but necessary to attract attention to the erosion of human freedom and dignity by modern technologies that require mass organization.[10]

[h1]If you loved previous Men of War titles especially Assault Squad 1&2 this is a MUST BUY! [/h1] 

I had been saying among my friends for years that what assault squad 2 really needed was a 64 bit engine and some minor tuneups for it to be my all-time favorite.  The Developers over at Barbedwire Studios are a team of devs made up predominantly of Men of War Modders who understand what fans want from this franchise, and they have more than delivered here!

All the best aspects of the Men of War titles with improved graphics and a MAJOR optimization pass that allows it to take full advantage of modern hardware.  It has full mod support and immense replayability for both hardcore PVP fans and casual COOP/Singleplayer modes.  For a game on the GEM engine it looks stunning too!  An absolute ton of new animations, sfx, and brand new high quality models have really breathed new life into this franchise.

[b]I'm personally not really all that into the PvP side of things so this review will focus on the COOP/SINGLEPLAYER side of things.[/b]  If that's what you enjoy too then this game is especially for you.  All the Singleplayer content can be played coop with friends in one way or another.  The three singeplayer/coop modes being [b]Campaign, Dynamic Campaign, and Skirmish battles.[/b]

[hr][/hr]
[b] Campaign [/b] is your standard scripted affair with greater historical context.  I'm a little sad the infamously bad MoW voice acting isn't there but I can understand why the devs avoided that(In my opinion it had a certain charm).  However there is only a small amount here.  Currently there are 5 per faction with 2 more (1 more per faction) not yet released at the time of writing.

[hr][/hr]
[b] Dynamic Campaign [/b] is by far the coolest addition to the franchise as a whole.  As it not only presents a fun challenge but provides a decent amount of progression as you unlock more and more units.  I won't describe it all here because its better experienced than described but it adds a HUGE amount of replayability to the game.  Give it a go, its super cool!

[hr][/hr]
[b] Skirmish Battles [/b] are basically your standard multiplayer battles against the AI, these are pretty fun for folks who just want to get a quick battle in and jump off.  They're a fun way to relax and challenge yourself but the AI doesn't seem capable of bringing in late game units like the player would.  So its best played when time is short.

[hr][/hr]
[b]As for downsides and negatives there are a number.[/b]  Some folks have reported repeated crashing but I have only experienced one crash so far and it seems rather stable.  Beyond that, the AI (especially vehicle) pathfinding struggles in dense (or especially urban) terrain and will not always take the most direct route somewhere.  This requires me to sometimes direct control them and move them directly to where I want them to go.  If you're a men of war veteran then be prepared to do this a bit more than usual with vehicles as they don't seem to like crashing through buildings as much as they do in previous titles.  

Also unlike previous titles the AI soldiers tend to carry out orders only once the entire squad has regrouped, this can be rather annoying when they come under unexpected MG fire and haplessly sit there waiting for that one slowpoke to rejoin the formation before running away.  Rather annoying so be more careful when moving your squads as a group so they don't get strung out like that.

Beyond those things my biggest annoyance is the CURRENT lack of factions.  If you're coming from Assault Squad 2 you're coming from 5 factions down to 2.  Only the USSR and Germany are currently available at the time of writing.  The Devs have already confirmed that more factions and theaters are going to be added in the future but the game does feel a little constrained without the extra faction variety.

[hr][/hr]
Despite all the issues listed above, for a filthy casual like myself this game is AWESOME.  The gameplay is immensely satisfying and it feels like a true sequel to the Men of War titles in every way.  I cannot recommend this enough for fans of the franchise and whether you're new or a grizzled MoW veteran, it's got something you'll love.

Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is a real-time strategy developed by Barbwire Studios and published by Digitalmindsoft. It is supposed to be a successor of the Men of War series, although Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront is not exactly belong to the Men of War series since that franchise is owned by Best Way and 1C Company.

[GAMEPLAY]
Long time players of Men of War series should be familiar with the gameplay of Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront, as most of the features are similar, with some improvement taken from the Call to Arms. Unlike Call to Arms though, Gates of Hell are more realistic and more resemblances of the old Men of War series, such as no hitpoints for vehicles and more realistic penetration and damage system.
One improvement that is brought over from Call to Arms are third-person camera for infantry and vehicles, like you can drive your tanks like in World of Tanks/War Thunder, not just driving them from top down camera with the old direct control mode. It's really awesome driving a KV-2 and blow up everything with its 152mm super cannon.
Conquest mode from Call to Arms also made a return here, with is much more better than current Call to Arms. You are given a little bit more time on attack mission to conquer your enemy and in defense mission the enemy actually spawn after a while so that you can have little time to prepare.

[GRAPHICS]
One of the notable improvement from Men of War is Call to Arms - Gates of Hell: Ostfront has way much better graphics, and thanks to the Call to Arms improved engine, performance is also much better, especially with bigger battles. The graphics looks similar to Sudden Strike 4, but with little more detail and since the camera can be zoomed closer, you can see better details here.

[SOUNDS]
The soundscape design is marvelous! At first I thought they're going to be similar with Call to Arms, which is nice but somewhat quiet I think. Gates of Hell have incredible sound design, it's loud, but not that crude loud that could break your ears. Explosions, tank firing, machine gun fire... it's a real war out there.

[MAPS]
There are 20 maps for multiplayer and 18 maps for conquest on release. They're supposed to be based on real locations. So far, I feel like the maps are so detailed, some provide lots of cover for infantry too. Imagine when they actually made western front maps... or maybe Africa and Pacific?

[CONCLUSION]
While currently there are only 2 factions in the game, the Soviet and Germany, they are planning to add more factions as DLC in the future. With all the game offers currently, I say this is a highly recommended game to play.

What an absolute gem of a video game. 

In short, CtA:GoH is CtA mechanics in WW2 with some of them being a little deeper, such as tripods, fire and such-- and more. Granted, it's set on the eastern front, so there isn't as many nations to choose from-- but damn is it well executed.
Yeah, bits are rough and that is pretty much granted with anything vaguely MoW-like, but once you get used to the jank (which took me like 10 minutes), it's a contender for my all time favourite WW2 strategy game seeing from the 4 hours I have played non-stop. 

Graphically and audio-wise, the game is astounding as it looks and sounds better than original CtA and all MoW on the market. I am surprised as I got fairly brutal frame drops in CtA, but here I got no such problem. 

Game play wise, it's CtA but slower, which suits it perfectly. There aren't 50mp/h strikers rolling down plazas firing on the move and BTR-70s rolling through walls shredding entire squads with DShKs. This change of pace works wonderfully and I am honestly glad it worked at the end, as it truly shines. Not to rant, it's much more manageable now-- it's the same amount of micromanagement as before, but slower, which makes it much more enjoyable.

New 3rd person camera is something I needed to adjust to but once I did, it's kinda like playing WT, but take it with a pinch of salt as I did see some weird physics wonkyness along the way. Overall, it works really well, but I wish the kept first person for the infantry in all honesty. I liked the gimmick of CtA being FPS/RTS in one, but it's not a biggie.

Lastly, singleplayer. Conquest is back, although still quite limited with the number of maps and such, but its liveable considering the amount and differing types of skirmishes one can have throughout it.  
Campaign though, oh boy is it improved. When I played CtA, most missions even on the hardest difficulty with hardcore realism seemed too easy to finish and especially cheese and exploit the game. Due to more limited technologies of 1940s and more of a 'defensive vs offensive' WW2 style of battles, missions on higher difficulties are truly challenging. It took me hours just to go through the first soviet mission-- multiple attempts per objective. Tactics actually paid off and zerg rushing with tanks wasn't a trump card as tank are slow, vulnerable and have very limited visibility. 

To cut it short, I'm so glad they made all aspects of single player so neat while making the game an absolute joy to play with the revamped pace and deeper mechanics. 
I don't say it often, but if this game does get DLCs (DLCs for a DLC I know, but still), I will be the first to buy them as it really feels like Christmas came early in my case. I see myself ramping up stupid hours in this just messing about, doing the campaign and replaying conquest. 

If you liked CtA, or like MoW or CoH-- this game is an absolute must have. 
Just be warned of physics bugs and general jank. But apart from that, damn-- I recommend CtA:GoH to hell and back.

[h1][b]The Best World War 2 RTS?[/b][/h1]
[i]I got this DLC for free for exchange as a closed beta tester, moderator of the Steam forum and a little bit of Discord as well.[/i]

When I first time saw Gates of Hell on Steam, I was very excited about it. I like GEM engine titles because they offer something special in the RTS genre. It's Direct Control, but I will talk about it later. I remember when Gates of Hell was in Steam Greenlight in 2015. It took a lot of time to release it because devs had some problems with engine licensing, they must ported Gates of Hell three times to a new version of the engine and they changed publisher. So it took a while to release CtA:GoH. It ends as DLC for Call to Arms. Devs have a big thumb up from me because they didn't give up, and worked on it in their free time.

What is CtA:GoH about? It's another RTS set in World War 2? CtA:GoH is historically correct and focused on realism. Don't expect your soldiers to survive heavy machine-gun fire or close explosion. You need to think more tactical about your moves. Get ready for micromanaging units and survive one of the darkest times of human existence. That's what CtA:GoH is about

It offers single-player and multiplayer. In singleplayer you can play 2 training missions, main campaign missions, conquest, and skirmish battles with bots. I highly recommend playing training at first. It will learn you CtA:GoH basics and its features. CtA:GoH is not easy to play. You must learn some basics about direct control and micromanaging your units. If you are new to GEM Engine titles, don't be afraid. You will soon learn everything that you need to enjoy it. One of the best parts of Call to Arms: Gates of Hell is the armour and penetration system. It's quite a complex thing. You can read more about in dev blogs [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/400750/old_view/356177263210682894]here[/url], [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/400750/old_view/289750654259080822]here[/url], and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/400750/view/6328093343576961288]here[/url]. Vehicles have components that can be damaged or destroyed. For disabling an enemy tank you don't need to explode it. You can destroy tracks, gun and turret. Or you can set the engine on fire with a Molotov cocktail or flamethrower. 

Missions are very nicely made. Devs made big research for every mission to make them as realistic and historically accurate as possible. It's not another WW2 RTS. DLC was made with passion and enthusiasm for the history of World War 2.

Conquest is a dynamic campaign where CtA:GoH will generate a map with nodes. You can set how big the main map will be, the difficulty of enemies and choose your factions. Then you choose your first place - node on the map where you will attack. If you were a success, then you will defend against an enemy counterattack. After each battle, you can research and buy new units. When you reach the enemy HQ and conquer it, you will win.

Skirmish is classic. You choose one of the multiplayer maps, add bots, set battle condition and play. DLC has one multiplayer mode at release. It's Battle Zones. Your task is to capture more zones than an enemy. A team that has more captured zones will start getting points. The first team which reach the point limit will win. The same goes for multiplayer. Both in skirmish and mutiplayer you will choose your doctrine. Each doctrine gives special units along with regular units which are the same for each doctrine. For example, if choose defensive doctrine you will get units focused on defence. CtA:GoH offers cooperation mode too. You can play main campaign missions or Conquest with your friends.

What is that direct control which I mention at the beginning? It is what it says. You can directly control your units. So you press E and you can control your tank by WASD + mouse. Gates of Hell takes this to a higher level. If you press T you will jump to 3rd person view. Vehicles and field guns have their own gunsight view if you zoom in. Zooming to 1st person works for snipers and officers with binoculars as well. It's a big step forward for GEM engine titles..

Another awesome thing about Gates of Hell and older GEM engine titles is the editor. You can make your own map or mission. What I most like in the editor is you can easily make your own battle. Spawn some soldiers, tanks and put them to fight each other. It's really easy to make it, and it's very entertaining. It's like a sandbox with toys. You can test units, learn how to destroy them, how a realistic armour system works, put one Tiger vs 20 T-34s, and so on.

So, I don't often review games, but i will for this one
of note, i did receive the game for free and was part of the closed beta testing team, at the time of writing i have 60 hours in the game with another 20, give or take, into the open beta. I will also be discussing this mainly from a MP prespective.

Gates of Hell is a great game, and honestly does everything that i wanted out of a sequel to assualt squad:

-grenade spam is much less prevelant (though its still there, especially in early game with F1 spam to some degree)

-combat ranges are longer, which give you more freedom in unit placement, and gives the game a much more realistic feel than previous titles 

-smoke ACTUALLY WORKS

- seriously, smoke is really important, especially when attacking entrenched fortifications, and should be used liberally when attacking in general, and its a change that i absolutely love

- to compensate for larger ranges, maps are much larger than in AS2, giving you adequit space to play with

-larger maps and increased ranges also tend to now lead to flanking being more viable than in previous titles as well, which i also love 

- the game looks fantastic as well, which is always appreciated

- capture points that actually represent the area they sit on! they arnt all just stupid circles anymore! this makes contesting points much more interesting, as having enough weight on a point can flip it, even if you dont control the whole area of the point

- MP is now sort of a combination of what used to be combat and assualt zones, where killing units will reduce your enemies score, but the goal is still to capture important zones on the map, which i really appreciate personally.

on the other hand, some cons:

-mid war is a bit too tank heavy for my tastes due to a general lack of good infantry based AT, and can have some balance problems as a result if the game drags long enough

- not a huge fan of unit timers, as generally i think units should just be balanced on their own by their cost and general effectiveness

- as of release, there's only 1 MP game mode, though I'm aware the devs fully intend to add more in the future

speaking briefly to singleplayer, there's also been quite a bit of improvement over AS2, namely no more stupid cookie cutter SP missions where you just take the 3 sets of flags every time, each mission is unique and different, making the SP actually worth playing!

there is also a dynamic campaign, which is cool, though i dont personally have a lot of time in it, so il going to refrain from meaningful comment on it in this review

all in all, very solid game that i think anyone who enjoyed mowas2 should pick up, and i very much am looking foward to what the devs add in the future!

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway, developed by Gearbox Software and published by Ubisoft, represents the most ambitious and emotionally intense chapter in the Brothers in Arms trilogy. Shifting the setting from the hedgerows of Normandy to the embattled towns and highways of the Netherlands during Operation Market Garden, the game continues the story of Staff Sergeant Matt Baker and the 101st Airborne Division as they attempt to secure vital routes through enemy territory. While it retains the series’ signature emphasis on tactical squad-based combat, this installment deepens both its mechanical systems and its narrative ambition, aiming to portray not only the strategy of warfare but also its psychological toll.

At its core, Hell’s Highway remains firmly committed to the tactical philosophy that defined its predecessors. Combat revolves around suppression and flanking rather than reflex-driven gunplay. Enemy machine-gun nests and entrenched infantry are formidable threats, requiring careful coordination between Baker’s fire teams and assault squads. The player must pin enemies down with sustained fire before maneuvering a squad to attack from a vulnerable angle. This structured battlefield choreography continues to provide satisfying tactical problem-solving, and the more open urban environments of Dutch towns introduce verticality and tighter corridors that vary the formula. Buildings can be entered, streets become deadly chokepoints, and destructible cover changes firefights dynamically, reinforcing the need for adaptability.

The addition of a modernized cover system marks a significant evolution for the series. Baker can now snap to cover, lean out to fire, and move between positions with greater fluidity, giving engagements a more immediate and contemporary feel compared to the earlier titles. The health system also shifts to a regenerative “threat” mechanic, where sustained exposure to gunfire results in a red haze and eventual death, encouraging careful positioning rather than reckless advances. Although some purists preferred the harsher health rules of previous entries, the updated system helps balance realism with accessibility, smoothing out frustration without abandoning the importance of tactical caution.

One of the most striking elements of Hell’s Highway is its presentation. Built on Unreal Engine 3, the game delivers a noticeable leap in visual fidelity. Character models are more expressive, environments are richly detailed, and lighting effects give the war-torn Dutch countryside a somber atmosphere. Smoke drifts through shattered streets, artillery blasts send debris scattering, and nighttime missions are bathed in an eerie glow that heightens tension. The sound design complements the visuals with sharp weapon reports, distant explosions, and urgent shouts from squadmates that create an immersive battlefield soundscape. A controversial but memorable addition is the dynamic action camera, which slows time and shifts perspective during dramatic kills or explosions. While some players may find it stylistically intrusive, it undeniably amplifies the intensity of key moments.

Narratively, Hell’s Highway aims higher than most shooters of its era. The story does not merely recount military objectives; it delves into the psychological strain of leadership and survivor’s guilt. Baker is portrayed as a man weighed down by past decisions and haunted by earlier losses, and these emotional threads weave through the campaign’s cutscenes and quieter moments. The game explores themes of responsibility, sacrifice, and the blurred line between duty and personal anguish. Squad members are given distinct personalities and arcs, making their fates feel meaningful rather than incidental. The tone is somber and introspective, occasionally bordering on surreal in its depiction of trauma, which gives the experience a gravity that lingers long after firefights end.

Despite its strengths, the game is not flawless. Certain encounters can feel scripted, and while environments are more expansive, the overall mission structure still funnels players along fairly linear paths. The action camera and cinematic flourishes, though impactful, sometimes clash with the grounded realism the series strives for. Multiplayer modes exist but never achieve the same level of depth or acclaim as the single-player campaign, leaving the core experience centered firmly on the story-driven tactical journey. Additionally, AI behavior, while generally competent, can occasionally falter, leading to moments where squadmates hesitate or enemies react predictably.

Even with these imperfections, Brothers in Arms: Hell’s Highway stands as a compelling culmination of the trilogy’s vision. It refines the tactical systems that set the series apart while elevating the emotional storytelling to new heights. The portrayal of Operation Market Garden provides a fresh historical backdrop rarely explored in mainstream shooters, and the focus on the human cost of war gives the campaign resonance beyond its objectives. For players who appreciate deliberate pacing, squad coordination, and character-driven narratives within a World War II setting, the game offers a rich and immersive experience that balances strategic depth with cinematic intensity.

Rating: 9/10

The portrayal of each episode is great with the exception of some more mellow circumstances that divert you from the importance of the situation and what's really at stake.

The gameplay always feels fresh and unique even though the level design is not the most complete or in-depth. Even then, it gives you plenty of routes to try different approaches and figure out the best solution. There are plenty of commanding sections sprinkled in with some solo situations. Here things get a bit messy with the AI, as it tries to kill itself at every step and ends up being really difficult to control and do exactly what you expect. But when it's able to follow your instructions and you reach the expected outcome, it's really rewarding. The shooting is okay; sometimes you feel like you can hit all your shots, sometimes you don't even know how you missed, but even that plays into the type of game it is, with some great mechanics implemented into this part of the game.

There's plenty of content to go through and even more after finishing the main story. The progression is fair, but towards the end of the game, missions get really hard, your character feels like it's not able to sponge as many hits as before, and you're being hit from nonexistent or non-shooting enemies.

The art and cutscenes look and feel polished and are accompanied by some great sound design. Would benefit from more weapon variety.

The whole series deserves a remaster and even a sequel.

Going into this blind I am very surprised how fun and engaging this game was. Its story, voice acting, and direction were believable for the time. And I believe Brothers In Arms is the only game that is a fps with meaningful squad mechanics, not like some top down game, no you are on the battlefield with them  You cannot defeat the enemies by yourself, you have to use your squad, they are at your command wherever you tell them to go and what enemies to concentrate fire on. When your squads and yourself fire enough at a enemy a grey circle appears indicating that the enemy has their heads down and its safe to move your squads. You got your bazooka guys, machine gun guys and the normal assault ones, and with every level having multiple flanking routes it gives a lot freedom for strategy. What really ties it together is the immersion, you really feel like a squad leader in WW2, Everyone yelling, bullets firing all over the place destroying cover, rockets launchers and tanks firing rockets, explosions going off, dirt getting kicked up, it does a really good recreating the chaos of war and its up to you to control your squads and push the line to kill the enemy. And since the ally AI will go where you tell them to, if someone gets killed its 100% your fault. The game isn't 11 hours long, but i restarted the checkpoint every time i got someone killed so i can proudly say I completed the entire game with no casualties. The game isn't perfect as it does show its age in places, you can only sprint in a straight line, the actual first person shooting ok but not good, for some reason there a few levels you are by yourself and its not that fun to play those and a couple levels near the end my ai wouldn't shot at the enemy at all, luckily quitting to menu and reloading fixes that, there are tank missions and they are okay its pretty basic. Overall I loved this game, especially when you are advancing in a area with heavy enemy resistance, and you use your strategy skills to position squads, move them when needed to and fight yourself to in the end kill everyone without suffering a single casualty on your team. Its worth the 10$ it costs but it goes on sale for 3$. Gearbox make another one of these! I would love a modern version of this

Very cutscene-heavy compared to the previous games, and I don't care for the linear tank levels. That aside, the gameplay takes a step forward with its destructible cover and new bazooka team. Shooting feels better too, and the contextual third-person camera makes commanding your squad notably easier.

This game aged so much more gracefully than the previous entries in the series. I can fully recommend it. Mainly due to its gameplay mechanics.

[h3] Gameplay [/h3] 

From my point of view previous entries are close to unplayable today. Gun accuracy there is so atrocious you can not take out an enemy from more than 6 meters away. Here this issue is completely gone. Especially with aim down sights weapons you often can hit an enemy on very long distance. However they still managed to balance the gameplay in such a way that player is forced to engage with squad mechanics. So while the core gameplay loop is the same - suppress enemy from front and flank from sides it feels much more natural here and not forced like in previous titles. Not like everything is perfect of course. The AI isn't the smartest so lot your squadmates deaths feel like the games fault rather than the players. Still these are minor gripes and the game is perfectly playable and enjoyable, even on harder difficulties. 


[h3] Story and setting [/h3]

The story is quite good, if you have played the previous entries. By itself it really doesn't stand on its own. The setting has been done to death at this point so it's hard to be impressed. In fact I don't know if the writers missed it during their research but there are other US divisions than 101 and 82 - many of them have done equally impressive things. The writers clearly have some talent so it would have been nice if they gave a try to idk Italy, Africa, British in Burma, or just any heck even other divisions from XVII Airborne corps.

[h3] Missions [/h3]

There are some 9 missions in the game. Most set it Neatherland countryside or small cities. Each one is fairly linear - with just enough sidepaths to enable the gameplay loop - suppressive fire and flanking. As for objectives they aren't anything special -  but given the story anything more special would feel out of place. You play as 101s not some super special forces operating deep behind enemy lines. So we get standard WW2 mix of shooting and disabling tanks/flaks. If the game was longer - currently it takes some 7 hours on harder difficulty, maybe 5 if you run on a easier ones - I guess it would get stale.  But the gameplay loop has enough substance to make even these generic levels feel interesting for the whole runtime.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

If you are in a market for WW2 shooter and don't strictly want a one man army experience give it a try. Also don't bother checking out older titles. Sure the story will suffer but the gameplay here is so much better representation of what the devs wanted to achieve it's almost uncomparable.

Stumbling upon this game in 2025 was not something I expected to do on the PC, but I'm glad it rang across my brain all the same. Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway was a great (but incomplete) leap forward for the World War 2 tactical shooter that both feels very well ahead of its time and scratches an itch that's been missing in modern gaming, while also showing a few hiccups that sadly held it back from being an all-timer.

Sergeant Matthew Baker leads a squad of 101st Airborne soldiers through Operation Market Garden, an ambitious failed attempt by the Allied forces during World War II to push through the Rhine River into Germany to end the war by Christmas 1944. It was by all accounts a disaster due to heavier-than-expected resistance by the Germans, supply shortages, bad intelligence and communication failures, and the difficulty of maintaining supply lines over a country with barely any real roads to facilitate the endeavor. One of the biggest reasons the series stands out as a whole against its competitors of its day was giving a great, comprehensive look into the tales of the 101st and their struggles with the war. Baker and his men feel human and share a sense of dread, laugh with each other, and fight like a real military unit would during a doomed invasion. Baker, Joe "Red" Hartsock, and the rest of the crew feel straight out of Band of Brothers, and it translates to the gameplay hearing their personalities shine when they shout banter at Nazis they shoot in the face.

The game's graphics and presentation is absolutely stellar even to this day. Troy Baker's first shot at video game stardom was from this series and his performance is fantastic as is the rest of the cast. The story is tight while giving great details of the battle unfolding around them in a way that feels immersive, with a beautiful Dutch landscape that range from beautiful stone cathedrals, to reddish flames of a burning countryside, to an industrial warehouse, to fields and windmills splattered with blood. The audio design is still some of the best in gaming, with Baker screaming orders to his troops with every crack of an M1 Garand or grenade hitting you right in the chest. 

Gameplay has always been one of the standouts of the series; while Medal of Honor and Call of Duty emphasized you as the gun toting badass that would punch a hole through the chest of every goose stepper near you, Brothers in Arms drags you back down to earth to remind you that you are a soldier who will quickly be Swiss-cheesed if you try to run out in the open for too long. Being a tactical shooter, you solely control your squad and let them know whether to follow you, set up in a position near cover, attack an enemy to suppress them, or now with destructible environments, blow up their cover. The friendly and enemy AI may have some hiccups (sometimes your men will refuse to find cover and get themselves shot up or run down an obviously dangerous path) but it's overall great to see in action watching an MG team spray down a small German squad for you to flank them from the sides. Each encounter goes roughly the same but it's a formula that never gets old from how you can approach it. Being a soldier who relies on your men to make it through the day is the best part of the series and one that makes you care about the soldiers you fight with.

Which is why it's a massive bummer when the game itself forgets this for some reason and makes you fight solo in many sections of the game. The game's controls and shooting mechanics are fine enough on their own, but the game is clearly made for squad based approaches. Its attempts to be a solo shooter for Baker always feel completely out of place and in terms of the plot aside from the hospital mission, nonsensical. Thankfully, the tank sections of the game control very well and feel exhilarating at times as a break from the boots on the ground action. 

I do absolutely recommend the game, and at $10 for it, the 5-6 hours it takes to complete it are a great easy thrill ride. It might be on the shorter side sadly, but the action, story, graphics, and pacing are all top notch.
