"What is it that makes a great soldier? Is it his brain? Or his heart?"

These are the words spoken by Sergeant Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division, and one of the iconic protaganists of the Brothers in Arms franchise. Brothers in Arms, as i've stated before in my previous reviews, is my favorite WW2 themed franchise; and with good reason. But Hell's Highway is it's own seperate animal. While retaining the core story, characters, and features that the series is known for, Hell's Highway takes the traditional BIA formula, and injects it with steroids. Everything the previous games did right, this game does it better. But, it's not my personal favorite in the series. That title belongs to Earned in Blood. The reason for that is because Hell's Highway has a few strange design choices, and nitpicks that hold it back from being my go-to. That being said, overall, I think Hell's Highway IS the best when compared to the rest of the franchise. Just not my favorite. But, enough beating around the bush. Let's get into it, shall we?

Story: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is set in the midst of Operation: Market Garden. The massive air and land invasion of Nazi-occupied Holland of which the end goal was to liberate the Netherlands, break through to Germany, and end the war before Christmas. However, due to the overconfidence of some Allied commanders that the Germans were on the verge of collapse lead to them overextending the Allied elements, and eventually to the failure of the operation. In Hell's Highway, you take on the role of Sgt. Matt Baker. A platoon sergeant in the US Army's 101st Airborne Division that takes part in the airborne side of the invasion (obviously). Baker finds himself in a tough spot at the outset of the game. Due to all of the casualties taken and friends lost during D-Day, the company has taken on many new uppity replacements. Those that survived the initial invasion are obviously a bit urked by how excited the newbies are for combat, and thus, Baker, as a platoon leader, must try to convey some sense of order. After the company settles with it's compatriots, it's time for the real deal. You'll be travelling to many locations throughout Hell's Highway. From the colorful and vibrant Holland countryside, to the bombed out ruins of war-torn cities. All the while coping with the sorrow and guilt of those that we've lost thus far. Hell's Highway's story is second-to-none in the realm of WW2 shooters, even today. Rivaling that of the HBO series Band of Brothers if followed across all three installments. That should tell you all you need to know if you're asking if the story's any good.

Graphics: Hell's Highway is an absolutely beautiful game, even by today's standards. The vibrant colors, overall fidelity, and lighting are stunning when looking at the time the game was released. Visual feedback and most animations are good as well, though there are some that could do with some improvement. Overall, there's not much to complain about on the graphical side of things.

Sound: Hell's Highway's sound design is well above average, i'd say. It's a definite improvement from the previous installments, but some weapon sounds could certainly stand for some improvements. The MG-42, for example still retains that downright annoying Hollywood stock machine gun sound. It sounds more like a broken chainsaw belt than the menacing "Hitler's Buzzsaw" that we all know. But, that's more of a nitpick than anything. Voice acting is great, as always in BIA. And they actually added more explosion sounds this time around! Overall, sound design is good. If you're not a stickler for it, there's not much to hate.

Gameplay: Now we're getting into the meat and potatoes of it. Gameplay is, by far the catagory that Hell's Highway stands out in. It's been completely revamped and streamlined for 7th gen, and it's a monumental improvement from previous installments. The "feature" where your character waves his weapon around like a cracked out zombie has been completely removed, the movement system is much more fluid with the addition of a sprint function, and the ability to jump and vault over walls, and with the addition of a sticky cover system, you'll no longer have to worry about having to run all the way across an open field just to hide behind a conveniently placed rise in the dirt. Additionaly, new weapons have been added, and many have been improved. The franchise's staple feature, the squad command mode has also been reworked and streamlined to be much more useful. This combined with some greatly improved level design results in the game being fun, and makes the player feel as though they're making progress, and not just going from firefight to firefight. Overall, the gameplay in Hell's Highway's the best it's been in the franchise, hands down.

Conclusion: Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a great game. And a great BIA game at that. As I said before, it's my personal belief that Hell's Highway is the best in the series from an "everything included" point of view. Just not my personal true favorite. It more than earns the title of "cult classic" in my opinion. And is one of the best WW2 shooters out there. If you're looking for gritty, emotional, blood-soaked rollercoaster of a WW2 game, you can't go wrong.

Final Score: 9/10

Hell's Highway feels a full generation away from it's predecessors - the graphics are vastly improved and the tech can finally tell the story with all the drama and tension that they've been aiming for since the beginning. 

It also feels like a new generation in terms of the fact that a lot of the gameplay has been streamlined (grenade throwing has been tightened up, thank god), and, in my opinion, these changes have made the game easier. The new appearance of OP weapons like the bazooka team and the player-controlled tank make it a cakewalk to mop up whole squads of enemies in one shot. Your Thompson is also replaced early on with a barrel-cartridge tommy gun that feels like it never runs out of ammo. You can, with relative ease, stand back and pick off enemies from afar with the new cover system that allows you to peek around corners and focus your fire, and if you do happen to flank the enemy, often they'll stand straight up and into your squadmates' gunfire, dying in seconds. All these additions detract from the immersion, and make the game feel a little more arcadey, even thought the core gamplay mechanics are nearly identical to the previous games. All in all, this game feels much more polished and fancy, but loses some of the pulse-pounding, gritty tension of knowing that even if you're prepared, bum-rushing that dug-in squad could get you killed.

The one thing this does best is make you feel. By the last levels of the game, you'll almost want to stop playing, and the push through burning wreckages and sand dunes, being harried by multiple enemy squads, will feel dreadful, but you know that you have to keep pushing through in order to complete the mission, which is exactly how the characters feel. The narrative continues the story of Matt Baker, who is experiencing some deep PTSD/mental illness. It's incredibly bleak all the way through, and centres around a specific and almost rushed-through moment in the original game, which is retroactively filled out to fantastic effect for the player, explaining the actions of some of the characters all the way through the series. There is a subplot about a cursed weapon that it also tries to retrofit, but this doesn't stick quite as well. 

So that's it - I've played all three games in the series, one after the other, in the space of a couple of weeks. [h1] "What is it that makes a great soldier? His brain or his heart?" - Sergeant Matthew 'Matt' Baker [/h1]

[b]Introduction[/b]
In Brothers In Arms: Hell's Highway you are playing as Staff Sergeant Matthew Baker also known as Matt. You are leading your men through Holland during [i][b]Operation Market Garden[/b][/i], an Operation that had the idea of punching through the German lines in order to open a highway to give a quick end to the war and be home by Christmass.
After Normandy (First 2 BiA games), Baker's platoon is folded into a brand new Reconnaissance platoon. 

[b]Gameplay[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Movement[/b] - Movement animations are great and realistic. Whether you are walking, running or getting behind cover it feels like you are really in the battlefield.

[*][b]Engaging An Enemy[/b] - Your squad has two modes of engagement. If the Squad is in stealth mod, which means the enemy didn't notice them they would move quietly, whisper and would not engage the enemy unless you order them to unless discovered your location which is when they switch to the other mod where they will open fire at engaging enemies even if you won't order them to.

[*][b]Grenades & Explosives[/b] - Your squad will throw grenades at an enemy if they are close enough. [b]The enemy will never throw a grenade at your squad, even tho they are equipped with grenades[/b], something which older games had featured which makes it odd. 

[*][b]Recoil[/b] - The recoil of the weapons in the game is as realistic as it gets with most weapons. Just enough to keep the game enjoyable but still making your life hard to get a kill on enemy that is far away from you.

[*][b]Tanks and 88s[/b] - Feels like the enemy tanks and 88s are just waiting for you to destroy them. No huge effort is in order to destroy them unlike in older games where you needed to strategise your approach to 88s and tank positions in order to take them out or you would get your ass kicked. 

[*][b]Sounds[/b] - The game has awesome sounds when it comes to the weapons and the ambient sounds that sorround you.

[*][b]Destroy Em![/b] - Plus, unlike the first two games, in this game you can actually destroy objects. For example you can destroy sorts of covers and get your enemy out in the open and kill them.
[/list]

[b]Story line[/b]
Unlike the first two games, this game has taken the cutscenes to the next level. Almost feels like you are watching a movie.The game has great writing. The cutscenes are adding a lot to the game and to the emotions you feel while playing it. Almost feels like you are there with Baker. The dialogues during combat are amusing and at the same time feel real. Unlike in other games where when your teammates die you don't feel anything because they were 'Badass', here you are connected to the characters, you care for them and you are concerned about them during battles. When a fellow team mate gets killed, it feels like someone has just kicked you in the stomach and it brings up feelings, almost to tears at some points. In addition to what I said, in this game Baker suffers from guilt as a result of the deaths of his friends during the battles in Normandy and you can see its affect on him through out the game. The locations of fights in the game are re-created real battles that took place in the real world, they were worked on by the developers team and historians to make the game more authentic and realistic.  

[b]Graphics[/b]
The game has amazing graphics. The areas that surround you in the game are just beautiful and mind blowing at the same time. The uniforms of Allied and Wehrmacht soldiers are just beautiful to look at, the weapons look authentic and more. There are beautiful locations in alot of occasions in the game.

[b]My Opinion[/b]
In my opinion the Brothers In Arms Series is the best World War 2 series to exist. Its the most authentic world war 2 series and most realistic. It has great game-play and story-line and brings a lot of features that other games don't. No other game made me care for my team like Brothers In Arms did. I am still waiting for Brothers In Arms: Battle Of The Bulge, or what ever the name of the next Brothers In Arms is going to be.

[b] Tips for game-play: [/b] 

1)Play the game without suppression bars or any other kind of miscs on your screen;
While playing with a clean screen you can enjoy the game way more than you thought you could. Playing with a clean screen gives you the feeling you are really there in the battlefield, ordering your men.

*You will need to remember where you placed each squad and what's the role of each firing team when you order them to move because it won't tell you which firing team you chose on the screen. You might wanna know who are the soldiers of each team before you order them around so in the battlefield you will remember by that which squad is located where and move them around correctly.

*You will need to keep an eye on your fire, yeah I know hammering the enemy is fun but when you don't know how much bullets you have left in the magazine or if you have extra bullets if at all you might run into some trouble in a battle - yeah running out of bullets in-front of a German firing squad is not a great idea nor fun.

2) Play the game on authentic. Playing the Brothers In Arms series on Authentic gives you the real feeling of the battlefield. It gives you the best out of this game. Every small move, decision or order can be critical in a battle. It also disables all I said above(miscs, etc) on default because of the exact same reasons I pointed out earlier. You need to be super strategic and careful when you move your men and yourself. Stay in the open for to long and you might find yourself dead, injured or losing men. 

Thanks for reading my review.

I was in the mood for a world war 2 shooter, since nowadays those are surprisingly rare. I read reviews on Steam and Metacritic to see what was popular and Hell's Highway came up.

After beating the game I am still not entirely sure if the game deserves a recommendation or not.

For starters, the game has some glaring errors in historical accuracy, such as German 88's firing at Sherman tanks at point blank range and failing to penetrate or a single such Sherman tank rolling through hundreds of men, tanks and 88's (for some reason there are no other antitank guns in this game, just the 88 anti-air -guns) with ease. 

The graphics (originally designed for the Xbox 360) are obviously dated, with character models warping and distorting uncomfortably and facial animation all but missing entirely. The voice acting is lackluster to say the least, ambients sounds are often missing, weapons sound muted and dull and even the music seems to be oddly off-key in few points (though this part might just be my lack of knowledge showing through). All in all, the game's audiovisual presentation is pretty terrible. Even the ragdoll physics are glitchy as heck (I shot a german soldier in the head and he jumped 50 meters in the air as he died)!

So far, then, this seems like a no-brainer: an ugly game with bad audiovisual design through and through.

And then we get to the gameplay, and here I find myself intrigued. You are acting as a squad leader for most of the game, and that means you cannot just charge the enemy Call of Duty -style, but have to order around your fireteams (up to three at a time, ranging from machine gun team to base of fire team to bazooka team to assault team), setting them up in cover, assigning them targets to suppress and maneuvering them to outflank the enemy. The levels offer a sometimes surprising amount of freedom in how much you can maneuver and the system feels surprisingly good most of the time. I especially enjoyed the frantic tension of emerging into a new area only to observe a german squad marching across a field, ordering my men into position and then watching the enemy spread out into cover as the shooting starts. The enemy AI is also surprisingly good, acting surprised where appropriate, falling back and regrouping into better positions as they are overrun our outflanked and generally putting up a good fight.

And then the game shoots itself in the foot again. Several times I had the AI completely glitch out, with my machinegun team or bazooka team simply freezing in place and refusing to move, getting stuck in walls or cover and such. The game hands you a sniper rifle on a few occasions, which immediately results in you, single handedly, gunning down literally dozens of germans within a minute or two, utterly breaking any immersion the game might have had so far. The tone of the game is all over the place, and then, in the end credits, comes the final straw. The story ends on a minor cliffhanger with "To Be Continued" -emblazoned on the screen. This game came out in 2008. I played it in 2016. There are no sequels, and likely never will be.

Game Over.

This game is pretty fun and not as much of a b-list game, as I expected for the price.  This is a fairly linear, old-school WW2 shooter, with a cool squad factor.  Beware of have far away you are and the path a squad might take though.  I've had them basically commit suicide by running through enemy lines, rather than behind something.

You are part of a glider team that lands in Holland sometime after D-day, and basically have to move forward and  clear out a lot of Nazis.  There is also an interesting back-story that unfolds, involving the main character's engraved .45 pistol.

As far as the game mechanics they are pretty much what you would expect with standard motions, weapons and shooting.  Strangely, there is no jumping, except for valting over a cover item.  If the game  recognizes an item as cover you can also vault it.

As far as the cover,  pressing Q benind a solid wall or other solid item like vehicles will put you in  in a temporary 3rd person cover mode, and you are crouched behind the cover item.  Using the arrows allows you to  move behind the cover or lean out to shoot.  This mode also give you a a much finer cross-hair for aiming, and a much steadier aim.   This is kind of  cool, but also has a  drawback, as you can' t control how far you lean out (or up if behind a wall).  So when shooting from cover you have to expose yourself to multiple enemies.   The method is to take fire until the view is starting to get pretty red, then go back into cover before dying-- and hopefully killing a Nazi or two in the process.  This is a little lame and would be much better if you could lean just enough to sight in on a single enemy, depending on the positioning.

Another really lame thing is that when sprinting you can't change direction very much with the mouse.  You can use A and D keys to kind of swerve--, but you basically have to stop sprinting to make a normal turn.  This is very weird to get used to, and I can't imagine what the  developers were thinking. Another weirdness is that while in cover and being flanked it is easy to get "stuck" to the cover.  The only way to get off is to move directly backwards, and that is easy to  forget when under fire.

Still, in spite of these negatives, this is a pretty fun game, especially for the price.

If you think you would like an old-school, ww2, squad shooter with a decent story then skip a fast-food lunch and you'll have the cash for this game.  Bon Appetit.

It's a good game - a strong example of a squad-based shooter. You control the position and focus of 1-3 fireteams, edging your way through battlefields to flank enemies and progress through linear levels. It encourages you to leverage your fireteams because your own weapons are unreliable to the extreme - on par with Counter-strike accuracy. Bullets spray for no particular reason, shots that are dead-on don't always register, and enemies take many shots to take down. While that's frustrating, it highlights that you are not a pure badass. Sure you may mow down hundreds of enemies in a playthrough, but ultimately it tries to knock you down to size with it's iffy gun mechanics - you need to use your squad to succeed. And while it is frustrating to not be rewarded for your own skill, i can understand that sloppy controls make you rely on your squad more.

It also seems to want to be Band of Brothers, the TV show. The game spends an enormous amount of time showing wooden characters (some of which are obviously derived from Band of Brothers characters, one of which even shares a voice actor) talking to each other about the war and each other. It spins narratives about cursed guns and lost loves which have exactly nothing to do with the game. The first ten minutes (not an exaggeration) is a series of unskippable cutscenes that awkwardly introduce a set of characters which it clearly wants you to be invested in. It keeps introducing new characters who have small quirks and different voice actors, but whom you really don't care about. When it kills off or maims a character, you're clearly expected to care, but there's no *reason* to care; the gameplay (controlling the position and focus of 1-3 fireteams) is identical no matter which characters are involved, and you're aways given replacements who are exactly as capable. Cutscene after cutscene is used, even with "shaky-cam" effects and close-ups of expressionless faces. It's all the more frustrating because this came out a year after Bioshock, a game which is almost purely story-driven, uses the same engine, and yet falls into none of the gameplay or storytelling pitfalls that this game does.

Ultimately, it's a fun game that executes a squad shooter very well, despite the flaws. I'd recommend it if you're certain you want a squad shooter, and wouldn't recommend it for any other reason.

Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway was an amazing experience and an example on what modern military shooters should do nowadays, yes, looking at you, Call of Duty and Battlefield. At thing which bugs me about modern shooters is that every single one of them has its focus on the repetitive multiplayer where as today most of them play essentially the same, just as the campaign. 

We need more games like Hell's Highway which are not glorifying war but show the human side the soldiers have instead of how many times they can yell "♥♥♥♥ YEAH, AMERICA!" while pulling out the flamethrower to "burn them, burn them all!!!"

The men you fight along in Hell's Highway feel human and just as in the older Brother's in Arms games, the main focus lies in the single player. If you want to buy this game for a killstreak loaded multi player to "pwn scrubs", you are wrong here.

A roughly about 10 hours long campaign (I played on Veteran difficulty)  will keep you motivated with a nice tactical component to command different squads such as the MG squad or the assault team as Matthew Baker, to surpress the enemy and use the element of surprise to flank clueless and somtimes dumb acting enemy soldiers. The commanding barely gets old and as you hop around different hubs of the hot areas during the war. Those range from wide fields to close battles in troubled cities and villages as well as asylums and collapsed buildings.

The thing which does get a little repetitive are the objectives you have to achieve using those methods of commanding. Most of the time you find yourself having to destroy 88 cannons and sometimes drive a tank around in which you are mostly safe even on the higher difficulties. Really annoying did those things only become in the end to me, as the game finally came to a closing, during the last hour of gameplay. The story itself kept motivating as protagonist Matthew Baker's mind started to crumble and he realized more and more and war is insanity. 
The "To Be Continued" in the end was a huge bummer to me though, especially because Ubisoft doesn't seem to care at all about this amazing series which could definetly standout amongst "Call of Boredom" or the recent development of the"Battlefail" games.

Also the sound design is great and as the bullets fly over your head  in cover and the enemies speaking correct German, which is a rare thing to see to be honest. The atmosphere is really great and makes you feel as if this was an episode of the critically acclaimed "Band of Brothers"-TV show. The developers really did a great job in capturing an unique and equally terrifying experience.

Overall Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway is a technically and gameplay wise far from flawless but also an unique and tactical game which definetly gets a recommendation for me, even if solely for the atmosphere and the long campaign.

Grab this game if you are sick of modern shooters and/or glorification of war.

Cover, destructible levels, multi-squad command, air recon, the map replacing SA view, sprinting, and the kill-cam all fit right into Brothers in Arms and don't make the game lose its identity at all. The levels are bigger and better than anything seen before, and the enemy AI is as great as it ever was. Other than that, this game is an improvement over the originals in every way.

Hell's Highway is a game with a solid gameplay experience, an interesting narrative, and some glaring faults.

As a direct sequel to the first game in the Brothers in Arms series Hell's Highway follows newly-promoted Staff Sergeant Matt Baker and his unit  through the Netherlands during Operation Market Garden. Baker's sanity wanes due to the contention of his men, rumors of a haunted pistol, and the memories of friends lost. 

The combat in HH holds to the tradition of the earlier titles in the series, while adding additional squads and features. Flanking and diversionary tactics are vital, as running into the open while an enemy fires upon Baker or his squad will result in a quick death.

However, Hell's Highway is a game that needs some fixing to enjoy. For anyone like myself who gets headaches or feels sick at a lower field of view, here's different methods of how to counter the horrid default setting.


--------------
Method 1: 
A simple binding to toggle the fov. This will change the fov when pressed, but will zoom out cutscenes, break sniper scopes, and disable zooming in when aiming.

Go to your "Documents\My Games\BIA Hells Highway\SumacGame\Config" folder and open "SumacInput.ini" in a text editor. 
under the"[Engine.PlayerInput]" section add the following.

Bindings=(Name="KEY",Command="fov DESIREDFOV",Control=False,Shift=False,Alt=False)


Method 2: 
Changing the action of the zoom hold command to change the fov. The fov will lower when aiming to zoom in, then zoom out to your desired standard fov on release. This will also zoom out cutscenes and break sniper scopes. I suggest a zoom fov of 60, and a standard fov of 100.

Under "[Engine.InputActionDefinition]" in SumacInput.ini look for the line that starts with "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias...".
Change the line to, "Actions=(Id=IA_ZoomHold,Alias=".ZOOMHOLD",Names=("Zoom"),Command="ZoomIn | fov DESIREDZOOMFOV | OnRelease ZoomOut | OnRelease DESIRED DEFAULT FOV")"

Other tips:
Creating a bind similar to the bind shown in method 1 set to "fov 63" will set cutscenes close to what they look like normally.

In the "[SystemSettings]" section of "SumacEngine.ini" you can pump up the graphics. I suggest setting "EnableHighPolyChars=False" to "True" and fiddling around with the MSAA.

A First Person Shooter with an actual storyline!    Not only do you get a fantastic shooter (with some very smart AI) but the storyline here was absolutely fantastic!  One of my favorite FPS!

No need to worry, while this is a sequel, this game is very welcoming to newcomers, offering a "Previously" cluster of scenes, summarizing the events of the prior games in the series.

Continuing the epic story of the two previous Brothers in Arms games, Hell's Highway puts you back into the combat boots of Sgt. Matt Baker to blow some Nazi heads off. Using Unreal 3 and new cover-combat with your cover being shredded before your very eyes, this game looks and runs amazingly. If you like World War II shooters and/or tactical first-person shooters, then you will enjoy this game. With the intensity of WWII, commanding small squadrons, the power of firearms, the vulnerability against firearms, and the cinematic shots of the final opponent being blown up or shot in the head is an incredible experience that closely relates to the HBO series: Band of Brothers.

If you like action, drama, WWII experiences, tactical combat, challenging first-person shooters, and captivating stories, then look no further than Brothers in Arms: Hell's Highway.

But the game ends on a freaking cliff-hanger! WHERE'S THE SEQUEL, RANDY?!

The whole BIA series is definitely worth a look if you are into first person tactical shooters.  You command a squad of soldiers during WWII in a series of engagements, wrapped in a story thats told welll with excellent voice acting.  It feels more like interactive drama, which for me is a good thing.  If you are into the story aspect of the game, you should consider starting with RTH40, the EIB, then this title.  HH is a big graphical leap forward and a joy to play.  Recommend the whole series.

If you have played the previous brothers in arms then this one will be a treat for you. It brings in the other stories from the previous ones and puts them all together in this one. It has gameplay that can get repetitive after awhile until you learn how to flank your enemy. You are in command of a squad the through the game and you have to direct them in a way that wont get them or you killed. You use strategy and timing to kill the enemy. The story was impressive. The graphics were very well done and great to look at. The cut-scenes were long and enjoyable to watch. The Multiplayer is still active but very small. The game is very well done and I really enjoyed it all the way to the end. If your into FPS and enjoyed the previous Brothers in arms then dont pass this one up when you see it on sale. It was awesome for me and I know you'll enjoy it too.

Gearbox Software is well known for putting out quality work. This game is no exception. Although the game mechanics are visibly older, it is a decent squad based FPS set in the WWII era. The story is quite immersive focusing on the bonding of individuals and the simple realities of war. The enemy AI forces you to use tactics and strategy versus just running and gunning. With a package price of $10 for all three titles, it is a good value.

The controls can be a bit clunky, but once you're used to commanding the squads, it's quite atmospheric. Story is a tad better than we're used in these generic WWII stories. Everything has an authentic feel.

This game was better than I thought.
The whole squad control thing didnt interest me at first, but the way you control your 1-3 units is just a two button execution. One to toggle between the teams and one to execute a order which are dynamic depending on what you are looking at. If you aim at cover, they move there, if you aim at enemies they shoot and if they are close enough they will use hand granades as well. 

Suppress, advance, flank and kill is the most common tactic. Every enemy has a icon over their general location which makes giving orders easy. While the enemy icon is red, they are a threat and can easly shoot you. If the icon are gray, they are supressed and you have a easier time advancing... and so on.

The gameplay is great, fun and works fine. The story is trying to be like the HBO series Band of Brothers, but considering the shorter time a game has to tell such a story it becomes very cheesy.

I would recommend it if it goes on sale again.

The game had a lot of potential. The map is beautiful and captures the feeling of Bolivia, with a wide variety of memorable locations that make the world feel immersive and realistic. One standout feature is how each underboss is introduced and concluded with well made cinematic videos that were a great touch.

The shooting mechanics are also very solid. Gunplay feels realistic, aiming down sights in first person gives off strong R6 Siege vibes, which I really enjoyed. The combat difficulty can also be satisfying, if you get surrounded by two or more enemies, you can go down quickly, which adds tension and makes combat more engaging.

Unfortunately, thats where the positives end.

The biggest issue and the reason for my negative review is the NAT status problem. My friend and I have played 30-40 coop games together without issues, but in this game it was a nightmare. Everything worked fine when we were in our hometown, but as soon as we tried playing from another city, the NAT status became inconsistent, switching between Open and Moderate and no matter what we tried, we simply couldnt connect to the same session. This completely ruined the coop experience for us.

On top of that, the game physics are very unrealistic. Vehicles handle poorly in terms of realism. You can drive at high speeds over rocks, downhill, or even through rivers with almost no difference compared to driving on a paved road. It completely breaks immersion.

Character animations and voice acting are also disappointing. They feel dull and generic, similar to many Ubisoft titles and none of the characters are memorable. I doubt I will remember any of them after finishing the game.

And speaking of finishing the game, we cant even do that the way we want. Due to the connection issues, we are only able to play when we are both in our hometown, which makes no sense. It feels like a strange hybrid between online and couch coop, and honestly, its just embarrassing.

While Steam’s automatic refund system denies requests made more than 14 days after purchase, you may have a legal basis to pursue a refund for a game that does not work on modern computers, particularly if it was advertised as functional. However, individual lawsuits are generally impractical, and legal avenues often involve consumer protection agencies or class action, rather than small claims court. 

Legal Basis and Arguments
Breach of Contract/Implied Warranty: A product sold must be fit for its intended purpose. If a game is sold on Steam, there is an implied contract that it will function on a reasonable, modern operating system. Selling a game that cannot run on modern hardware without declaring it in the system requirements can be seen as a breach of this contract.

False Advertising/Misleading Practices: If the store page explicitly states the game works on Windows 10/11, or fails to disclose that it requires complex community fixes to run, it could violate consumer protection laws.
Misleading Advertising: If the game is advertised as having functioning features (e.g., multiplayer) that are non-functional, this is a stronger case for deception.

Ghost Recon Wildlands puts you in Bolivia and sets the environment up into a big open world map with a ton of outposts/bases full of cartel and military enemies, and repeatable side missions scattered throughout. You get a glimpse into the full game early on and the game is much easier with AI teammates. One of my main complaints about the game is how over powered the AI are. On the higher difficulties, the AI will kill you almost instantly once you are in their line of sight, that's why going for a stealth approach is so important, because once you get spotted, you're pretty much screwed unless you know how to use the additional tools the game gives you. The game's tier one mode (which is like a prestige system for the campaign), will eventually set the game to the highest difficulty too. 

I will warn anyone buying this game, you WILL get frustrated at times, because of things like; AI that can shoot you through a wall, getting spotted instantly by enemies, a helicopter crashing on you or having to restart a mission from the start.

Overall, for me, it's one of those games where if there was a "mixed" button i would have chose that. The game would just be a bit better if some things were ironed out, like the overpowered AI, more checkpoints in missions and more variety in activities. Ultimately though, i think this game is worth the time.

These aspects, and many others, sound good on paper, but once you sink 15-20hrs into this game you begin to see that all them have drawbacks that ultimately left me feeling meh about them. Only pure negative is the campaign. While absolutely chock full of content it's a brutal gameplay loop of interrogate what's-his-face, destroy cache of supplies or drugs, kill boss, then next region.

Biggest thing that left me conflicted is Tier 1 mode; basically, prestige mode. Once you reach max lvl 30, you can begin Tier 1 where you work from tier 50 up to tier 1 while the game gets progressively more difficult. The AI doesn't become smarter tho, they just become flat out OP. It eventually takes an entire mag to drop one guy in a white tank top with no armor. Their aim is laser and their TTK against you is legit two shots. Cartel weren't horrible but holy crap was Unidad a nightmare in this mode. Add onto that a bug in some missions where some enemies continuously respawn and you'll lose about 45min of progress if you're not perfectly stealth. And the cherry on top is you can completely cheese Tier 1 by turning it off during the mission, making the game easier, then turn it back on right before you finish said mission. Only XP you're missing out on is kills, intel, and spotting.

So yeah, overall fantastic first 10hrs, rough 20-30hr mark, frustrating slog 40hrs+. On sale? Why not. Base price? Nope

GAMEPLAY
If you want something to play while watching a streamer, listening to a podcast, or rewatching a show, Ghost Recon: Wildlands is fine. If you wanted to play a game that will do something interesting with its mechanics or tell you a story worth paying attention to, do literally anything else with your time. The only reason I even put the time in to finish this is that I have a high tolerance for monotonous gameplay as long as its basic functions are decent. 

The only aspect of this game that makes it stand out compared to other first person shooters is it’s environment. It genuinely showcases a wide variety of unique landscapes, terrains, and aesthetics that highlight the beauty of Bolivia. Sadly the only thing it can think to do with that environment is populate it with thousands of identical, bald, tattooed men in white wife beaters. 



TECHNICAL/PERFORMANCE
The game won’t work if you don’t have ubisoft’s terrible DRM software installed and running in the background the entire time. But it doesn’t make this clear, so instead it will likely just refuse to launch until you fix that. 
Even after I did this it still wouldn’t launch and I had to look online for other users help with troubleshooting because ubisoft is incapable of being helpful. I ended up having to ‘repair’ the installations of every C++ library installed on my PC and then it finally launched.



STORY 
This game is some of the clumsiest and laziest propaganda I’ve ever seen. You play as four members of the US Army who enter Bolivia to wage a war against a drug cartel and the military police force that has turned a blind eye to them, in a country in which you have no jurisdiction or right to operate.

You work with the local rebels to fight the cartel, which actually means feeding them into the woodchipper, sometimes using an ability that specifically calls them in as an explicitly expendable distraction.

The game is so unwilling to cause friction in its gameplay that it is willing to toss any sense of narrative under the bus to avoid it. A great example of this is how the missions which involve you taking out supply convoys and marking them for the rebels allow you to blow up everything in the convoy and just chuck a GPS tracker on the burnt out remains, as though you actually accomplished something productive for them.

Killing civilians results in little more than your teammate calling you juvenile names and slapping you on the wrist. The game warns you that killing civilians will cause you to fail missions, but I have had instances where I accidentally killed several in separate, but back-to-back instances and the game was never willing to actually follow through and punish me for my recklessness.

There is a mission in which you are searching for the General in charge of La Unidad, the military police outfit formed in response to the cartel. To arrange a meeting with him, you are sent to find his daughter and coerce her into contacting him. On the way to find her, my character talked with his squadmates about how they were upset with their handler telling them to use an innocent woman as leverage. 

Then when I turn up, she is inside a school building with half a dozen children still in the class with her. I got the feeling that this may be a moment when the game may finally say something interesting about how the actions of my character are brutal, illegal, and that the vague gesturing towards helping the Bolivian people is nothing more than a façade to justify violence that serves geopolitical goals. 

But no. The only way to progress is to grab her and hold a gun to her head to “Interrogate” her the same way you have to dozens of others throughout the game. The difference being that the other people where all armed criminals involved in drug and/or human trafficking who try to shoot you on sight, but she is an unarmed civilian in the middle of teaching kids that look no older than 12.

The game specifically points out that this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and has my character voice a displeasure with being asked to do it. But the developers couldn’t be bothered to actually write anything meaningfully critical of these actions, so you just continue being terrible people while unironically referring to yourselves as the ‘good guys’.
And I’m not kidding on that last point. When killing enemies your squad mates will routinely make comments like “one less bad guy”. I’m hesitant to call them characters, but the characters in this game genuinely feel like they were written by 14 year old boys.



TLDR: This game is at best; repetitive slop and at worst; jingoistic propaganda written by people who’s understanding of morality is less complex than most children’s.

I absolutely love Ghost Recon Wildlands because it delivers one of the most immersive and flexible open-world tactical shooter experiences I have ever played. The game places you in a massive version of Bolivia controlled by the Santa Blanca cartel, and the main objective is to dismantle the cartel piece by piece by targeting its different branches and leaders. What makes the game incredible is the freedom it gives the player. Missions such as rescuing Amaru, investigating La Yuri and El Polito, tracking targets like El Cerebro, La Santera, El Pulpo, El Cardenal, and pushing through the cartel’s security forces like El Muro all feel unique because there is rarely only one way to complete them. You can infiltrate bases silently with suppressed weapons, coordinate synchronized shots with your squad, scout enemies with drones, or simply storm a compound with helicopters and heavy weapons. The progression system where you weaken production, influence, security, and smuggling operations makes the story feel like you are slowly collapsing an entire criminal empire. The world design is also one of the game’s biggest strengths, with deserts, jungles, mountains, villages, and cartel-controlled territories that make exploring Bolivia incredibly enjoyable.

Another thing that makes Wildlands stand out is the tactical gameplay and squad mechanics. Even when playing solo, the AI teammates feel like a real special forces unit because they help mark enemies, perform synchronized kills, and support you during firefights. Flying helicopters across the massive map, scouting enemy bases with drones, and planning stealth approaches made the experience extremely memorable for me, and I spent a huge amount of time simply exploring the map and clearing outposts. Of course, the game does have a few glitches; for example, during the final mission against El Sueño, it is sometimes possible to dodge missiles by aggressively maneuvering a helicopter, which makes certain moments easier than intended. There are also occasional AI or vehicle bugs, but they rarely break the experience and often end up being funny rather than frustrating. Overall, despite these minor issues, Ghost Recon Wildlands remains one of the best open-world tactical shooters ever made, and for me it is a game that perfectly balances freedom, strategy, exploration, and action, making it one of my personal favorite games.

Repetitive Missions and Weak Narrative: The main missions are highly repetitive, often consisting of nearly identical objectives that fail to challenge or engage the player. Combined with a shallow and poorly structured narrative, the campaign lacks emotional depth or sense of purpose, leaving the experience mechanical and uninspiring.

Inconsistent Enemy AI: Enemy behavior is erratic and unreliable. AI frequently fails to respond logically to player actions, either ignoring threats or overreacting without cause, undermining tactical planning and frustrating both stealth and combat engagements.

Flawed Vehicle Mechanics and Open World Design: Vehicle handling is clunky and unresponsive, particularly over rough terrain. The open world, despite its scale, is repetitive and sparsely populated, with regions that feel recycled and lacking meaningful content, making exploration tedious rather than rewarding.

Ineffective Cover and Combat Systems: The cover mechanics are unreliable, often leaving players exposed even when used correctly. Shooting controls are stiff and imprecise, while explosives and weapon physics behave inconsistently, reducing the reliability of tactics and overall combat satisfaction.

Technical Bugs and Performance Issues: Wildlands suffers from numerous bugs, mission-breaking glitches, and missing audio lines that disrupt gameplay. On PC, performance is inconsistent across systems, with frequent crashes, stuttering, and long load times, reflecting insufficient testing and optimization.

Poor Checkpoint and Fast Travel Systems: Checkpoints are poorly placed, respawning players in inconvenient locations that compromise strategy. Fast travel and mission tracking are unintuitive, forcing unnecessary backtracking and navigation challenges that detract from immersion.

Ineffective AI Teammates and Cooperative Play: AI squad members are often unhelpful or counterproductive, failing to provide meaningful support in combat. Multiplayer and co-op modes are further hindered by connectivity issues, lag, and synchronization problems, limiting the effectiveness of cooperative tactics.

Side Activities Overshadow Main Story: Side objectives dominate the open world but rarely provide meaningful engagement. This imbalance distracts from the main narrative, leaving the campaign feeling directionless and diluted.

Ubisoft’s Corporate Decisions Impact Design: The game reflects Ubisoft’s reliance on a formulaic open-world approach prioritizing scale and monetization over innovation and tactical depth. Recycled environments, predictable AI, and cosmetic-driven incentives suggest design decisions driven more by corporate metrics than player experience.

Regression in Tactical Design: Overall, Wildlands represents a significant step back for the Ghost Recon series. Tactical depth and cohesion are sacrificed for an expansive but hollow open world, leaving an experience that feels unfinished, unpolished, and ultimately less satisfying than prior entries.

Tom Clancy’s Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a tactical open-world shooter that drops players into a massive, detailed version of Bolivia dominated by the Santa Blanca drug cartel. It’s a game built around freedom of choice in how you approach missions, whether that means silent stealth operations, coordinated assaults, or full-on vehicle combat. Steam’s community rating for the game is Mostly Positive overall, with tens of thousands of positive user reviews, showing that many players enjoy what it offers.

The core strength of Wildlands lies in its co-operative multiplayer. Playing with up to three friends transforms missions into tense tactical scenarios where teamwork, planning, and communication matter. The world is large and varied, with diverse environments to explore and multiple ways to tackle objectives.

Customization is another high point. You can tailor your character’s gear and weapons to fit your playstyle, enhancing the sense that you are building your own elite Ghost operative. Vehicles play a big role too, with dozens available to traverse the terrain by land, air, and sea.

However, the game has some trade-offs. Some missions and enemy placements can feel repetitive, and the solo experience isn’t as satisfying as co-op for many players. You’ll also need a Ubisoft account linked to Steam to play, which can sometimes complicate launch or connectivity for some users.

This game looks beautiful and plays well.  There are hours upon hours of content in it and it entertains throughout.

That isn't to say that the game isn't without faults.  Audio barks are far too consistent, particularly with the enemies; no variations in either what they say or who says it.  The gameplay loop is fairly standard ... travel to a new area, do some light intel gathering, go to a particular area to gather materials / do a mission / unlock equipment, scout the area for badguys then have your team pick them off one by one, until you either screw up, your team makes a sound in some way, or you manage to clear them all without issue ... do what you came to do then ... repeat.  Bases have different layouts but are immediately forgettable so while it technically is different each time, it doesn't feel like it.

Further for a game that lays in heavily on stealth, it certainly makes it hard to be stealthy.  You can be lying down in the grass far off the road and a vehicle will drive by and the driver will spot you.  Characters VERY quickly detect your presence even from behind.  Enemies have a supernatural ability to know exactly where a single sniper round from several hundred meters away originated from and will hone in on that area.

It's almost as if the devs wanted the characters NOT to be stealthy so as to have high action combat ... but then not equip you well for that at all.  Your team doesn't really support you once you enter the 'Engaged' status (the enemy knows where you are and are shooting at you), unless you pick targets for them, which is hard when you're running and gunning.  And, even on the lowest difficulty, you can't survive long in a gunfight ... but when you go down THEN your team will sweep in, clear out a few of the guys near you, and get you back on your feet (only for one of the enemies to 'spot' you before you can get your gun up and start shooting at you again, all while your team seems to ignore them).

In that regard, it doesn't feel like there was a clear idea of where the game should land ... stealthy shooter or action gunner ... and it suffers because it feels like it doesn't do either particularly well.

Ghost Recon Wildlands feels like Ubisoft just gave you Bolivia to play with and told you to wreck a drug cartel however you want. I mean you start out as this Ghost operative and your main goal is breaking down the Santa Blanca group step by step. No big dramatic talks or anything like that its mostly about sneaking around or going loud with guns and maybe blowing up a helicopter if things get messy.

The freedom in how you approach missions is probably the best part I think. You can try to be all stealthy and quiet one time and then next thing you know its total chaos because someone messes up and alerts everyone. Like you might be coordinating perfectly with your team and suddenly youre running after a target down a hill while the convoy flips and the whole area lights up. It happens a lot especially if youre playing with friends in co op where nothing goes right but its hilarious.

Gunplay works pretty well and theres a ton of ways to customize your gear which keeps things interesting. The map has all sorts of areas too jungles and deserts mountains and those big salt flats that look amazing. You look at the map and figure okay just one more outpost to clear and before you know it hours go by youre still taking down radio towers and wondering why you cant stop.

The story is there I guess but its not super deep. It mostly just gets you to different spots to take out bad guys from far away. What really makes it fun is all the random stuff that pops up during missions that emergent chaos as people call it. In co op it seems like everything falls apart in the most funny ways possible.

Its not without problems though repetition starts to show after a while and the AI acts weird sometimes. Realism dips in places too like it takes a break now and then. Still as this big sandbox for tactics it delivers a lot of chaotic enjoyment.

The only reason to consider Wildlands superior is the chaotic and unpredictable nature of the combat. Unfortunately, the price to be paid for this chaos is that enemies spawn practically on top of you. They are not entities in the world, they are constantly appearing in a way that’s trying to convince you that it isn’t a COD type of constant spawn—though it is. Turn the difficultly up, and the randomized spawns increase. In other words, another game with idiot difficultly—instead of offering an opponent who is better at chess, you just give the opponent 8 queens to start, thereby making it difficult for you in a disingenuous way.  

Adversely, though Breakpoint uses reinforcement mechanisms for the enemy characters, they don’t randomly spawn around and behind you. They are characters who have to walk/drive/fly through the environment to get to you. Not so in Wildlands. On max difficultly, a character shoots directly at your head, then looks around and then notices you. The order of operations means that the enemies become closer to drones than human combatants.

The game runs well. The physics are good and the fighting is fun when some randomized nonsense that breaches the idea of what you’re doing doesn’t get in the way. The difficultly is because you’re fighting a simple mechanisms.

One full multiplayer playthrough and a partial singleplayer campaign rounding out at 65 hours total on extreme difficulty later, Ghost Recon Wildlands is about a 5.5/10 that I can only honestly recommend if you have a partner on hand to play this in full plus a deep sale price. In a sea of Ubisoft slop gameplay structures and general lack of polish that I can no longer stomach beyond the 4-hour mark, the fact that I was able to eliminate every Buchon and finish most of the side missions is more commendable than most. That being said, the experience is never able to transcend beyond tedious yet functional white noise, with the few outlier instances being terrible moments rather than positive ones.
Wildlands eschews most of the drawn-out hand holding and boring cutscenes present in a modern Assassins Creed or Far Cry title for a quick yet still effective opening act that acclimates players into its core gameplay loop without much issue. On a technical level, the game looks great at a glance. The environments are varied and detailed, and the open world makes great use of Bolivia’s mountainous terrain to work changing elevations into it’s gameplay. However, the urban environments are utterly flavorless and obvious copy paste jobs, and the military bases are more hit and miss. Sound design likewise is mixed. The voice acting and sounds mixing is fine enough, but gunshots lack the crackle and punch you would expect, and the vehicle noises all blend together (more on those later). Character animations are basic and stiff, and the physics engine is weak. For example, characters react to getting run over by cars the same way they do to fall damage or getting hit by an AR, and momentum on the aircraft doesn’t possess any real inertia. 
Gameplay wise, what we have here is a “babies first rainbow six tactical shooter” placed in a MGSV-lite open environment. There are ostensibly multiple paths to complete a mission, but the objective cannot be deviated from in any way. This means you will always going to need to assassinate, kidnap, steal the files in each mission. Consequently, the more outside the box decision making found in the aforementioned games is diminished here. Just about every encounter will begin with a reconnaissance phase using a frankly completely overpowered drone to get a lay of the land before deciding on a course of action. The drone can later on be upgraded to contain a bomb for sabotage or assassination, a lure to distract enemies, or an instant revive heal (this will surely not be totally busted).  The stealth system is decent enough; there is enough time between you being seen and being spotted to react quickly, and enemies are just smart enough to be taken seriously while still being predictable enough to map a route through an encampment and carry your plan out afterwards. Once you are detected, however, enemies bring the hammer down on you immediately and with absurd levels of precision, with cartel minions dual wielding mac-10’s able to down you from 150 meters away in an instant, and the AI is able to identify and assault your position in the blink of an eye. Thankfully their own healthbars are equally squishy, and with the right preparation you can play a more aggressive ambush style, especially with multiple players assigned different roles, and destroy the enemies fast. Vehicles can act as an effective force multiplier, and the ai rebel faction can offer a variety of different support functions for stealth and assault operators. Weapon variety is numerous and diverse: the different models of firearm within a given category offer tangible differences in performance, and all guns can be modified extensively for extra customizations. The same cannot be said for the vehicles, which all handle like the default car asset in Roblox. Suspension and transmission are completely unmodeled, which isn’t optimal for a game set in the mountains, so civilian vehicles are best left for travel while the armor is best left for the occasional full-scale battles that the missions occasionally require. These missions highlight the weaknesses of Wildlands combat system, mostly boiling down to save scumming in order to prepare the perfect Maginot line of mines, chokepoints, and rebels to blunt the hordes of cracked out marksman enemies.
As for the games’ story and characters? You obviously aren’t coming to a Ghost Recon game expecting Black Flag or Far Cry 3 levels of storytelling and characterization, but what is here is so poor that the games action can hardly justify itself. Picture a Tom Clancy group of spec ops army guys and the archetypes they would each fulfill, then melt them all into a broth and hand it to the four guys in this game, and you have what Wildlands refers to as characters. The game’s actual protagonist ends up being CIA-lady Karen Bowman, who if nothing else has a stake in the games narrative and expresses what at times could be mistaken for a personality. The game has, on paper, a couple dozen characters in the various captains, underbosses, and operations heads you combat, but we are never given the chance to actually see them do anything that might flesh out their motivations or build the reputation of the Santa Blanca cartel as a malevolent organization to be feared in any way. Instead, they are quickly introduced in a brief before being killed or captured by our heroes to be interrogated by Bowman in The Shack. What is The Shack you might ask? It is the place where EVERY SINGLE CUTSCNE IN THE ENTIRE GAME TAKES PLACE, thanks for asking. Even the final encounter with El Sueno in his cathedral uses the same lighting fixtures as the clay walled, dirt floored shack, so get used to it quickly. The game’s open structure in the way you can complete any story arc in whichever order you choose means that no plot developments can take place beyond the premise to set things up and the conclusion, and as a result there is no pacing in the plot Eliminating the security operation doesn’t weaken the enemies you face, destroying production doesn’t reduce their numbers, etc. so the opportunity to create some kind of lasting impact from the story onto the gameplay is lost. As for the DLC missions, the less said about those the better.
There are a number of different prisms from which Wildlands is contextualized more broadly that are often more interesting than the game itself. In some respects, this is the infamous standard for the ubislop we know and hate with its drawing the most surface level and focus tested mechanics from tactical shooters, sandbox games, and stealth games and churning out a smorgasbord of uninspired content to grind out for a few dozen hours. But this impression is less charitable than the game deserves. The premise of a fully co-op drug war in a massive environment is a genuinely interesting concept, and in the hands of a studio with more talent and direction (say, Rockstar) there could have been something really special here. This is also in many ways the last respectable piece of media Ubisoft would ever produce. We would soon be subjected to a Far Cry game in a developed country with a silent protagonist and an RPG Assassins Creed that would serve as a final embarrassment to each of those poor franchise’s cultural relevancy, not to mention Wildland’s own disastrous sequel. But all of these broader schools of thought belie what at its core is a just an ok game that treads water without making waves or sinking to the depths. Bizarre minor choices like the game’s good ending requiring you to get the bad ending first even if you’ve fulfilled the requirements for the good ending, the atrocious Rainbow Six Siege tie in, the DLC/extra half-baked game modes, etc. Aren’t enough to balance out some nice landscapes (the salt flat part is cool) and decent third person cover shooting. In summary, a fun and inoffensive slop shooter from an era where even slop was held to a standard.

As a longtime fan of the Ghost Recon series it was definitely a big adjustment getting used to the open world, third person, vehicle, and story driven gameplay as opposed to a purely tactical mission based experience. Once you get the hang of it the game is a lot of fun and mostly rewards the player for learning how to navigate the world, take down enemy bases, and complete missions. At the same time some missions felt exceptionally difficult and not in a way that requires a learning curve, rather, some missions felt bugged in that you could die during cut scenes and/or had to essentially cheese the game to win. When it worked it was one of my favourite games to play and allowed for so much creativity, at its worst it felt like smashing my head against a wall. Overall it is worth it, and is arguable one of the most underrated games, but it also has some flaws.

I played this through with my friend and we had a great time.

It's a massive game that will take quite some time to clear all provinces especially if you are going for all collectibles and side activities. The missions are varied and the player is rewarded for stealthy approaches and prior surveillance using a drone and other tools.

In general the game is quite forgiving in terms of difficulty, especially with the admittedly lackluster AI however extreme difficulty proves to be a better challenge as the player is forced to not rely so much on the radar and non stealth approaches are punished.

There is also a permadeath 'Ghost' mode for those that was a challenge.

As per usual Ubisoft excels when it comes to the environment and world immersion, and Bolivia is full of varied biomes and lived in towns and cities.

Some of the characters are quite two dimensional including unfortunately the main cast of characters.

The first DLC 'Narco Road', is disappointing in its jarring change of tone to a more comedic style, however proves to fun after settling into it.

The second DLC 'Fallen Ghosts', arguably improves on even the base game in terms of difficulty and atmosphere, the missions are demonstrably harder and new enemy types makes the gameplay generally more engaging.

Overall a great game that the player can get a lot out of and generally serves as a great open world stealth and action game.

After nearly 50 hours of playtime, I FINALLY beat this game. For those of you who don't know, when Ghost Recon: Wildlands launched back in 2017, it was an unoptimized mess. Most PCs could barley run the game, including my own. So I uninstalled and forgot about it. Fast forward to the holiday sale in 2025 and the game was $10USD here on Steam. So I snagged it, installed the first person mod (which I HIGHLY recommend) and started my 3rd playthrough. See, every other time I tried to complete it I just fell off and never got back to it. This time I was going to roll credits, and about 5 minutes ago I did just that.

THE BAD: 
The game has some serious ISSUES, out of date game design (tailing missions) and a handful of other problems that almost killed my drive to complete it. For example, one mission has you hijack an enemy cargo truck and park it in an enemy "garage" without being spotted. Seems easy enough? Until you park the truck 4 feet to far forward and you "leave the mission area!?" Causing you to have to replay the entire mission from the start. No checkpoint once you park the truck. There are a few missions with seemingly idiotic design that really kills all momentum you can have in a playthrough. Also the way the skill point system works becomes a pain in the 2nd half of the game. At first you can rack up enough gas, food, meds or com gear to upgrade skills pretty quickly. After you take out your 2nd part of the cartel however, you'll end up with upwards of 100 skill points you can't spend since you don't have enough resources. I ended my playthrough with 110 I couldn't spend. Could I have taken the time to do all the convoy missions, heli drops and airdrops? Yes. But that would have added another 5ish hours to an already 50 hour game. Also, sometimes enemies just shoot you through walls, spot you in the dark with no lights from 50 feet away and even glitch into the gameworld. There's just a bunch of poor design and jank here. Also collecting weapons and attachments is just not really worth it. I found the best AR, Sniper and pistol by looking in my inv to see where they spawn, getting them, finding a high zoom sniper scope and that was that. The MK17, MSR and Lady Killer were my most used guns, and while the Lady Killer is only obtainable via a "buchon" the m9 handgun is pretty solid and looks cool. But if I would have collected all weapons and weapon attchments, there's another few hours added onto the game. And once you have the best guns, collecting anything else is just not worth the HOURS it would take.

THE GOOD:
The game would is beautiful. Like the game on "Very High" settings is breathtaking, I found myself stopping to take pictures of the game world quite often. I do have a very powerful system with an RTX 4090. and could not push "Ultra" above 70-80fps at 3440x1440. This game is almost TEN YEARS OLD? But regardless, very high looks very good... The game also nails gunplay. Once you level up your bullet resistance, you can run and gun pretty well. Or you can stick to stealth, which takes a lot more time, but is very satisfying if you can pull it off in 5 skull areas. The score is also very good, and the overall audio design is solid. Enemies will talk and it allows you to locate them based on their voices alone. During stealth they will sing to themselves when they think they are safe, or just have basic conversations. Now you'll hear the same "santa, santa, saannntaa blanca" lyrics over and over and over and over, but it's still a nice touch. Also, most missions are pretty fun. But the forced stealth and tailing missions make me want to punch concrete.

TLDR:

For the age of this game, it does get a pass on some of the outdated game design, as it is almost 10 years old. But the tailing missions are just bad. Shooting feels solid, game looks amazing and for a solid $10-$20 it is 100% worth the pickup. I played the whole game solo with limited HUD and the first person mod, but the game does support full Co-op... just hope your friends are good shots lol.

I'm a bit late to the party, as the game is essentially dead, but Ghost Recon: Wildlands is sh!t, to put it mildly. And here's why:

From the outlook until you get into the swing of things it feels alright. Then, once you have completed a few missions the realization slowly sets in: You're just doing the same tasks over and over and over, run through copypasta village after copypasta village. It gets real mundane real quick.

To go a bit more into depth:
Design:
The concept of this game is a 1 v 1 v 1 kind of "stand-off". Cartel vs Corrupt Military vs Rebels.
Except 90% of the time Cartel and Military work together, so it's really a 1 v 2.
The landscapes are quite pretty, but also extremely poorly made. What do I mean by that? A lot of the mountainous terrain feels like taking a rock and just copypasting it over and over. Sometimes that leads to little V-shaped notches that you can drop into, but never get out of again. Over 70 hours of playtime I have gotten stuck at least 30 times. That is attrocious as you either have to reload a checkpoint or, if you're fighting the military, just kill yourself using grenades.

As I mentioned above, the map is too big. Instead of making a huge "open world", half of that size would've been enough for the scenario without making it feel quite so "low-effort copy-paste".

One more huge negative aspect fits into design, but also into gameplay, so I'm putting it into the next one.

Gameplay:
The gunplay is.. meh.. at best. Nothing feels quite satisfying to use.
The driving.. well the choppers are actually kind of solid. The planes... they are fly-able. It's not that hard.
But any ground vehicle is just pure, unadulterated ass. They're floaty, slip around everywhere and as soon as you go offroad, start bouncing and breaking physics like it's nobody's business.
Again, if you make a huge map, you kind of rely on solid vehicles to get you from point A to point B.

Then, the problem that is both "by design" and "gameplay-related".. so you have the Cartel, they occupy a spot, have a limited amount of resources and possibly one or two reinforcements. That's it.
And then there's the motherf**ckers that are Unidad who just get infinite reinforcement and spawning out of thin air plus an aimbot that always knows player position, even if they have never actually seen you before. You take an enemy out from 400 meters away in a bush, they trigger the alarm and after not moving for 4 minutes suddenly Unidad soldiers pop up next to you as if they were watching you the whole time. Say you attack a Unidad base, hunker down in a fort and destroy 50 choppers. They just don't care, because they have endless resources and manpower. They will just keep spawning out of thin air, chasing you until you're either successfully killed, or managed to get away 500 meters or more.

Then there's the teleporting bots that break all physics and rules. From headshotting enemies through 2 concrete buildings to literally phasing through solid objects or randomly teleporting around. Nothing about them makes sense.

In the same way, most of the upgrade system feels completely wasted. Yes, at first you unlock some new gadgets to play with, but afterwards it just becomes a tedious grind to find the right parts you need to progress.

As a positive, albeit a single one, I do appreciate them putting in their other franchises with missions related to Splinter Cell or Rainbow Six. But that's about it.

Now for Execution:

Everything just feels.. unpolished. Like wiping your ass, putting everything correctly into the toilet bowl, but forgetting to flush. The whole game stinks. The longer you play it, the more you realize, what a mess the game actually is.
I honestly can't think of a single thing they did exceptionally well.
The bot AI sucks, the Rebel AI sucks and the enemy AI can either smell you from 50 meters away against the wind, while it's raining or they're as oblivious as if they're trying to look for stars in the daytime sky.
If I had to guess, enemies have a 180° field of vision that goes 90° upwards and 90° downwards. So even if you're directly below a chopper with no possible line of sight or are behind 3 trees some 300 meters away, a sniper is going to see 1 pixel of your character and will start targetting it.

And to sum it all up, as you progress through the game, progression becomes meaningless. You take out cartel bosses, get a quick cutscene and some skillpoints and that's it. DJ Pelico still keeps talking about bosses you took out months ago and you striking a deal with Unidad changes absolutely nothing in their behaviour. Everything just feels meaningless. Like what you do in Bolivia has no goal, you're just endlessly running in a straight line, never seeing the finish line.

And for that, and more stuff I couldn't be bothered to write down here, I'm giving this game a 3/10.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands offers a massive, beautiful Bolivian open world with fantastic co-op tactical shooter fun, strong gunplay, and rewarding exploration for weapons/attachments, but suffers from repetitive missions, a weak story, and sometimes clunky single-player AI, making it a solid but flawed experience best enjoyed with friends for strategic chaos.

I’ve spent a lot of time in Ghost Recon Wildlands and it’s a solid open‑world tactical shooter. You pick your loadout, sneak or fight through Bolivia, and the game lets you approach missions however you like. Squad AI works okay solo, but it’s better with friends in co‑op. Vehicles and helicopters make travel fast, and maps are huge with lots of side activities. Stealth feels satisfying when it works, and gunplay is solid with a variety of weapons. Missions can feel repetitive, but exploring, taking out camps, and coordinating attacks keeps it fun. Graphics and weather effects make the world feel alive. Regular updates added new events and gear. If you enjoy tactical shooters with freedom and co‑op, Wildlands is worth your time.

Hours Played: Enough to clear a cartel base twice and still hang out
Verdict: ⚠️ Mixed‑Positive (Great Idea, Patchy Execution)

Ghost Recon Wildlands drops you into a massive open world and says, “Go stomp cartels with friends or alone.” And that promise is mostly delivered but not always smoothly.

The open world is huge, gorgeous, and packed with missions, outposts, and secrets. Driving across Bolivia, flying helicopters, or sneaking into a base feels cinematic and fun. There’s a real tactical freedom here: stealth approaches work, loud gunfights work, or that middle ground that ends with explosions and regrets also works.

Co‑op with friends is the game’s sweet spot. Coordinating flanks, reviving teammates, and executing plans makes every mission more satisfying. AI teammates are serviceable, but friends do it better.

However, the game often feels repetitive. Missions can blur together (“kill target, blow stuff up, repeat”), and enemy variety isn’t huge. Some mechanics feel shallow compared with the size of the world. Early releases also had plenty of bugs many fixed now, but occasional glitches can still pop up.

What Wildlands does right:

* Huge, varied open world to explore
* Fun tactical freedom and approach variety
* Excellent co‑op experience
* Satisfying gunplay at its best moments

Where it struggles:

* Repetitive mission design
* Occasional bugs and AI quirks
* Can feel shallow compared to its scale

Ghost Recon Wildlands isn’t perfect, but it’s a blast with friends and a solid tactical shooter in a massive playground. If you love towering maps, flexible strategy, and coordinated chaos, this one’s worth your time just don’t expect perfection at every turn.

My Experience:
The game doesn't start-up and gets stuck in loading... basically, it is completely broken on modern processors. I am running an Intel Core Ultra 9 285K (Core Ultra Series 200s, released in Oct 2024), and despite having a high-end rig, I spent my entire time fighting the software instead of playing.

If you have a modern CPU, especially from the 12th, 13th, 14th Gen, or the new Ultra Series 2, be warned: this game suffers from a severe incompatibility with hybrid CPU architectures (P-cores and E-cores). The issue lies in an outdated OpenSSL library the game uses, which misidentifies the capabilities of newer processors, causing it to crash instantly or hang on an infinite loading screen.

I tried absolutely everything to get it running. I went through the hassle of adding system environment variables (like the OPENSSL_ia32cap command), fighting with command prompts, and disabling the Ubisoft Connect in-game overlay. I even looked into the community "fixes" that involve downloading shady ZIP files from GitHub to manually patch the .dll files or replace the game executable, messing with file paths in the Steam directory. Nothing worked seamlessly.

Some guides even suggest going into your BIOS and disabling your E-Cores (Efficient Cores) just to run a game from 2017, which is ridiculous when you are running a flagship CPU like the Ultra 9. Whether you are on the latest Intel chips or potentially facing similar issues with newer Ryzen architectures, it is a lottery. Most laptops are unaffected by this problem; it mostly occurs in desktop architectures. You shouldn't have to become a software engineer, edit system variables, or cripple your hardware in the BIOS just to launch a product you paid for.

Until Ubisoft decides to officially update the game executable to handle modern instruction sets without needing third-party bypasses or manual file surgery, do not waste your time or money. You will likely spend your two-hour refund window debugging their code rather than playing. Refunded.

I'm not sure how people can like this game, but to each their own. It's basically just a less goofy version of Far Cry. Why do I have to grind my butt off just to get a scope for my weapons? As for the gameplay, it is far from realistic as the game seems to want to be. For example, I was playing with a friend, and during some scripted ambush, he was shooting at a couple enemy soldiers who were returning fire in his direction. I took that opportunity to shoot at them from the place I was hiding, thinking that I could get the drop on them. It took three headshots to take down the first guy, which is absolutely ridiculous. Not only that, right after the first shot hit him, he immediately turned to face me and shot me effortlessly. Talk about an aimbot. And this kind of stuff happens way too often in this game, which completely ruins the immersion. 

Of course, I guess I should have been thankful just to be able to actually play with my friend; it was a real chore just to try and do so.
