To be honest, I have a love-hate relationship with this game. I'm giving it a thumbs up because for the most part it's a really fun stealth shooter that gives you a large open world, a slough of bad guys to shoot and a lot of tools to get the job done. I've poured a lot of hours into it and even then I'm only halfway through the game because I'm taking my time picking up guns, gun parts, and upgrading my skills. It's also a big plus for me when you provide a great amount of customization for your character and your NPC squadmates to make them look awesome.  But as much as I love the feel of being a cool, customizable commando squad leader, this game has its moments that have made me rage quit on a couple of occasions. 

The story follows a team of commandos taking down a drug cartel that's taken over Bolivia. That's about it for narrative. You have a bunch of mini-bosses to take down on your way to the main antagonist, and they do come with their own cutscenes and backstory if you're interested, but I figure most of these guys are either going to die or going to jail so I don't really care.

Gameplay is what you'd normally expect from stealth shooters; you sneak around, take out bad guys if you can, and if you are detected it's run and gun time. There's a bigger emphasis on stealth here though, especially in the first part of the game when you're weak and don't have as many tools at your disposal. Even when you've fully upgraded your health, it's still really easy for a simple grunt to take you down if they flank you, so stealth is typically your best approach to any situation if you can help it. The enemies are a little more sensitive in this game as well, able to detect you at farther distances and able to hear silenced weapons if you're shooting them too close to patrolling guards. This means you really have to plan out your approach and scout out enemy positions with a camera drone or binoculars before you move in, because being detected in the middle of an enemy base that has a army of guards, mounted gun emplacements, mortars, and alarms that call helicopters can lead to a very swift death for you and your squad. In fact, there are some moments where it's ridiculous how quickly these guys can detect you at a distance. More on that later. 

Your NPC squad is a bit of a mixed bag. They can be really handy a lot of situations, being able to fire at targets from passenger seats in vehicles, being able to revive you when you are downed, and able to simultaneously snipe marked enemies with flawless accuracy. They're also able to help you with recon by marking enemies for you. Often, they see enemies through buildings and landscape like they have X-ray vision, which is a bit of an immersion-breaking bug, but it is helpful so I'm not going to complain too much. On the other hand, there's moments when they feel completely brain-dead. They'll normally hang back when you're infiltrating an enemy base, which is good because if you tell them to follow you they'll throw caution out the window and end up getting detected, forcing you to fight for your life. They also get stuck on the landscape or objects in the area on occasion, though I mostly noticed this in underground areas which you don't encounter very often. 

However, my biggest gripe with this game comes from the Unidad. THE FRICKING UNIDAD. I'm not gonna lie, they're one of the main reasons why I'm writing this review. I cannot stress enough how much I hate these guys with a passion. Basically, they're Bolivia's military police that are low-key allied with the cartel, and they're supposedly dangerous and elite soldiers. Why, you may ask? Because they have high quality gear? Because they have military training? No, it's because they crap their pants and call for reinforcements at the first sign of danger, no matter what the situation is! 

"Oh, we just caught four lone guys in the middle of our base full of trained soldiers, machine guns, mortars, APCS and helicopters, BETTER CALL REINFORCEMENTS." 

Like, I get it, they're an enemy that's meant to make the game challenging and make you think twice before taking the direct attack approach. Still, I can't help but wish that these guys got a little bit of a nerf, because as soon as they start calling for reinforcements it is nonstop soldiers, armored cars and helicopters. Like, at the very least, give me a little more of a cushion between waves of reinforcements so I can consider my options. To make things worse, they always show up at the worst times possible. If you're trying to infiltrate a cartel base on the side of the road, then you'd better get the heck away from that road because I promise you a Unidad patrol car will drive up behind you, spot you, and start ripping into you with a mini gun while calling their entire army to back them up. I've lost count of how many times a stealth mission went south because a lone Unidad car just so happened to pass by me while I was scoping a base out. 

Some of the most aggravating missions in the game revolve around fighting these guys; I wouldn't call these moments hard, I'd call them outrageously unfair. Like a mission where you have to sneak onto a base without killing anyone, defend a computer download while all the soldiers you could have taken out beforehand start swarming the area like crazed serial killers, and then make a mad dash out of the base while being chased by endless armored cars and helicopters. Or a mission where you have to kill an Unidad commander while his base is attacked by cartel gangsters. The cartel gunmen last like thirty seconds before they get smoked, and then the base is on high alert the rest of the mission. That means the guards on the ground can spot you and alert everyone much faster, and snipers in the guard towers can see you a mile away like they're the freaking eye of Sauron. And if that wasn't enough, there's a helicopter just camping above the base, and it can see almost everything too, though it wasn't as bad as the snipers. I was on normal difficulty for this mission, so I bumped it down to easy, but even then it felt like it barely made a difference on the difficulty. Maybe I'm just stupid and there was a better way to do these mission, I don't know. But as an average player, I'm having a hard time believing anyone play tested those missions and deemed the difficulty fair. IT WAS THAT RIDICULOUS! 

Overall, I do really enjoy this game and I love the stealth/action vibe it gives, even if it does have some frustrating aspects here and there and the Unidad is annoying beyond belief. If you want a game that offers fun stealth gameplay, action packed hit and run warfare, and a fair amount of character and loadout customization, this game might scratch that itch. However, if you want a game with a compelling story, gameplay that isn't repetitive, or to feel like a demigod destroying everything in your path, this might not be what you're looking for.

Wildlands is a game that you'll either love or hate. For me, I personally loved it. If you aren't 100% sure about buying this game (on sale or not) watch some videos of its gameplay on youtube. Everything I put is obviously from my experience, and I just think its time to review this game.

First is the graphics. I play this game running an i7-9700k, GTX 1070, and 64GB of ram. Overall, I can hit 50-60 fps 1080p on almost all settings maxed. I don't think I ever really got a frame drop, Maybe like once from blowing up a few to many things at once but other then that the game runs very nicely. And so, with this game being system-heavy, the visuals follow suit. For me, it is absolutely beautiful. The water, sky, grass, vehicles, people, mountains, all of it looks great on Ultra/high settings. And the vast variety of landscapes like snow, swamps, salt lakes, Rocky mountains, Desert, etc. It is overall just breathtaking and you will find yourself just roaming around because of how pretty it is.

Second, the main campaign. Wildlands has a plethora of bosses controlling regions, in which it lets you choose which ones to go after and when. As you dig your way in, you'll find harder bosses with different difficulties of levels. and eventualy El Sueno, the big bad boss. I found almost all the characters in the game intriguing, good and bad guys alike. They put a lot of backstory into there characters and I think it really plays out well because you end up really getting to know them, whether you are going to kill them, hunt them, kidnap them or whatever. It really feels real. The cutscenes held character, and the differing missions surrounding bosses were enjoyable. It feels and plays like a natural and unrestricted experience.

Third, the side missions. This is where I find a lot of hate, even something I noticed right at its release. They are the same thing over and over to get resources for upgrades, throughout the entire game. But, oddly enough, I didn't mind them. I think, at least for me, is because the changing location always allowed for different circumstances. I like it because of the fact its all somewhere different even if the mission is the same. Hijacking a truck, for example, could be way different in an urban city vs. the mountains with thin roads and little traffic. The good news is, whether you like them or not, they are in no way required. It is very much possible to finish the game with the starter gear and weapons.

Fourth, the driving. Vehicles come in variety, with different purposes and characteristics. Say, perhaps, you take a van and stow your newly aquired short-term prisoner in the back. Take a sports car, and there is only room for one passenger, so you have speed but no friends to come along. On the PC specifically, it works well in one case and horrible in another. If you're trying to be slow and seaky, or perhaps just obeying the rules of the road, goodluck. Just to keep my speed down I have to tap the key at a consistent rate to stay on par with traffic. However, once you're accustomed to the driving, you'll find it quite useful. The high speed chases are much easier, as just holding the key keeps you at max speeds, drifting comes naturally, and split-second maneuvers are not just a thing of legend. Although this was my experience, and I noticed A LOT, or more so the majority of people hated the driving system.

Fifth, customizability. (Did I spell that right?) Weapons, well most of them, have several interchangeable parts that you can unlock to increase performance or change from that scope you hate. There's lots of paint jobs, even part by part. I loved playing around with different weapons, It really lets you play around with your own playstyle, whether you like stealth, loud or both you can really play around with what you want and how you want it.  Your character can be changed to your heart's desire, You have the disposal of ghillie suits, Costumes, Masks, Basically anything you can think of. Which is one thing I think ubisoft does really well is the customizablilty in a lot of there games.

Seventh, my verdict. I have endured easy success, endless failure (that one city mission in Narco Road MY OH MY), but overall I found it to be worth my time. I honestly think its a little underrate, I really found myself invested in the story and really enjoyed the experience. Get this game on sale, and I'm sure you'll get something out of it.

There's no other way to put it. This game and the followup Breakpoint are bad Ghost Recon games. 
The entire aspect of Stealth was sacrificed for the novel concept of an 'open world game'. And in the aspect of what an open world game could have been, managing a guerrilla insurgency and having a more engaging gameplay experience, this game falls painfully short. 
It's one similar mission after the other with repetitive objectives. There's one immensely irritating mission that flaunts every little issue with the game's inherent design and the painfully poor friendly AI (The El Pulpo mission for everyone who's played the game). 

All in all, it has its moments of being fun. I haven't done any of the PVP, but there's surely reviews abundant about that floating around. And if you're a total gear-eccentric, there's a lot of fun stuff to deck your operator out in, thought you're going to have to purchase some DLC to get 'kit' that isn't just a 5.11 drop. 

As an old game, it's worth getting on sale for just a few hours of messing around WITH friends. Otherwise, save your money, and definitely avoid Breakpoint like the plague.

I put almost 400 hours into the game, from the bug-ridden launch through 100% completion in every DLC. Wildlands is one of the most enjoyable co-op, tactical shooters I've played. Its a nice balance of arcade-y input and tactical action that lets a four player team take it super serious (mandatory at higher difficulties) or go in guns blazing. The transition from a perfectly executed tactical stealth op to a scrambling gun fight when someone drops the ball is seemless and constantly entertaining. 

In particular, Wildlands has the gold standard for drop in / drop out co-op multiplayer. You can play the game 100% co-op from the beginning. If a player jumps in to join you on a mission / zone they haven't reached yet, the game has no problem allowing them to participate and even gives them credit for any missions that are completed and unlocks that are found in their own save game. Players can easily go back and replay old missions to help out a friend who hasn't completed as much of the game. Players are also free to roam anywhere in the open world, which allows the team to divide and conquer or spread out for multiple angles of approach on an objective (ground, air, sniper / LMG overwatch, etc.). More co-op games could learn from what Wildlands does so well in this space.

I would personally consider Wildlands a game with few flaws, but they exist and are worth being aware of. The Teammate AI is a little lack luster, this is a game that was built from the ground up assuming you would play with other people and I strongly recommend playing it that way. The story is a pretty by the numbers, spec-ops military story; partly par for the course for a Tom Clancy military story line but the simplistic story is also what enables the seamless drop in / drop out multiplayer to work so well. There's not a lot of shocking twists and turns or personal character growth throughout the story, but its also not really the point of the "fun" in the game (for the record, the "fun" is infiltrating an enemy base to grab intel and then shooting your way out when the plan invariably goes belly up!). Compared to historic Ghost Recon games, this outing has definitely tilted more arcade-y and less tactical. If you're looking for old school Ghost Recon, this isn't it, but I feel the modern upgrades are what made this title so successful.

Long and short, I recommend Ghost Recon Wildlands for anyone who enjoys tactical shooters with their friends. Roaming the Bolivian countryside getting up to hijinks and taking down cartel strongholds with three friends is some of the best times I've had gaming in the last few years.

This game was fun for approximately 30 hours.  I played the majority with one friend in multiplayer.  The graphics are amazing; especially at night! It was nice that there was no tether so you could move as far away from other players as you want.  The game provides a decent open world where you can pick what order you want to do things and attack each mission/challenge as you please.  There were levels of realism to things that we enjoyed.  There were a LOT of options for customizing your character's appearance which was nice.  Unfortunately...

The guns available were fine but it didn't seem that one weapon was much different from another.  We spent the majority of the game playing with the same weapons and never traded them out for something else.  It didn't feel like we needed to collect all the weapons and parts on the map as a result.  

While we enjoyed a lot of things about the game, once we reached the 4 skull difficulty levels, we became frustrated by how the game chose to increase the challenge.  We  liked the added siren warning system, choppers in the air, and Unidad presence (bad guys with armor), we were very irritated with how the game would spawn random bad guys, sometimes right beside you, even while you were hiding and out of sight.  Somehow, the AI always knew where you were at, even when hiding or moving through heavy ground cover.  There is almost zero ability to be strategic because even though you could place proximity mines around a building you were camped, the AI would spawn directly beside you.  Strategy is further complicated, when one player is detected, the other player is detected as well, even if they are on the other side of the compound and not near you.

Whatever you do, don't let them out of their cages because the game will start spawning more bad guys randomly around you, even in places you have already cleared.

The vehicles were not great.  They were hard to control and easily damaged.  We had the most fun on the dirty bikes which were great at getting around off road.

In the end, we enjoyed the game for what it was, but didn't complete it.  We started to feel like we were just struck in a loop of doing the same thing over and over in a different location.  We wanted this to be a more tactical shooter game but strategy became almost impossible for the above reasons.

This game has a bit of a learning curve, but after a few hours of gameplay you will start to get the hang of it.  The single player campaign has a loose structure, but is quite entertaining. Although not quite as interactive as some, Wildlands boasts arguably one of the best open worlds ever created. It is a jaw-droppingly huge and incredible world to explore. Although it is scaled down and only a rough impression of the real-world Bolivia, it still feels like the full entirety of an actual country (albeit minus any large metropolitan areas, unfortunately). Still, as the title of the game suggests, the focus is on the wilderness, and Wildlands' map does not disappoint. Amazon rainforest, paradise lake resorts, cocaine farms hidden in the depths of the jungle, high-altitude woodland, snow-capped mountains, arid, rocky foothills, and even the famously desolate expanse of Bolivia's salt flats.

The best way to play this game is with a strict no-fast-travel rule - including fast travel at all is frankly a crime in a world this fun to traverse. When you take fast travel away, you actually have to hike across these expansive wildernesses, talk to locals for intel, put around in "borrowed" old cars on lengthy road trips, dodge military patrols and checkpoints, and generally inhabit the backwoods of a fictionalized country.

Speaking of fiction, the story content is relatively good. It's much more reminiscent of classic Tom Clancy stories of civil unrest, powerful terrorist organizations, and outnumbered and under-resourced special forces, as opposed to the tediously bland techno-vomit of newer, posthumously ghostwritten "Tom Clancy" dreck (prime example: Breakpoint). This is also where the gameplay excels, because where it lacks in open world depth, it makes up for in dozens of engaging, elaborately-produced mini-campaigns in each region of the map as you target the various bad guy lieutenants in order to expose and go after their bosses in turn.

One mission has you abduct, extract, and interrogate some flunkie for information, and the co-op possibilities really shine here: My friends and I nabbed the target at gunpoint and took out his guards while one of us pulled up in an escape vehicle. We stuffed the target into the trunk while the bad guys closed in, so we peeled off into the desert. Eventually we shook the pursuit and found ourselves alone, at night, in the middle of afore-mentioned desolate salt flats. So, naturally, we did the only Correct & Proper thing: dragged the guy out of the trunk and put him in front of the blinding headlights of our car in the middle of nowhere and interrogated him there. One we were finished with him, we knocked him out and left him for dead, driving off to find civilization again and our next objective...

The story missions really carry a lot of the gameplay, especially in co-op. Unfortunately, as mentioned, the gameplay outside of those missions can get a little thin. Combat encounters tend to be pretty formulaic, the difficulty settings suck, and once you've been at it for awhile you can start to see the simplistically-exploitable rules of what is a sadly rather shallow simulation.

Still, that one flaw is the only thing really dragging this game down. I wish it had some of the more evolved features of Breakpoint, because aside from that Wildlands is a far superior game - damn near a work of art on account of what is by far my favorite open world I've ever played Make Believe Soldier in.

The graphics are nice and the lighting in particular is really great as it transitions between night and day and all the weather effects. Its a pretty nice atmospheric game and captures the Ghost Recon environment from older games really well. The weapon customization is awesome, you can tweak nearly every part of each gun. Long Story: Ghost Recon Wildlands is something of a strange game when it comes to the Tom Clancy name. It's not a tactical shooter and it's not an in-depth military game, instead, it's a game that tries to be this hybrid open-world shooter without ever perfecting the formula. You're dumped into the surprisingly immersive war-torn Bolivia, chalkful of people to shoot, places to explore, and more. Something Ubisoft is very capable of doing, the game worlds are usually their strong suit. However, their faults lie in some important parts elsewhere in the game. The big issue that primarily plagues Wildlands is that while it's not exceptionally bad at anything, it's not exceptionally great either. It's just an open-world military shooter. The game does become exponentially better when playing with friends though. The game SLIGHTLY reminds me of ARMA in that I can play with some friends and infiltrate a base together and get immense satisfaction successfully clearing a base using tactics with each other. That's what I think this game was designed with in mind. That being said, I do have some personal complaints. First being that the customization is fairly lackluster, half the customization options make you look as if you're dressing up for an airsoft match which isn't very good (this problem is mitigated by the much more tactical-looking special outfits but those offer no customization, detracting from player agency). Second is the AI, it's either dumb as rocks and couldn't spot you in an open-field or it's spot you from 3 miles away in a jungle and snipe you with a pistol, there is no in-between. I wish the AI was just a bit better to go up against. At the end of the day, Wildlands is a pretty good game and there's not really a whole lot out there to offer what it does on the scale that it does. It's better with friends but servicable as a single-player title. I can however promise that it is so much better than the trainwreck that is GR: Breakpoint.

Ubisoft basically only makes one "open world" game these days.  If you've played any of the later Far Cry games, Watchdogs, etc. you already know what you're getting with this title.

All of these games offer a couple of hours of refreshing, novel content before they start to feel like a mindless slog.   The fictionalized version of Bolivia in this game is a beautiful landscape of arid hills and shimmering lakes, but it feels hollow - like a theme park version of a real country populated by soulless animatronics.  It's  "Westworld" version of South America for you - the player - to live out your action movie super commando fantasy.

NPC cartel soldiers and rebel guerrillas alike just roam around the many (many... many...) roads brainlessly until you decide to take some action.  The game dialog suggests you're dropping into the middle of a shadow war between the Bolivian army, the Santa Blanca cartel and the rebel faction but in practice there's no sense of a bigger stage.   All of the action takes place within 50 yards of your location at that precise moment and as soon as you leave that location everything is reset.   Military outposts you wipe out are spontaneously re-garrisoned, lavish casinos you destroy are rebuilt and filled again with wealthy party goers. 

The title of the game and the designation of your squad, "Ghosts", seems to suggest that you're there to act invisibly; to get in and get out without anyone ever knowing about your presence.   To infiltrate using guile and stealth and accomplish your objectives without leaving so much as a ripple...  Yet there's no disincentive to roll up to each and every mission marker in a fully loaded attack helicopter and just lay waste to everyone.   Need to plant listening devices in a lieutenant's personal estate?   Murder everyone, stroll in and place your bugs, and then stroll out.  Mission accomplished!   No one raises an eyebrow at the pile of bodies left behind, and indeed the bodies all vanish after 30 seconds anyway.

As always, you can rely on Ubisoft to make a competently mediocre game.  It's an experience which captures all of the elements of what technically makes up a video game, while managing to avoid any of the soul or engagement that makes a video game actually fun and memorable.

The game offers a bonanza of different weapons and weapon attachments, but who cares?  All you do is headshot everyone from the bushes and it hardly matters what gun you use or what the "handling" stat is for it.  I don't even know what the Handling stat does, because the game never bothers explaining it.  I guess the developers realized it didn't actually matter too.

The premise of the game is that your squad is assigned to travel from province to province within Bolivia and systematically dismantle the Santa Blanca narco organization (sorry - "narco TERRORISTS"), but after the third such province I just didn't care any more.  Each region offers the same basic structure - 6 Story Missions to find out where the head honcho for that region is hiding out, followed by a final mission where you go kill or capture them.  Along the way you can help out the rebels with some pointless fetch quests which unlock better versions of the pointless "Rebel Support" call outs, but who cares?  Kill the 'buchon', blah blah blah some vapid dialog from your CIA handler about how much of an impact what you did will have (Spoiler alert: it has zero impact and everything in the region stays exactly the same), and then you steal yet another helicopter to fly over to yet another region to do it all over again.

I'm not even sure why the late Tom Clancy's name is still attached to any of these games.  Sure, back in the 80's and 90's he wrote some popular military thrillers but how is any of this connected to his work?  Did he write a book called "Ghost Recon Wildlands" or does any Ubisoft game where an M4 carbine appears qualify as existing under the "Tom Clancy Military Action" umbrella?

tldr; by this point I should no better than to keep paying actual money for Ubisoft games, and so should you.  Let's all do our patriotic duty and demand better games than this.

Pros:
+ Gorgeous game. Seriously, the graphics make basic navigation and exploring fun.
+ No framerate / GPU issues. Game has run flawless for 133+ hours which seems unheardof for modern games.
+ Extensive weapon customization.
+ Weapon mechanics are fun to use and unique to each gun.
+ Immersive combat and environment.
+ Stealth and non-stealth gameplay are both rewarding.
+ Consistent development and updates to gameplay.
+ DLC is actually worth it.
+ Impressive colorblind mode options that ACTUALLY help.
+ Interesting storyline and lots of side content if you explore.
+ Has replayability. If you liked a mission or storyline, you can replay it as many times as you want.
+ Up to 4 player coop. This game is fun as hell to play through with one or more friends.


Cons:
- Absolutely zero gore aside from blood stains...kills aren't very satisfying or unique to what weapon you're using (aside from shotguns maybe).
- Enemy AI aren't very challenging or dynamic, even in TIER ONE mode. All they do is make the player more susceptible to damage.
- Teammate AI only really exist to revive you. If you do leave them enabled, they wander around in the open in the middle of enemy compounds and looks hilarious.
- Everyone else complains about repetativeness so I'll put this here because it does exist, but that's expected with a title from Ubisoft. It can be averted if the player changes their gameplay style throughout the campaign which keeps the game somewhat fresh. Doesn't bother me though.
- Escort missions are annoying because the NPCs get stuck on random environment objects.
- Has microtransactions for weapons that cannot be unlocked through natural gameplay or progression.
- Interrogations are not interactive and feel extremely half-a$$ed. They should have implemented a similar system to splinter cell conviction. I want to beat the ever living $hit out of lieutenants/enemy informants, not give them a wet willy with my m9.

I'd give this game a fair 7/10, I think. It's not a classic, it's not particularly memorable, but I've played it fully 3 times now and had a fun time doing so. (Note that I've always played with another player, never with the AI companions.) I enjoy trying to figure out how to execute a mission perfectly so the enemy never knows we've struck, and when that inevitably fails and we have to shoot our way out -- well, that's fun too. The plot doesn't try to be anything more than an excuse to kill a lot of drug dealers and corrupt cops, so don't bother playing this one for the story. The side missions add a little variety, or at least a fun diversion as you explore Bolivia. Overall, it's a good game. Not great, but not bad. Merely good.

It does have flaws, of course. There's one side mission type where you hunt down a truck convoy, for example, and quite often multiple convoys will spawn on top of each other, making the mission bug out and impossible to complete. A lot of the guns feel superfluous, and you'll likely end up only using a handful of them because the others just aren't good. Similarly, there's a group of consumable items, things like grenades and mines. Of these, I only end up using half of them, because the other half don't help solve problems you'll encounter in game. Take the "diversion lure," for example, an item that is supposed to distract enemies and draw them away from you so you can sneak in. All it actually does is put enemies on high alert so they're more likely to see you.

Similarly, there are a lot of skills that I never end up using. One skill tree is devoted entirely to giving you more items, so those aren't helpful when I don't use those items. Other skills actually make the game harder, or at least more annoying: a skill tree that makes your scouting drone faster has two levels, and the second level makes it nearly uncontrollable. There's another skill that makes you do more damage to vehicles. Maxing it out makes you destroy most vehicles with a handful of bullets, which is cool! Except a lot of missions require you to _disable_ vehicles so you can catch the driver. Blowing up the car just kills them, making you fail. Yet other skills provide bonuses so small that I don't bother giving more than one or two points total. So, by the end of the game, I have dozens of skill points I'll never spend because the skills aren't worth investing in.

I don't play many games like this but Ghost Recon: Wildlands is an exception. The amount of control and customization is insane.  The immersion in Bolivia is convincing with all the violence, bodies hanging from signs, cartel attacks, corrupt goverment, ect. You can play co-op which is probably the best and most fun way to play, or go it solo with 2 AI partners as I do. I play solo due to online toxicity and being extremely introverted, so I was really hoping the AI wouldn't be bad, like Sheva (you know if you know) bad. Your AI teammates are always with you, they'll teleport to you, even if you make a run for it in any vehicle. I died waiting on my posse to get in the truck MANY times before realizing this lol. There are many missions and places of interest in this massive, literally wide the ♥♥♥♥ open sandbox. It's on you to dress up like a bad mofo and find these places, people, intelligence, supplies, weapons, vital gun accessories, armor, vehicles, ect. Ghost Recon: Wildlands is truly the epitome of the term "Sandbox" title. There are over 20 Sicarios, which are drug cartel and their goons, and you have to make your way to each one and eliminate them. At any costs. It's not easy though, because they are looking for you as well, setting up frequent roadblocks and ambushes. It all feels like a big sequence and repercussions of a years long drug war, or really the war on the Cartel. You can choose to approach your target(s) like a Banshee with big guns, or use your drone, binoculars, and other sneaky snake tools to mark supplies and "Tag" the ugly bad guys. Tagging baddies is vital and here's why: when using your drone to Tag or have a clean line of sight on 2-3 enemies you can assign the 1st Tagged guy to AI #1 and assign the 2nd Tagged baddie to AI #2 and hit Fire to have them Sync up and snuff both targets cleanly, quickly, and quietly (if you have YOUR suppressor on that is lol). If there's a 3rd enemy near the Tagged targets line him up for yourself to headshot to initiate the Sync kill. Boom! You just killed 3 ugly birdies with 3 silent lead stones! You can unscrew and screw your suppressors on the fly even while aiming, as well as change your fire mode with the Right D-Pad. You have the standard shoulder swap for those pesky doorways and corners, and can toggle scopes, iron sights, first person views while aiming. It's handy to switch from Semi-auto to Auto and change positioning so fast to snap a clean, quiet headshot off and be ready to let loose when the poo hits the fan. You have a few Skill trees, branching out a bit to improve or add more vital combat improvements, toys, ability to call in vehicles, modify drones to reach farther and have better batteries, or even eventually equipping a "Payload" to drop off as a gift to your nearest friendly neighborhood drug dealer. I haven't even gotten close to understanding everything Wildlands has to offer, but I see that as a great thing, because Ubisoft actually gave the map depth, not just useless "collectibles". You collect guns and equipment now, and the Collectibles are actually Medals/trophies that raise certain Skills and Stats beyond the Skill Tree's capabilities, kind of like Vault Hunter Class Mods in Borderlands. I know I didn't cover everything, but by the game and start surprising yourself! You can ignore everything and go nuts, for real. Ghost Recon: Wildlands is more fun than Just Cause 3 and 4 ever were and Wildlands is a serious game! I have to get off here now. I'm coming for you Sueno...

You're a special forces team like in Strike Back Vegance (the TV show) comprised of four operators called Ghosts (Delta Company, First Battalion, 5th Special Forces Group) and you're working for a CIA agent called Karen Bowman (bit like Homeland but she doesn't looks stressed out constantly and is actually badass) on a joint taskforce thing with DEA and JSOC etc taking down the biggest baddest cartel from Mehico called Santa Blanca that's taken over the Bolivian salt flats and their headed by a Dominc Toretto looking beefy badass with a cross tattooed over his face called El Sueño. 

If you're a fan of those TV/movie references (apart from the Fast and Furious one, sorry no mention of family in this game) I just mentioned then you'll love the story and setting of the game and a fun and more grounded departure from the miliatristic futuristic setting of Ghost Recon Future Soldier!

Gameplay wise their is a decent customisation for your charachter's gear (you play as Ghost Lead nomad) and you determine their basic look and gender to start with (You can also change the look, gender and customise gear of your AI teamates too). For all the Tacticool nerds there's plenty of cool gear such as Ghillie suits (for the snipers), 5.11 pants, oakley gloves, aviators (or the classic CrossCom glasses the iconic image of the Ghost Recon series), comtac like hearing protection/headphones and FAST helms with the night vision goggles etc and even cigars for those who want to cosplay a cartel member. Most importantly for the truly Tacticool the wide arrange of firearms at your disposal to pick from (unlock) and the Gunsmith makes a return for an indepth gun customisation so you can pick whether you want an APITAL or Laser 3Dot for your ACR to aim assist in getting some sick headshots on those Santa Blanca fools or to add a suppressor to your MSR sniper rifle or Vector smg for those stealthy players.

The drone also makes a return with easier controls,the ability to utilise night vision and thermal modes and more importantly marking enemies Assassin's Creed style. With your 3 AI teamates the Sync Shot makes a return allowing you to aim up to 4 enemies (including your own) and headshot them all in one go. You can use it to command which eneimies your AI teamates should attack. There are a few basic orders you can give to your AI teamates whom helpfully revive you when you are downed (trust me you get shot easily if you play "I started blastin" style. They also provide light commentary on the situation but unfortunatley these lines can repetitive af as they only have a few recorded.

CIA agent Karen Bowman is a great narrator giving you the mission brief and intel and really drives the narrative forward. She definitley stole the show for me and it felt more like her story and our badass team are the soldiers deployed to do the action. Karen is no "karen" as you see the game go on. Although in the background with her feeling like the narrative lead it really gives you more freedom as an open world game and makes you feel as if you can do whatever you want and have free reign from the start (literally if you want to fly your helicopter to the hardest zone in the game from Level 1, go for it but you will ♥♥♥♥ bricks as the AI are ridicously accurate, how da fuq is a sicario with akimbo scorpions aiming me from 500 metres away?) and start blowing stuff up all over the place.

Their are enough mission types to keep you entertained although it can seem repetitive at times it doesn't feel like a RPG grind fest. Another positive is outposts don't get cleared, enemies will respawn allowing more replayability across the map.

Conclusion the game is pretty fun and I've racked quite a few hours on it. It's probably even more fun with friends (I played solo) and the story is enjoyable enough to keep you hooked. The game is open world from the start so it really has a sandbox vibe if you just want to play a game to live out your Tacticool fantasties or just start blasting away.

You can play anyway you want (until you get to Tier mode, wow,  now that's a story for another day)!

Enjoy plummeting to your death because you can't actually look down to see where you're landing, and you just smashed off your rotor blades on that tiny little tree you couldn't see under you. Oh, and what's up with the magical ability to slide down a vertical cliff, then auto-summersault INTO the cliff face at the bottom to avoid damage?

Hope you like replaying the entirety over and over and over, because there's no checkpoints, and you'll have to listen to the same intro audio/video every single time. 6) Slowly sneaking along and need to switch into night- or thermal-vision? Enjoy reaching across the keyboard and hoping you hit the right key because you will be reaching a LOT. And missing, because you're expected to be hitting multiple widely spaced keys very frequently.

Ghost Recon Wildlands: The Good, The Bad, and Better Than Breakpoin

First things first, let's talk about how it compares to Breakpoint. Now, I don't want to throw shade, but let's be real – Wildlands is like the big brother Breakpoint wishes it could be. It's more open, more engaging, and just...better.

Now, onto the nitty-gritty - gameplay. It's fantastic, no two ways about it. The freedom to tackle missions in any order and the ginormous open world to explore is a blast. You can go all tactical, sneaking around like a ninja, or go in guns blazing, and both ways are satisfying.

But here's the kicker - it can get repetitive. Clearing out yet another cartel outpost, stealing another chopper, it starts to feel like a Groundhog Day scenario after a while. But, hey, isn't that what we signed up for in a sandbox game?

What's great about Wildlands is that it feels like you're playing with your buddies. The AI team members are surprisingly competent (and you don't have to worry about them stealing your snacks).

The story? Well, it's not exactly Oscar-worthy, but it's enough to keep you moving from one breathtaking locale to another. You're on a mission to dismantle a drug cartel, and let's be honest, it's a pretty solid excuse to explore the stunning landscapes of Bolivia.

Now, I can't finish this review without mentioning the vehicles. From dirt bikes to choppers, you've got an impressive garage at your disposal. The driving physics are surprisingly solid, and there's no greater joy than catching some air off a cliff in a stolen sports car.

So, in a nutshell, Ghost Recon Wildlands is an action-packed sandbox, a little bit repetitive but hella fun. It's the better sibling compared to Breakpoint, offering an open-world playground with plenty of toys to keep you entertained. If you're into tactical shooters with a dash of chaos, you've found your game.

As a lifelong, OG player of the Ghost Recon series, I had played the original Ghost Recon (2001), its two expansions, viz. "Desert Siege" and "Island Thunder", as well as GRAW 2.

After reading the reviews, I understandably went into this game expecting to absolutely hate it. To my surprise, I fell in love with Bolivia, its landscape and people, and took it personally upon myself to rid them of the Santa Blanca drug cartel. Also, the short film, [B]"War Within the Cartel"[/B] by Ubisoft immersed me fully into the story. It is so good that it deserves to be its own Netflix series. Seriously, you should check it out!

The open world setting is a refreshing addition to the series and perfectly lends itself to tactical gameplay. [B]While this game isn't designed to be exclusively tactical like its predecessors, that doesn't stop you from exclusively playing it this way.[/B] 

It is up to you - the player - to create your own rules of engagement. The open world simply provides you with the tools to do so. I rely heavily upon sniping and stealth. In fact, the sniping is tremendously fun, and at a high vantage point on a cliff or hill, it turns into a competent sniping game. I have also taken out entire bases with upwards of 20 enemies completely undetected with just a silenced pistol and a crossbow, without raising the alarm. 

To do so, you have to pick your targets carefully and prioritise stragglers on the outer edges of the base and work your way inwards. You must develop tripper discipline and resist the urge to shoot everyone in sight, lest you wish to find yourself out-manned and out-gunned (especially on higher difficulties, which is what I play on). You are an elite, 4-man team that is far behind enemy lines with little reinforcement and surrounded by hostile forces on all sides...so act the part. Wait till an enemy's patrol route leaves him alone and out of sight of his buddies and only then should you go for the kill. 

Make your enemies fear the jungle and the dark, and let them know that they are not safe anywhere - even behind their seemingly-impenetrable fortifications. Expose their weaknesses to them! As the Ghosts, we will strike at any time, and we especially love the night, where we will strangle cartel members in their sleep. The resulting nightmares and insomnia alone would be sufficient payback for Santa Blanca's crimes. All of this, along with the thrill of sneaking around a base within inches of guard towers and enemies, brought back memories of old-school stealth masterpieces such as Splinter Cell Chaos Theory and also newer titles like Sniper Elite 4. 

The weapon and clothing customisation is extensive and allows for even further role-play. You can kit out your guns with specific attachments according to your preferred play style, viz. loud or silent. Make strategic use of flashbangs to incapacitate enemies and swiftly capture or dispatch them, and also use the flare gun and other distractions (Eg. diversion lure, drone noisemaker) to lure them into a kill zone. You can also dress up your entire team in the uniforms of your favourite, real-life Special Forces units from across the world and role-play as them. Similarly, you can tailor your camouflage to blend into Bolivia's diverse topography, from jungles to deserts, salt flats and ice caps.

For outfit ideas and gameplay immersion tips, I highly recommend [B]Darkdally[/B] on YouTube. As for me, I decked out my Ghosts in Jungle Warfare (US Woodland) attire, similar to what [B]Brent0331[/B] showcases on his YouTube channel. This allows me to blend into the thick, Amazonian rainforest and strike unsuspecting cartel members with swift and deadly precision. They never see it coming, and before they can alert their buddies, they are sync-shot by the Ghosts. 

The opportunities for role-playing are endless, especially with your buddies in co-op. But, I have personally stuck with single-player only [strike]because I don't have any friends and I have trust issues around strangers online[/strike] because the AI teammates are more reliable in stealth and never miss their sync shots. Yeah...that's why.

Some reviewers, especially [B]"Worth A Buy"[/B] on YouTube, have complained about the enemy-tagging system that allows you to see enemies even without a clear line of sight. Also, the drone is apparently OP since it allows you to spot and tag every single enemy. To these critics, all I have to say is that this is meant to simulate hours upon hours - or even days - of reconnaissance whereby the Ghosts have studied and memorised the patrol routes of every enemy. This is not practical - or even fun - for the player to carry out in real time; hence, the in-game "wall-hacks". Furthermore, the Ghosts also receive live updates of enemy positions from Bowman's CIA team back in the US who are conducting surveillance via satellite. This is what the enemy cloud on your mini map is meant to represent in visual form: the "Recon" part of "Ghost Recon".

With this being said, I will admit that the third-person shooting mechanics aren't very engaging, and they fall flat. They aren't terrible, but other games do them a lot better, while Wildlands leaves a lot to be desired in this department. If this is how you have played the entire game thus far - just like any other random, generic shooter - I can understand why you might find it to be sub-par. 

But now, I implore you to play it the way that it's meant to be played - [B]as a stealth game, and on advanced difficulty[/B] - and I guarantee that you'll experience some new-found appreciation for this criminally underrated title.

ps: Also, Steam review editor is totally wanking out on me and has failed to save several versions of this review, so I won't be updating it much any more as it doesn't seem to get stored.

Maps are also insanely repetitive. Many times I've been in different parts of the map looking at EXACTLY the same layout as I was just at. Besides, it doesn't matter, since what you do has not much effect overall except to advance the story a little (or grind out another skill point). Taking out something is always just temporary, everything just respawns as it was, hostility and all. So no clearing a path through a maze of anti-air missiles (in the harder parts of the map) before doing a supply mission. This can't happen since by the time you've found the next one (since you can't mark them, another lack), the one you just destroyed has probably respawned already. Just one example. 

List of pros:
- The graphics are kinda nice, I guess?
- The AI teammates are useful, I admit.
- What I got of the story is OK, but it's pure grind going through it.

List of cons: (from minor annoyances to major beefs, in no particular order)

- The driving sucks, but it seems most missions require you to do it at one point or another. 

- airplane controls aren't great, but was worse earlier. Because  "mouse mode" is turned off by default for airplanes. Turning it on and adjusting mouse sensitivity improved things a lot here. Useful video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z5WtLYsvxU4

- When you "capture" a location and free the rebels, it just resets to hostile as soon as you move away from it. So everything is hostile all the time, no matter what you do, or how much you help the rebels. Example: take out an anti-air missile system. Within minutes, it has respawned and the airspace becomes impassable again. (NOTE: I'm noticing that some locations seem to remain in rebel hands. More later)

- Can't repair vehicles, so have to find new ones all the time. 

- I can destroy an opponent's car with 4 shots of a sniper rifle, but they'll take dozens of hits from a minigun and keep going. So trying to take out vehicles defending a convoy is an exercise in frustration, mostly. Especially since even if I ram and flip them, they'll just automatically right themselves, and NOTHING happens to the crew unless I can get it to explode. 

- Massive lag spikes. In single player. Game just freezes for anything from 2 to 15 seconds, then continues. No idea why. (NOTE: definitely a game issue. Doesn't happen anywhere else.)

- if you "fail" a mission, such as losing a target, it respawns you and you lose your vehicle/helicopter. Even if you took no damage. Annoying as HECK!

- on a deserted mountain road, soon as you approach your target it's rush hour in London, with dozens of cars, civilians, and others around. Of course, the game penalizes you for hurting said civilians. Also, civilians just stand in the middle of the roads and DON'T FSCKING MOVE! Another annoyance.

- you can't shoot from a boat. As in, if you're in the water, there is no way to get ONTO the boat without either driving or being a passenger, neither or which allow you to shoot. Soon as you get out of your seat, you dive off the boat. WTF?

- can't CLIMB except in specific designated locations. Even if the thing is only waist high, can't climb it if the developer didn't put a "climb here" sticker. Sigh. Also, apparently chain-link fence is a completely impassable barrier and wire cutters don't exist.

- AI teammates will clip into surfaces and get stuck. Sometimes when they're supposed to be reviving you. Doesn't happen often, but it happens. 

- Parachute doesn't always deploy when you hit "space". I usually have to spam space to get the thing to open, and even then it doesn't always work (like, about 1/3 of the time it just does NOT open). The delay seems to make base jumping that much more dangerous, as there's a min time before you can open, and it won't open once you're "too close" to the ground.

- Can't put my own markers on the map. So no way to mark the infinite respawning anti-air missiles so I can disable them and hopefully get my chopper out before they respawn. 

- Bullet physics seem off. I've never seen a shot curve sideways before...

- The "predator" mission is a fscking joke. Or rather, it's pure trolling on the part of the developers. Direct hits with explosives don't touch it, multiple clips into it don't touch it <spoiler>thermal works great to see it</spoiler>, but it one-hit-kills anything it's aiming at and there's no dodging because it's explosive. Took me a while and several retries to realise this of course.  It *might* be possible if you have the maximum number of respawns available to you do it doesn't end the mission quite so quickly. If I don't rage-quit (or "I'm bored now" quit) the game I might come back to it.

- Can't JUMP. So if I'm going over rooftops or through scaffolding and I want to bridge a TINY gap? I CANNOT! A 50cm gap is the same as a gaping canyon as far as this game is concerned.

- and the final straw: they know EXACTLY where I am, ALL the time. Even when I move in a wide circle, they'll FOLLOW, despite not seeing me. I can trigger a C4 from max distance, and they'll know exactly where I triggered it from. I can shoot a drone jammer, and they'll know both where I shot from, and where i moved to. That's just not right.

Where Breakpoint failed, Wildlands delivered. I feel like this game is critically underrated, and if you enjoy a game that has a sense of realism to it with stealth and plenty of different ways you can go about missions, especially in co-op, this game is at least worth a try.

Pros:
- Graphics; the game is beautiful and has multiple landscapes all the way from snowy mountains to plateauing salt flats. If you like in-game photography and scenic vistas, this game is amazing for these points.
- Gameplay; this game provides multiple different ways to play, and many clever options to explore when going into combat. When assaulting a facility, you can run and gun head-on, be stealthy from up close or a distance, or tactically parachute in with all your friends. Speaking of friends, the game gets much better when you are communicating with friends in a 4-person squad,
- Multiplayer (PVP); This game is definitely interesting with it's PVP element, and while PVP definitely isn't my forte, I can safely say that it takes a little bit from R6: Siege and turns it on it's heels, giving you several operators to choose from to compete against the opponent's choices. Again, much more fun to play with friends.
- Customization; Oh boy, this game has a lot. If you like a huge variety of guns along with a huge variety of appearance options, this is a game for you. The game allows you to change your loadout on the fly to better suit certain situations. It also allows you to keep appearance presets to make you look the part of every mission.
- Mechanics; Specifically the Buchon hierarchy tree mechanics. Basically, this has you start at the bottom of these hierarchal trees fighting minor enemy characters with various different personalities and backstories, and never is one boss quite like another. As you go up, missions get harder and harder until you finally fight the Buchon, which is needed in order to progress to the end of the game. It's a really interesting system that works very well in an open-world game like this one.
- One World, Several Franchises; If you like this game enough, you'll end up finding yourself in missions that are crossovers between other Ubisoft games and other popular media. It's a really cool experience if you've played other Ubisoft games.

Cons:
- Voice lines; Something about the dialogue in this game just doesn't really do well. Every character always sounds soulless and tries to have banter that just doesn't end up being funny or amusing in the slightest.
- Story; On the surface, the story seems interesting, but the story ends up being more along the lines of a gameplay mechanic more than an actual story. El Sueno, the big bad, takes no effort to come across as just that. He preaches a better world where people of Bolivia live in harmony, while also very blatantly interrupting this ideal by killing anyone that goes as far as breathing in his direction. He's very flat overall.
- Travelling Mechanics; Honestly, driving and flying in this game is just all over the place. It's not bad but also not good, leaning more towards not good. Controls don't make sense and are very janky. Honestly it would be a lot better to switch to a controller for these bits.

Final Verdict: 7/10

Small but good enough variation & variety of missions types.
However the main missions, often times you accidentally take 1 step out of the mission zone which is not indicated at all, you fail the mission, then they boot you to loading screen & you spawn far away.
SUPER IRRITATING.

Gameplay
THE SAVING GRACE.
The graphics & Animations are beautiful to admire, and really immerse you.
Movement & interaction is amazing, your character reacts to corners & slopes smoothly,
prone, sprinting all feel natural & tactical, vaulting climbing have urgency to them,
aiming and walking all make you feel badass, & you can holster your gun for roleplay.
And the voiceacting & dialog is excellent, really tactical for almost everything you interact with.
Tons of controls to use for your character and weapon handling, even the scopes.
Irritatingly tho, is that my character often auto switches to left hand, or that the drone button is the same as attachment button.
Control scheme not very good so rebind them.
Gadgets are abit hard to navigate & choose.
The RPG elements are great, you level slowly but at a good pace, unlocking/upgrading perks & gadgets,
making you an efficient killer, but even level 1, you already are based on skill.
You carry 2 primaries & a sidearm, ammo & gadgets are based on perk unlocks.
The weapon variety is sufficient to meet anyone's liking & you pimp them with attachments & camo of your choice, beautiful.
Clothing Customization is SUPER FUN, & you can save loadouts for any terrain, change them anytime accordingly.
All aesthetic but REALLY great for immersion.

Open World
Not sure if this was the best choice, cos getting around is quite painful. The good things are that the world is very immersive, and when running around your character moves fluidly.
The vehicles, not so much. Cars, Trucks, Bikes, feel like Steel boxes moved around via magnets, the steering is horrid, driving is slowish, and if you go offroad, its over, you can climb a hill, but you cannot go over the smallest of rocks & gaps. INWHICH ITS ALL OVER THE MAP.
Boats, while they look cool & feel great cruising the water, steering sucks too.
Planes, you cannot turn properly.
Helicopters, the only sustainable mode of transport, also feel kindaweird, like hover cars, and the detection from enemies are abit weird, sometimes flying over them you dont get detected, but when you are miles away, you get spotted.
Good thing is that vehicles dont immediately blow up, they gradually get damaged, stop working then blowup on sustained damage, great details.

Dynamic TOD & weather
This is one of the better parts of the game, grass looks like grass, rain looks like rain, snow is chunky, sand is sandy, AND THE ROCKS, LOOK LIKE ROCKS. Night & day is amazing, with a unnoticable change, night has sufficient obstacles lights, which can be sabotaged or shot out, you have NVG / Thermals which looks highly realistic.

BOTS
The enemy bots are actually great, they flank, they use cover, they coordinate, they feel like ex-military, hell even the friendly rebels are useful.
They spot you realistically, which i really like.

The ''Elite team" that you have is non existant. NOW, they sound and look like an elite team, they help to point out targets & have reactions with great dialog, and you can dress coordinate them accordingly, they do rush to help you when downed.
Thats it, thats all, if you want to be immersed, turn them off in options.
The Sync shoot is horrid, they shoot thru walls & floors to hit the target, & when needed the most, they lose tracking. During stealth, they can walk strait up to an enemy, sorry, they ALWAYS do it, and they dont cover you when using the drone.
Sorry, they don't cover you AT ALL, not even when an enemy is beside you or them. I tried to use them as a shield at least, BUT they dont even block bullets for you.
Enemies always seek you and target you, even when my "elite team" is nearer or blocking.
While in vehicles, you can get them to shoot things which is good, THAT IS IF THEY CAN AIM, even when driving or flying next to a target, THEY CANT HIT ANYTHING.

Play Multiplayer / without Bots, then all is rectified & you get to be the elite team you dreamed of.

[h1] CONCLUSION [/h1]
Meh,  if you can afford the steep price point, recommend FarCry 5 instead, SO MUCH BETTER.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a largely uninteresting, open-world grindfest from the studio that has done essentially nothing but create collectathon shooters for close to a decade straight. Progression is slow and dragged out, with skillpoints tucked all over the map into areas that become largely irrelevant once collectibles have been gathered. Gunplay is interesting, but mired with half-baked stealth mechanics that largely don't operate as intended. Enemies will occasionally notice you through walls or walk right over a body without noticing.

Singleplayer and multiplayer alike are abound with recycled content, repetitive missions, and unbearable bugs. This extends even to paid DLC content, as even the very expensive weapon DLCs recycle both damage values, statistics, and animations. I care little about graphics fidelity, but extreme enemy pop-in at long range - even while on "Ultra" settings - is unacceptable in a game where snipers are a prevalent piece of the game's formula. Microstutters and complete freezing upon asset load is an extreme issue, and one that appears to have gone unfixed despite being reported mere hours after this game's launch three years ago. AI behavior is largely pathetic, especially considering it took nearly three years for friendly AIs to even be added in the first place.

It is par for the course that Ubisoft games launch in a state of disrepair, but with three years of development time after what might as well have been an early-access launch, Wildlands is still incomplete and filled with problems. Moreover, with development on this title having been haltered for well over a year in favor of their newer title Ghost Recon: Breakpoint, don't anticipate any of these issues ever being fixed.

To put a cherry on top, this game's microtransaction scheme is atrocious. Extending even beyond the metric buttload of useless cosmetics tucked away inside of lootboxes and unimaginative cosmetic singleplayer content, some paid DLC and lootbox offerings are statistically superior weapons to the base game that dominate much of the multiplayer gamemodes. Being competitive in this game's multiplayer necessitates you spending money on weapons outright or opening lootboxes in the hopes of unlocking a new weapon.

This title is not worth your money no matter the price. If you are hungry for a open-world looter shooter, look instead to Ubisoft's sister series, The Division. At the very least, those games function on the most basic level.

[h1]Plot[/h1]
The story is pretty simple. The government is turning a blind eye to allow the drug cartel, Santa Blanca, to do what they like, resulting in the largest cocaine production in the world. Your objective is to take out the leader, El Sueño. 

[h1]Customization[/h1]
Character creation is decent enough in this game. Very limited options for hairstyles and colors for hair and eyes. But thanks to all the clothing and accessories and the colors for them all you can still make a very distinct character. Clothing consists of various Tops, Vests, Pants, Footwear, and Ghillie Suits. Accessories include Eyewear, Facewear, Headwear, Headsets, Handwear, Backpacks, and Patches. You can also save outfits to preset slots if you wish to try out different outfits and cycle through them at various times. Fun for immersion if you want jackets and beanies in the snowy areas and t-shirts and sunglasses in the sun.

Customization is also available for the other 3 AI members of your team. I personally made everyone wear the same clothes/accessories to make us look like a uniform team, and just gave different colors to each person's clothing to differentiate who is who. There are also 121 different paint presets for weapons. 

[h1]Open World[/h1]
Enormous open world with seamless transitions (never experienced loading screens aside from fast travel and respawning). Vehicles include motorbikes, cars, jeeps, trucks, buses, helicopters, and planes. Yes, you can jump out of planes and helicopters to skydive and open a parachute (once you've unlocked it which is one of the first options you have.) All missions take place at locations in the open world and are approachable from any direction (even parachute in if you want to drop right into the middle of the bases).

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
General gameplay is in third-person view and aiming down sights can be alternated between third person or first person. Stealth-oriented. Scout out the area for soldiers, turrets, drone jammers, alarm systems, and power generators. Mark everything with binoculars, drone, or even just aiming your weapon at it. Everything marked will stay marked until it's been taken care of. Take care of soldiers by shooting or sneaking up and grabbing them to knock out (some can be interrogated to reveal locations for resources and upgrade points.) AI teammates can be used for Sync Shots, if you need to take out multiple soldiers at once. For most difficulties, enemy soldiers will appear on the mini-map as a large blurry circle to indicate there's a soldier in that vicinity. The blurry circle will then change into a dot once that soldier is marked. When playing on Extreme difficulty, that blurry circle will not exist, leaving you unsure if you've spotted every enemy. This one small change makes the game much more difficult in my experience and also more enjoyable as I'm now being caught off guard more often and things are less predictable. 
For those who like a challenge, feel free to disable AI teammates in the Gameplay tab under Options and play completely solo.
In terms of gameplay to progress the story... In order to lure El Sueño out of hiding, you need to work your way up the hierarchy throughout the various branches (Security, Smuggling, Influence, and Production) of the business. Search the open world for clues in order to track down Buchons. Take them out to track down an Underboss. Take out an Underboss to track down the Head. Take out the Heads to track down El Sueño. (You're only required to eliminate 2 out of the 4 Heads to get to El Sueño). You can complete these in any order you wish, but they do have an established Difficulty associated with them as a sort of "intended route".

[h1]Loadout (Weapons/Items)[/h1]
You get a loadout of three weapons, a drone, your parachute, and some items. 
Your weapons consist of two primary weapons and one secondary. 
Primary weapons include Assault Rifles, Light Machine Guns, Submachine Guns, Sniper Rifles, Shotguns, and Crossbow (only one crossbow available from what I can see).
Secondary weapons include Compact Machine Guns (one-handed SMGs, basically) and Handguns (pistols).
Weapons and their attachments can be obtained by finding weapon cases spread throughout the world.
Choose one of four types of drones: Explosive, EMP, Noisemaker, or Medic. They can all be used for scouting out an area and they each do what you'd think. Explosive blows things up, EMP disables electronics, Noisemaker makes noise (to lure enemies around for stealth) and Medic revives a fallen teammate.
Parachute can be customized with preset designs. Some can be obtained from ost are unlocked through Spec Ops Crates or Prestige Crates (as far as I can tell these are microtransaction lootboxes).

[h1]Multiplayer[/h1]
Got a few friends? Definitely play it together. I didn't play co-op because I have no friends patient enough to deal with stealth and planning tactics but I'm sure it could be way more fun trying to coordinate everything with a team of real players rather than dealing with the AI that can be pretty dumb sometimes. You can co-op any mission in the game! You can also join open lobbies. Most people seem to just go off and do their own thing in the lobby but occasionally somebody will join another player's party to help with their mission. Any progress made in co-op will transfer to your solo world and you can even do missions not available to you yet.

There's also PvP modes but I haven't gotten into those yet (even though I usually prefer PvP over anything else in games) so I can't say what the playerbase is like over there in terms of population, toxicity, and all that. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1] 
Overall a great game and I'm looking forward to completing it all again on Extreme difficulty. I don't have the skill or patience to play Extreme mode without Drones or AI teammates for sync shots. Feel free to take on that challenge if you're crazy enough! And if you want more of a challenge than that... Don't get any of the upgrades. Good luck on that. 
Anyways...

As someone who was forged in the holy fires of OG Ghost Recon, back when Desert Siege and Island Thunder were practically my personality traits, and when downloading mods required actual spiritual commitment, I was ecstatically yeeting myself back into the franchise with Ghost Recon Wildlands.

This was Nostalgia on Epic Proportions.
No. Bigger.
Nostalgia on Biblical Proportions.

Fallen Ghosts—chef’s kiss. Hard, intense, fun, and just the right amount of “Oh wow I definitely wasn’t emotionally prepared for that.” I 100%ed it too because apparently I have commitment issues unless it involves video games.

But then…
Narco Road.

It doesn’t feel like Ghost Recon.
It feels like someone said, “What if we took everything serious and tactical about the franchise… and replaced it with Monster Energy and questionable life choices?”

Still, Wildlands overall? Absolute blast. 10/10 would destabilize a fictional nation again.

[h1] Ghost Recon Wildlands [/h1]

Developed and published by Ubisoft in 2016. This is a review of PC version of the game written in summer 2020.

The game takes place in Bolivia. In the game you are a member of "Ghosts“, under a special operation to take down a local cartel called "Santa Blanca“. As a Ghost you are supposed to be invisible, unfortunately, that doesnt always work. I played the game coop with a friend. For the most part my friend and I tried to be as stealthy as possible, though this became increasingly more difficult late-game. There were times when we would remain undetected under the noses of 20 enemy NPCs without being noticed, then there were times that we would get shot by an NPC with dual wielding Uzis from about 300 meters away without having done anything to call attention. Overall, if you are considering buying this game, keep in mind that its not always easy. I personally would suggest playing with a friend, in my opinion, playing this solo wouldn’t be all that fun.


[*] [b] Story [/b]

The story progresses with you taking down members of the cartel, first the peons, and lower tier members, eventually escalating to taking out more challenging targets. I feel the need to note this as I claimed that there would be no spoilers, all this is explained in the main menu cutscene, I dont consider it a spoiler. The game is a pretty simple concept, although, if you play it on higher difficulties it can take you about 50 hours.


[*] [b] Gameplay [/b]

The gameplay is good in my opinon. I think the best part of the game is the weapon handling. It is responsive and you really need to control the weapons to keep aim on the target. Customization of your character is also great, with a variety of options to choose from, you can make a loadout that fits your playstyle very well. Unfortunatately, there are other areas that are lacking I think, forexample, the driving is just horrible, so for bigger part of the game, you will be using a helicopter.


[*] [b] Graphic design [/b]

The game looks amazing, especially for its age. For example, you can feel that they really captured Bolivia‘s diversity in its weather and geographical features, you may be driving across salt planes, trying not to die while sliding down a hill full of palms on a motorcycle, but you can’t help but to take in the beauty of the scene even still. This attention to detail on the bioms is great. You won’t find yourself bored even when nothing too exciting is going on as you can enjoy the scenery. The guns and your character look as realistic as possible with details like accurate badges on your uniform.


[*] [b] Characters [/b]

You play as the character Nomad, a ghost operative, an American super soldier, impressive weapons, strong voice, very much a patriot. Then there is a girl named Bowman, a CIA operative, she is your boss and guides you thoughout the game. Every time appearance she has, she is quite the badass. As to your allies, you have none, besides the rebels that you can call for help. There is no shortage of villaines characters though, and they’re not all the same stereotypical villain types either, they’re quite unique in their own ways.


[*] [b] Sound design [/b]

The game does a few things well, but, most others seem to have been done with very little effort. With the soundtrack there are some nice songs, unfortunately to me they are relatively easy to forget. All but a few of the weapons sound the same, one of the exceptions being miniguns, although, those are different in a bad way, they’re are unnecessarily loud in comparison to the rest of the game. Vehicles leave much to be desired as well, like the guns, they all sound the same, no real variation which shouldn’t have been difficult to do. I am aware that the game’s focus is not audio authenticity but I feel that a little variation would have gone a long way.


[*] [b] Bugs and technical issues [/b]

You’re sure to run into bugs relatively often, my friend and I frequintly got stuck under rocks, in the hills, or even ended up flying under the map. It’s as annoying as you can imagine, so you do have to be patient. As I said before, the driving in this game isn’t great, there is a bug that occurs far to often, where if you hit a small rock, knocking yourself off a motorcycle, you’re likely to fly pretty far away, and end up dead because there isnt a way to open your parachute. Also, and I won’t spoil anything, but due to a bug near the end of the game, we ended up not having the best time. As few as the bugs may be that I mentioned, they’re so common and cause so much stress that I feel they’re worth thinking about. There are of course some funny bugs, for example, running with you team and them being upsidedown for you.


[*] [b] Final rating of the game [/b]

Objectively, this is not a bad game, but its not above 6/10 overall. However, the fact that you can play this game with friends gets it at least one addition point from me. Its just fun to play with friends. The bugs can be fun as well as you can laugh about instantly dying, or mess around and exploit some of the game’s mechanics to see some wacky stuff. Then launching a mortal fire on top of your heads, because you are so stupid. My personal opinion is that if you have friends to play with, have fun with it. Buy it, laugh at the some of the stupid moments with your friends, be shocked by others. I’d say this gets a solid 7/10. [b] It’s decent [/b]

There was so much potential with Wildlands, but it fell short.

1. Failure to utilize a large, beautiful open world
2. Poorly Designed Campaign & AI Dynamics
3. Non-Existent End Game. 
4. Mercenary Mode

1. Open World. The developers created a large, beautiful open world, but only about 20% is truly utilized for its mission sets with the remaining parts rarely explored because there is no reason to venture into those areas. 

2. The Campaign. Initially, the game was marketed to to a feature a series of surgical operations, targeting key personnel and nodes of the Santa Blanca drug cartel. The campaign missions were a mix of some exciting and some poorly designed missions. The campaign didn't stray too far from the marketing scheme, in the sense that the player IS targeting high value individuals. In many cases, the player must locate and gather information for the whereabouts of high value individuals - in some cases, you are detaining personnel for interrogation that drive the story. 

However, the campaign is also LIFELESS; there is no cause-and-effect within the story. For example, if the player disassembles Santa Blanca's security wing, there is no reduction in patrols or degraded relationship with the Bolivian Military wing, Unidad. At least in Far Cry games, the enemy forces attempt to take back outposts. There is no attempt with the meta-game AI. They just sit there and take it, and it is very disappointing. 

3. There is no end-game. Unless you enjoy chasing convoys for pointless points that you don't need or running the mundane, boring, and senseless daily challenges. As stated, the only available challenge are resource convoys that players can capture for unnecessary resources, or awful, lazily designed, and mundane Daily Challenges. 

The End Game is an area that had a HUGE missed opportunity. An opportunity that could've used something similar to The Divisions 'contract' missions. Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Wildlands is another 'open-world' title by Ubisoft that allows you and up to 3 teammates to traverse a massive world, fighting enemies and their 1000 outposts, unlocking new weapons, skills etc. Aka your average Ubisoft game. Without going too indepth with the game, in summary its a "sum-of-its-parts" situation. Not all of the parts are fantastic but its the fact that they are all consistently solid that make playing this an all around great experience. Sure there are some features that faulter and there are so many nitpicks that can be made but generally that doesn't bring down the rest of the game.
The unrestricted open-world aspect of it is really the cherry on top here. Any one of your teammates (up to 4) can be doing separate missions at different corners of the map and everyone can receive the xp/progress rewards for them. While I haven't completed the game yet, at no point was I prevented from just leaving a mission. Or tackling the mission any way I wanted to. A colossal step up for Ubisoft. Character customization is also pretty solid with enough options to really keep you satisfied for the most part

As for the woes: for the most part cringy and boring dialogue, various standard ubisoft glitches. Thats it. 
I highly recommend this to anyone considering it, its fantastic. 8/10.
