I love this game. I've been playing it since it was released and have l logged almost 500 hours worth of completing the different stories and just plain ol' messing around. Having played many of the other great T.C. titles, this one by far is my most favorite as it is very well done in virtually every aspect.

There are probably as many merits to this game as there are problems, so this is not really a recommandation for everyone.

Pros:
- Gun physics is well done, the ballistics is similar to sniper elite IV without wind.
- There is a good variety of weapons and attatchments to choose from.
- Drones and night/thermal vision work nicely in this game. It is satisfying to learn to use drones to gather information on higher difficulties.
- The plot, albeit generic for some people, is supported by well conceived lore items (audio/video recordings, paper files). They are interesting enough that I (a quite impatient person) will go out of my way to collect them.
- The landscape and open world looks beautiful.
- The co-op has a lot of potential when you increase game difficulty and remove HUD.
- Performance is rather ok. 60fps with 2k resolution on a system with 1060 on medium/high setting.

Cons (there are a ton):
- AIs (friendlies and hostiles) are just awful, awfully awful:
 = Enemies will instantly pinpoint your location if they notice anything bad (see a dead body, hear an explosion, etc.). They are also telepathic.
 = AI squadmates are not a choice in single player, they will follow you anywhere unless you tell them to sit at a location.
 = AI squadmates ignores flanking enemies completely, consistently. This means if you sit on top of a tower reconning with drones, it is entirely likely that your squadmates guarding the stair case will watch enemies running up the tower to shaft you with dispassion. I've watched this happening on my drones too many times.
 = Enemies on all difficulties have ridiculous aim, meaning they can land an uzi burst on you hiding in the tallgrass in the middle of a moonless night while a storm is going on from 300m away. They can make Shroud look like a blind old lady.
- Mild cases of invisible walls, meaning a well aligned shot can hit something along the trajectory with a bigger hitbox than visible. 
- Stealth gameplay is a trainwreck. Most of the missions will make you face overwhelming number of enemies, hence stealth is essential on higher difficulty (due to AI aim prowess). But the mechanic is so poorly done it feels like an added feature on a finished game.
- Some missions are, imo, very poorly designed. One type of mission requires you to defend a radio broadcast in the middle of the street for 3 mins, while enemies pour in from all directions, with your position exposed. Let's say it feels like fighting 30 Shrouds high on coco at the same time, while protecting a truck sized hostage in the open.
- There are a handful of bugs in my 80 something hours of gameplay.

Things you may or may not like:
- Uplay.
- Ubi-grind.
- Ubi dlc items. It means you have to pay $ for certain weapons, so if you are a compulsive hoarder this may upset you.
- Barely existing cover mechanics. People feel differently about cover shooters.
- Certain game mechanics. E.g. the Bolivian popo that works like gta popo that will send unlimited reinforcement unless you run.
- The shooting mechanics (bullet drop, muzzle velocity, ADS etc). I am a huge fan of Sniper Elite IV gunplay and accostomed to rainbow six siege weapon handling, so GRW feels like a watered down hybrid of both (no wind, no leaning, no rapelling). If only they just copied either of the two, if only.
- It's a finished game, so devs won't be changing anything significantly.

In conclusion, GRW is worth the price if you can get it on 50% sale (for average FPS gamers), as it has a good deal of content and is a decent shooting simulator even without it. If you want a polished experience, know that this is a Ubi game, so you will be triggered left and right, and looking elsewhere will save you some torment.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a good game.
The action takes place in Bolivia, where powerful drug cartels are ruling the land.

As part of a four-man special ops team, you have various missions and side missions to complete.
There are also pieces of intelligence placed around the map (which help you level up), as well as various gun caches (which give you new guns to use).

You don't have to follow the story-line, but can just roam around the map if you like, looking for fights to get into (the drug cartels are happy to oblige).
There are several types of vehicles you can use to get around, with a wide variety of cars, motorbikes, and helicopters (and some boats too).

I've played this both as a single-player (you and three AI guys) and multi-player game (up to four players), and have found that both work well.
I have been able to complete most of the missions in single-player mode, except for one sneak mission (where the AI guys kept on getting the attention of the guards).

All up, it's a good game.
I can recommend Ghost Recon Wildlands for a bit of shooting fun.

SHORT REVIEW:
Ghost recon Wildlands is a game that thrives on immersion and on the overall experience it provides to the player. Some of the individual features of the game might have flaws (the AI, bossfights  and driving most of all) but the overall experience makes up for most of the hiccups the game has. Going from stealthily taking down snipers in enemy camps in a series of coordinated shots with your teammates to chasing a convoy in an helicopter while making bullets rain from a minigun on the armored truck feels smooth, exciting and fun. I often felt like I was a victim to the circumstances the world presented, forced to adapt and freak out a little when the enemy VIP tries to leave the base via helicopter the second an enemy spots me. Still, motocross drifting  through the muddy roads and lush vegetation of one of the (if not the) largest, richest (in biomes and missions) and best looking open world maps I've ever seen in a videogame feels incredible. I'll go as far as saying that for the discounted price, the game is worth picking up solely for the way it looks, it will stress you computer, but the risult is worth every FPS you loose. Jokes aside, the game is just fun. The story and map achieve a great level of immersion, missions (main and secondary both) don’t feel like a waste of time and everything you do is excting, packed with action, useful, and (if you’re into customization) you can look damn good while doing it. To me, if it wasn’t for Uplay and the lootbox thing it would be an 8/10, but honestly, for the discounted price, it’s a must have


DEEPER ANALYSIS AND CONSIDERSIONS:
Aside from my general considerations one very important thing to point out is the quality of story. It is a well written tale analyzing the "drug cartel" topic quite deeply asking a question that is "what if a cartel got so powerful it would end up running a country?". The Santa Blanca cartel isn't just a random evil organization, carachters themselves admit the genius of the corrupt system they have created, the same system you as the main carachter are trying to dismantle. The game provided me with entertaining Intel, recordings, pictures and videos on every single enemy I hunted down, trying to make me understand who the person is, what are his/her motifs, and why I should take him/her out. The focus put on making enemies feel like actual people and not your everyday NPC takes the immersion and the story telling value of the game to a whole other level. The ones who actually end up lacking personalities are the "good guys" who's reasons to even be in Bolivia I found to be very arguable without even touching on points like their oddly blind obedience during morally ambiguous moments and the way they joke about in-game events, theese things kind of mess with the feeling of immersion because I ended up in a situation where the game tells a very detailed and serious story about drug-trade, tradition, poverty, power, culture and corruption while in-game carachter sometimes are like "yeah right LOL". The feeling that the game portrays carachters as actual people but the carachters don't take themselves or events seriously kinda made me scratch my head. 

Regardless, the main protagonist of the game is without any doubt the map. Bolivia is beautiful, alive and filled with things to do and places to explore. From mountain tops to forests, little islands and salt flats, swamps and dry deserts, crop fields and ancient ruins the map really has it all. The quiet, calm moments I sometimes spend resupplying and regrouping with my squad after clearing an enemy camp can feel meditative, leaving me in awe to the beautiful, fictional, world of Wildlands. I often choose to walk or drive rather than fly from place to place just so I can let the view sink in deeper. The map is also the canvas on which the action takes place being filled with all kinds of missions, collectables, military and non-military vehichles that with the aid of the autosave mechanic allow for fun, exciting action moments to which you must adapt (being unable to load a previous save) making the experience feel different at every enemy encounter and genuinely challenging at higher difficulties. The tasks you have to complete hardly ever feel like a waste of time, there are no useless collectables or tedious secondary missions, everything you do or collect feels somewhat useful or it helps progress towards and objective. Honestly, the game is just fun. If you add to the mix things like the chance to join other people in the co-op mode, the surprisingly deep weapons and carachter customization, the fun easter eggs missions, the challenges, ghost mode, the surprising longevity of the story, the amazingly well done gun play, you get a huge game with a tons of content that, most importantly, manages to be FUN basically all the time


However there are low point,  in my opinion they are the driving, AI and bossfights

The driving is arcadey, and there's nothing inherently wrong with it, but driving Humvees, Jeeps and Trucks that feel too fast and weightless doesn't feel right and breaks the immersion, still, bikes, helicopters and boats, feel amazing to drive. A honorable mention must go to the offroad bike driving experience, without any doubt, it was one of the single best in-game driving experiences I’m ever had in any game, ever.

 The AI of enemies is bad but not terrible, point is, sometimes enemies just act dumb; the one of single player allies, on the other hand, is just lacking. Ordering them around simply feels bad, the commands are always too generic both for stealth and guns-blazing and when left alone allies seem to have no idea on how to preserve your and their lives. I also don't understand why can't allies drive when NPCs do and it triggers me a bit having to trash every helicopter I parachute off of because none of my allies can safely land it or fly it away. Honestly, I felt like the only point of NPC teammates was to take out marked enemies

However, after playing for a while, these issues seemed to fade in the background of the general experience the game provides. Unfortunately the lowest point of the game, the one I still just can't ignore (of course in my opinion) are the boss fights. I spend over 2 hours to track down a boss (I take my time). The process of gathering Intel, watching videos and completing mission builds up to the moment you capture/kill one of the bosses, unfortunately this highly anticipated missions are not always particularly satisfying. This completely shatters the immersion for me that's why it's the one thing I consider a proper negative point of the game

Ultimately the absoultely worst part of the game are Ubisoft and Uplay. Things like the Alt + F4 Uplay drops on you if you loose connection because you can't play offline to over priced DLCs and lootboxes that literally offer 2 weapons and 2 cosmetics for THE SAME DAMN PRICE OF THE DISCOUNTED BASE GAME feel like a genuine dropkick of the face by ye olde french developer 

Just to wrap this up, the game isn’t perfect, but it sure is pretty and fun to play, for the discounted price it’s a no-brainer

Honestly? I guess it isn't the worst game in the world, but Ghost Recon Wildlands isn't a great game either. There is nothing that has been done in this title that hasn't been better done somewhere else before, and there is a handful of issues that essentially boil down to Ubisoft being a goof that kept this title from reaching it's true potential.

The main problems I see with this game are; Technical issues Ubisoft has failed to fix, boring gameplay and anti-consumer business practices.

Google Ghost Recon Wildlands for technical glitches and compatibility issues and your jaw will drop. These range from the minor and goofy(having your helicopter launched to the top of the map after trying to land) to downright critical gameplay issues, like game crashes. I experienced several random game crashes. Every time i logged in to the game i had to toggle Fullscreen > Windowed > Fullscreen to actually play the game in full screen mode. My Ai teammates were an absolute nuisance as they flat out ignored commands and stood at my feet while i would bleed to death without reviving me. Simple mechanics, like traversing terrain, were awkward and buggy, often leading to comprimising situations you intended to avoid. I flat out gave up on the stealth mechanics in this game, as they were unpolished to the point of being an unviable strategy. I was clearly spotted through walls, tracked by non-alerted enemies through cover as if they were locked on to my character and even got killed by a grenade on the other side of multiple walls. I was reading other reviews where people would have their game file or earned items disappear. This game has been out for far too long, and Ubisoft has had the tools to fix these issues. Instead, they let critical issues interfere with the game experience, to focus on wringing more profit out of the game, like DLC and MTX's.

The gameplay itself, for being an elite team of tier 1 operatives given free range to take out a cartel in Bolivia, is incredibly lackluster. Being a Ubisoft game, about 90% of this game is generic objectives and side missions that supposedly add "depth" to the game. From the first hour to the tenth hour, the gameplay didn't change. I was doing the exact same things in the first area, that I ended up doing in all of the other provinces i conducted operations in. Even the pattern for reaching a Buchon was copy paste throughout the game. Mess with production, put a gun in someones face, capture someone close to the buchon and then capture/kill the HVT in an obvious ambush. "Free to operate your way" feels like a meme the fourth time you're forced to walk into an obvious ambush. In later provinces, the developers tried to modify the missions by simply piling multiple missions you've already done elsewhere into a single missions which gets irritating quickly and seems like a waste of the player's time solely so Ubisoft can proudly exclaim they have "hours and hours of content".

These issues are an adamant deal breaker for me because I know for a fact that Ubisoft can do better. The fact that they had day one paywalled content and continue to release DLC's and microtransactions while there are still critical issues with the game, proves that yet again, Ubisoft is putting profits before the player experience. Ubisoft's development team has all the tools needed for success. They have the money, the creative tools, the manpower and the fanpower to create well polished and cutting edge gameplay experiences.

If Ubisoft put half of their effort into THAT goal, as opposed to finding a way to jam in as many microtransactions as possible, They might have produced a more memorable and reputable title in the past few years. 

Another thing to note too - This game was easily shallow enough to beat on the free weekend if you ignore doing a full clear of the provinces, like me. Despite there being play time left on my account for the free weekend, I only had access to the game for 24 hours so i was unable to finish up the last few missions i would've had to finish the story.

Perhaps Ubisoft knew i was close to knocking off El Sueno and decided to bench me.

Just wait for another free weekend and you'll beat it if you didn't this time. Maybe you won't get suckered into having to pay for the base game and all of the DLC's too.

All the roads and environments are so ragged and cluttered that you cannot maneuver a vehicle through them. The only viable, quick form of transport are the helicopters, which fly decently. This ruins the game's pacing, the fun of world exploration, and how quickly you can get to objectives. Fortunately there is fast travel, but even that has faults.

The shooting mechanics are actually quite enjoyable - that is if you ever can find yourself in circumstances to be firing your weapon. Stealth isn't tenable, since the cover mechanics are shoddy and unreliable, and enemy sensors are too unpredictable. The gun customization looks great on the offset, but actually isn't once I started using it. Same goes with the character creator - easy to use, but in retrospect not that great.

TL;DR:
It's fine. It's a Ubisoft game. Bullet travel time is dope. Everything else is see-sawing between meh and aaight. Decent deal for 20 bucks. Otherwise ignore.

Extended thoughts:
It's a Ubisoft game. With all the good and the bad that comes with that statement. It's got quality in presentation, sure, but it varies very little from other titles released since 2012 onward. 

It's like they managed to mush together both Far Cry 3/4 and The Division to make the best of their mediocre inspirations. Which, unsurprisingly, ends up still pretty mediocre. It's servicable, sure. Plays fine. Looks great. But you've played this game before. Nothing here to merit full price. At 20 bucks I think it's a pretty good deal for what you're getting, it shoots better than the Division at least. But other than that, you could just skip this title and miss nothing of value. A statement that is becoming sadly ever more prominent when relating to Ubisoft titles.

I will say however that I like that the bullets have travel time and bullet drop. This goes for all of your weapons, making you place your shots more carefully. I also like that - contrary to what you might think - that you don't capture outposts and then suddenly control that part of the map forever, á la Far Cry 3/4. This time they have the bad people respawn if you've been away from that particular place/outpost/etc. Which is nice, because you never really run out of things to shoot. I haven't yet felt like I was lacking in progression in the story, but at the same time, it does somewhat invalidate the impact that you're supposed to have. I mean, after you've killed the the Local Villain in Sesame Street Bolivia, nothing much changes it feels like. You just get out of the region and begin the cycle anew, which wears out fairly quickly. Moreso because of the fact that missions are structured very similarly, and never really demand your full attention when you've played enough and realize how every mission will play out. The game shows its hand in terms of content very early, and never really improves. Locations change. Missions don't. A region will play almost exactly like the other region, only now with Bigger Boys, Tougher Dudes, different scenery. Which is typical Ubisoft Sandbox Progression.

Besides that, the customization is dope. But I then immediately have to retract the statement about customization due to just how much is locked behind lootboxes or other menial nonsense designed to waste your time. And I can already hear the argument of 'But it's just cosmetic' ringing my ears. To which I reply to that strawman: frankly, even the 'just cosmetic' parts are an integral part of the game experience. If you didn't care about looking cool, or we didn't care about graphics at all, we'd be playing with untextured polygons in vague shapes. If only gameplay and merit carried games, we wouldn't have half of the gaming demographic made up of people who play mobile games. But this is starting to sound like a soapbox. The lootboxes in Ubisoft games have always been tolerable, and this title is no exception. But they're still in the game, and just because they're the least obtrusive with implementing them doesn't mean they're void of scrutiny altogether in that respect. 

That'd be like praising a cook because they only put a little bit of dung on top of your meal, which you think is better just because other cooks have a horse directly defecate on top of their meals. In both scenarios, you're still willingly eating dung. In the former case just less of it. My point is that lootboxes are stupid.

After a great many attempts and continuous wishes to have an open world Ghost Recon game where stealth is greatly rewarded, and you can enjoy driving and flying whilst having countless options to combine all of theese, I must say that this is just too far away from what it sets out to be to even remotely deserve my support. Let alone anyone else's. 

In honesty, this is what this game is: 
A content-rich third person shooter with sneak elements and many stats, skills and abilities to combine with just as many weapon, appearance and attatchment options in order to create a Ghost Recon operative that you'll love playing as
The graphics and scenery leaves little to be asked as this game along with a clear majority of Ubisofts' games are above all graphically impressive.

But then we arrive at the second layer... And the fact that this isnt a movie, or a photoshoot. It is a GAME. Which also far too often seem to pass the minds at Ubisoft entertainment by. 
A game needs gameplay. And I do not think that the crew spend even a fraction of their time spent painting the landscape on forming the gameplay itself.

This is sad, but to the point and honest, how the game works:
Your controls of the character you play as are quite varied, your moves are a little bit unrealistic at times, but far within reason (and personally I think they are great). 
Vehicles however, are controlled in a rough, speedy and very unpolished way. Which makes it very unrealistic in a stealth game, where smooth turning and careful planning are crucial to the "soul of the game". And vehicle integration as it is does not go well with this at all. There are a great many vehicles to choose from, but they all drive relatively the same. 
And the only smooth driving there is would be the linear, predefined driving of the NPC's. Who when even driving at all, only have two speeds: Normal or supersonic. "But this is only in driving" you think? No. 

Unless enemy NPC's are set to the first 3 out of their 5 stages: Stationary. Walking. Suspecting. Hunting and Engaging.
The game's weakness starts to show. And bugs appear. The alerted NPC's will for a time know exactly where you are are shoot you as soon as it is possible with insane speeds, let alone accuracy if you are playing on a high difficulty. The time it takes an NPC to ready their weapon and shoot you down may be less than 0.5 seconds. Making bot fights as unrealistic as they are annoying to deal with. 

In a game like this the whole idea is to try avoid as many engagements as possible. But you would think that this would be because it is a game about stealth, and not because the actual engagements are tedious and boring.

Interactions with bots is what the mostpart of the game is all about. So why have the dev team put as little effort into this as humanely possible?
Instead all they are adding now are more cosmetics and premade weapons for their microtransaction crates. Lots of content that you will not be able to unlock just by playing. 
Mistake upon mistake will and probably have... Killed yet another game that has and had all it needed to become great.

I got a lot of enjoyment out of this game, but take that with a grain of salt, as this game has a lot of flaws that could very well turn someone off.

But first, what I like:
- Easy to pick up, put down, repeat
- Gorgeous scenery, great graphics
- Huge map with different terrain / climates
- Tons of gun and character modifications earned in-game
- Crossover missions are super cool 
- Satisfying gun mechanics / physics 
- Synch Shot is pretty darn cool
- Drone is a cool gadget
- Story is pretty well done, especially with all the King Slayer files adding details

The Bad:
-  Awful AI. Enemies have eyes in the back of their heads and will shoot you at 150yds, dual-weilding machine pistols. Your AI teammates are clunky to control, will waltz right up to enemies without being noticed (thankfully lol), and other than for sync shot are kind of just spectators excxept to heal me when I get plowed over by a civilian in a truck. 
- Missions can be done out-of-order, but do not account for it. For instance, you will have a current mission / cutscene referencing someone whom you've already dealt with in a prior mission. Def an immersion killer. Either have the main missions follow a set order or make multiple variants to account for people who go a differerent route. 
- Repetition. Side missions are just dozens of the same 5 things in different areas, some story missions are very similar. However, there is no one way to go about any of them as base / hideout layouts and terrain are VERY different. As are the defenses present.

Neutral:
- Driving. Driving fullsize vehicles and helicopters was easy for me to pick up and become adept at. Motorcycles and airplanes were a pain. Motorcycles are unweildy off road (where you want them most), and I dont know what the deal is with the planes, but I was terrible.

MY opinion:
I bought it on sale for $25 and I would absolutely do it again, and would for sure play a sequel that is hopefully more polished.  If you like Far Cry-esque open world military games, I would give it a shot next time its on SALE. You'll know if its right for you within a couple hours.

After over 300 hours in to the game and l'm still looking forward every day to get to play this game with my friends. Overall the game is somewhere between a really good and a masterpiece game, 9/10
 Here's a little more detailed review:

Graphics
You'll need one hell of a PC to enjoy this game to it's full potential, but if you can manage that, you'll enjoy probably one of the best graphics ever made in a videogame.

Gameplay 
I personally love it,with one exception. The cardriving mechanics suck in this game. But to make up for that, bikes are really fun. The gameplay itself offers a variety of stuff to do, real fun sidemissions where you get to blow doors off and rush to a building, defend a position from a horde of cartel sicarios and so much more. The main storyline is mostly fun to play as it offers an insane amount of options for you to choose how to capture or kill the target you want. 

Combat
Sometimes all-out combat is your only choice and that is awesome. I've had so many epic moments with watching out for the choppers my friend just blew out of the sky, driving down extremely steep hill with hotdes of Unidad after me, and epic car chases that end up in a helicopter extraction or ♥♥♥♥ blowing up. I just love it

PvP
Okay, so there's not much about the PvP. It's sometimes fun to just kick back and relax in multiplayer with all these different - but all fun - classes.

Extreme difficulty
OK, now read the next line carefully:
THE EXTREME DIFFICULTY IS NOT A JOKE
the game says it's "a realistic simulation scenario", and that's what it is. Enemies spot you really easily, one shot means you're dead. But boy, is it fun? Hell yeah! Once you've played the game through on regular (which is what l recommend for new players), try playing it again on extreme and.. see it yourself

Also the game offers the ghost mode, perma-death extremely difficult mode. I recommend you try it out with a few friends and feel the frustration when one of you dies 

Overall l higly recommend buying this game, especially if it's in sale.

Waaaaaaaaaay back in the day (the early to mid 2000's) Ghost Recon was a tense tactical shooter with an emphasis on stealth and teamwork over blowing ♥♥♥♥ up. Ubisoft seem to have looked at this idea and thought to themselves "maybe what the fans really want is a boring linear third person cover shooter with some stealth elements?" It was this line of thinking that left us with the snore fest known as Ghost Recon Future Soldier a few years back, but what about Wildlands? Ubisoft threw off the linearity issue by swinging the pendulum so hard the other direction that they lost the point again. Wildlands is an open world action game that is trying to be comparable to Just Cause or Grand Theft Auto, but with none of the freedom offered in those games. You are ostensibly a government agent working on behalf of the United States within Bolivia to take down the Santa Blanca drug cartel. A cool concept but when put into the context of an open world sandbox, it results in the game kneecapping itself to stay consistent. For example, you cannot shoot civilians or you will get a game over. There are also numerous missions that will result in a failure state if you break stealth, which is fine if that's how you want the game to be but there is zero indication based on the available equipment that stealth is the best or even a good option. Yeah, you get suppressors  and a drone but most of the upgrades are combat oriented and many weapons cannot mount suppressors. There are also times where the game just alerts the enemies based on a scripted event, so even if you were running a perfect stealth op it gets ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. The point is that the game never gives you an indication of what to expect so you cannot prepare accordingly. 

How is this a ghost recon game exactly? Yeah, I know your unit is called the "ghosts" but they seem awfully under equipped. Like for example, the ghosts in Future Soldier had futuristic active camo, but our ghosts in Wildlands have hoodies? And don't come at me saying "oh they're trying to blend in" when you can wear a plate carrier and a ghillie suit with three guns strapped to you at all times. 

But none of that matters if the game is fun. Is the game fun? If you have a full squad of friends, and even then only for probably 15-20 hours max. After a while, you realize that the game is one big repetative loop. Your goal in the game is to take out underbosses to get to overbosses to reach the big boss himself, El Sueno. The problem is that all of these steps take the form of 3 things: kill someone, break something, steal something. Now imagine you are expected to do those same 3 things for upwards of 50 hours to beat the game. Sound boring? You're not wrong my friend. 

Look overall, the game is just boring. It's not bad, or broken, or offensive, it's just the gameplay equivelant of plain oatmeal. No variety, no flare, no fun. And what, I ask, is the point of a game if it isn't fun?

Pros: 
- Combat is very enjoyable; it has the nice Far Cry gameplay loop of scouting out a base, thinning the herd of enemies, and then clearing out the rest in a firefight
- The presence of multiple factions hostile to each other can lead to interesting engagements
- Finding collectibles by collecting intelligence is fun, as it means when you enter a new province you need to capture a few lieutenants or find some intel caches to find out what's in the area, rather than just climbing a tower and revealing everything
- Finding weapons and attachments is also enjoyable, as the things you want to get tend to be in enemy camps, giving you an incentive to raid them
- Skill progression is well-balanced; I never felt the need to grind for resources
- Allies are actually upgraded as the enemy advances so they don't end up underpowered, although this is based on stat bonuses rather than improved equipment
- It's generally very enjoyable mechanically
- There are a lot of nice touches, like if you interrupt certain conversations your character will apologize for the interruption before it continues.

Cons:
- The game is really buggy. In the last five hours I played, I fell out of the world once, clipped through terrain at least twice, got stuck on terrain thrice, had prone animations bug out such that I was running really slowly and my body was pointed in a direction tangent to the terrain I was on, and had the game crash when loading a cutscene. Objects held by characters in cutscenes also tend to desync or float away from their hands.
- People's accents, even supposedly native Bolivians, are pretty bad, although theirs are somewhat better. The most egregious example of this is a line where your CO pronounces "madre" as /mædrə/.
- The male voice for the player is particularly bad for this, but 
- they seem to have forgotten to record some of the voice lines for the female character, most egregiously in the entire ending cutscene for the Splinter Cell crossover mission.
- Lip syncing is really bad.
- Mission checkpointing is pretty bad, often forcing you to restart from the beginning.*
- The game includes missions with instant fail on alert conditions, which has been recognized as bad game design for running on a decade now.
- Side missions like disabling two antennae on a time limit or doing wave defense aren't all that interesting and I tended to avoid them, except the convoy ones and the raids which are pretty fun.
- Your squadmates are invisible to enemies during stealth and teleport to you, especially when you're in a vehicle. This makes them feel unreal, especially since
- sync shots ignore LOS, so you can use them to eliminate enemies none of you could hit instantly. They also look really bad since enemies just get shot in the feet then collapse. To be fair, you generally can't use them against enemies in buildings.
- In contrast, escorted characters from the crossover missions don't teleport, which actually works just fine but make the allies' powers more immersion-breaking.
- AI is generally pretty bad. I saw allies and enemies alike running directly into a wall until they teleported to me or got shot, respectively.
- Enemies cheat a little in the "hunted" stage of combat, sending people to locations you're at in addition to your last known position.
- There's no real sense of front lines, which is a shame because actually having to help the rebels secure and control territory could've been pretty engaging.
- Factions' relationships to each other are unintuitive. They tend not to engage each other unless they see the other firing their weapons, which essentially boils down to whether the player character's around. I saw plenty of rebel technicals moving through cartel-infested areas or Unidad checkpoints without a shot being fired. This could've worked well if the game's thematic message was about Americans ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ things up, but 
- aside from a few "subversive" lines acknowledging that you're playing as Americans operating in Latin America and that cartel torturers use American techniques it's pretty standard post-Tom Clancy Tom Clancy: your CO regularly orders or suggests doing some pretty despicable things without much comment. 
- Back to the checkpoints: if you don't stop in them, you won't be spotted, even if you're driving an armed Hummer. It really makes the factions operating them less threatening. 
- The lack of squad customization is a bit disappointing; all of the default squadmates wear standard dudebro attire which makes an actual uniform stand out. 
- Vehicle handling is atrocious. It's not as bad as Just Cause 3 but it's up there.
- The world could do with some more detail. For example, to my knowledge the rebels are never given an actual name, and many settlements are named something like <province> Outpost #1. Also, naming your Aymara rebel leaders [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%BApac_Katari]Pac Katari[/url] and [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%BApac_Amaru]Amaru[/url] is pretty lazy.

TL;DR It's a really fun game, but I can't recommend it because purchasing it would give Ubisoft more data in support of lootboxes. If you really want it, which is totally understandable, wait for it to be in a Humble Bundle and make sure you give Ubisoft none of the money. Your charity probably needs it more anyway.

*This was most egregious in the Splinter Cell mission because you aren't allowed to kill enemies or be spotted until you reach Sam Fisher, which means that you'll die a lot when assaulted by the entire base and then have to reinfiltrate, doing the whole process of reconning, without a drone, since it's jammed, but under a (pretty generous tbf) time limit. The game's mechanics are not suited to nonlethal runs, and it shows, since your only option is throwing a diversion lure, which you don't start with and even once unlocked you only have three of until the end, and knocking people out counts as killing them. It ended up being easier to simply wait guards out and then cheese the fight by camping in a room.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands is a game that takes you into a fictitious Bolivia where the drug cartel called Santa Blanka essentially takes over the country. Your job, should you choose to buy the game, is to take on the cartel, remove it from power saving the day.

Why 8/10?

The campaign map is huge, divided up into territories controlled by members of different branches of the cartel. There is no set order to which territories you investigate and which cartel members you can take out. Its all up to your discretion in what order this occurs. There is a plethora of weapons to choose from with equally as many weapon upgrades to customize your gear.

Problems with the game come in two flavors: Repetiativeness and the need for multiplayer campaigns. 

So what do I mean by repetativeness. When you go to a province, you find the intel you need by either interrogating people or finding intel caches, you find the weapons cashe or weapons crates, then you can find the main cartel memeber you are looking for and do his/her mission. Once you are done you rinse and repeat this for every province you come across, kind of like in Assassin's Creed 1 except with automatic weapons instead of swords and the cool assassin's blade.

With reguards to the multiplayer campaign, this stems from two undeniable factors: less than helpful AI "buddies" and the infanite revives you get when playing with actuall people.  The AI team mates are not as helpul as one might think leading to the sense that there is one of you taking on all of the Cartel, this includes when you get the squad upgrades. When in a solo campaign, your allies may only be able to revive you at most once for the majority of the campaign until you get the upgrade that allows you to be revived by them twice. When you play online with real people, this gets thrown out the window and you can be shot, stabbed, ran over by civies, have a helicopter crash on you, your teammates run over, have Unidad run you over, fall from the maximum game hieght etc as many times as you like and you can still have your people revive you.

In the end though, would I recommend this game to someone... absolutely. Nothing is quite as fun as taking down a cartel with a bunch of buddies in a far away fictitious land.

Wildlands has its issues but I think the good outweighs the bad. Graphically it’s one of the best looking games on the market at the moment, almost photorealistic at times. The draw distance is amazing, flying in a helicopter and seeing trees, roads and towns kilometers away is great and it makes the game world feel massive in scope which it already is but it’s nice to actually be able to see how big it is physically without things popping in from the distance. The game has the ubisoft formula where the map is cluttered with all kinds of things to extend the length of the game and it’s to a massive extent in this game because the map is so huge. There is an abundance of side missions, upgrades and collectables in each area/region of the map making this a really long game. A lot of the game is collecting weapons and weapon mods, skill points and doing side missions which make the game feel like its on auto pilot mode at times but because I played in coop it lessened that feel quite a bit because we often found our own way to keep the game fun. I think this is a really good coop game because there is a lot of ways to cooperate and play the game together like the way you approach missions together or the way you navigate around the world together. The game also has that unpredictability and randomness feeling that open world games often do which leads to a lot of fun, weird and unscripted moments. 

I think the gameplay is pretty good overall, the shooting feels great, headshotting feels great, especially with a sniper and syncing shots together with your coop mates is awesome. The game feels really satisfying when you complete a mission in stealth but it’s also fun to just go loud at times and I love the amount of equipment and customization that’s available. The vehicles feel and handle pretty good, the animations are good but the transitions between first and third person and changing between the two when aiming can take a while to get used to and even when you are used to it it’s not exactly a smooth tradition because you have to aim down the sights first before you can change perspective and then once you do you have to check if you have to change the shoulder position of your character, doing this while in a gunfight can feel pretty clunky.

 I like how challenging the game is overall and how relentless the enemy ai is but there are times where the bulls*it meter goes up like an enemy having perfect accuracy from a hundred meters away while dual wielding uzi’s. We started saying ‘I got lazered’ at times when we got downed because sometimes the enemy feels like its shooting lazers at you that can’t miss, it can get pretty annoying. Overall if you’re looking for a coop game to play with the bois this is one worth playing through and one that you can spend a lot of hours in.

I swear, this game is an enigma to me. It's not a game I would usually like, yet I've had quite alot of fun with it. First things first, I'll start out with issues or things I disliked. Even though it may try to act like it at times, this game is really not a "tactical" game in my opinion. And it really doesn't have alot of similarities to the older Ghost Recon games, so forget about that. I say this because, I find that at certain parts, the game just isn't entirely sure what it's trying to be. (Then again, that's just my opinion) The game also has a considerable amount of issues with bugs and performance, even after all this time, you'll find most negative reviews come from these 2 factors. Often times parts of the game feel really uninspired and lacking, and the gameplay mechanics can be kinda bland or not well thought out. Playing solo can be rather boring as well. However, the game manages to be fun in the weirdest and dumbest ways, seriously, and this is what really redeems this game imo. This game is such a blast with friends it's crazy, I didn't expect that at all. I'd go as far as to say that coop with friends is what seriously makes this game worth playing. *There's also ghost war pvp which was surprisingly fun as well, but it personally is a little too janky and bulletspongy for my taste. (It's definitely still worth checking out however) In summary, although this game is definitely flawed, it manages to be a fun and unique 3rd person shooter experience. To start, I was on the wall about this game when it first came out. I had been burned by "The Division" and though I can say I also enjoyed that game, it did have a lot of issues that made me hesitant about purchasing anymore ubisoft games. However, I was hearing good things about Wildlands and figured that since it was on sale, then it would be worth picking up. The game is a third-person shooter that transitions to first, when aiming down sights. It is a huge open world map, with lots of side missions, lots of guns and parts to collect, and a lot of main missions to do in general. The overall story is okay for what it is, and the gameplay is pretty good, but that's really it for the good parts. Now for the bad parts. The map may be huge, but there really isn't much to do. You will probably spend more time flying a helicopter/looking for one just so you can get to whatever your next destination may be, also there are anti-air missiles with no way of avoiding them, other than turning sharply. There is a cover system for the game, but when you engage enemies they usually sit behind cover and just wait for you to pop out into the open. Your 3 bot allies are actually very useful when taking out enemy units, but will sometimes be unable to revive you because you fell in a spot that they can't get to. [b]TOM CLANCY'S GHOST RECON: WILDLANDS.[/b]

You ride alongside your teammates, 
callsigns [b]Midas[/b], [b]Holt[/b] and [b]Weaver[/b]. 
All monikers and all specialists as 
demolitions, communications and 
the sniper, respectively. As the 
person from the pilot cabin steps in, 
you remember where the burning 
sensation came from, the product 
of your last [i]'jump'[/i] to this game, 
this world. 

The aid worker [b]Karen Bowman[/b] makes 
small talk and briefs you on the 
recently-deceased DEA mole who 
was the catalyst for your Ghost team
being deployed to this oft-overlooked
corner of the world. But you recognize
her for who she is. Despite her tired,
world-weary features and full-blonde
hair [i](which is unexpected)[/i], you knew
the moment she stepped in that this
older, wiser woman is none other than
this world's [b]Summer-Rain[/b]; your new
mission controller in Bolivia.

A version of Bolivia, ruled through 
proxy of the [b]Santa Blanca[/b] cartel. The 
organization reaches everywhere, with
their [i]Sicarios[/i], or hitmen, operating 
freely, sometimes even with the 
blessing of the paramilitary police 
[b]UNIDAD[/b], despite both factions coming 
to blows repeatedly against the other.

Led by the mysterious, enigmatic man
known only as [b]El Sueno[/b] [i](The Dream)[/i],
You begin to establish a groundwork
for the local rebels, the [b]Kataris 26[/b] to
better reestablish order and take the
fight to Santa Blanca. After liberating
the second leader of the Kataris 26, a
man named [i]'Amaru'[/i], you coordinate
with the first rebel leader [i]'Pac Katari'[/i],
who, like El Sueno, does not look too
favourably with the interference from
a [i]'yanqui'[/i].

Summer-Rain, in her aid worker cover
of Karen Bowman, liases with you,
the Kataris 26 and the home offices,
constantly cross-referencing the CIA
facts with any potential leads or intel.
The mission variety is divided along
these lines - assiting rebels, raiding
drug caches and destroying them, or
uncovering new weapons or their
respective attachments for a greater
range of flexibility, customization and
potential efficiency.

The entire game, or world in itself is
in line with Kyrat from Far Cry 4 with
its sprawling expanses, rivers, lakes
and mountain ranges. Its biomes 
vary from snow to jungle and even
desert, with wind and rain affecting
visibility and how you approach each
mission and tackle enemies.

Like Pagan Min's Kyrat, each section
of Bolivia is headed by an underboss
under El Sueno. Like you and your
team, each character assigned to be
removed by you goes by a moniker,
with narrated and animated files
providing background on each mark
with Karen Bowman detailing them.

You notice over time that this version
of Summer-Rain is extremely hard-
edged, cynical, and sometimes even
flighty or flirty with the targets you
are assigned to capture and extract.
Perhaps it was the death of the DEA
agent who was her close friend, or
maybe it was her rough-and-tumble
upbrining in this world. 

You find that you actually don't care, 
and would rather be hunting the next 
target to take one step closer to 
ending the threat Santa Blanca poses 
to the wider world. You cannot help 
but remember your time in Far Cry 3
Blood Dragon, where the constant
repeating of the reagon-era adage
accompanies you on each mission- 
[b]WINNERS DON'T USE DRUGS![/b]

After weeks of fighting across Bolivia,
you storm the mausoleum at the apex
of the game, having toppled all lesser
underbosses and lieutenants, leaving
El Sueno marooned on the monument
to his vanity, his cult of personality.

With your weapons drawn and Karen
Bowman alongside you, El Sueno is
dismissive of everyone, having worked
out a deal with both the DEA and CIA.
Robbing Karen of her justice she was
pursuing on behalf of her dead friend,
she draws her weapon on El Sueno
once more as he calmly walks out,
expecting to be chauffeured by Karen
to her handlers. 

The game has two outcomes based on
your actions as a Ghost Operative, but
this time, you find yourself taking aim
at Karen herself. El Sueno is still walking,
and Karen realizes that you have drawn
your rifle on her. She demands that she
do this, but you reprimand her that this
is not the way, and that in both possible
outcomes, there would be no winners.

You know deep down that she would
either kill El Sueno and take the fall for
justice, or allow his usage as a potential
informant help the CIA for a time before
he rebuilds elsewhere, stronger, but the
Ghosts will be ready. Karen has foreseen
this, as it is the reality, and the game's
will through its code and laws. But you
are free. You are boundless. A lone
Assassin in Bolivia through the lens of
Far Cry.

Karen Bowman takes aim and fires at
El Sueno. You crash everything that 
this world knows and rush forward 
between both of them and the bullet.
Another shot rings out, instinctual from
your rifle. Karen is stunned before she 
realizes that El Sueno's head blossoms
red, and he falls to the ground.

Instead of blinding heat like how you
first arrived here, there is now a slow,
growing of dread and cold. Your three
teammates rush to attend to you as you
fall, having taken the bullet from Karen's
gun and circumvented her prosecution
from delivering justice. You have dealt
with El Sueno and closed the case in
Bolivia. All that was forfeit was your life.

You see Karen and your teammates 
around you before you ebb away and
feel elation, accomplishment in your
missions together. With Holt calling in
for medevac and Weaver and Midas
trying to stop you from bleeding out,
you see Karen scared and forlorn, and
recognize that young girl behind all 
the harshness, bluster and cynicism.

Your Summer-Rain.
The love of your life.
Horribly changed and worn down
by the horrors of this world called Earth.

[i]"You'll... be alright... please... be okay..."[/i]
you hear her whispering now, but all
is going black, dark. 

Quiet.

[i]"I know, Summer. I will be."[/i]

Old review:
Beware! You might lose your save files randomly. It happened to me twice, so you want to make sure to look up how to recover your last save files form the cloud before hitting "new campaign" on the menu as it will replace your old files.

Now about the game:
It feels like a mix between GTA V, Far Cry 4 and Just Cause 3. It's kinda realistic, but at the same time pretty goofy, which is fun. Unfortunately there's no wingsuit or grapple hook, at least that I know of, but general gameplay wise, it does feel similar to those games in my opinion.

It has a large map and there's lots of stuff to do. As other people has already stated; it can be pretty repetitive with the missions, but I don't mind as the combat feels so nice! I really enjoy planning my attacks and shooting enemies in this game, it feels pretty "rewarding" when getting kills due to the general feeling of the weapons and the sound they make (+ hitmarker sounds).

The vehicle physics in this game are horrible to be honest. It's pretty similar to how you drive in another title from Ubisoft: Watch_Dogs. The vehicles kinda feel unresponsive, but at the same time too responsive (it sounds strange, but if you try the game you will see what I mean), and there's a slight delay between input (keypresses) and the actual turning, so if you're trying to avoid collision or doing some drifting or whatever, then you will most likely have issues controlling the vehicle. Helicopters feel "stiff" and weird to fly with as well.

But on foot, it feels pretty good actually. You have a drone you can use to take a look around the area and use it to plan your attacks. While using the drone, you can request different powers, such as mortars, helpers (friendly bots) and an ability to see enemies easier.

You can customise a lot. Both the character and the weapons.

There's a possibility to play CO-OP with your friends so you can help each other out with missions you can't do on your own, or if you just want to team up and wreak havoc together.

Every now and the game will be glitching {
For example, during CO-OP, you and your friend might have the same enemy left to kill, but where the enemy is at is completely different. So one of you could see an enemy 50 meters away and your other friend would see him 300 meters away instead. And if your friend would walk in front of the version you see, nothing happens, and if he kills his version of the enemy, then the version you see will die as well.

Sometimes you can get "launched" or pushed away if you stand near moving objects in a certain way.

Sometimes mission/special event vehicles can spawn inside each other and get lauched away while being ablaze (I think this might be due to the code not validating if the first vehicle actually exists before spawning the second one), so two or more vehicles can spawn inside each other and they get stuck and explode, then flies away (It's fun to see when it happens).
}

Conclusion:
- It could be a hassle getting your save files back if you lose them
- The vehicle physics are atrocious
- You will see glitches often (some fun, some not as fun)
- Repetitive missions

+ Awesome combat and sounds
+ Slick drone you can have with you to tag enemies and call in powers/abilities with
+ Lots of customisation (character/weapons)
+ Fun with friends, so if the game goes on sale, make sure your friend(s) buy it as well

I have very mixed feelings about this game. On the surface, the graphics are nice and the open world is vast and very beautifully done. There are some exceptionally good elements like bullet drop and finite bullet flight time, which you don't see in many shooter games.

That's about where the good things end. There is hardly any plot in this game. The whole plot is known from the very beginning: kill everybody in the drug cartel's organization chart, bottom to top. (Well, some have to be captured alive, not killed.) But the main characters have nothing at stake in this task. They are just empty shells, soulless mercenaries, we know nothing about them. In fact, from somebody's point of view they are the invaders of a foreign land, the bad guys.

The quests are extremely repetitive. Mostly they just involve killing people and/or blowing stuff up. The world is large so there is a whole lot of that to be done. Well, there are a few missions where you have to prevent somebody from being killed or prevent something from being blown up. Also there are five types of side missions which repeat endlessly. I must have stopped a hundred convoys and stolen 50 aircraft.

The difficulty level of the game is rather high. After the first ten or so missions I found it practically impossible to complete more missions on the second-easiest difficulty level, and had to complete the rest of the game on the easiest difficulty. Still some missions where you had to prevent somebody from being killed or something from being blown up, or not being detected were extremely hard, even after maxing out all the skills.

Morally, the game is of course quite appalling. While some social problems like poverty and inequality are mentioned superficially, the moral of the story is that it's fun to fight a perpetual war on drugs, let's just keep killing people, yee. It does not even touch any solutions to any problems. It would have been fun to see an alternative ending "world legalizes cocaine, all cartels collapse overnight" but no.

After grinding for a hundred hours or so, the plot gets just slightly more interesting in the very end of the game. So I guess I have to give it a thumbs up after all.

[h1][b][u]My Review For | Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands[/u][/b][/h1]

[u][b]The Background and Gameplay[/b][/u]
The background of the game is; That you and 3 other operators from the United States special forces group called: Ghost's, are sent into Bolivia to take down one of the worlds most dangerous cartel groups; Santa Blanca.

You achieve this by gaining intel from the local area and disrupt cartel leader's operations until you have enough progress to eliminate them personally.

You take out santa blanca's Security, influence, smuggling and production arm's.

In true tom clancy style - the game plays tactically and realistically.
From shooting enemy personnel from afar with a sniper rifle or by conducting cqb fights with assault rifles and smg's; you feel like your playing as an elite operator, skilled, calculating and precise.

The Game can be played from behind cover for dug in firefights and can be played as stealthily or as aggressive as you like.
Surgically removing enemy, or by steamrolling through their fortified positions.

All in all the Gameplay is on Point and can be played by Stealthy or Aggressive playstyles.

It also features an online mode for tactical firefights with real players from around the world.

[u][b]The Customisiation[/b][/u]
The customisation in this game is without a doubt; [b]One of the best i have seen[/b].
Coming from a military background myself, i truely appreciated the little things; Such as Molle Pouches changing on your PLCE depending on what rifle you are carrying, and that there were clothes for all enviromental conditions; like jackets and fleeces for cold nights and t shirts and polo tops for the sunny day, it truely allows you to tailor you and your ghost squad to how you want them to look and operate.

The customisation for your firearms is great too. You can put on a wide vareity of attachments to your gear, such as CQB sights and scopes to rail guards and laser sights, Not to mention the wide variety of paints you can apply to your gear and each individual part.

[u][b]The Run Down[/b][/u]
In Conclusion;
Ghost Recon Wildlands is one of the best 3rd person tactical shooters I have seen on the market in recent times.
The realism and attention to detail is truely great, using real military gear, some from real brands such as CamelBak and 5.11.
The Gameplay is great for people who want to play stealthy or aggresively, and is a great addition to the Tom Clancy Series of games.
With Great Graphics, and all of the above taken into consideration, your in for a great experience with this game.

10/10 - Must Buy.

Spent enough hours in the game to make the following conclusions:

Pros:
- From the very beginning – a vast variety of customization options for Your characters. For me it’s very important.
- Very nice choice of weapons.
- A very beautiful game, a huge world with different types of landscape.
- Great and interesting story. Well, I cleared only two branches of the Cartel, and can say that story missions were quite different and diverse.
- Nice selection of vehicles for transportation + fast travel option.
- A possibility to play with friends.
- Very nice modern combat features like a drone with different options.
- Interesting system of your allies support (Recce of rebels, rebels delivering vehicles on your request).

Cons:
- Quite lame optimization. If you want a smooth picture be ready to sacrifice some beauty of the environment.
- Very dense concentration of enemy forces. Well, I think Bolivia is big enough. Even having a real army of the Cartel sicarios You cannot physically put them on every road crossing and ensure patrolling cars each 500-1000 meters. The same is regarding the Army. Patrols appear on the roads with a 20-30 seconds interval + very frequent checkpoints. The only way to avoid this – get a chopper.
- Very stupid respawn of the enemy. Well I played the hardest difficulty, but even so it’s too much. I mean, 15-20 seconds after a loud attack You have an endless row of enemy combat vehicles coming in with a separation of some 10-20 seconds. When You hit local military, it’s even worse. 10-15 seconds – 2-3 combat vehicles. After that – combat choppers.
- SAM sites. Oh, Yeah Baby!!!! In areas with high difficulty SAM make your flying very difficult, but interesting. And it would be much more interesting to have a possibility to take out SAM sites. And you have one. But guess what? They respawn as soon as you get away for a couple of kilometers. A very stupid system. You cannot clear an air corridor in the area for a considerable amount of time, the game won’t allow this.
- Very stupid controls and physics of ALL vehicles: cars, choppers, planes. Uncomfortable.
- Some missions a very annoying. The last mission… You have 6 minutes to get to the Mausoleum, which is far away. Only two options and both of them almost cheaty. This game has been the surprise of the summer for me. As a game that has been on radar since E3 2015, I am very happy I finally pulled the trigger on this one. Wildlands is an open world third person shooter with loot boxes, PVP, a Rogue-lite/hardcore mode, and Online Co-op. I typically try to avoid games that bill themselves as gaming as a service. But this one hooked me pretty well.  

The best thing I can say about this game is that it takes the best parts of Metal Gear Solid 5 (one of my favorite games of all time) and puts it into an absolutely huge open world. This might be one of the biggest open worlds I've ever seen actually. The world is full of military bases, outposts, and hidden lodges which can be taken in any manner of ways. For me, the true test of a sandbox game is that it gives you tools, and objective, and then says "Go figure it out". 

You see a base, you can stealth in like Solid Snake or Sam Fisher and eliminate enemies one at a time at a variety of ranges. You can sit on a cliff above the base and snipe em out. You can take to the air in an attack helicopter and take em out that way. Or you can even steal an armored car and just bash your way in. It is fun in single player, and it's even more fun in Co-Op. I don't have friends that play this game and the randoms I've been matched with have been alright. 

There's always something to do/find in this game whether it is a convoy that needs to be destroyed or a weapon/attachment you need to pick up. The devs are regularly adding new (free) missions and just added a perma-death mode. 

The main gripe I have heard about this game is that there is nothing to do after you finish the main campaign aside from helping people in Co-op or starting over in permadeath mode. While that is true, I am currently at 50 hours played and am maybe half way through the campaign. Much of that time played has been spent messing around in Co-op where missions you finish are counted toward your single player campaign as well .  This game finds its fun in the times after stealth goes wrong, and after you fail a mission. When you can rethink your strategy until you get it right. 

Endgame edit: The best thing I can say about this game is that after I finished 100% of all missions, I still have the desire to jump into random co-op. The game is still fun and I am eagerly awaiting additional content. 

I highly recommend.

Wildlands is a game that you'll either love or hate. For me, I personally loved it. If you aren't 100% sure about buying this game (on sale or not) watch some videos of its gameplay on youtube. Everything I put is obviously from my experience, and I just think its time to review this game.

FIrst, is the graphics. I play this game running an i7-6700k, GTX 1070, and 16GB of ram. Overall, I can hit 50-60 fps  1080p on almost all settings maxed, with only shadows and distant textures turned down a bit. I rarely have frame drops, with them lasting about 20 seconds and they only occur every few hours of gameplay. It's never been an issue for my experience. And so, with this game being system-heavy, the visuals follow suit. For me, it is absolutely beautiful. The water, sky, grass, vehicles, people, mountains, all of it looks great on Ultra/high settings.

Second, the main campaign. Wilands has a plethora of bosses controlling regions, in which it lets you choose which ones to go after and when. As you dig your way in, you'll find harder bosses, and eventualy El Sueno, the big bad boss. I found almost all the characters in the game intriguing, good and bad guys alike. The cutscenes held character, and the differing missions surrounding bosses were enjoyable. It feels and plays like a natural and unrestricted experience.

Third, the side missions. This is where I find a lot of hate, even something I noticed right at its release. They are the same thing over and over to get resources for upgrades, throughout the entire game. But, oddly enough, I didn't mind them. I think, at least for me, is because the changing location always allowed for different circumstances. Hijacking a truck, for example, could be way different in an urban city vs. the mountains with thin roads and little traffic. The good news is, whether you like them or not, they are in no way required. It is very much possible to finish the game with the starter gear and weapons.

Fourth, the driving. Vehicles come in variety, with different purposes and characteristics. Say, perhaps, you take a van and stow your newly aquired short-term prisoner in the back. Take a sports car, and there is only room for one passenger, so you hae speed but no friends to come along. On the PC specifically, it works well in one case and horrible in another. If you're trying to be slow and seaky, or perhaps just obeying the rules of the road, goodluck. Just to keep my speed down I have to tap the key at a consistent rate to stay on par with traffic. However, once you're accustomed to the driving, you'll find it quite useful. The high speed chases are much easier, as just holding the key keeps you at max speeds, drifting comes naturally, and split-second maneuvers are not just a thing of legend. Although this was my experience, and I noticed A LOT, or more so the majority of people hated the driving system.

Fifth, the DLCs. I bought the gold edition for a hefty $120 CAD, which I don't recommend. (I did it for the sweet shotgun mostly, kinda a shotgun fan) If you are willing to spend the $40 CAD to get both DlCs, I will say they were quite enjoyable. Fallen ghosts was a fair challenge and took a lot to complete. Narco Road was cool to infiltrate a gang and do neat stunts with new vehicles. (But the boost on sports cars was even too much for me to control) They are seperate saves than the original, which I didn't mind. HOWEVER, from day one I have had this bug where if I try to exit to the main menu (so that I can switch between the DLCs and main game) it kicks me straight out of the game. Quite wierd. Also, had to restart my entire Narco DLC due to a bug that wouldn't unlock the final quest arc.

Sixth, customizability. (Did I spell that right?) Weapons, well most of them, have several interchangeable parts that you can unlock to increase performance or change from that scope you hate. There's lots of paint jobs, even part by part. I loved playing around with different weapons, but still got too addicted to the Wilderness shotgun. (Used to do max damage and killed even from like 5m away, but they nerfed it......so sad........) Your character can be changed to your heart's desire, but I stuck with the rebel leader costume I got from the Gold Edition. 

Seventh, my verdict. I, out of my 100+ hours, have endured easy success, endless failure (that one city mission in Narco Road MY OH MY), but overall I found it to be worth my time. Get this game on sale, and I'm sure you'll get something out of it.

Essence of the game: Kill all drug cartel fiefs (everyone cartel related really). 

The game overall plays out like this: 
1. Enter a region. 
2. Receive a radio communication from the task giver, where she tells you about the fief in the region, that she has no idea where that person is. However she knows about a couple of points of interests (typically 4-5) which are then marked in gold on the map. 
3. You travel to each POI and as you reach each of them, they transform into another POI on the map, some distance away. 
4. You travel to that new POI location. 
5. Once you've visited all of POIs in the region, a final POI is marked on the map. 
6. You travel to the final POI and is tasked with killing or kidnapping a person. 
7. You again travel a fair distance to some specific safehouse where you drop the kidnapped person off, and the story progresses a bit. You are told about the impact of the loss of this fief to the cartel organisation. 
8. Repeat 26 times from step 1. 

This game is long. The main reason for that is cheap padding. 
1. A constant back and forth travelling (backtracking) where travelling between a single POI to another may take 3-4 minutes by helicopter or many times that with a land vehicle. 
2. In between each step above, you will face an infinite number of enemies, that respawn "as soon as you turn your back on them". Or more accuratly, as soon as you've moved a short distance away. 
3. In order to not be annihilated you need to upgrade your skill tree and that is accomplished by... you guessed it, boring fetch quests, travelling to yet other POIs on the map, where you have to kill hordes of respawning enemies. 
4. You can't just acquire new and improved weapons and addons for your weapons stash from killed enemies, no you need to travel far and wide to hundreds of additional POIs, where the same "Crate" will exist with a trophy in it. 
5. Each item you seek is typically placed as far away from you as possible, while still fitting in the overall story segment. For example, it's almost certain that if there's a village with an item in it, then the item will be located in the highest building, at the top floor, as far away from the stairs as possible. It seems UBI used an algorithm for travelling salesman problem where they inverted the heuristic to produce the location with the furthest travelling distance from any other point on the map. 

Liked: 
Even though the game has all its problems, the cheap tricks to pad its length, and the constant repetition, I still found it a blast to play, in small chunks. 

* Performance, it ran beautifully at 90/120 FPS on my Intel Core i7 4790K, with a Geforce GTX 1080ti and 16 GB RAM at 2560 x 1440 (1440p) G-synced resolution. No crashes. 
* Voices. Acting was rather good I found and added quite a bit to the immersion. Your team mates respond to surroundings. In the beginning I was impressed by the variety of comments by the AI mates, but found they ran out of ambient dialogue after about 10% into the game. A potential for improvement in UBIs future titles, but as a proof of concept, I think it turned out rather well and applaud the devs for the idea. 
* Graphics. The scenery is absolutely stunning. From snow covered mountains to dense jungles. Nothing beats flying a helicopter over cities, canyons, bridges, the jungle and the alps. It's something very relaxing about it. The character models also looked great. Attention to detail was overall very high imo. 
* Gunplay. Bullets have trajectories! Head shots are fatal! Unarmored enemies are not bullet sponges! Weapon handling feels a bit on the realistic side when compared to other titles, with weapon weight and stats playing into how the weapons behave. Overall I found gun fights highly enjoyable, which really is a saving grace as you wade through the hordes of zomb... I mean cartel and unidad soldiers. 
* Rebel assistance. This is a new thing I believe in UBI titles. Along with your skill tree, there is a separate branch which allows various forms of assistance from bolivian rebels. The types include sending grunts to help you in gun fights (can make a HUGE difference, especially for timed challenges), calling in mortar strikes (Awesome, especially for taking out pesky drone jammers), helping with recon etc. I found the former two great, while the rest I never saw a use for. 
* Your AI mates aren't completely useless! They're definitely not Rainbow six good, but they're much better than in your average FPS title. 
* The story was OK. It definitely wasn't CDPR good, but much better than other UBI titles. It also served a purpose, giving you enough of a justification for exploring areas. But it sure as hell is better then Farcry 5's cornucopia of nothingness.

Lastly, i wont buy the 2 DLCs... dont seem worth it, i mean 90+ hours was enough for me. And those microtransaction LOL just LOL.

Anyone looking to buy this because you have some hope that the original, hardcore, painfully difficult and tense Ghost Recon game elements were going to resurrected in an awesome way, abandon all hope because it doesn't happen. This game was good in its own regard but was almost certainly NOT a Ghost Recon game if you hold it to the standard of the first couple games. The originals, even 2 and the expansions of 2 were still in keeping with original feel. That butthole-clenching tension that made you anxious every time you moved your squad because you knew that you could die in about 1 second from any enemy and that you weren't some gun-toting superhuman who could destroy a tank with a firearm - THATS the feel I'm talking about. THATS the feel that I want when I play a game in the Ghost Recon series. 

WIldlands was more of a cross between GTA, Red Faction and the Division, just with a Ghost Recon nameplate slapped on it. Sure, you get to do some operator stuff. Sure, you get to meet Sam Fisher in the DLC. Sure, you get to use squad commands. But you can outrun attack helicopters in a car. You can also be shot over 10 times before being "downed", a mechanic that I whole heartedly disagree with, given that it removes all tension from your play through since you can just be revived. That’s why games like Dark Souls are so awesome. You genuinely don't want to die because you know how much is riding on you staying alive and finding that next bonfire AND because you don't want to squander all your hard work by losing all the souls you harvested. In games with that type of death mechanic (i.e. classic Tom Clancy games), you value your decision making and sense of self-preservation that much more. In Wildlands, because it doesn't have this, it feels like you just got into a bounce house with a bunch of other people, threw on some protective padding and smashed into each other for a couple hours. No real consequences, you more or less already know what's going to happen and you can see everyone coming. 

Maybe I'm a Ghost Recon snob because I played every single one of the originals and have incredibly high standards, or maybe Ubisoft finally sold out and catered to the lowest common denominator - i.e. 15 year old’s who LEIK TO DO AWPERATER STUPH and feel cool driving cars around pointlessly for hours. 

Either way, I can't recommend and not recommend a game at the same time, so I'll just say buy it when it's on sale but don't expect it to be on par with other games of the same name. Like I said earlier, it's good in its own way but is nowhere near as interesting or difficult as the others.

Revised: Yes it does have flaws and the repetition is best avoided by skipping the side missions and the endless collecting. 

What it does have going for it is the beautiful environment, careful detail of characters, props, weapons, and so on. You can't fault Ubisoft for skimping on the artwork for its titles. Likewise, the map is large and the game allows you to explore it however you choose; there is no set path, but obviously the harder opponents will likely need better gear to beat than what you start out with. 

The main criticism I have is that the AI of the enemies is poor. They have the amazing capability of pinpointing your location (and relaying this information to all of their mates) perfectly should you get caught out. The AI doesn't seem to notice that their friends are missing unless they discover the body, but only within a critical time because the bodies are rapidly claimed by the earth soon after death. Moreover, like Far Cry 2, areas you clear are repopulated by the same band of cretins you killed earlier, but there's no indication why this happens. Did I fail to clear it properly?

Your own team is hindered by poor AI and a number of contrivances to seemingly work around the AI limitations. For a while I waited patiently while my three teammates carefully lined themselves up, opened vehicle doors and sat down. Then I realised that it doesn't matter if you just drive off because they magically teleport into the vehicle anyway. 

There are loads of weapons, but it's a confusing mess of restricted choice. You'd think that unlocking (via a pick-up on the map) an attachment for assault rifles would work on all assault rifles, but this is not the case. Some require purchasing from the Ubisoft store or trudging around additional locations on the map. 

Speaking of weapons, the design of the game seems to imply that sniping beyond 500 metres is off limits. The game world doesn't seem to render beyond a certain distance and luckily so, because the gravity in this game is pretty strong. So strong in fact that shots over 200 metres require a lot of compensation to connect. And you do want them to connect because alerting the enemies to your presence means the magic pinpointing of your location to everyone all the time.
