Genuinely enjoyed the game. Anything from world, graphics, gameplay, amount of (meaningful) content, and overall package has left me really happy with my time spent with the game.

Graphics, world design, atmosphere, tone and feeling of the game are unrivaled.
Taking a walk around these stunning Bolivian landscapes is a factor motivating me to play this game more even after finishing it. World not only looks really believable, it feels like it. It's not as alive as it could have been, which it suffers from it a lot at times, I would consider it to be good enough given GRW was Ghost Recons reboot title. The game keeps it's tone fairly consistent. It's not gloomy or depressing, but it's not wacky or clowny either. Most humour comes from chats between your team members, which is quite enjoyable and doesn't spoil the tone of the game (which tackles drugs, murders, kidnappings, human trafficing, slavery, to name a few. Sadly, it tackles a lot of them in a very shallow and safe way).

Ambient audio is fantastic, and music extremely satisfying (although I felt the lack of more memorable combat music).
Voice acting on the other hand is a mixed bag. While Ghost squad and Bowman are nice to listen to, everyone else has the classic Ubisoft's xbox 360 microphone quality. 
Sometimes, game has made me mute music completely, simply so I can walk through jungles or mountain tops or savannahs and enjoy the ambient sound of the world.

Core gameplay is a "ubisoft formula" of an open world. Albeit repetitive, and generic at times, with lots of meaningless blips on the map to do, I did enjoy it all things considered. It was a perfect game to kick back and scratch that "tacticool" itch of feeling like a spec ops badass killing anything in their way. Biggest issue gameplay wise other than repetitiveness of missions is certainly content bloat. The game offers A LOT, on paper, but most of that content is mind numbing, boring generetative content that doesn't bring in anything interesting to the table. It was clearly in there only to stretch out game duration, and was a bane of Ubisofts game design for years to come. 

The gameplay wears you off, however. It is worth noting I didn't finish this game "in one sitting". I think that it's a perfect game to come back to after few months to get that itch of exploring vast open world, and running around shooting enemies, especially considering you don't really have a story to follow. 
When it comes to interacting with the world, movement, operating gun and cover system works really well and is intuitive. Movement is weighty, meaty, and for the most part you feel like you're a running blob of flesh, and not a capsule with artificial camera attached to it. Vehicles are a completely different story. Every car feels like it's light like a plastic toy, and physics on them are extremely exaggerated. Helicopters and plane controls feel almost like they were an afterthought. Animations are really well made, and make everything seem fluid and on point. 

Gunplay was serviceable enough to make me want to pursue exploring map for guns that I am interested with and mods to kit them out. Customisation of both ghosts and their weapons was quite surprisingly complex given the time.

Story was serviceable at best, it was there only to push the player around provinces. I really liked the concept of taking on a cartel, very real and mostly overlooked conflict today, and undermining drug empire. I enjoyed how grounded and somewhat realistic the story was *trying* to be, and I think with a proper effort they could've made something really interesting here. However, for what it was, only a handful of stories, or "buchons" really picked my interest enough to make me read about them more. 90% of them you won't be able to remember as soon as you turn off the game. (except Nidias huge assets.)

Really fun game, quite repeditive though.  The story is 7/10, some missions are awesome and challenging, some are annoying. The player customization is incredible and the gun customization is good too. 

I'd recommend playing on the hardest difficulty for the most fun. Otherwise it's kind of easy (shows enemies on mini-map and such).

No matter which part of the map you explore, Ubisoft’s in-game version of the South American country of Bolivia looks great. From the get-go, you’re free to roam the entire map, which includes jungles, mountains, deserts, salt flats, lakes, swamps, quarries, and caves. These biomes aren’t just eye candy; they have a major impact on how you play. Areas thick with foliage are perfect for hit-and-run guerrilla warfare. Deserts have little or no cover, so fighting from range works well and having an escape vehicle ready is imperative. In the mountains, with a bit of leg work, you can usually hike to the high ground and assault your enemies from above. Wildlands leaves the strategy up to you, and because vehicles and fast travel points are so plentiful, the wide-open Bolivian landscape feels like a land of opportunity, not a burden.

Speaking of vehicles, yes, the chatter is true: many of them don’t control well. Even on a bone-dry dirt road, some cars and jeeps feel like they’re skidding around on slick ice. After 15 or so hours I was able to pilot anything without much trouble, but it took far too long to nail Wildlands’ “feel.” Choppers, in particular, take a while to break in: once you’re cruising, you’re good, but building up to that speed requires a weird dance of tipping the nose up and down and easing up on the throttle. And, because the map is so large, you’re forced to spend a ton of time in vehicles to get to locations between fast-travel points. Also, it’s very common for high-priority targets to jump into a vehicle and flee, and if they get too far away you’ll often lose them and fail. These situations take an already uneven driving and piloting system and push it to its frustrating breaking point.

Wildlands’ main issue, however, is poor mission variety. For the first five or so provinces everything felt exciting. The next 15? Not so much. Until I switched to playing co-op, it descended deeper and deeper into repetition.

The cycle begins with a boss hunt. Each province has a boss, and to learn that boss’ identity and draw him/her/them out from hiding you need to complete four to six missions. That’s not a major ask, but the missions are usually a rote combination of the following: blow up an inanimate object (cocaine cache, equipment), extract and interrogate a high-value target (an assistant, a family member), steal or photograph something (a car, documents), or just kill some stuff. It doesn’t help that enemy variety that stands between you and your objectives is almost non-existent. There are standard enemies, heavily-armored enemies, and snipers – that’s about it. Even common video game mainstays like The Flamethrower Guy, The RPG Guy, and The Guy With The Big Shield don’t make an appearance. Sometimes you’ll face other obstacles, like an enemy chopper or a jammer that keeps you from using your drone. They definitely crank up the intensity, but you’ll quickly learn how to deal with them, too. Even the variety that comes from the diverse locations isn’t enough to mix it up.

These issues might have doomed Wildlands if not for its highly satisfying sandbox antics. When you’re a kid and you only have four action figures, what do you do with them? You fire up your imagination, go outside, and make your own ridiculous fun. The same goes for Wildlands.

Yes, you may be on your umpteenth extraction mission... but this time, what if you throw your target in the trunk of a car instead of lifting him out by helicopter? That seems like a good idea, but before you can get into the driver’s seat an enemy truck rams that car down a hill. Now you’re running downhill to check on your VIP passenger, all while shouting at your friends to find a new escape vehicle. In the distance, you hear mortar fire. A second chopper is closing in.

Then, maybe next time you’re on an extraction mission enemies may take out your escape vehicle and you’ll have to run through the woods at night, holding your target by the neck and taking out pursuing enemies with only a pistol. Just when you think you’re home free, you’ll get spotted. The chase continues.

Yes, the missions are too similar in design. You’ll undoubtedly feel the deja vu. But most of the time things don’t go the way you’d planned. The madness that ensues is what saves Wildlands, and what compelled me to keep playing well past the hours a human being should normally be awake. These are the moments I talk about when people ask me how I’m liking it.

Some of those moments are made memorable by the boss characters. Wildlands’ standard enemies may not be special, but it does a fine job of turning cartel bosses into more than just targets. None of them will join the pantheon of great video game villains, but in games like this, it’s often the case for underlings to simply feel like rungs on a ladder, something you just step on in order to move up. Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor got around this issue by imbuing its minibosses with personality, and so does Wildlands. These characters are outlandish, unnerving, and pulpy. Remember when Walt and Jesse dissolved bodies in barrels of acid in Breaking Bad? One of the cartel bosses does that too, but he also has a beloved stuffed animal and the mental capacity of a child. Another boss duo of former doctors plays weird sex games while they torture and interrogate the cartel’s enemies. It’s decidedly silly, and often more than a little bit on the nose, but they left a mark on me nonetheless.

- The Verdict
This huge, wide-open shooter constantly shows its flaws in its mission variety and vehicle physics, but its strong, sandbox-style gameplay and seamless co-op kept me coming back for more madness. If you must repeat experiences over and over, you could far worse than helicopter chases, assassination missions, or drug busts gone wildly wrong.

[h1]Ghost Recon Mildlands[/h1]

Ghost Recon Wildlands is a third-person tactical shooter that continues Ubisoft's long-running Ghost Recon series. Wildlands sees a team of Ghosts taking on a drug cartel in Bolivia. Set in an enormous open world, you and your squad of three are tasked with disrupting the cartel's drug production with the ultimate goal of taking down their leader. You'll use a myriad of weapons and a few different gadgets to assassinate targets, blow up drug stashes and stop supply convoys. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Bolivia is a huge open map with plenty of locations to visit, the map is well-designed and while it doesn't quite feel lived-in, it doesn't feel empty either
+There's a wide variety of guns to unlock and customize, ranging from fast-firing compact SMGs to sniper rifles that will quite literally blow your enemies away 
+Gunplay is pretty satisfying but it's let down by the lack of enemy variety
+Quite a lot of customization options for your character and your squad 
+The whole game is playable in co-op, in fact it's probably more enjoyable with friends though only the host gets story progress when playing in co-op
+The map is split into different regions, each region has its own leader as well as weapon unlocks, attachments and special skill points (boosts a specific skill) unique to each region. You'll also find missions to upgrade rebel skills (calling in reinforcements, vehicle drop-off, recon etc.) and to gain supplies (used to unlock skills)
+Due to the game's shallow nature, it's good if you just want to switch off and have some 'mindless' fun

[b]Cons:[/b]
-The first few hours are really good fun but you quickly realize that the game is very repetitive and lacks the variety it needs. All of the missions boil down to either rescuing someone, killing someone or blowing something up
-Most of the regions are pretty similar visually
-There are only three types of enemies: soldiers, heavies and snipers. I feel the combat would have been a lot more interesting if there were other specialized units such as explosive focused enemies and stealth focused enemies
-Unlocking new skills is far too easy, levelling up doesn't really matter as you can pick up medals throughout the game world which can grant up to five skill points each and the resources aren't hard to come by
-Wildlands has some of the absolute worst vehicle physics I've ever seen. All of the vehicles feel very floaty and fake. It's hard to describe but you never feel like you're actually driving/flying a vehicle and it's even worse than ubisoft's previous attempts at vehicles in the Watch_Dogs series
-The AI is too simplistic, enemies are easy to predict and your squadmates are pretty much useless compared to you/other human players
-The story is so uninteresting that I nearly forgot to mention it in this review. You have a handler who tells you a little bit and then you get videos that are optional to tell you about the characters you're trying to kill. I found these videos pretty dull and they didn't make me care anymore about the characters so I just stopped watching them

[b]Verdict:[/b]
Wildlands is a solidly mediocre game, it'll give you some decent fun but it doesn't do anything interesting and it really lacks variation. Gunplay is good but the enemies aren't good enough to keep it interesting. The open world is well designed and pretty to look at but getting around it isn't fun because the vehicles are so badly designed/implemented. If you enjoyed Ubisoft's other open-world games you'll probably get some fun out of this one but just keep in mind that it doesn't do anything new and it gets really repetitive. Only pick it up at $20 or less.

For example, the AI is next to useless with 4-5 basic commands that execute for the whole squad preventing you from accomplishing even the most basic tasks whilst relying upon them, thus forcing you into co-op. On top of that stealth is hindered by glitches. I was deeply dissapointed that Ubisoft dropped the ball on this. As a long time fan of the series I hope that the next installment (and we all know there will be another) refocuses itself on providing a solid experience for both singleplayer and multiplayer as Future Soldier did so well. If Ubisoft could just focus its ambitions more tightly, forget about giant maps and amazing graphics I just want to be able to enjoy Ghost Recon by myself rather than trying to coax my friends into purchasing an 80 dollar game just to play with me (as I'm sure they'd like me to do.) 

So to conclude, if you want to pay 80 dollars for a pyramid scheme of a game that is not nearly as enjoyable as the previous games; go ahead and make this purchase, but if you're like me looking for the classic Ghost Recon experience you're out of luck unless your friends are 1. This game was great. I've completed it 100% twice (all areas found, missions completed, and "hidden" items discovered) and it took enough time for this game to be worth the price and then some. Lots of fun things to do and a myriad of ways to take down baddies and complete objectives. Truly a play-as-you-want style game. I definitely recommend to anyone who enjoys shooters and open-world sandbox style games.

There are a few downsides:
First and foresmost is the lack of anything to do once you've beaten the missions. They added a Tier One mode in which you continue gaining XP to level your character and weapons. This leveling system begins at Tier 50 and you have to gain XP until you've leveled up (or down?) to Tier 1. Each Tier level increases enemy difficulty, IE their ability to spot you, damage buffs, and accuracy. Unfortunately, even beating the game 100%, I found myself at Tier 21. You can replay any missions you've previously beaten for XP, but each time you beat that mission the XP reward drops, which makes leveling up that much more time consuming. As far as I can tell, there are no real benefits to getting to Tier 1, so my drive to continue playing the game has greatly diminished. It essentially turns into a slow, painful grind.

My next biggest complaint is bullet speed. Bullets travel way too slow in this game. And equipping a suppressor makes bullets travel 50% slower. In firefights I've had to lead targets that were a mere 40m away and sprinting. That's insanely slow bullet velocity. Granted, it makes sniping fun because it allows for bullets to drop over a distance instead of being hitscan, but there are other games that have handled bullet trajectory and velocity better. The Battlefield franchise manages to do these things well.

My last complaint is the shaky-at-best physics. Helicopters I've shot down occasionally decide to bounce off the ground, enemies glitching through rocks (this happens rarely, to be fair) and anytime you get in a vehicle you are at the mercies of whatever physics the game decides should exist - or not - at that point in time. I've got tons of footage of various glitches which were, for the most part, entertaining, but it's still a minor inconveniance at best and if trying to do a driving mission can be a massive setback.

Overall though I really loved this game. I put over 200 hours into it, which imo is more than enough time to warrant a strong recommend even if it does have the drawbacks I talked about above. Again, if you like single player with AI teammates getting you through engagements like I do it's a must try for anyone. You're free to be tactical and stealthy, ordering your teammates' movement and telling them who to kill 1 by 1 to quietly take over an area. Or you're free to just bash their gate down and take the base guns-blazing.

It's a solid FPS. Give it a try.

Ghost Recon Wildlands is perhaps my favorite game from 2017, though I didn't play it until a few weeks ago.

It's a perfect mixture of military shooter (Call of Duty, Battlefield, etc) and open world action (Grand Theft Auto, Saints Row, etc) in an Ubisoft package done right. This means you get some of the tactical goods and options that Ubisoft has been dishing out for years via Ghost Recon and Splinter Cell. This isn't to say you have to play swift, silent, deadly, but it's certainly a lot more satisfying to do so! Wildlands was pure satisfaction!

Gameplay is what you'd hope in an open world action game. Easy to traverse foreign terrain and a sense of being somewhere to explore. From running around, sneaking around, driving a car, or flying a helicopter, it's all you would expect from GTA or SR. Combat is all you'd expect from Call of Duty or Battlefield. Pick your weapons, modify them to fit your needs, pick a loadout, aim, double tap! Ubisoft really nailed it, and I rarely find a game to have gameplay this enjoyable.

On the single player end, you've got 3 AI teammates. They are a bit flakey at times, and seem to have the rare issue of not following you. So in rare moments, you will find yourself alone, wondering, WHERE THE FRAK IS MY BACKUP?!? That's what you get for trusting some toaster AI buddies. Still, they're otherwise pretty great. You can sync shots with them to take out small groups of cartel members, and 99.99% of the time, it goes smoothly. You can however play co-op with friends, and hope they can do the same. I have no useful friends though, so it's the lonely, solo road for me. Lastly, missions rarely have checkpoints, so if you mess up, be prepared to start over! 

Graphically, it's pretty great. Ran the game on both an ultrawide (3440x1440) and via Steam Link to my 86" 4K TV where I eventually finished the game. Running at ultra settings in both conditions, I was as happy with this as I was Final Fantasy XV. Environments looked great, and overall, it felt like a place worth exploring. Didn't have any fps issues, no memory leaks, and not a single crash in the 70+ hours I played.

The story is pretty simple. You lead a black ops team lead by a woman from the CIA (a rather familiar theme) into a foreign country (in this case, Bolivia) to systematically rip apart a drug cartel. The story is never quite as black and white as we'd hope, and like real history, there's more black ink than there are sharpie makers. Some of it is rather predictable if you listen to what these characters have to say. All in all, it felt good to rip apart the cartel and dish out some "American" justice. There's a lot to do in this game!

This game was great! I imagine it would have been greater if I had real friends with play with. Maybe that's a good thing though, they'd probably get killed all the time or screw up sync shots. Or crash a car and get everyone killed... YOU KNOW WHO YOU ARE! Anyway... Yeah. 10/10. I haven't been this satisfied with a game in a long time.

EXTRA: If you're only into the single player part of the game, just get the base game. There's no need for the DLC. Read DLC reviews. They don't add to the base game. They're separate stories with different characters, and poorly reviewed.

This game has been so much fun. 170 hours, I finally finished the campaign, with 100% map explored, all guns and mods found/equipped, every mission done (took down all four underbosses before taking out the big bad guy). I saved the two "special" missions for last. I am still short on resources (food and comms) for my last two perk unlocks, but I have no doubt a few more supply convoy raids will net me the 20k of each that I need to wrap that statistic up. 

As for the game, Wildlands is absolutely gorgeous, handles very well, feels like a shooter should. The gameplay is fun enough that the repetition isn't bad when it strikes, and you learn a lot about Bolivia, Spanish, and the local culture/history, not to mention a little bit about cocaine :-) 

My biggest gripes having played this game all the way through are: 

- the NPC teammates. They can get annoying sometimes, and we ought to be able to disable them (or choose how many we want). We also can't customize them... I'd like to pick the gear they have or at least change the *type* of weapon they have. I'd also like to change one or two to women, but apparently only the player can be female.

- failed missions always give you a black screen and then you respawn nearby. This is incredi-dumb; you should just fail the mission and then stay where you are. I would much rather continue doing what I was before, and/or fight my way out of a failed stealth mission and survive, than get magically teleported away. 

- you can't detect enemies, even with binoculars or a drone, from more than about 400m away. How am I supposed to attempt shots at 1km or 1.5km if I can't even see the NPCs, let alone target them/mark them? My longest shot was from 592 or 596m or so, and that was because I marked a guy out in the open at max distance, then ran up a mountain for another 100-200m and took pot shots at him. 

- killing innocents/bystanders. The game says that you'll "fail" if you kill too many rebels or civilians. I would often kill them inadvertently (sometimes they would just walk right in front of my gun while I was firing... which was annoying), and while I never reached a point where the game failed me, I feel like that's something that should just be removed from the game. I'm a disavowable ghost asset, persona non grata, in a hostile country. I should have full latitude to kill whomever I want, because honestly who is gonna report me and to whom are they gonna complain?

- During the mission to capture the old woman buchon who then turns on you in an ambush, the game should still let us capture her. I stumbled upon her base earlier than I expected and the first building I ran into had her, so I captured her before the audio about the scripted ambush even happened, and drove her all the way back to a rebel hideout to try and "extract" her, only for the game to just sit there silently. Ultimately I shot her while she was standing there by the car we drove up in, and then I got a "mission succeeded" notification. Pretty lame.

- The handling of the armored cars and APCs is laughable atrocious. Like, not "handles bad" atrocious, but "implemented poorly" atrocious. An APC is like 2 tons, it should not slide around like a car in an avalanche. 

Even with those gripes (and many more smaller ones), this game was an absolute blast. Fix those gripes I mentioned above, and the game would be pretty near flawless in my opinion. 

I did not play with other people at all, so I can't speak to the multiplayer, but I hear from Reddit that it is loads of fun.

You basically run around kidnapping dozens and killing thousands of people, destryoing the infrastructure of Bolivia and throwing the country back into the stone age without even one serious thought about why you're doing it. The protagonists constantly berate the Bolivians for being to weak to stop Santa Blanca from taking control, for being poor or for wanting to survive by making deals. This game is huge and intricately woven, looks beautiful, sounds great, is fluid and dynamic and gives you an eye watering amount of customistion options for your weapons, character (and now) team mates. Awesome.

Squad AI, while lightyears ahead of what it was before, occasionally leaves something to be desired. I like how you can leave them to their own devices instead of having to micromanage them CONSTANTLY like in previous titles, but they do occasionally goof around and alert enemies during stealth raids which is somewhat irritating. 

Other than the above, I've really not got much in the way of complaints. The biggest grip people seem to have with this game is the lack of mission variety. If Ubisoft look to correcting this in the months to come, they'd be on to an absolute winner.

One additional set of gripes is the notion of shared stealth - again, in another part of the world, a player does something to become detected - hundreds of kilometers to the east, suddenly an enemy base of a totally different faction is alerted to you, and suddenly sends pinpoint accurate mortars in your direction despite no one reasonably being able to even know you were there. FEELS GHOSTY.

I still recommend this game on sale, but it'll make you consistently angry enough to not buy the DLC and to seriously reconsider putting money into future iterations of this or other Tom Clancy games, so take that for what it's worth. These aren't even difficult things to have considered (or fixed), so if you're like me it will really give you pause when reaching for your wallet.

Full review:
I'm going to be real, at first I expected Guerilla Division. But it was much better. So much better. Yes it has its flaws, but for once, the good outweigh the bad.

The driving for starters was pretty cancer at first. But you can get used to it. There's something about the devs and the "physics of friction" getting along like you would with your in-laws, but you do eventually adapt. If you use a controller like I do (just for vehicles) get ready for the automatic transmission system to be utter crap. For some reason, the land vehicles just can't seem to grasp the idea of shifting out of first gear without me tapping the throttle a few times to wake it up. Maybe it's the deadzone on my particular controller, maybe the game is just sh*t, whatever the case, I've never had that kind of problem before where an automatic transmission in a game refuses to upshift.

Aircraft flying is a nightmare. 

I'm an avid helicopter pilot in nearly every game that has them. From Battlefield to Grand Theft Auto to Arma 2 and 3, I've always enjoyed flying helicopters. But this game really made me want to drive more than fly. It's kind of like Saints Row, or sh*tty aircraft pack from Garry's Mod. You fly them like you would a drone. Up, down, left, right, forward, and back. There's no true control over the physics of the rotors and trim and pitch etc...

Fixed wing airplanes? F*cking forget it. Don't waste your time. For some reason, the dyslexic monkeys on crack on Ubicrap's developer team thought it was a good idea NOT to give airplanes rudder control. That's all I'm going to say about that.

The Artificial Intelligence in this game is mind boggling. 

The enemy AI are pretty standard and honestly I enjoyed being up against them. They acted predictably (in a good way) and did what typical 'bad guy' AI are supposed to do. Their aim wasn't OP korean MLG FPS players WITH aimbots. **cough cough GTA cough cough.** They can be a neusance at times, but at least they're not teleporting, shooting you through walls, and predicting your location like they have a radar too. Unfortunately though the game has a problem with bodies dissapearing really quickly or if you look away for an extended period of time. While this does make for much easier stealth... it's kinda TOO easy as I'm not expected corpses to dissapear before even clearing a single zone. Maybe it's a setting, I don't know, but if it is, it's definitely a flaw.

Your friendly AI however... What the actualy t*tty f*ck were the devs thinking? 

For starters, the Rebels are equally as cancer as the CS:GO community wrapped in burnt leathery bacon smoking cigarettes. I've probably killed more rebels due to their ignorance and stupidity than I care to mention. I've lost count how many have fallen infront of my car, or ran RIGHT in front of me while I was laying down automatic fire. The reasons just go on and on.

Then there's your squad. Holy f*cking @ss crackers. They cause you more problems than anything if you want to take them on to the battlefield. The command system they give is supposed to be helpful, but the way you select the commands on the wheel is more of a hinderance than an aid. It has much too many steps for a 'quick select' feature. You're honestly better off telling them to f*ck off on a nearby hill, and only use them to take out enemies with the Sync Shot. That's literally all they're good for. 

Other than these obviously sh*tty points about the game I've made, I actually do recomend you play it. Wait for a sale though. Don't bother with any of the DLC.

Not Fun at All
- Grinding mission is less variation, it just seems there are only 15 kind of missions (or something) in different areas, not creative. A small base can be done in 5 mins, medium in 10-15. - Some buildings are the same in different regions, so same tactics in different regions, kinda boring. Almost every building has no doors, if there’s one then that means you cannot go in there, or you need to kick it down or blow it up.
- Health; There is no health bar, which is great. Unfortunately, there is Health regeneration which makes this game less realistic. I ran like hell for hundreds of meter, then I went on crouch then snipe some sicario on the tower, no recoil and I still got a clean shot, so my character has a very great breathing ability.
- Enemies bases & patrol are less variation; I expected a vast enemy base with hundreds of personnel, especially when facing the four cartel bosses, how come there are only (around) 20 – 30 personnel? 1 magazine was enough for the whole troops if 1 bullet per person.
There are some enemy bases that connected with some old-unused mine, it felt a bit big, unfortunately, enemies are not as many as I expected.
- AI for NPC are sucks; some rebels might just attack the base I tried to infiltrate (in some missions) randomly then it failed the mission, how come? Rebels won’t attack enemies when they are on patrol, silly. Then somehow there’s a pedestrian just walk in the middle of a forest and waiting to be hit by a car.
- Team/the AI Squad; they are a bullet sponge, they are a jumper (do teleport), corny conversation & jokes, not stealthy, wear the same clothes but won’t wear the same as mine and caused me a lot of missions failed just because they standing/crouching in front of the enemies. 
Team Squad has only 4 commands: Fire, Hold, Move To and Regroup.
Fire: They’ll shoot anyone and kill almost everyone, sometimes you don’t even need to waste a bullet.
Hold: Won’t move. Won’t budge. Even they were spotted & got shoot at.
Move To: This is the funny part. They move to the spot that I asked them, actually I need 1 of them but instead 3 of them move to the spot. Then they stay still until I got shot and semi-die after that one of them move to revive (or sometimes teleport) which left the spot I asked him to be there.
Regroup: I rarely use this command since it will only bring me problems, either they got spotted or shot or whatever. I use this when I need them close to revive me.

I expected that I can give a command to each of my squad, so the stealthy infiltration will be more realistic. I noticed that one of them is a sniper/spotter and the other an assaulter, however when we sync shot, every one of them was a sniper.

There is no history about me, my team or my superior. Hell, I even didn’t know who I work for after reaching El Sueno. Well, we are just a ghost after all. Right?



CO-OP Gameplay
I must say, despite all those negative experiences. This is what I found fun in this game. When I play with friends, damn, it was so much fun. You can see in people’s reviews, I didn’t believe it at first but then I’m kinda addicted to it. Then I met people I didn’t know, we played together for a couple of hours. It’s fun.

Now for the EXTREME Difficult, I mean I played it on Extreme Difficulty.
It is Hell even with the HUD turned on.
The Tier doesn’t award me much. Yeah, I can upgrade my guns and add it with more damage (small). Maybe you think it’s nothing, wait until you can bring down a heli with one-shot. 

When people commented on how bad this game is, I don’t blame them, but you should try with the HUD turned OFF. Then you’ll know why we were named as a GHOST. It requires a lot of Patience, Precision and Tactics. You can’t just come in and kick the front door down, you’ll be dead (semi-dead if you can be revived twice per fight) in a Second. If enemies see you then you are Dead, they shot just like Lucky Luke, you’ll be dead when you realize it, hahaha.

The ’Extreme’ mode really requires your guns on silencer all the time and you have to kill them silently. Enemies only aim & targeted at you if you were spotted, even your team was the one who’s spotted.

Basically, this is Far Cry without crafting, attacking/attackable animals, less collectibles, no towers and less weapon options. In other words, Far Cry Light.

The main questline so far, is mostly good. Same with voice acting. Graphics are excellent, and the huge world is beautiful.

But there are tons of negatives, unfortunately...

- Vehicle controls, especially for planes and helicopteres, are absolute garbage.
- Enemy helicopters is a constant annoyance, at least after first zone. They are almost contantly on to you. It's sometimes so bad that I have my toons commit suicide just to get rid of them.
- The skill system is among the worst I've ever seen. You get skill points from certain quests, by finding them in the world, and by leveling up. But you need resources to spend them. And the main way of getting resources, is doing side quests like stealing planes and helicopters. Due to the terrible controls mentioned earlier, I haven't done a lot of those, which is why I currently have 69 (!!) unspent skill points... The only positive here, is that most skills are garbage and you can do absolutely fine without them.
- Respawning after dying. Sometimes you respawn extremely far from where you died, in fact several kilometres. This is VERY annoying since you have to spend several minutes just getting back to where you was.
- Some missions does not make sense at all. For example, one mission requires you to sneak into an enemy base, without killng anyone and not being seen. And once you get there, you need to hold the posion right there in the middle of the base, killing everyone who's coming for you. And, if you fail to defend your position, you have to do EVERYTHING all over again. And you may not even be able to do that right away. Because if the time goes past 4 a.m. when defending, and you fail, you have to wait till 9 p.m. to try again... What kind of scumbag came up with this garbage?

So, is it worth it? Well, yes. Kinda. But it's certainly not worth the full price. If you're on a tight budget, go for Far Cry 4 and/or 5 instead, and you'll get similar games but much more value for you money.

Great game. Lots of fun. Some real shortcomings, but the strengths outdo the weaknesses. 

POSITIVES:
Game mechanics are strong. Good graphics. Good stealth (though the enemy is not aggressive enough when searching for you, trying to find you). Fairly large game world, free to roam. Very entertaining.  Great fun. 

Great camera angles, giving you the option to easily toggle between 1st person and 3rd person view. I've never liked only playing in 1st person, which is usually your only option in most similar type of games. Spent most of my time in 3rd person and it was great. 

NEGATIVES: 
The story was not entirely bad, and it serves a purpose, giving you direction and a sense of purpose. Yet, to me, the story feels a bit lacklustre. Hunt down the cartel leaders and eliminate or kidnap them, then repeat the process... That's it. If there's a sequel I'd hope for a stronger story. To me, a strong story that drives the game forward and gives the protagonist plausible and justified reason to do all the things he/she does is absolutely fundamental. Story is everything. 

Car-chases could have been an absolute highlight in this game, but the enemy can't drive for ****, they're so slow and pursuers give up easily when you outpace them. Also, during car-chases, friend and foe alike is literally hanging out of the car windows firing at each other like insane when the cars are supposed to go at max speed. Realistically that would be suicide (a simple sharp turn and *snap*), and because they they fire at each other constantly the cars blow up in a fiery inferno basically before the car chase can begin... It takes away the joy and thrill. If friend and foe could behave reasonably and stay inside the cars, it could instead have been a fight to push each other off the road. What can be more satisifying than driving your target or pursuers off a cliff through skillful driving and see the car rolling down the hill? But thing is, on the rare occasion that enemy veichles don't blow up too soon, if you do manage to push them off the road/cliff, the enemy is always unscathed. Unharmed. No matter the fall. The steering of cars are not the best either, as many others have agreed.

Also, you have 3 companions, or co-agents, that are forced on you. You can't choose to leave them behind or temporarily go solo. They're always with you! Always. Even when you don't want them to. They can't die. They can "fall" in battle, but they're back on their feet and healthy as healthy can be once you stick a medic-aid-something in them to revive them. When my soldiers can't die, then what's at stake??? Nothing. From a story-perspective, my crew is invincible. It takes the edge of the story, plausibility, immersion and sense of danger/hostile environment. It becomes a case of unlimited respawns/chances. It is very, very rare though that the enemy actually shoots at your 3 co-agents, because the enemy AI is so poor that all enemies ALWAYS will shoot at YOU, even when you are farther away and partially behind cover while your allies is out in the open, standing almost right in front of the enemy. I would prefer if my co-agents were mortal... and replaceable. Like, if 1 or 2 of them died/suffered serious wounds, I could recruit new ones at certain safehouses, though I don't think the agents should come in unlimited supply. There should be a cap, and a case of "work with what you have, if you lose them all and your own character, you die and fail. Game over. Try again." I also would have greatly preferred to create my own agents, all 4 of them, not just the main character, and then swap between using them as I see fit, like was the case in the very first and original Ghost Recon game, back 2001 +/-. In effect, there wouldn't really be a main character, but the focus would be on the unit/squad itself. So, squad-wise, Wildlands is a step back from the original. Lots of good things from the original could/should have been kept. Imagine if we started out with a larger squad and used them on rotation as we saw fit. Wounded agents obviously would have to be put out of action temporarily or permanently dependign on the severity... A bit of squad management then.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Wildlands.

 OR: The Backpacker's Guide to Bolivia (MilSim, it ain't!)

Are you considering going on an adventure? Do you like to rough it out in the wild, taming nature armed with nothing but your wits and your innate curiosity? Well, the good people at Ubisoft (UBI) have designed this useful and innovative Virtual Tourist Guide just for you! This time: Bolivia.

Take in the stunning beauty of the Bolivian countryside and the charming rural communities scattered along scenic routes or nestled in breath-taking wilderness. Visit Klaus Barbie's (now) abandoned hut - complete with a hidden door and underground tunnels - and see Messrs. Cassidy and the Kid's last stand at San Vincente. And don't forget all the fascinating drug-lord hide-outs and private estates, each one more complex and luxurious than the other. And of course, learn useful phrases such as "Come la m****a, cabrón!" to ease interaction with the local populace,  and greet passers-by with a cheerful "Míra, p*****o!"

I know it says "Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Wildlands" (GRW) on the cover, but just ignore that and traverse this immensely beautiful country designed in great detail and with impressive graphics. UBI clearly have found a new and much more promising use of their game designers and developers, one which I hope they'll stick with because they sure as f*** don't know anything about game development!

But it's not all bad news. In fact, GRW is so close to achieving a "Recommended" rating it almost feels the coin could have landed on either side. But it ultimately comes out as "Not recommended" for the following reasons (in no particular order of severity and for PC using keyboard/mouse):

1. The "Shoulder View Shuffle" is insanely annoying and so disruptive as to make it almost impossible to engage enemies without constantly having to adjust the shoulder view thereby losing critical split-seconds. Why is this not a user-defined option?

2. The dozens of "Black Holes" littered around the map add another difficulty level not to mention endless frustration, especially when extracting an HVT after 30 minutes of intense stealth or all-out fire-fights with 150,000 Unidad and SBC enemies - only to walk or fall into a Black Hole that you can't leave or get out of. Your only option is to exit to the Main Menu thereby losing everything since the last AutoSave, which is always some 30 - 40 minutes ago.

3. This brings me to quality control and testing which are either woefully underfunded or out-sourced to people who clearly don't give a flying f*** - or maybe everyone at UBI is too busy making "Ghost Babies" instead of checking for obvious bugs like these. On that note, the average keyboard has some 119 individual keys, and UBI seem hell-bent on  using every single one of them, making GRW an absolute nightmare to play.

4. The player characters (female and male) are beyond non-descript. I know they're supposed to be secretive people who don't really "exist" - hence the title - but even  with this in mind, Nomad must qualify as the single most boring, one-dimensional player character ever devised. And Andrea Deck's voicing does nothing to suggest that Nomad is even a carbon-based life-form. Jane Perry does a slightly better job with Karen Bowman, but sadly you can't play as Bowman (to my knowledge).

5. The Squad is so useless it's almost a joke. You literally need to semi-die before they act; they will walk past a cartel soldier running towards you and do absolutely nothing until you're lying on the ground waiting to be revived. As you upgrade the Squad skills, they will become marginally more useful, but no matter the level or the situation, you still need to semi-die before they act.

6. The story-line is mundane and clichéd, and it utterly fails to engage me. This is a shame, because UBI clearly spent a lot of time with all the Kingslayer files and tape recordings, but it all comes out as: "Oh, another drug-bust - this time in Bolivia." The extra material - all the info about Bolivia, its history, legends, and mythology, while certainly interesting cannot possibly compensate for the thin-legged, re-hashed "US vs a random drug cartel" template. And just when you thought it couldn't get any more predictable, after some 130 hours in my case, you get the same hackneyed "Villain cuts a deal with the US" ending that you've seen a milion times before. (Unless you activate the Sueño mission by mistake at 99 % completion, as I did, and get a slightly different ending. This ending, BTW, is so much more rewarding I'm surprised UBI didn't choose it for the 100 % option).

7. Replay value is zero point zero. Once you've completed the game at 100 % (with all collectibles and trophies) and enjoyed all the good stuff and endured all the bad stuff, replaying this game only offers all the insanely annoying bad stuff and no sense of reward or accomplishment.

8. No matter the difficulty level, every single encounter with SBC or Unidad precipitates World War 3; the moment you're spotted, GRW goes from ambitious stealth action á la Metal Gear Solid V to the cheapest zombie hack´n´slasher imaginable, with enemy soldiers, vehicles, and choppers piling on endlessly. I wish I was exaggerating, but you can spend 20 or 30 minutes just picking out soldiers with your rifle, vehicles with your HTI sniper rifle, and choppers with your rifle-based rocket launcher (after 30 minutes of doing exactly this in Koani Province I simply got bored and left, but I bet I could have continued for hours!)

If you check the CIA Statistical Yearbook, I guarantee you the actual Bolivian Armed Forces do not possess anywhere near this amount of helicopters. And this happens every f***ing time you're spotted! And you're just sitting there thinking "at some point they must run out of soldiers, vehicles, and choppers - right?" Nope!

9. The 'dynamic' day/night cycle could have been an excellent feature, but UBI need to understand that users want to be in charge. In Metal Gear Solid V you can smoke a 'Phantom Cigar' and accelerate time; in FallOut 4 you can sit on a bench and indicate how many hours you want to advance in time. This makes it possible to conduct most of these games in daylight - when you can actually SEE something (and, yes, both games have dynamic night/time). The day/night cycle in GRW works like this:

A. You die during day-time. You respawn at night.
B. You die during night-time. You respawn... at night!
C. Every time you die, you respawn AT NIGHT! Every f***ing time!

This means you spend some 80 % of GRW in total darkness. So you use your night-vision which gives you a vomit-coloured maxi-dot screen in "glorious 240p". Gee, I'm so glad I spent hundreds of dollars/euro on a high-end GPU!

In conclusion GRW emerges as either a very innovative Virtual Tourist Guide to Bolivia, OR a total waste of 130 hours of my life and €60 gone from my bank account. Hoo-ah, and Bowman out!

I LOVE THIS GAME

Now let me tell you why.

Going through the review sections, you will find many reviews pointing out that the game's story is not all that diversified or rich, and that it mostly just accumulates grinding. However, You must understand that they are overlooking the main attraction of this game which is teamwork and tactical gameplay (admittedly not the most realistic) but still.

I for one, adore the tactical gameplay that this game provides. It is not too simple nor too forgiving, the difficulty scales very well based on how you want your game to be with enemies being harshly unforgiving on the hardest difficulty and your minimap offering no aid whatsoever as to enemy positions unless you sport them. 

Stealth approaches have a very satisfying feel when you pull it off whereas the game gives you the opportunity to run and gun if your heart so desires.

There are obviously flaws to the game too, the major one of which is ubisoft's joke of an attempt on driving/piloting physics, and the weapon ballistics aren't all that accurate either. But, it is important to note that these aspects are not what this game was intended to perfect. The game gives you a wide variety of missions and landscapes to plan your approaches on. A heavily fortified base in the mountains is going to allow you a lot of sniping cover but a similar scenario on the salt plains isnt going to play out very well with the same strategy. Which is why every zone feels different and refreshing.

The game also supports a lot of weaponry to fit your playstyle and in a similar fashion to "The Division" allows you to carry two primaries and a secondary. So you can easily adapt from a patient sniper to John Wick. 

If I had the money, I'd buy this game at full price and would not be dissapointed, but at a sale, it is a must have for all you guys who like to plan out your attacks and feel satisfaction in a perfect execution.

I've been a huge fan of Tom Clancy games since the 1990s, including the original Ghost Recon, so I wanted to get at least 50 hours of play time before I reviewed! KEEP IN MIND I HAVEN'T DONE ANY PVP, only co-op and solo in the open world.

First of all, a statement meant for you to take neutrally: The only thing this has in common with the original Ghost Recon is the fact that the words "Ghost" and "Recon" are in the name... Also, this game has many difficulty settings. I got kinda bored with it after about 30 hours until I realized I was on the "Casual" setting, and cranked it up to max! Now it's actually a challenge.

All politics aside, Wildlands really is its own, unique, amazing game... and there will be more on that later. But when I describe this game to my gaming buddies that haven't played it yet, I say that it feels like a combination of Grand Theft Auto 5 and Sniper Ghost Warrior 3, so I'm going to use those as comparison points for certain things.

What do I mean it's like Sniper Ghost Warrior 3? Well, if you've played SGW3 you can easily understand the concepts in this game and will recognize certain familiarities in the UI. In my opinion, it's freakishly similar. You can even fly a drone around marking targets like in SGW3. But Ubisoft did it sooooooo much better. You can work toward improving your skills/character to hold more items, unlock other items, improve accuracy, larger explosion radius, etc. You can work toward improving your drone through skills, and even turn it into an EMP or IED. You have fast travel points on the map just like SGW3. I swear someone at Ubisoft must have played SGW3 and said, "This is kinda alright, but let's do it better and rake in the lewtz!"

What do I mean it's like GTA 5? Firstly, if you've played GTA5 -- the 3rd person "mechanism" on this feels a lot like that. The clunkiness of movement and shooting, the at-times difficulty navigating radial menus during a firefight... It DOES give you the benefit of better situational awareness, since you can see around objects and plan your actions. But for me at least, every time I come up with some awesome plan, I get stuck on a wall, or end up needing extra time to "swing around" from my current viewpoint. Secondly, it has a lot of interactive "stuff" around! You can kill civilians and helpful rebels, though enough of it brings a penalty. You can fly helicopters, airplanes, boats, cars, trucks, ATVs, big rigs hauling stuff -- either empty ones or jack ones that are currently occupied ;)

Other stuff:
- YOU HAVE AI TEAMMATE SUPPORT you can order around when playing solo!! (which is something I was hoping for when playing Lone Wolf in Rainbow Six: Siege)
- HUGE open world to explore, with things to do all over the map. Even after 50 hours there's just a never-ending array of tasks. Yeah they all kinda start to feel the same after a while, but it's a video game after all.
- The initial load time seems to take forever when first starting a game or after you die and are respawning -- BUT you can move around the entire, massive map freely with no additional load time after the initial load.
- Do whatever you want. Sure you can do the storylines and the missions. Or, just drive around and look at the scenery. Practice drifting in a van. Dive out of a helicopter into a lake from almost 4km in the air. Drive down a dirt road at 200mph in a Lambo and see how far you can get before you crash it in a fiery blaze. Pretend you're the world's worst big rig driver and plow other vehicles off the road / over cliffs. Go dirt-biking across a salt flat. Lie down on some train tracks, or run across traffic without looking both ways. The power is yours! (Individual results may vary. Do not try this at home.)
- Many of the objects in game are actually objects. That stack of boxes over there? You know your inner toddler wants to knock it over!
- Lots of weapons, accessories, and utilities.
- Attention to detail and ambience. NPCs act drunk, sing, interact with each other, eat, and even go inside and sleep! Including the enemy cartel you're hunting. The radio station even changes its programming as you do the storylines, to match all the explosions, chaos, and death you've created!
- Multiplayer co-op is awesome! You can plan team stuff or just go in blazing together, or even go your own separate ways if you're feeling antisocial.

I waited for a sale because I'm a miser and can't justify spending 80 bucks (Canadian) on ANY game regardless of how good it might be or how much money is burning a hole in my pocket. However, that being said -- had I paid full price, I would NOT be regretting it! I imagine even after I get bored with it, it'll be a game I come back to every so often.

There are more negatives on this list but the positives outweigh the negatives in quality, not quantity. There are flaws but they don't ruin the game.

Essential features that function as expected:
►Fully rebindable keys.
►Adjustible field of view.
►Well optimized performance.
►Support for high framerates.
►Raw mouse input.

Things that are good:
▲Extensive options to customize everything you need, with preview images included.
▲All HUD elements can be invidually disabled or enabled and there's an instant hotkey ingame to turn everything off.
▲Very good character customization, with save slots for different cosmetic item loadouts. Extended to AI squad mates in an update. However there is no option to replace squad mates with completely custom or female characters even though they have voice acting.
▲Dynamic cover system that works perfectly and never gets in your way. Whne your character approaches a wall, they take cover in a realistic way automatically without the need of a "cover" -button.
▲Ubisoft has always been very good at making ground vehicles that have handling that's reasonably good and not too arcade and not too realistic.
▲Ubisoft's best implementation of ledge mantling so far. No pre-determined points, basically everything that looks like you can climb it, you can climb it.
▲The best implementation of dynamic day/night and weather cycles to date. Every combination of lighting and weather seems to produce an accurate representation of what it would look like IRL. All the materials change to wet variants from rain and slowly dry in the sun.
▲Vehicular stealth works fairly well and in a way that makes sense. Enemies will not look twice if you drive past them in a civilian car or a vehicle of their faction, unless already alerted. It is absolutely not like the Far Cry games where every road encounter leads to combat.

Things that are bad:
▼When aiming in 3rd person, the crosshair doesn't accurately reflect what your character can actually hit. You can accidentally shoot at an obstacle in front of you because your character is shooting towards the crosshair from the side, but the crosshair is pointing at your target straight ahead. It's that same age-old FPS game flaw where you blow yourself up with a bazooka after shooting at a wall right in front of you even though you could clearly see that your weapon is pointing past the wall.
▼In 2018 it has been ten years since Ubisoft forgot how to save a game. In all Ubisoft AAA games, "savegames" save almost nothing. Nothing you've done before the game makes its autosave will be restored upon loading. Your equipment will reset to full and your position will be a default one for that autosave. Most insultingly, you will not lose any XP progress or items you have found, you will literally restart from the location you died so no progress is lost, even the time of day will stay at the time of your death because the game simply will not revert to a state that it supposedly saved. Gone are the days of DOS-games like Doom where a savegame would record the location and trajectory of every airborne rocket on its way to a target. It's embarrassing how inept Ubisoft is in this regard. It's like they think saves must still fit a 1MB PS1 memory card.
▼"Return to the area of operations" has a 15 second limit that is often barely enough when you accidentally pass the borders in a flying vehicle.
▼Even though the microtransactions are for cosmetic items, the system is predatory and dishonest. You have to buy packs of ingame currency, and items are precisely priced so that you can only ever have too much or too little currency for what you want. There is no way to get exactly your money's worth.
▼There is no "wait" mechanic. If you really want to do a mission during nighttime, you'll have to actually wait for night to fall, or to zigzag across the map using the fast travel system to speed things along.
▼Even though your AI squadmates are almost invisible to the enemies, still sometimes they can act so stupid around hostiles that they will blow your cover. The only alternative is to leave them behind and sneak into enemy territory by yourself, and their stealth is completely disabled while they are following an order you've given. If you tell them to wait, they will do nothing to avoid being seen by passing patrols.
▼Stealth is very important but you can't move bodies to hide them unless you very conspicuously grab them as human shields and then knock them out in a safe location. Fortunately bodies disappear very quickly when you look the other way.
▼Some missions that should logically have a stealthy option insist on "helping you" with rebel reinforcements who will get you into firefights that you will not survive on the hardest difficulty.
▼Sometimes you are arbitrarily forced to physically enter an area in order to do recon, even though you can very easily use your drone instead.
▼Sometimes a rebel group will randomly wander into an enemy base like they own the place and put everyone on alert while you're trying to sneak around. It's not a useful distraction. Your enemies be more alert for any intruders.
▼The game incentivizes dispatching targets very quickly to avoid alerts, but you are also not supposed to kill surrendering targets. You will never have the time to check if someone is surrendering or not.
▼You get a game over if you shoot civilians, except children. You can empty all your mags into kids and the game doesn't penaltize you for it. Because they're inexplicably invincible. Is this a value judgement? Shooting up an elementary school has no consequences but executing the elderly forces you to restart?
▼Tier Mode AI is artificially difficult. They can snipe you from long range through walls with dual-wielded automatic weapons, and even spawn-kill you by materializing behind you.
▼Raiding comm stations on higher difficulties usually involves at least one knockdown and revive because your AI squadmates simply will not help you take down the hostiles inside, and flashbangs you use are randomly completely ineffective. It's exactly like trying to do a SWAT raid on a building in real life on your own. Walk through a door checking the wrong corner without anyone checking the other, and you're instantly dead.
▼IR-goggles can't see through infrared-transparent materials such as thin walls, but can see through infrared-opaque materials such as glass.
▼Anti-aircraft missile turrets can only be avoided by flying low, and "low" means literally on the ground. They will acquire you if you rise above 2 meters. If you destroy a turret, it will respawn as soon as you go beyond 700m from its position, making some of the aircraft theft missions a nightmare where you simply do not have access to proper tactics due to technical limitations of the game engine.
▼Helicopter controls are insane and have no consistency. Why is it that Rockstar can trust their players to learn to fly a chopper in a way choppers actually behave but Ubisoft has to insist on some weird compromise between chopper controls and ground vehicle controls? They released alternate controls in an update but didn't actually fix the problem, just gave you an option to replace it with a variant of the problem.
▼Some of the weapon stat balancing is nonsensical, namely the SR-3 Vikhr, which in real life is one of the most silent subsonic anti-armor covert weapons ever made. In this game it's one of least silent ARs on the roster and doesn't even have good armor penetration.
▼Randomly there is a bug that prevents you from deploying the drone. You only hear a sound like a menu telling you "access denied" and for no reason the drone doesn't work.
▼The Splinter Cell themed special mission is ironically the least stealthy mission in the game. An onslaught of pre-aggroed enemies, and attack helicopters that literally spawn 5 copies of themselves instantly when you shoot one down. Not something that should have anything to do with Splinter Cell.

My god, the draw distance for the map is phenomenal. But the fact you can't see enemies at a mere 600 meters is a total buzzkill for anyone trying to do any long-range sniping. TL;DR: Being quite different from earlier Ghost Recon games, this one tries to do stuff better than Far Cry and Just Cause series and occasionally does, but losing much of the fun parts in the process. If you don't mind repetitive missions, Wildlands can provide dozens of hours of sniping entertainment. Probably great in co-op, although I haven't tried that yet.

While both main and side missions are quite repetitive, at least in most cases you have some freedom to choose how to complete them. Mission descriptions could use more hints of what to expect. It's dumb to fail a mission because a target has a sports car next to him and you only have your legs for a sudden chase, which obviously becomes a problem. There are some nearly impossible missions that were clearly badly designed and/or not playtested properly (especially a particular truck depot). I haven't played co-op so I don't know if those missions are easier with friends.

Faction wars between rebels, cartel and Unidad are sometimes useful, but there really should be some code to prevent them in mission areas. It's terribly annoying to successfully snipe dozens of enemies but then fail a mission because of getting dragged into a big gunfight someone else started.

AI teammates are useful in sniping (sync shots), but when things heat up, they become rather useless. Often they just watch their commander (you) getting shot at, and at that point there's usually too little time to order them to do anything useful to prevent player death. A couple of times they even left me bleeding to death for no apparent reason.

It's unfair that enemies can aim perfectly through vegetation while I can't even see what's coming at me. In the hardest difficulty levels their reaction time and aiming become so superhuman that attacking radio stations becomes nearly impossible; in such tight spaces you're dead before you can even spot the enemies. Tossing grenades is surprisingly ineffective.

Vehicles handle quite well, so driving and flying is generally enjoyable. Mountain roads are an exception, though. Besides being narrow and full of hairpin turns (one of them is even named Death Road), there's also WAY too much traffic, disturbing all the frequent car chases. There should be more like one car per minute instead of one every few seconds, as the mountains are supposed to be the titular sparsely populated wildlands – not GTA cities.

SAM sites are awful, and their respawning is nearly game-breaking. For example, I tried to blow up missile sites around a runway to be able to steal a plane, but after destroying the last one I turned around and saw that the first one was already back in action!

The game could've used some more humor. There is some funny banter between your team, but all in all the tone of the game is a tad too serious.

There's not much music, but that's good. The subtle use of music creates atmosphere and tension.

It was exciting to meet a famous scifi villain in the jungles, and I've read there are plenty of smaller easter eggs all over the game. That fight was hard, but later I managed to win (hint: Tier One weapon upgrades).

It's unfortunate that there's no endgame content, so there's not much to do after you complete the story missions. This could've been easily fixed by adding random intel recovery missions to enemy bases. Right now there are some "season challenges", of which I played the Yeti hunt. Those don't seem to provide much additional gameplay, though.

The keys for drone, binoculars and possibly others randomly stop working. Apparently this bug has existed since beta. Not cool. Other than that, bugs seem rare, although I got stuck in a couple of cars and experienced a trippy fall to the void beneath the game world.

Despite all my complaints there's still a good sniping game beneath the problems, so I can recommend this – but only barely. Wait for a sale, just in case.

-As I said earlier the looks and world are stunning, but the interaction with it is really weird and goofy at times. So let's start with the very basics, the movement. It feels .. clunky, like a game from 2007-2010. When you run and want to go in the right of left direction, your character immidiately turns and goes to that direction, no change in animation , no momentum and no weight to it. Just watch a youtube video and you'll understand what I'm saying. You are pretty much just glued to the ground and a simple Can of beans on the ground can stop you from advancing forward, the way you go over cliffs is simply by finding a good rock which prompts a " Climb " option to it. - Why can't I see the laser sights from my team mates?

My review of this game is mixed. As this game doesn't offer a complete ranking system, I am recommending base on the cost of the game upon time of purchase. I bought this game complete for 25 dollars (Season 1 Pass + Base Game). Based upon the price of that alone I can recommend it. 

I will go over some Pros and Cons like other reviews before me so one can judge before purchase.

Pros:
- Graphics. The game looks gorgeous and runs smoothly with a GTX 1060 (6 GB) and I6700 Processor. I ran 60 FPS a majority of the time with little to no hitches on max settings. Just staring off at the distance had me in awe, if not when you are on the ground watching the grass sway as you walk through it.
- Guns (Lots of guns with LOTS of customization, from camos to the barrels themselves), Keep in mind you have to locate all weapon attachements and extra weapons. Base weapons are passeable, and all guns are serviceable. Gun use is almost a preference.
-Plenty of side quests and tasks to keep you busy.
-Coop available (I never got to experience, but just after dealing with the AI, I could see having a friend or 2 would help significantly, and be fun as well).
-Addition of PVP (I haven't played, but the addition is there)
-Customization of character. (While somewhat lacking, it is present, and lets you get creative with some wacky stuff, or just being a operator)
-Tier 1 mode (adds end game incentive to replay, and is challenging, if not somewhat frustrating)

Cons 
-Redudant gameplay, almost every task is completed in a similar manner, and while there is a dynamic it isn't pleasant.
-Forced stealth gameplay. I will emphasize this, as it has never been as heavily forced on a ghost recon ever before. Not using a silencer is almost a punishment in this game. This is negating the facts that alot of missions FORCE you to not be detected or mission failure.
-Connecting off the stealth is the stealth mechanics. Stealth mechanics don't feel fun or fluid, and are almost always ruined by AI.
-Now  to the AI. Ally and enemy alike, it becomes infuriating. You could successfully bypass 30 guys with some smooth stealth technics, just to have a mission ruined by a random group of rebels blowing your cover. Likewise a random helicopter or car patrol could spot you a mile away, even while hidden, the consistency in detection never felt present(even while fully upgraded)
-Story not extremely compeling, but at the same time it is not forced. (Good or bad) 
-Your accomplishments never really feel like..... well accomplishments. To put this short, no matter how much the computer tells you through dialogue how you are impacting Bolivia, you never see it. Bases will always respawn infinite enemies, respawn SAM turrets, and so on. This isn't Far Cry where once you take that base, you literally take it. 
-SAM Turrets and Unidad. I have no problem with adding a challenge, but being blown out of the sky constantly because that SAM turret you killed 5 minute earlier respawned is infuriating. Then imagine traveling 10 KM with a supply plane just to have 5 missiles lock onto you in your last .5 km...... Think of Unidad as GTA Cops. They don't stop coming no matter how many you kill, and they WILL ruin your missions atleast a good few times. 
-Bugs, I am gonna throw this in, they are here. Just haven't experienced too many beyond some clipping and weird lighting on occassions. 
-While not entirely necessary, things like requesting a vehicle could become infuriating. It could spawn next to you, or...... 1 km away in an enemy base. You have no control over it.

As I previously stated this is a good budget game. The designers really went all out with the feel of an imaginary Bolivia. Even the cartel had some appeal to it. The story wasn't invalid, but I felt was heavily weighed down due to the lack of impact you actually had on the world around you. I understand that they kept respawning enemies for end game, coop, challenge etc, but that could've been more confined to after completion of the story, or even upon a preference of the player. Once you get the hang of the gameplay, it did feel a tad redudant. I felt that the fun of the game got weighed down by man of the cons stated. It is entirely worth 20 dollars, maybe even 30. The content time is there, but I believe the maximum enjoyment would be with friends (as I believe developers may have intended). Playing Solo was painful at times.

The AI squad members, let's say were not smart, or even useful beyond reviving you and the occassional kill or 2. The forced stealth may have made it worse. The player really never was in control of how a mission played, more the skill of the player's stealth ability came into play. That and patience. This at times felt more like Splinter Cell, than maybe even splinter cell. To top this off, we have a open world game with such flaws, when other games years before it had corrected or added improvement systems. 

With that said I did enjoy the game for the most part, and hope they make some vast improvements in the future (1 being adding character preference in play, and maybe slightly smarter allies). Ironically Ubisoft had 2 titles in both categories that they could have borrowed from to make an optimized experience (Far Cry and Splinter Cell). They got graphics down, now lets go more onto the gameplay aspect. The switch from 3rd to 1st was actually done well done though, so props for that.

Once you've taken out a province in most games, the random encounter enemys seem to dissapear. This is not at all the case of Wildlands, where you can still get in gun fights with Cartel Sicarios even after you've butchered their regional boss. I love this, as this aspect made me get bored of Just Cause 3 once I had 100% it and liberated all the towns and bases; in Wildlands you can wipe out the Santa Blanca men in a base, take a little trip across Bolivia, and come back to some more angry guys, and do it all again a different way. The replayability will deffinitly keep me coming back for at least a year or 2 on my 15 fps laptop, and I hope you get to have a similar experience playing it but with better frames.

It's a neat tactical shooter where proper recon, planning and execution are in the foreground.
However, I can only recommend it if you play it like me:
* Always with friends, never solo
* Only on hardest difficulty

Playing on anything but the hardest difficulty makes it a shooter game, and it's nothing special in that aspect. However, turning the difficulty up to max forces you and your friends to act reasonable to some degree. To plan ahead, stay hidden, do proper recon and keep the upper hand at all times. Successfully executing a plan in this game is pretty fun.

This is why I cannot recommend playing solo. As soon as you are not in a game with other players, you get three horribly useless AI teammates. The core of what made this game fun for me is planning and cooperation, and the teammate AI doesn't offer that.

In addition, you'd better be bug tolerant, as this game often does weird and slightly unfair things that can lead to frustration.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Recommended when you [b]and your friends[/b] are into cooperation, planning and communication.
Not really recommended if you want to play alone or are looking for a shooter.

After putting off for buying this game for over a year, I finally purchased the Gold Edition for $32 on the Steam sale, which is an aboslute steal. 

Not only do you get all content except Year 2 pass, but you also get a great game. When I first played the open-beta, I had a problem with the game's difficulty. We were, (my friends,) playing at the hardest difficulty in the beta and were breezing through everything. But the game's difficulty now has extreme, as well as "Tier One" after you reach level 30, and it definitely makes the game more challenging and fun.

[h1][b] STORY [/b][/h1]
I haven't even started on the story yet, i'll try to edit this review after i've completed the story. But for now, i'm having too much fun just going around and taking out Unidad outposts stealthly, going around and collecting all weapons/attachments/skill points/etc., and stealing supplies for skill(s)... It's a great game, but it does have it's flaws.

[h1][b] PROS [/b][/h1]
1. Great gun selection, far better than Far Cry 5's gun selection. 

(I know that's not a hard thing to beat) but for real, the gun selection in this game is amazing. All weapons are very well balanced, and I feel there isn't any "best" weapon. All weapons are basically even as far as performance goes, and you basically choose in your opinion the best. My favorite is the m4a1, and G28 sniper. 

2. Massive open-world.

Definitely the biggest open-world i've ever played besides DayZ, and the "difficulty's" for each region don't really effect you. You can go to any region you want right off the bat, and not have to worry about OP enemies that basically force you to play in the lower level'd area(s) like some other games (*cough* The Divison)

3. 4 Player co-op is some of the best co-op experiences i've ever had in a video game. Especially when defeating The Predator ;)

4. Character customazation is also great, however it's annoying how some of the clothing options like the "Predator Helmet" w/ dreads is locked behind a ~$20 paywall. :(

also, beards! Gotta love having a bushy beard.

[h1][b] FLAWS [/b][/h1]
The first few I can think of are
1. Driving

The driving is absolutely horrendous. Vehicles drive like they're on ice 100% of the time, heli's have low health so any standard NPC can shoot it down, and plane's are slow, and also have low health. The maneuverability in vehicles is terrible, it's hard to get away from enemies chasing you, doesn't matter if you're in the air, or on the ground. I recommend taking down heli's before you get in a heli to escape your patrol.

2. Bullet Travel Speed

The bullet travel speed is also quite bad, I believe Wildlands *highly* exaggerates suppressor's slowing down bullet speed. So, without a suppressor the bullet speed is about what it would be in real life WITH a suppressor. I say [b]about[/b] because it might be a tiny bit slower, but definitely not as slow as it is in the game WITH a suppressor. It takes about half a second at ~15m for a bullet to connect once shot. That's ridiculous. The human eye shouldn't even be able to process the bullet when fired, it should connect INSTANTLY when shot. At least, to the human eye "instantly." Considering most of everyone who plays this game has a stealthy play-style, you basically need to use a suppressor. Enemies can't hear unsuppressed shots ~150m out, so sniping unsupressed is fine.

3. Friendly AI when not playing co-op

Your Team AI you get when not playing co-op is quite idiotic and stupid. The only thing they're good for is sync shots on the supply missions, or reviving you when things get heated. Thankfully, their stupidity doesn't affect you as far as enemy AI is concerned. They'll sometimes crouch right up and be basically touching enemies when silently taking out a base, and not get detected. So that's a plus, I guess. Breaks immersion though.

4. Microtransations

'nuff said.

No but seriously, the fact there is not a SINGLE way in-game to earn "Credits" to use in the store is absolutely atrocious. If I put 100s (hundreds) of hours into your game, I should at least have a way to earn credits so I can buy my predator mask... >:C

In a genre with fierce competition from able and high-budget products, Ubisoft simply turns the page with this game, I am surprised and impressed I must say. It makes all the competitors suddenly look and feel very yesterday, setting a new standard. 

Not much is really totally new, you can clearly see the various lines of development from previous Ubisoft games and influence from other titles. But it is perfected. The game is slick in performance, loading very fast and using smooth and fast interface throughout. 

The virtual world is huge, divided into regions (new for Ghost Recon and vaguely resembling Far Cry but incorporated into the main plot in quite another manner). Opponents are generally effective, if predictable in the long run, reacting reasonably to your actions and you are able to regulate just how effective they can be.
