Title: Ghost Recon Wildlands - A Thrilling Covert Operation in the Wild
Overall Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5 stars)

Gameplay: ★★★★★ (5/5 stars)
Ghost Recon Wildlands delivers a compelling gameplay experience that combines tactical shooting with open-world exploration. The freedom to approach missions in various ways adds a dynamic element to the gameplay, allowing players to experiment with different strategies. The vast array of weapons and gear, along with customizable characters, cater to diverse playstyles. While the AI can be inconsistent at times, overall, the gameplay remains engaging and enjoyable.

Graphics: ★★★★★ (5/5 stars)
The visuals in Ghost Recon Wildlands are nothing short of breathtaking. Ubisoft Paris has crafted a stunning open-world environment in the lush landscapes of Bolivia. From dense forests to arid deserts, each region is meticulously designed, creating a realistic and immersive world. The attention to detail, day-night cycle, and dynamic weather contribute to the game's stunning graphics, making exploration an awe-inspiring experience.

Sound: ★★★★☆ (4/5 stars)
The sound design in Ghost Recon Wildlands is well-executed, enhancing the overall immersion of the game. The ambient sounds of the environment, gunfire, and explosions create a realistic atmosphere during missions. The voice acting for main characters is commendable, though some supporting NPCs may lack depth. The soundtrack complements the gameplay, adding to the intensity of combat and moments of suspense.

Story and Narrative: ★★★★☆ (4/5 stars)
While the premise of dismantling the Santa Blanca drug cartel sets the stage for an intriguing storyline, Ghost Recon Wildlands falls short in its narrative execution. The plot can feel somewhat predictable and fails to fully engage players emotionally. The character development lacks depth, making it difficult to form strong connections with the protagonists. Despite its potential, the story doesn't reach the same heights as previous entries in the Ghost Recon series.

Multiplayer: ★★★★☆ (4/5 stars)
The cooperative multiplayer mode is where Ghost Recon Wildlands truly shines. Joining forces with friends to tackle missions and take down targets offers a more enjoyable experience compared to playing solo. The seamless transition between single-player and multiplayer modes ensures a smooth and immersive experience. However, the absence of competitive multiplayer options might disappoint players seeking PvP gameplay.

DLCs: ★★★☆☆ (3/5 stars)
Ghost Recon Wildlands' DLCs, "Narco Road" and "Fallen Ghosts," add exciting content to the game, including new missions, weapons, and storylines. "Narco Road" introduces thrilling undercover missions within the Santa Blanca cartel, focusing on daring vehicle-based gameplay. "Fallen Ghosts" ups the challenge with tougher enemy factions and intense survival gameplay. While some DLCs lack impact and suffer from occasional technical issues, overall, they enhance the game's lifespan and offer additional value to fans seeking more adventures in Bolivia.

Bugs and Updates: ★★★☆☆ (3/5 stars)
Ghost Recon Wildlands had its fair share of bugs and technical issues upon release. While Ubisoft Paris addressed many of the early concerns through patches and updates, some issues persisted. The occasional AI glitches and mission bugs could disrupt the gameplay experience. However, the development team's commitment to providing updates and addressing player feedback deserves recognition.

Conclusion: 
Ghost Recon Wildlands successfully blends tactical gameplay with an expansive open-world, offering players the freedom to chart their paths in a visually stunning environment. With solid gameplay mechanics, cooperative multiplayer, and outstanding graphics, it provides hours of enjoyable gameplay. While the story could have been more compelling and certain technical issues lingered, the overall experience remains engaging and satisfying. Whether you're a fan of the series or a newcomer, Ghost Recon Wildlands is a thrilling adventure worth undertaking. if you come here after playing Breakpoint then this is a much better option.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a co-op open world game where you and up to three buddies can take on the Santa Blanca Cartel, across a fictionalized version of Bolivia where this massive organization has essentially taken over the country. You and your team of Ghosts can systematically take down piece by piece. All at your own pace, the game doesn't guide you by the hand past the first zone. Recently, the game also includes a PvP component. Ghost War, a 4v4 class based tactical elimination gamemode. Is it worth your time? Well read on to find out.

Pros
-Immersion. Top notch if you let it. Or not, you can ignore the story and just kill these bad dudes.
-You can do this, by blowing up, knocking out, shooting, or stealthily taking down the cartel.
-Some members of the Cartel are actual characters and you can change the outcome of the story based on how you take down the Cartel.
-Loads of firearms and gunsmith to customize your guns. You can carry two large guns, and a pistol on you at all times.
_> Gunsmith: You can make any gun better suit your playstyle with a large amount of attachments.
-Lots of objectives and things to collect. The world is actually very much realized for what it is. Easily 50 hours of content.
-Gunplay is chunky and feels good in both PvE and PvP.
_> Why? Ballistics. The game utilizes an exaggerated bullet drop system where bullets fly 3x slower than in real-life. This makes bullets feel weighty and makes the gunplay more skillful.
-The game looks amazing in some spots, and can feel like you are going on a vacation in Bolivia sometimes.
-Both stealth, and brute force are valid tactics.
-Loads of vehicles, super cars, helicopters, planes, jeeps, armored personnel carriers, and trucks with miniguns on them.
-PvP has a role for many play styles. Teamplay can really make or break a team composition.

Neutrals
-Average character creator, it's passable. You can operate in proper tactical gear, or you can walk around in a t-shirt and jeans.
-Game is HUGE, both in map size, and in real estate on your hard drive. This is a double edged sword.
_>Map has 21 regions, and 11 different biomes from the desert, to swamps, forests and even snowy mountain tops.
_>Game is about 50 gigabytes big.
-Co-op can get slightly monotonous for some people. As there are a set amount of objectives.
-PvP is currently only elimination. Across 8 distinct maps. There are 12 classes, that keep the game fresh.
-Some missions autofail, if a player is seen. These can be annoying if you aren't good at hiding.

Cons
-Game needs a bit of optimization. And by a bit I mean quite a bit. Most PCs, cannot sustain a solid 60 fps.
-Crashes tend to occur if you have an antivirus that the game doesn't like.
-Has a few odd bugs, physics based usually. Falling through the world sometimes, etc.
-Sometimes hangups occur, and the game may not register certain things like launched grenades.
-Very odd bug, where your teammates aren't shown where they actually actually are. I've had this happen in both PvP and PvE.
-PvP can be a tad bit imbalanced toward higher leveled players, because they have access to more classes. For example, the Medic character is unavailable from the beginning and has a very powerful abilty to revive a player from a distance.

Feel free to ask questions in the comments. Overall I give the game a solid 8/10 it has it's problems, but what game doesn't? I'd say that you should definitely pick this game up, and on sale this game is an absolute steal. There's a lot of fun to be had in the Wildlands. Good luck out there, Ghosts.

This game is a masterpiece; One of my favorite of the last 10 years. A major departure from most Ubi games, in that all the features feel fully crafted to thrill the player, rather than just left at "good enough." Love almost everything about it, but here are my top three:

1. Realistic in all the ways it needs to be, arcade-y in all the others. Bullet physics are great, and enemies typically die in one hit, driving is really fun. But also, you don't have to practice for two hours to make helicopters fly right.

2. Missions don't force you to run them a specific way; the player is genuinely free to improvise based on a wide spectrum of tactics. Parachute onto a rooftop and blast everyone, or stealth in while your (robot or human) teammates give you sniper cover, or run a rebel assault from above using a drone, strafe with helicopter-mounted mini-guns, et cetera, or any combination. Folks are complaining that missions are all similar, but that's looking at it from the wrong perspective; variety isn't forced on you, it's given to you in a big fat tool kit to use however you want. (If you get bored, it's because you're a boring player)

3. The options menus are rad, which is a weird thing to type. The game allows you to tweak a heap of settings, so everything feels exactly right all the time. Car steering sensitivity is a different setting than helicopter steering sensitivity, which is different from airplane settings, for example. Also, all the graphics tweaks come with a little demo of what that option actually does, and tells you how much it will impact your CPU. A great example of how Wildlands is very consciously-crafted player experience.

The downsides? It's a CryEngine game, so you need a moderately beefy computer to make it look pretty (I get 40~60 fps on moderate/high graphics settings with a GTX 1050Ti). Also, even single-player is dependent upon a server connection, so when they do server maintenance, the game is inaccessible. Not the worst copy-protection Ubisoft has ever implemented, but still irritating.

Full Review:

Ubisoft have had a bit of a troubled past for me. The Assassins Creed series took a nose dive after the first few titles, and it seems they are absolutely flooding the market with game after game and to be honest I can't keep up (nor do I want to anymore).

And while I've played a few of the Tom Clancy titles, I wasn't holding out much hope for Wildlands after reading a significant number of people talking about the famous "rinse and repeat". Then came the play free weekend, topped with a 20% discount if you buy direct from Uplay, and I now own a copy of the game.

It's true, if you play the game mission after mission, I can see why it would feel like the old rinse and repeat is coming back, but that's only seems true to me if you rush through the missions/side missions one after the other eager to complete the game in record time.

I've spent countless hours (19) just wandering around the streets looking at stuff, driving around, collecting items you need to unlock weapons and skills, and I've been in awe of the views and landscapes this has to offer. I've tried all the different settings, and this is packed full of them - from easy/normal/hard/extreme difficulty to a highly customisable HUD (or no HUD at all if you want complete emersion).

The characters are often amusing and your squad cracks jokes when you aren't in combat or just hanging around. The whole feel of the game for me is superb, and a credit to the Ubisoft franchise. And what day doesn't feel a bit rinse and repeat... we do something different to make each day different and I see no reason why this shouldn't be applied here.

If you see this on sale again and appreciate 3rd person shooters (1st person when right mouse button held) then grab yourself a decent shooter. It's definitely one of my more recent favs of Ubisoft's

Thanks for reading - Enjoy!

Wildlands is an interesting open world take on the Ghost Recon franchise. It is similar to The Division and the FarCry series. It feels easier, more "casual" than the old GR games, but on higher difficulty you are better off sticking to stealth.
The shooting mechanics are well done, gravity is actually affecting bullets, so you need to compensate in long distance shots. The open world feels authentic, living. With cars traveling the roads, people living in towns. The environments and scenery are beautiful and varied, from swamplands, mountains, deserts and so on. The graphics are good, weather effects are pretty. Locations are well designed, they do not feel as a level in a game, they feel like farms, towns, factories, etc. As it should be. You have a good variety of vehicles (cars, boats, helicopters) to get around the fictionalized Bolivia, 
but driving and flying feels a bit off. It is usable, but not as well done as it could be. There are lots of weapons to find, and the customization is definitely a highlight. You can change almost any component of a weapon to tailor it to your play-style with silencers, scopes, magazines etc. There is a lot of attention to detail, like that enemy vehicles act as disguise, the paint job of your guns will scratch and wear over time, guards have different behavior in day and night etc.
Although it works as a single player game, Wildlands really shines in co-op, it is meant to be played with a group of friends. Especially on higher difficulty levels, where squad communication and coordination is essential. You can play drop-in-drop-out coop with random people, but the results is as you would expect...
After a while it does get repetitive, but this is the characteristic of open world games like this. There are some small bugs, like climbing on rocks and your squad members freezing up, enemy soldiers spawning from nowhere, but I did not encounter any game-breaking ones.
If you have a group of friends to play with, or you just like open world games with a bit more tactical and stealthy game-play, I can recommend it.

So far, it's been a pretty fun game. I'm a huge fan of the Far Cry series, so naturally, I came to enjoy Wildlands. The graphics are great, runs smoothly  (with the right graphic tweaks), and the gameplay can keep you playing for several hours. The co-op is incredibly fun with a friend or even a random person. I hate to use Far Cry in comparison, but it plays just like Far Cry 3 & 4. 

[b]Graphics[/b]
The graphic are excellent. I'm able to get 60-80FPS on medium-high settings on an XFX RX 480 8GB paired with a Ryzen 7 1700x. Even at lower settings, the game looks great. It's hard to complain about something in this area.

[b]Audio[/b]
The audio is pretty nice. I play with my Apple earbuds and sometimes with my Turtle Beach headset and the sounds are great. You can hear explosions in the distance, the direction of gun shots, and not to mention Ubisoft did an excelent job on the audio for the weapons. The dialogue seems a bit half-assed, but it's irrelevant in most situations outside of the main story. I'm not even sure if every member of the squad that follows you around has their own voice actor, it's always the same guy it seems.

[i]Dialogue example: 
*Finds weapon attachment
*It's a long barrel for a machine gun
"This will go great with my boots"[/i]

[b]Gameplay[/b]
The overall gameplay is pretty solid. The gun mechanics are great, the bullet drop makes distant kills satisfying, and the sound the guns make feel real and varied. The customization of each weapon is pretty awesome, though, it takes a bit of time and effort to unlock the things you would like to have for your gun. Unfortunately, due to time contraints of my life, I had to spend about $5 to get the weapon unlocks in a timely manner. You do not have to spend money to acquire weapon attachments and the base-game skins are readily available.

[b]Content[/b]
The content of this game is pretty interesting. It's similar to that of Far Cry where you go to a base and essentially take it over by taking out bad guys using whatever method you desire. Want to run in and guns-a-blaze? Go ahead, but you'll probably get outnumbered if you're not quick enough or have proper gear/skill points. There's plenty to do in Wildlands. There are side missions, collectables, and bases to attack. Though, the missions do get repetitive, but there is more than one way to play each mission. You could try different tactics, there is no "right" way to play this game. There's not a lot of variety to the enemies, either, There is the Santa Blanca cartetl and the Unidad, each faction with their own set of soliders, snipers, and armored guys. The AI, however, is becomes more challenging as the game progresses and awards stealth over run 'n gun in most situations.

[b]Story[/b]
There's a lot to do to finish the story. I'm about 25 hours in and I have yet to make it to 50%. The story, at this point, seems a bit uninteresting and the interactions with the underbosses are anti-climatic. Plus, they seem very easy to manipulate for a drug cartel. Each underboss (sort of like a mini boss, sorta) has their own set of missions designed around their weaknesses in order to take them down to get to the final boss. These missions do add some variety to the game, but  most of the stuff outside of the main story missions get repetative very quickly. If it wasn't for the great gameplay, the missions wouldn't be very interesting.

[b]Vehicles[/b]
The vehicle mechanics are pretty terrible, especially with a keyboard and mouse, but this is to be expected as most things are generally better with a controller (with the exception of shooter games). Most of the vehicles handle very strangely. The dirtbikes are pretty fun off-road, if you can manage to stay alive when you're flying down a massive hill. 

[b]Character Customization[/b]
One thing that I really like about this game is the ability to change how your character looks throughout the game. I'm not really sure if your apparel makes a difference when it comes to visibilty to the enemy or whatever. But, you do look pretty snazzy in an all-black attire with a ski mask. You also have the option for gilly suits, which is neat.

[b]Multiplayer[/b]
Not worth writing about. The PvE and story mode is where it's at and it's even better with a friend.

[b]Micro-Transactions[/b]
I know, it's like word vomit to a lot of gamers, but I think Ubisoft does it right here. There are no loot crates, instead, you can either choose to buy the guns for the story through the store with real money, or, find them in weapon crates hidden throughout the game. I don't have a lot of time to play video games these days and I really wanted the M4A1, so I ended up spending about $5 to get the things that I wanted. The rest is just cosmetics. And honestly, I think the base-game has some really nice character customization options.

Overall, I think Ubisoft did a great job with this game. It's worth the $60 price tag and could easily suck you into its endless gameplay and gun mechanics. Though, with repetitive missions and difficult AI, frustration could soon be an issue if you play for long periods of time.

Completionists aside, even a speed-player will have to spend hours grinding or finish the game with starting gear - and that's another thing about this game - I'm usually a sucker for getting new, more powerful guns (but I love precision, tuning, not raw firepower) and upgrading them to perfection - having gone through the entire list of weapons in this game - I maybe found 2 others (besides the starting one) that I wanted to try. There were honestly too many brute assault weapons (that don't really fit the gameplay) and boatloads of freak (called signature these days) weapons - a.k.a. copied from Far Cry. There is absolutely NOTHING original here. The story, apart from "briefings", is just basic cutscenes with poor dialogue (which is becoming a Ubisoft signature feature) that simply tell you what is going on. And that's it. As for bugs I haven't encountered any yet, except teleporting AI teammates but that's just the usual AI programming laziness of Ubisoft, so no shocker there.

It amazes me that people would actually pay 60 EUR for a game like this. I wouldn't pay 30, I wouldn't pay 20. Played the free weekend 10/13-10/15 2017.

I was able to clear the first zone purely in singleplayer mode. While the gunplay and gameplay was pretty good, I can't justify spending 29.99 for this as a full title. There just isn't enough here.

My strategy was largely as a sniper and true ghost. I prepped the area of interest by observing guard numbers and movements. If necessary, I thinned them out with long range suppressed shots. Which...in this game...is cartoonish. No supersonic round is going to be totally silent. At the very least, the other guards would hear the supersonic crack of the round as it went over their head and into their buddies' noggin. They just stand there as though nothing happened. But I digress. After a recon, I would park my team outside and go in solo, get the intel, object, or lieutenant solo, and get out. This worked fine for a while. It was like playing a more pretty version of Far Cry, which I am experienced.

Though after the first section, the difficulty ramps considerably. You have to park your NPC allies further and further away. Before long THEY get spotted which instantly puts the whole compound on alert. As far as I can tell, there's no way to disable alarms either. And there's nothing more infuriating to stealth masterfully through a section of bad guys for 20 minutes only to see "Murray spotted" on your screen and have to settle in to the certain death you will face, through no fault of your own. I just wish I could send my allies back to base, with a box of slim jims and just...MGS my way through the campaign.

Though you can't do that. That's a problem. Also this game has UBISOFT-itis. Inflammation of the map area. Communication towers, and boxes you have to dig through. For some reason, you went into a fortified area filled with some of the most dangerous enemies in the region, and only brought a 4x acog with you... like...what? Everything else has to be scouted and ground out, in regions where you may not be high enough level for yet. You just have to OSP them. It's like come on. You had a helicopter. Load the gear. I get it. It's an unlock system for players to slowly be exposed to the game and progress with increasing difficulty but decreasing overall challenge. Well, Rainbow Six Vegas gave you a full arsenal of weapons and scopes from the start. It ramped up by giving you more complex terrain to navigate. TL;DR - Not worth 59.99, open world concept is good but removes urgency, not a singleplayer friendly game, not as exciting as previous Ghost Recon games, boring story, missions lack variety.

1) The open world aspect of this Tom Clancy release is very agreeable, however this same feature removes any sort of urgency that is present in previous Ghost Recon games.
2) The level of customization with the weaponry is also very agreeable, however, lack of options from the outset makes the first hour or so of gameplay a scavanger hunt trying to get a half-decent outfit suitable to one's playstyle.
3) Compared to previous generations of GR, squad orders are clunky and vague, being unable to individually assign orders is a huge handicap. Until "Efficiency" is upgraded, early missions rely heavily on the player, who can expect little-to-no support from their AI squad members, all of which have terrible pathfinding and target aquisition/termination.
4) Very disappointed with the "sniping" aspect of the game. Max range (solo) is only about 500m beacuse the max character render distance is only a bit more than that. It is almost pointless that there are sniper rifles in the game, because at such a short range most assault rifles fitted with an ACOG or Hybrid sight can easily make that shot and still be useable for short range encounters.
5) The drone is extremely useful for solo play, but it is also strangely undetecable by hostiles, I can imagine this feature makes it definitely OP for multiplayer, being able to launch multiple drones in MP squads would allow an accurate scout of hostile bases in seconds.

Although I am continually finding more frustrations, I find myself wanting to play it a bit more. I think I will purchase the game on sale, perhaps it is better online.

Imagine if Splinter Cell and Just Cause 2 had a baby.  Next, GTA and Rainbox Six had a baby.  Then, the "Splinter Cause" and "Rainbow Theft Auto" babies hooked up and had the ultimate hybrid baby.  Then, hybrid baby fell in love with Far Cry.  Their baby would be Wildlands.  It's online or offline, your choice.  It's a tactical, squad-based, third-person-shooter sandbox with optional co-op, and you can approach missions Rambo-style, or plan your attack with careful recon, and get in and out like a shadow.  You collect loot and mark supplies to earn a type of currency that lets you upgrade your stats.  You can just go sand-boxing around the world, looking for trouble and loot, or you can concentrate on the missions.  I know it's fun to hate on Uplay these days, but you really should play this if you enjoy these kinds of "clear-the-map-of-side-missions-and-collectibles" kind of games.  You'll fly helicopters and planes, drive SUVs and motorcycles, and fire tons'o'guns.  The game is very story-driven, which was a surprise as well.  Ultimately, this is a sandbox RPG in every sense of the term, except that there are no dialogue choices.  I got the game for 50% off, and although $30 is a bargain, if I had truly understood what this game was before the free weekend, I would've gladly paid $60. As of now, I've passed 60 hours, so I'm now getting entertained for less than 50 cents an hour, and I'm only halfway-or-so finished. I highly recommend this if you enjoy open-world shooters with upgrades.  This is really fun.  As for all the negative reviews... look at their play times.  People who play a game for 100-200 hours then give it a thumbs-down are strange.  If you don't like a game, why do you play it so much?  -and if you "only" liked it enough to play it for 200 hours, doesn't that mean you only paid pennies per hour to be entertained?  How do you not recommend that??  It's not about the destination, it's about the journey.  /rant.

Its a decent and visually pleasing game. The map is huge and the gunplay fair. I found the driving aspects of the game very weak, but was able to over look that. I encountered no real bugs although I see from other reviews that some did. 

Avatar customization is very good, although some items are locked behind achievements and/or cash shop buys I was very satisfied when making my avatar look the way I wanted.

The *progression* system is very slow and leans towards alot of grinding. I compleated the first area and was 80% done on the second area when my free playtime ran out. In that time I had gain a fair amount of skill points, but very few new weapon unlocks from the massive list of available items. 

The story for the first two area's seemed ok (In that I can remember it and the major players) It does seem to play alot like Witcher 3 with its open world map, free form playstyle and many objectives. However, the many objectives in GRW are the same few objectives over and over, there is very little variety in the side missions. Attack convoys, Steal plane / helicoptor, Defend radio broadcast ... got old pretty quick. Maby list this expands later on? Many missions boil down to the same assault type missions where scouting with your drone, deciding a route in and sync-shotting as you pick your way through defenders. I read that this gets harder later on with jammers being installed, early-game its very "samey" on every assault though.

I had the most fun assulting the Uni bases (Local corrupt police forces) as they could bring some pain to you if you messed up the assault. 

Drone usage is your friend. I did find the squad site Sync attack to be a little overpowered though. Using Sync attack to pick off foes I had very little chance of getting LOS on for a shot, yet my AI team mates could shoot though buildings and cover to take out these foes while I mopped up the overlook sentries. 

I was'ent thrilled with the *order wheel* to give commands to rebels and your teammates, its standard controller design though so playing with a controller would be better. There may have been options to remap these commands to keys, I never bothered though since outside of sync-shots and revives my AI teamates seemed pretty useless. Later missions may require more finesse with teammates and rebels, however early game I did not encounter that and just let them do thier thing.

I never played co-op or PvP so can't comment on those areas.

Overall I did enjoy my time in the game, although towards the end it became a game of grab a chopper, hunt down all the skill point / weapon upgrades / kingslayer files. My final impressions are that its a poor witcher 3 game with guns. It *is* fun in small doses and maby had my friends been around I'd have had more fun in co-op or PvP. My limited trial did not convince me to buy the title though, even on sale. 

I'll still give it a thumbs up, simply because I did have some fun, but it's a very borderline recomendation.

It's beautiful, and expansive -- there was no way I was able to cover more than a tiny percentage of the map during the free weekend. It was missing a crucial component of the "getting started" -- even the "tutorial" misnormer under the pause menu was just a slide deck, and didn't cover anything to do with the other 3 members of the team. Maybe I am the outlier in that I don't like playing with other humans until I have gotten the game mechanics down. It's like learning to skate at a skate park: you don't need to be there to learn.

But it was cool to have 3 other NPCs that basically operate independent from you, but that you can give rough directions to them. Thankfully, they are never the reason the enemy gets spooked, meaning your partners never make mistakes. Then, when you acquire the 2nd and 3rd "Q-mark" ability, they are absolutely essential in being able to take down a cluster of bad guys in ways that might be hard for even an experienced FPS player to do by themselves.

I loathe, loathe, loathe that it doesn't have the essential mechanic of moving dead bodies like you can in Splinter Cell. Or even, as best I could tell, taking out enemies without shooting them. That matters only in the circumstance where you have to "extract intel" out of a mid-level character, and the only way to do that is to get [b]REALLY[/b] close to them and press the "use" key. That is in contrast to a game like Splinter Cell where the game understands that the [u]intention[/u] is to grab or takedown, and one need not be inside the clipping box of the target to carry that action out.

Overally, it's a recommend, modulo I only played it for a little while. It's certainly in my IsThereAnyDeal.com list, but it's not currently worth the $30 asking price.

When I started, I thought I was gonna hate GH:W. I thought it was gonna be a stupid hispanic-people-shooter unsubtly spreading the word of American exceptionalism. While I was sort of right on that front, and I never really forgot about it, that premise sort of faded into the background as I stealthed my way around.

Really the best way I can describe this game is by calling it "Tacticool Spec-Ops Sim", but that would be pidgeonholing it a bit. It's yet another Ubisoft open-world game, which means it's a gun-based collect-a-thon, not unlike Banjo Tooie. Except instead of collecting Jiggies, you're collecting intelligence files and interrogating the disenfranchised at gunpoint, which makes some semblance of sense. And these allow you to collect supply drops, new firearms (there's a surprising variety, but in the end they all make nasty men fall down), new tacticool gadgets for your firearms, bonus medals that help get your skills up like an aptitude viagra, and yes, there is a leveling system.

There are story missions as well, but these are mostly all variations on "Blow things up" or "Stealth things up", some of these being extremely samey, but that's mainly par for the course with a Ubisoft game. I'd like to just brush this whole experience off, but I find myself actually somewhat enjoying the gameplay here, and I'm not entirely sure why. Maybe it's Ubisoft's perfection of the Skinner Box, what with a little rush of dopamine every time you collect one of its hundreds of blinking map icons. Because I sure as ♥♥♥♥ know that the story doesn't interest me enough on its own to get me invested.

Bottom line, this game is neutral-good, but really only serves to illustrate how Ubisoft has stagnated creatively over the years as far as sandbox shooters go. It's easier and more amusing to think of it as Yooka-Laylee with high-powered armaments and actual speech, with a story based on one South American cartel's struggle with a crippling collective addiction to getting shot in the face by me and my three mates.

Oh, and Co-Op is very entertaining, in so far as it's a crutch used to keep yourself from getting bored.

Played this during the free weekend with no expectations whatsoever: ended up being the only game I played through the duration.

Personally, I did not see a lot of the things people are complaining about in the game:

I did not come across any bugs in 15 hours of in-depth gameplay and I literally explored at least 75% of this huge freaking map. Which in itself is amazing. It's probably the nicest open world map I've ever seen in any game. From salt flats to jungles, from forests to the areas punished by forest fires, to the peaks of the snowy mountains to lakes, this game has pretty all terrains combined into one map and it is extremely well done. 

I can see how the game can get repetitive, but you get what you want out of this game. If you go into every mission the same exact way, yeah, of course it's going to get repetitive. I, however, took different approaches to each mission, and I had a lot of fun doing it. From being completely covert to run and gun, to using an aerial assault to get the job done. The tools are there for you to use, if you do not use them, of course you'll get the same experience every time.

I played on advanced difficulty, and I didn't think the AI was too bad, and the game was definitely not easy as some have claimed. If I got into an active gun fight, I got lit up quick and was forced into cover (which is good). I imagine extreme being even harder. One thing that I did notice was my AI team mates would put themselves in obvious positions, but they still were not spotted by the enemy. From a person that understands programming and AI, getting this down realistically would be pretty difficult; actually it would have been insanely annoying trying to be stealthy af only to have your teammates completely ruin it for you. 

I averaged 80 FPS on my machine with max drops to about 50 FPS at max settings and I'm not on a top tier machine. I'd put it in the medium-high range. 

The vehicle dynamics aren't the best, but they weren't terrible. I still enjoyed exploring this huge map with a whole range of different vehicles, from dirt bikes, to LAVs. The ability to order your team to assualt from any vehicle you're driving is a bonus and actually works well. 

I thought the story is actually pretty good, and the videos they made for intel are extremely well done and really dive you into the story. In exploring the entire map, I tried to unlock as much info as I possibly could on all the high value targets in the game and in doing so it really had me looking forward to completing the missions. It also showed me how in-depth and huge this game really is. Not only is the map huge, so is the story that goes with it. 

Last but probably not least, until I play this again - I loved the customizability of everything! You can change almost every part of your firearm, including how it looks. The level of detail in customizing your character is great. I dig the idea that you can change just about every peice of clothing and accessory of your character at any given time, and make him look or blend into the environment that you are in. I just wish that this tied into how stealthy you character can be. If your running throught he forest with jeans on and a blue plaid shirt.. you should be spotted pretty easily. lol 

Anyhow, as it is right now, I would give this game an easy 8.5/10. Would I say it's worth $60? No, but at the same time I do not think any game is worth $60. Buy this game on sale for 50% off or more, and I think it's a pretty damn good deal. I will absolutely be revisiting this game in the future, and look forward to it.

Time for my "8 hours in review"

Pros:
-The combat is what I wished the Division could have been. No bullet sponges, it forces you to take it slow and steady on Extreme difficulty, and so far most of the times I've died are due to my own stupidity, or bad timing.
-When playing co-op, if you go down there is no bleed-out counter, so you could go down, leave to make a snack, and come back and still be down waiting for revival and not need to respawn and loose progress.
-There is a penetratable cover system, so some materials you can shoot through while others you cannot.
-You can skip all the "game starting splashscreens" and boom, you're right on the main menu.
-You don't have to load into an online session to play. I'm looking at you, Division.
-Customization and outfit saving, gawd this one rubbed me the right way. I have 3 separate outfits saved that I can change to whenever, and the guns you own have a plethora of mods you can apply to them, that is, when you find the mods, which are scattered in weapon crates across the map.
-The map size is big... really big. 8 hours in and I've pry only discovered 1/4th of the map maybe?

Cons:
-Going back to the cover penetration system, we've had instances where we've been shot through floors or multi-story buildings. The floors were thin metal though so, not really sure if it's a con or not, but watch out for that.
-You can't shoot through chainlink fencing for some reason.
-There's this military base called Goyo, and there is a sniper set up on top of the garage. You can see that he isn't behind anything. Turns out there is a concrete barricade lining the roof that you can't see when you're not inside the base. Wasted so many rifle shots hitting invisible concrete trying to get him, and I don't doubt there's a handfull of other LOD issues like this.
-Audio logs.... Look, I understand you want to tell a story, but listening to a guy leave a voice message that's two minutes long in a co-op game is a drag-on. This isn't Metal Gear V. You marketed this to people who play Co-op. Keep it short.

Notables:
-Vehicle handling is a mix between GTA 4 and Just Cause 2 where your car rocks like a boat and wants to break loose if you push it's limits, but it has instant response times to acceleration, braking, and steering. It's VERY acrady, but for how large this map is, it works. I cannot imagine how many times you'd be stranded if it had realistic handling and you'd get stuck on ever hill, rock, tree, and gutter.
-Do not use your mouse when menu navigating. Just straight up use the keyboard. If you use your mouse and hover over certain hotspots, the game will think you've clicked on said hotspots and change settings like what clothing you are wearing or what gun you have selected. 
-Rebellion flag is a Wiphala flag. Don't be like me and think "Missing textures!?"

Final verdict: I like. I buy.

- It's a 45GB download, if your ISP charges extra for exceeding a monthly limit (eg: some BT contracts with only 25GB/m) this could cost more than you expect.

I get better performance in The Witcher 3 using Hairworks. However, if you CAN run this game maxed, it is actually a very good looking game.

The controls are kind of weird. Vehicles on keyboard suck, they're manageable on a controller. With keyboard they are really twitchy but start to straighten out rather than continue in the direction you turned, which is what makes it so weird. There's options to change this but I haven't fiddled with it.
Helicopters are basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥. There's Little Bird-likes with mounted mini guns but they may as well not be, there's no possible way to fly it stably enough to use them effectively. It's basically for taking out other helicopters in boring rounds of cat and mouse.
On foot, the thing that really gets me is the cover system. It's the most vague system I've ever seen. I understand why they did it, but it just ends up not working very well. Most games now have a form of sticky cover where you basically get sucked into cover and you can get stuck in weird ways or get sucked into cover when you don't want to. Wildlands makes a good attempt at making a sticky cover with no stick whatsoever. But unless you really push up against objects, you don't really enter cover which ends up being more annoying than you'd think. There's also no way to actually peek around corners... at least in first person, I never bothered with the third person. This is great for when you're trying to peek around a corner not quite behind cover and you step out entirely and get spotted.

On the subject of being spotted, maybe it's just me, but I hate the "You're being spotted right now" sound. It takes over every other sound and just doesn't give me any useful information. The spotted sound is either played through stereo (with no directional) or through all speakers and in either case doesn't tell me where I'm being seen from. I'd really rather just remove the sound entirely, but unfortunately cant. And that's basically how all the audio is. It goes from being disappointingly poor to outright annoying. I have a 5.1 setup and the surround option in game, but directional audio seems almost nonexistant. This is also hindered by the games ridiculous audio implementations. Gunfire is ludicrously quiet, and without suppressors sounds more like a kick drum than bullets. Getting shot? Oh, we'll help you out by removing all sound altogether so you can't tell where you're being shot from. Nothing really seems like it correlates to the volume of other objects, and it doesn't seem like they're recorded from real guns, or they did a whole bunch of processing effects on them.

The customization is absolutely bizarre. Want a new gun or part? Find it in a crate somewhere in the world, as picking up enemies guns do not unlock the guns or parts attached. Congratulations! You found that random weapon crate and have unlocked the Battlefield 4 style customization options! I hate this. It's at best a PVE game, with a PVP JUST released. Why do we need this stupid upgrade customization thing where one foregrip increases accuracy and lowers stability and the other is vice versa? It's super dumb and that's not how grips work. You don't have to balance the game when it's PVE. 

You also just magically unlock guns as you arbitrarily level up, which is something this game has zero need of. The perks/skills/whatever skilltree is absurd. It makes no sense in a "Realistic" warfare game such as what Ghost Recon is supposed to be. You get perks to get stable sniper scope aim, increase hip fire accuracy, make you somehow more bulletproof, make your vehicles somehow more bulletproof, make enemy vehicles somehow less bulletproof, get more invincibility time after being revived, get revived quicker, get revived more than once.... where the ♥♥♥♥ is Ghost Recon? 2. Tracking of Enemies
I felt that using the drone to tag enemies was something tactical. The batter and range are fine to have. At least that might be something Tom Clancy-ish.

[h1][b]CONS[/b][/h1]
1. Blocking of Movment
Beds block your movement, small crates block your movement, heck almost everything blocks your movement.

2. GTA Again?
If you attack the government forces, Unidad, the gameplay proceeds exactly like GTA. It's the same situation as when you attack the police in GTA. You gain stars to up your notoriety, vehicles come in with reinforcements, then at the end an attack helicopter flies in. 

3. Pea Shooter Guns
Trying to "level up" automatic rifles is kind of a strange thing. Bullets either pierce or don't pierce. Sure, they can get stuck but this is absurd.

4. No Auto Mission
You have to manually search for missions on the Map View. Why they don't automatically update with multiple options is a wonder to me?

5. Grenade Launchers as a Skill
This really didn't make any sense to me. It's not a high level skill you need to learn.

6. GTA-Style Hijacking
Point a gun at civillian cars, force them out and take their car. If this is not GTA, I don't know what is.

[h1][b]NEUTRAL[/b][/h1]
1. Helicopters being Blown up by Drones and Power Lines
Realistic but very boring. 

2. Sync Shots
Really only carried out in Solo Play with the AI. No one in a public game is going to sync their shot. It's interesting to see but you can't do it with other people.

It's fun to play with friends and the graphics are beautiful, but it just gets boring after a while. Once you beat one or two provinces, you pretty much just start repeating all the missions, which comprise of sneaking into someone's house without being seen, capturing a vehicle/person and bringing them to an extraction point, blowing up some drugs, protecting a building, etc., and once that happens everything just seems like you're doing what you've already done before over and over again, especially in singleplayer. In multiplayer, things are a lot more fun and you can do a lot that you can't really do with the singleplayer teammates, but playing with friends often just results in everyone trolling and trying to kill each other with explosives. The scenery and graphics are amazing, and it's very enjoyable to just explore the area and look at everything.

Additionally, there are a lot of glitches/issues that haven't been fixed ever since this game came out. The game crashes every time you go back to the menu, the performance has gotten considerably worse since release, and there are several glitches that can get you killed. These can be easily overlooked in a regular playthrough, but are a serious problem if you try to play through a ghost mode campaign, which deletes your save if you die. It is extremely frustrating to try to play in ghost mode only to have enemies spawn literally on top of you, your teammates disconnect or have desynchronized revive timers, or be killed by buggy physics.

tl;dr: Really fun, but is glitchy and singleplayer can get pretty boring. I'd recommend waiting for it to go on sale or wait until some of your friends get it too.

Only played 40 hours of this game (haven't tried the pvp since it didnt sound too interesting for me) but so far I am loving the experience.

Things worth mentioning : 

1. Single Player (Campaign)
Many other reviews mentioned the redundancy of missions and how you could quickly lose interest in this game, and to be honest that is exactly what i felt when I played my first 20 hours by myself. The missions are truly flat and doesnt have a lot to offer, you "infiltrate" an area and you either blow things up, gather intel, steal something, or kidnap some unfortunate soul. Your 3 AI buddies are VERY inconsistent. They could be useless 3 year olds running around not knowing what to do or they could be freakin beasts with their OP aim bot. In single player, you could babysit/carry your AI pals through missions or tell them to stay at one place and while you solo everything. If things go crazy and you got shot down, your AI pals have built in teleportation. Single player is probably the biggest problem i got with this game.The game is so much better with friends, and you just have to experience it to get what i mean.

2. The Grind
The plot in this game takes REALLY FRICKIN LONG to complete if you are someone like me who bothers to do the collectables, not to mention that the collectables (the files are not necessary IMO) are essential if you want to get the full experience. You arrive in an area, you collect intel on main missions, side missions, and collectables , and then you travel around the gigantic map completing these tasks so you can finally see some cinematics here and there. The map is unnecessarily huge, which IMO is the source of this tedious grind.Although a larger map may sound appealing at first, the terrain feels copy and pasted and the lack of variety just makes it seem like the developers are tried too hard in the wrong attempt to make the game be more "open world". 

But this for some reason doesn't bother me at all. Why? I play Warframe, and that should be self explanatory. In addition, it also feels pretty dang good when you can brag to your friends about how you got that sniper rifle with that sick scope that you bothered to collect when they are just trying to rush through the campaign. 

3. Tier One
TIer one mode can be activated once you reached lvl 30 in the game and it basically makes the game harder for you in exchange of rewards (cosmetics, resources, weapons, etc) when you lvl up (Starts from 50 and all the way down to 1). In my experience the enemies are mentally challenged before turning on Tier One so having the difficulty turned up (better eyes, ridiculously op here and there, and better aim bot , which could also be too op from time to time) could be a fun experience for many others. For you grinders out there, this is simply another thing to grind. 

There are so many other things to discuss about his game i.e: mechanics, plot, realism, but since there are so many other gamers out there who can come up with a better analysis, I'm not gonna bother 

Summary:
Have Tier One Activated, play with your friends, be prepared to play alot, and feel like you are doing the world a big favor and you are mercilessly lighting up drug cartel members with bullets.

Oh and get the HTI sniper rifle asap, you can thank me later.

I bought this game after testing their PvP beta, which was VERY promising.

The singleplayer mode of this game is okay. Very nice graphics. Interesting missions. But it's not something that will keep me playing longer than 20-30 hours.

However, the PvP mode is really good. The beta mode (which basically still had half of the game content locked) was  already so enjoyable that I could easily put 26 hours without being bored.

Ghost War (the PvP mode) is a tactical game that is a bit more slow paced than other games, but heavily relies on strategy and tactics rather than solely on shooting skills. There are 16 classes that you can choose from. And each class comes with its own advantages and perks. 

I am really a fan of the new suppression mechanic that they added which certainly makes the game more challenging. On top of that, drones can also make sure that you just can't run around shooting everybody with your gun in this game, as drones make your movements easily detectable if you're making reckless moves. These mechanics make you think twice before going in a specific direction.

The revival mechanic is also a good feature, which makes the game interesting in the sense that, once someone is killed you face two options: either rush to their aid and risk being shot by the enemy (since they usually keep an eye on the surroundings of someone they just killed), or play it safe and try to pull it off despite the enemy's team number advantage. Downed teammates is sort of a trap right now, which certainly makes it fun and brings a dilemma to the equation.

[h1][b]TL;DR:[/b] GTA5 with a lot of features cut and set up in Tom Clancy's universe.[/h1]

I really don't know how to expand on the TL;DR I just gave you. It's a typical TC's game, with a lot of shooting, some stealth, some gunsmithing. It's a blend of Division, GTA5, Far Cry and the latest Splinter Cell titles, basically.

The concept of getting smaller bosses, to get to bigger bosses, to get to final boss is alluring -- you have your metric ton of audio and video files to listen and watch through, which is going to make your ADD go hard on you in no time. On the other hand, if have 3 friends who bought the game too, you'll have a lot of fun -- just make sure to turn on the toughest difficulty, as anything less than that is just too easy for four people.

And now I'll make a quick pros/cons list for people who're into that.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]

+ Game looks great. Lighting, fire, fog and all of the VFX are just awesome. Flying on a heli at night is spectacular.

+ Gunplay is okay. Recoil is easily controllable and there's no aimcone to speak of.

+ Gun customization looks neat. Tinkering about your guns is a great addition to your gameplay experience.

+ Co-op options are limited, but still satisfying. Landing 4-synced shot feels just great.

+ Non-linear story is kind of bland and predictable, but still okay, as you can choose your path through main boss' cronies to get to him.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

- Limited gameplay. This is very important, as most players are turning game down because of this. There are 5 secondary mission types for rebels, 5 or 6 resource missions (which are mostly repetition of the same -- either destory a convoy or steal a heli/plane), and a ton of campaign missions that aren't too different between each other too. At some point you'll feel like you're playing some MMO, grindning an instance to get to the next level (which isn't too far from the truth).

- Car/heli controls. Worse than a lot of arcade games (I won't even bother comparing it to simulators). Shooting miniguns from a heli is just painful. Motobike physics are the worst too.

- Worst Season Pass in history. I've reviewed both major DLCs included -- one is decent, second is just a money grab from Ubi. Anything other than that included in the season pass are crappy skins and laughable guns. Do not purchase it, I mean it.

- Price. That's just my beef with Ubi and it's prices for CIS region -- they're absurdly high (twice as high as Doom is, for example). Price is not a problem for me, but most of CIS community are torrenting the crap out of Ubi's games because of this sole reason: price is way too high for the region.

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 

All in all, TCGR:W is a good game that a lot of Division (and TC in general) fans will find appealing. It takes ~25 hours to complete the main campaign. If you want to get all of the bosses, double the number. And if you're going to collect everything in the game, triple it.

I'd say it's worth a buy -- just don't buy Gold Edition, play vanilla. And maybe wait for a 25-33% discount (or even 50% if you're not a fan of TC's games).

The atmosphere of the game is impressive, and the ability to approach missions in different ways really enhances the feeling of guerrilla warfare. I like the classic specialization of the different heroes and the way they can be upgraded. The camp management mechanic is also an interesting idea.

A more combat-oriented stealth strategy game with cover, freely deployed traps, and chances-to-hit based on each character's level of mastery of certain firearms. If setting up ambushes is not your thing, the game can be played slowly and more-or-less stealthily, attracting enemies one by one with lures and whistling to knife them - and this seems necessary for some achievements - but it is more frustrating that way, in part due to bugs and controls. I experienced quite a few issues with traversal, picking items off the ground, items vanishing from inventory if sorting too quickly, several crashes, and general lack of responsiveness when controlling characters, which hinders swift playing. Literally every action is performed with a simple left click, which becomes problematic when there are multiple interactive objects too close together.

Remember to always perform melee attacks on enemies from behind or from the sides, as they waste almost no time going into "red" alerted state when confronted up close, thus probably ruining the achievement run and instantly failing the occasional "do not be discovered" mission requirement, even if that enemy is neutralised shortly afterwards. At a distance on Normal difficulty setting, enemies' detection times are pretty forgiving, though. Some enemies turn their heads, and officers have a much wider field of view. Annoyingly, windows are treated as perfectly transparent openings at "ground level" and do not hinder enemy vision at all - bodies and characters in a room will get spotted by enemies patrolling outside through a window, even at a considerable distance (though this is mostly only a problem for challenge missions with all modifiers on).  The only way to hide a character by the window reliably is to click to take cover by the window sill. In addition, accidents will always attract nearby and sometimes even pretty remotely positioned enemies, and cause them to go into "yellow" search mode.

Each operative gains experience to level up and improve abilities. The descriptions on some of them could be a better, and there does not seem to be a way to reset allocated skill points. Some abilities seem more useful than others, so save in advance to experiment freely.

There is loot to be found in the levels and stashed in the operatives' inventories, even if said loot is pretty scarce in the name of balance. Some of it has to be taken back to base where it gets converted into food and "supplies", while some of it can be used in combat - stuff like weapons, ammunition, mines, grenades, lures, and healing items. There are no silenced weapons, but gun shots have limited noise range. There also don't seem to be any heavy weapons. Keep in mind, that loot cannot be placed on the ground or in containers for sorting purposes, only discarded.

Managing the base of operations is a cool concept, but it feels somewhat undercooked. It may eventually start feeling a little tedious having to assign tasks to each squad mate - things like procuring food or supplies, and performing passive "missions" with a chance-to-resolve. On the other hand, if you end up feeling some emotional attachment towards the characters, even such basic management along with equipment sorting can add to immersion. Problem is, the characters get very limited exposure because there isn't really any dramatic story here - the campaign feels more like a pack of independent missions and ends pretty abruptly.

The game features an entirely optional Hard mode which disables manual saving, and Missions mode which allows for replaying five levels with modifiers enabled to increase difficulty (only the latter mode has achievements for playing it). Get comfortable with level layouts and game mechanics first because the reinforcements modifier seems pretty savage -  it spawns squads of enemies after certain time intervals, and they just bee-line to engage player characters. Still, it can be fun to run away from them through pre-mined narrow passages.

All in all, it is good when it works, but it really needed more time in development - if for nothing else than to work a bit more consistently.

Partisans 1941 had potential, but it’s a frustrating experience overall.

Achievements are misleading: On Steam, DLC achievements (from Back Into Battle) are mixed right into the base game list. This makes it look like you can unlock things like Missions Mode and Defense Mode, when in reality they’re locked behind paid DLC. If you only own the base game, you’ll never be able to 100% the achievements. It feels unfair and misleading for completionists.

Unresponsive UI: The interface often doesn’t respond properly. Menus lag, commands fail to register, and inventory management is clunky. In a tactics game, where precision and timing are critical, this is unacceptable.

Story & execution fall flat: Compared to Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, which delivered a far better story, polished UI, and flawless execution, Partisans 1941 feels like a rough imitation rather than a true competitor.

Unless you’re willing to buy extra DLC and tolerate buggy systems, I can’t recommend this game. If you want a polished, challenging, and satisfying tactics experience, play Shadow Tactics instead.

Partisans 1941 is a tactical stealth strategy game developed by Alter Games and published by Daedalic Entertainment, set against the brutal backdrop of World War II’s Eastern Front. Unlike many titles that focus on large-scale battles or famous military figures, Partisans 1941 zooms in on the gritty, clandestine operations of Soviet partisans fighting against the Nazi occupation. This focus on small-scale, guerrilla warfare and stealth tactics creates a unique and immersive experience, blending elements of real-time strategy, squad management, and resource gathering into a tense and challenging survival narrative.

The game’s story centers around a group of partisans struggling to survive behind enemy lines after a devastating defeat in 1941. You lead a small, ragtag team that grows over time as you rescue civilians, recruit fighters, and build a makeshift resistance base. The narrative unfolds through character interactions, mission briefings, and environmental storytelling, painting a somber and personal picture of war’s human cost. While the storyline itself is somewhat straightforward, the emotional weight comes from the survival struggle and tough decisions you have to make, rather than plot twists or grandiose drama.

Gameplay in Partisans 1941 is defined by tactical stealth and careful planning. Missions often take place in dense forests, villages, and enemy encampments where loud gunfights are a last resort. The game rewards patience and creative problem-solving—silencing enemies quietly, setting traps, and using distractions are key strategies to avoid overwhelming odds. Each mission is essentially a puzzle, where awareness of terrain, line of sight, and enemy patrol patterns can make the difference between success and annihilation. The AI is generally competent, forcing players to think several steps ahead rather than relying on brute force.

Squad management is a core pillar of the experience. You control a team of diverse characters, each with unique skills, strengths, and personalities. As you progress, you can assign roles like scout, sniper, or demolitions expert, and tailor your team’s loadout with weapons and equipment scavenged or crafted from resources. The characters develop over time, gaining experience and new abilities, which adds a light RPG element that increases investment in their survival. However, permadeath is a constant threat—losing a veteran member can be a significant blow, adding emotional stakes to every encounter.

The base-building aspect offers a strategic layer that complements the tactical missions. Your home camp serves as the hub where you manage resources, craft items, and upgrade facilities. Scavenging for food, ammunition, and medicine is essential, and managing limited supplies forces you to prioritize certain upgrades or risk the health and morale of your fighters. The base also acts as a narrative anchor, showing the gradual growth of your resistance and offering moments of respite between missions. This balance between intense combat operations and quiet base management helps pace the game well.

Visually, Partisans 1941 employs a muted color palette and detailed environments that capture the grim reality of Eastern Europe during the war. The isometric perspective allows for clear tactical views of maps, with plenty of environmental detail that supports stealth tactics—bushes for hiding, buildings for cover, and terrain features that affect visibility and movement. While the graphics are not groundbreaking, they are effective and serve the gameplay purpose well. Animations are fluid, and the sound design further enhances immersion, with ambient noises of wildlife and distant gunfire contrasting sharply with the tense silence of stealth operations.

The soundtrack is subtle but effective, blending atmospheric music with the sounds of nature and war to create an immersive auditory experience. Voice acting is competent, with dialogue that adds personality to characters without feeling overdone. The game also includes text logs and mission reports that enrich the worldbuilding, providing historical context and personal stories that deepen player engagement.

Despite its strengths, Partisans 1941 is not without flaws. Some players may find the pacing slow, especially early on when resources and personnel are limited, making missions feel punishingly difficult. The AI, while generally smart, occasionally exhibits pathfinding issues or inconsistent enemy awareness, which can lead to frustrating moments. Additionally, the game’s learning curve can be steep, particularly for players unfamiliar with tactical stealth games, as success often requires trial, error, and careful micromanagement. The UI is functional but occasionally cluttered, and some mechanics could benefit from clearer tutorials or in-game guidance.

In summary, Partisans 1941 offers a thoughtful and immersive take on World War II tactics, focusing on the gritty reality of guerrilla warfare rather than grand battles. Its blend of stealth, squad management, and base-building creates a compelling survival experience that challenges players to think strategically and value every life in their small band of resistance fighters. While it may not appeal to those seeking fast-paced action or historical epics, it shines as a tactical gem for players who appreciate methodical gameplay and a sobering portrayal of wartime resilience. For fans of strategy games with a focus on stealth and story-driven survival, Partisans 1941 is a worthy and rewarding journey into the shadows of history.

[h1]Intriguing ideas, but fumbles too often to be truly great.[/h1]

Partisans is a strange game, it has some very unique features but the actual product still leaves a lot to be desired.

Unlike similar isometric stealth games Partisans has a loot system where you can pick up equipment, weapons, and ammo for use on the field. This includes food and materials which are used for the base management side of the game. It's a neat idea and your party members can make use of literally anything at their disposal no matter who they are. Need someone with rocks to throw as distractions? sure. Want a dedicated medic? easy. Party members have a couple of individual skills to differentiate them, so team member choice is important but it doesn't gate-keep specific strategies.

Another feature is the camp management between missions. You have to produce enough food to keep your team healthy, enough materials to help make improvements like weapon upgrade benches, better food production, creating items, etc. So long as you assign everyone a job around production and food each day and upgrade as soon as possible it quickly becomes a non-issue and sadly kind of redundant, which is a shame since as a concept it's pretty solid.

That's also kind of where the good points end...

The first and biggest problem with this game: it has fog of war. From a planning perspective this is a terrible idea for real-time stealth when timing and line of sight is paramount. Enemies can even sometimes see you but are covered by the fog so you end up being spotted by someone you didn't even know existed. This really slows down some levels where you're consigned to moving to a crawl inching forward hoping no one is in the distance. There isn't a dedicated crouch or prone action and instead you have "stealth mode" where you move slower and crouch once you get close enough to an enemy. Their FOV cone is their full absolute vision...sometimes anyway, not often with how buggy this mechanic is.

The next problem is the controls. Left click as a command literally does [b]everything[/b]. Movement, picking up bodies, interacting with objects, the lot. When areas get cluttered you quickly end up doing the wrong action since something else was either close by or in the way. Having ctrl + click would prevent this but you can't remap any controls at all. The pointer precision is also off so you can't be exact with your movements or actions so sloppy looking mistakes are genuinely through no fault of your own.

Another dealbreaker is the map scrolling with the mouse bugs out constantly. Fighting the camera and having to correct it with the arrows keys was painful and shouldn't still be an issue after the game has been out for so long.

AI detection is probably the biggest offender though because it doesn't even play by its own rules. In every other game of this kind when you're seen the enemy's view cone becomes focused so you know who it is, but here you get nothing but a small exclamation mark above the enemy's head, and if they're in fog of war? nothing. The detection gauge also fills based on noise. Fine in theory, but the noise detection radii doesn't match the noise radii you make as yours is apparently way bigger than what it says. Enemies will still hear you even if you think you're out far enough away. Even moving slowly into bushes can set it off so everything you think is safe carries some weird disproportionate risk. There's no delay between being spotted and the alarm being sounded so multi-kills can be unnecessarily hard to execute properly.

Sometimes an enemy can instant alert the second you hit their FOV with no detection gauge fill - I can't work out if it's something to do with being spotted beforehand or if it's a bug? Being in vision whilst carrying a body is also an instant alert, made worse with carrying bodies being incredibly slow even with party members who can upgrade that stat. I've sometimes even had enemies who are off my screen the other end of the map being "alerted" to my presence?

The next issue is the "tactical mode". For some reason you have to execute the plan the second you leave the mode, which can be awkward if you want to scout before confirming your actions. It's a small quality of life difference but a big thing when compared to other games that use the same system. With the tiny detection alert window on top I mostly gave up using this and opted for strictly using solo kills instead since they were far more reliable.

For a stealth game there's a lot of combat you're forced into. Sections of the map act as cover, and hit chances are calculated based on range, weapon stats, and enemy cover much like an XCOM-esque title. If in cover you can normally let the fights play out themselves and you'll come out mostly unharmed. Overall though I'm not entirely sold on this concept since more often than not these fights are against an army of 12+ enemies vs your 3 team members, and slow methodical stealth mechanics here are clumsy enough. If there were smaller groups to deal with and not have the whole map be alerted when you fight then maybe this could work, but definitely not in its current state.

The map design is your standard fare of large forests, train stations, enemy bases, however there's no verticality so no ladders or vantage points to make use of. These maps are also massive but also where the designs have problems. 90% of the time you can skirt around the perimeter of a map and avoid a lot of troublesome stuff. [spoiler]The last mission becomes trivialised by doing this as you can just sneak to the top corner, fetch the key needed and you're into the main building with zero effort. After that, I opted to just run and gun my way through to the final room because apparently there's one type of enemy that refused to walk through open doorways so I could spam grenades through until they were all dealt with.[/spoiler]

In summary, Partisans has a novel approach to real-time stealth with a unique blend of RTS, top-down shooter, and resource management but is severely bogged down by a very finicky system, odd bugs, and mechanics that just don't really mesh well together on the whole. There's some interesting foundation being built here though, but it still needs a fair bit more polish to really make a dent on their competition.

I want to give this a 'maybe' or a 'neutral' rating, but I'll settle for a tentative 'yes'.

At its core, the game has a decent idea. Stealth real-time-with-near-pause, with party control. It is also point-and-click with simple mechanics. 

However, the execution leaves much to be desired. Given how it is point-and-click to execute actions, there really needs to be more feedback to the player as to how the characters will behave in certain situations. For example, if a door is locked and the player attempts to move a character into a position behind it, the character will attempt to path into the room by any means necessary. Even if this would put the character in a position where they can be seen. There is no indicator that pathfinding was not able to find the shortest direct path and is, in fact, attempting to go a longer route to get to where the player clicks.

Combat is not particularly satisfying in this game. Your characters and the enemy both go down in one or two shots, and there are far, far more of them than you. By virtue of sheer number of shot attempts, if your stealth breaks and things go loud, you are pretty much done. The enemy will overwhelm your position with sheer volume of fire, and it doesn't seem like they have limited ammunition either while you are limited.

Stealth is where this game is strongest. Each level is essentially a puzzle to be solved. Which enemies do you eliminate first? How do you choose to eliminate them? These choices can make or break each run. However, it has to be said that the optimal path is often the ONLY path you can take, because doing anything else would break stealth - and doom your run by virtue of loud firefights going very badly for your partisans.  Taking a leaf out of Sniper Elite, you can use bottles and rocks as distraction tools as well, which helps things along. 

All in all, there are frustrations with the game with regards to both the level design and the way that the  controls behave. A little bit more feedback to the player as to how the characters will move with a given input would be nice. There are bugs with detection triggering well beyond sight cones, and sometimes with enemies detecting things behind walls. But if you can overlook these, you can certainly have a pretty good time in the game.

Worth your while if you are a fan of Commandos style tactics-games. Ideally get it on sale as the technical side leaves a lot to be desired. If you can't stand communisits don't play.

PROS
- Most of the missions are wonderfully designed, great looking, with multiple ways to complete your objectives. They're not too long nor unreasonably difficult. Mission 14 is genuinely a masterpiece of non-linear stealth action.
- Soundtrack and sound overall is very good and atmospheric, good weapon sounds and nice ambience. Visuals have a nice artstyle and are overall very pleasant.
- Characters are reasonably well balanced, they all offer different flavours and unique approaches to missions. Cracks in their balancing appear only at very late game or at higher difficulties.

MIX
- Story is pretty much non-existent as there isn't an overarching plot. The characters don't go through arcs or change, although for this type of a game it isn't much of an issue. You are given missions to complete and that's it. Extra interactions between characters would've been nicer though.
- The camp managment side is very barebones, you get most of your camp upgrades very early and after that there isn't much to do. Also the camp UI is kind of messy and you never get quite used to it.
- The game feels like playing through a Yuri Ozerov movie, it very much uses USSR WW2 propaganda, the Partisans are all super heroic, the Germans are all super bad and there are one-liners straight out of propaganda posters. Now this might be on purpose to create an atmosphere reminiscent with what the state media would portray the war as, shortly after it's end (think post-war US WW2 movies). Or the developers genuinely believe this and are old-school USSR apologists. Either way be warned, it might rub some people the wrong way.

CONS
- The game doesn't have fully customisable graphics, you cannot choose textures, objects and post processing individually, you can only chose low. medium and high presets, that's it.
- The inventory is total crap, not the idea, but the implementation. The game will scream at you that you don't have anymore space but you actually do, you just have to make it manually. Items of the same type often won't autmoatically stack together, so you get three incomplete stacks of the same ammo instead of one full stack. You cannot reload your guns in the inventory by dragging ammo onto them, you have to unload the gun and then put it into the Partisans hands. Every time you move an item or change a weapon the game lags. The auto sorting is almost useless as it sorts very strangely and makes a mess. The icons are very difficult to read at first glance, you will confuse different ammo types till the very end.
- There are many moments where the game hiccups and you'll have no idea why, it's classic Slav-jank. 'Cause I'm a Slav myself I don't really mind and just use the F5 button religiously as I was taught, but it's noticeable enough to where it can be sometimes frustrating.
- The last 2 missions are exactly the opposite of why I liked the game. They are very linear, ball bustingly hard and feel like you need to cheese to finish them. Absolutely appalling ending to an otherwise good game.

(-) Bugs:
a. Partisan stuck in a object. I have to restart mission 14 because of this.
b. Input Command not registered 
c. Placed trap suddenly disappear 
d. Partisan suddenly stops when placing trap/mine 
e. Partisan suddenly stops when activate a skill 
f. Hard time to examine/loot enemy body. Have to move the body first or rotate the camera, before the “Bag” cursor properly work.

At first, It reminds me of Commandos 2 mechanic… but:

b. There are too many items to manage. Foods, medical items, medical parts, materials, weapons, weapon parts, traps, etc... it feels like survival game rather than RTS game.

You won’t be able to save in 3 conditions:
